items.title: We Need to Talk About Markwayne
items.description: You might think that someone who took over for Kristi Noem would have a solid sense of why saying and doing dumb things is unwise. The former Department of Homeland Security secretary was such an embarrassment that she earned the honor of becoming the first ou
items.author: Chas Danner; Benjamin Hart
paragraphs: You might think that someone who took over for Kristi Noem would have a solid sense of why saying and doing dumb things is unwise. The former Department of Homeland Security secretary was such an embarrassment that she earned the honor of becoming the first ousted Trump 2.0 Cabinet member, lost her plane, got exiled, no longer even has a job in MAGA Siberia, and was last seen shooting more animals with Greg Bovino. Senator Markwayne Mullin got the call to replace her, but as we’ve now seen over the past several days, he may not have reviewed Noem’s Wikipedia page as closely as one of his aides probably recommended.

Mullin is having a big moment in the national spotlight, thanks to last weekend’s epic FAA air-traffic debacle, plus an assortment of other apparently coincidental tech outages that are now causing alarm. It hasn’t gone well. Here’s some undoubtedly unwanted advice for the Homeland Security secretary about the lessons to be learned since Friday.
Don’t try to make “SI” happen during a national emergency, even if Trump is watching

On Friday, soon after the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop for as of yet unknown reasons, you spoke with reporters in an attempt to calm Americans’ nerves and assure them that the Trump administration had things well in hand. That was a good idea! But then you took the opportunity to correct a reporter who used the term “AI” instead of the Trump-mandated rebrand for artificial intelligence. This was not something a serious person does.
Avoid saying “this isn’t another 9/11” in almost all circumstances

We get it: It’s not unreasonable to assume that people old enough to remember September 11, 2001, may be worried about another nationwide departure ban. Still, though, you can probably just say something else to communicate the same idea, particularly if you run the agency that was created because of 9/11.
Don’t start a White House press conference during a crisis by saying, “Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”

Yeah, okay, it’s a joke, and you’re the kind of head Homeland Security honcho who likes to cut the nervous tension of a confusing nationwide transit emergency with a little humor. But the problem is this: It’s a confusing nationwide transit emergency during which there has been scant official information from the government officials who release information, and what people have been waiting for someone to say, out loud, from some place like behind a podium in the White House briefing room, is this: The cause of the emergency has been identified; it has been or is being fixed; planes can fly without any additional risk; and the nationwide ban on flights taking off has been lifted. All of this information could have been bullet points written on and read from your hand (though reading notes off your hand at the White House would have looked even more amateurish).
Also, watch the face of your colleague, Transportation secretary Sean Duffy, after you say that line. That was not a good reaction!
Thanks, though, for not also coming to the podium wearing a Jason hockey mask. It was smart to leave that backstage.
Think about how things look before saying, “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like”
Outside of Trump’s inner circle, we call this common sense.
Don’t throw the Transportation secretary under the bus while he’s standing right next to you blaming everybody else
Well, unless he deserves it. You do you, Markwayne.
Don’t take your government plane to a college football game in the middle of an air-travel crisis you just fumbled

According to the New York Post of all places, “While thousands of Americans were stranded in airports around the country on Saturday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was on a government plane, flying to Baton Rouge, La., to take in the Texas-LSU college football game.” It’s okay, though, because he paid for the flight, his spokespeople told the Post.

This was not a good idea! Sure, you deserve to watch a Texas-LSU game as much as any American — but sporadically, on your phone, when you can steal away glances at the score because you are so damn busy managing a national crisis. And for goodness’ sake, don’t fly to Louisiana on a government plane to see the game in person when average Americans are re-creating their own private Odyssey fueled by snacks from Hudson News and stuck in a car rental line at their third airport in 24 hours while their suitcase (unbeknownst to them) has somehow ended up in Wichita and (also unbeknownst to them) they still have another 40 hours to go until they’ll finally be able to get home, get three hours of sleep, and then go to work — all because, you know, they don’t have their own government plane.
Markwayne, it would much cooler if you did not try to live like Matthew McConaughey in this situation.
Do not, under any circumstances, claim your football-game flight was leading by example

Just apologize! Why can’t Trump officials ever just apologize for doing something stupid instead of digging an even bigger hole? Comments like “We still gotta live our lives” — or worse, suggesting that your trip was necessary to prove air travel was safe — are not a good defense.
Here’s what Mullin told the Homeland Security Committee on Tuesday:

I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece who has never been to an LSU game and she’s a huge LSU game fan to a game. We had discussions at ten o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace was completely open, it could bring confusion. Because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there, that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly. There was a lot of stuff going on in the news saying, “Is it safe to fly?”
Markwayne Mullin took a government plane to a college football game over this weekend for you, America.
Don’t be the DHS guy who shares some random other guy’s theories about AI suddenly breaking everything
Especially when you used to be the guy assuring everyone that “SI” wasn’t to blame:
Don’t make such of a fool of yourself that your new boss has to give you a TV timeout from abroad

On Thursday, Politico reported that Mullin’s various media appearances since the ground stop had gone so poorly that newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had intervened to yank him off the airwaves:

Mullin’s missteps hit a fever pitch Tuesday afternoon Washington time when White House chief of staff Stephen Miller intervened in the early morning hours from Manila, where he was traveling with President Donald Trump, to swap the floundering DHS secretary for the steadier hands of DNI Jay Clayton and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to message for the administration, three people close to the White House told Playbook.

It wasn’t just Mullin’s string of strange gaffes that landed him in trouble with Miller, though; per Politico, Mullin had already provoked his ire last week by floating a possible immigration deal that would give legal status to American residents brought to the country unlawfully as children. Read the (xenophobic) room, Markwayne!
This post has been updated.

items.title: San Francisco’s Congressional Earthquake
items.description: This year’s contest between Scott Wiener and Connie Chan to succeed Nancy Pelosi as San Francisco’s U.S. representative didn’t get much national attention on Election Night, partly because it was a Democrat-on-Democrat battle (thanks to California’s top-two pr
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: This year’s contest between Scott Wiener and Connie Chan to succeed Nancy Pelosi as San Francisco’s U.S. representative didn’t get much national attention on Election Night, partly because it was a Democrat-on-Democrat battle (thanks to California’s top-two primary system) and partly because we count votes very slowly in the Golden State. But it’s worth looking back on. The race to represent CA-11 was a fascinating microcosm of the California Democratic Party’s love-hate relationship with the tech community and the still obscure but important internal dynamics of the companies involved in AI. That the story also involves the legendary House Speaker Pelosi (who held this seat for 20 terms) and Wiener, the OG pioneer of the Abundance movement that has swept some Democratic precincts and alarmed others, makes it even more compelling.

Back in late 2022, Pelosi formally stepped down as Democratic House leader after 20 years (eight of them as Speaker of the House, the other 12 as minority leader). But she chose to remain in Congress for two more terms as potential successors waited for her to announce her retirement.

State Senator (and former San Francisco supervisor) Scott Wiener was long interested in moving up the ladder to Congress, having already established a statewide and then a national reputation as the author of up-zoning legislation seeking to force local governments in California to accommodate multifamily-housing development instead of endlessly prioritizing the mythic single-family-house-with-a-yard residential land-use pattern. Wiener’s battles with powerful NIMBY forces added to the local fame he had already achieved as a champion of LGBTQ+ rights. Meanwhile, Pelosi was perceived by many observers as keeping her seat warm until her daughter, Christine Pelosi, a political consultant and veteran staffer in both the federal and local governments, was ready to occupy it.

Then other would-be successors ran out of patience. First, tech mogul, Justice Democrats co-founder, and AOC chief of staff Saikat Chakrabarti declared for the seat in October 2025. He was quickly followed by Wiener, with both entering the fray before the former Speaker had publicly announced her retirement. This formidable field chased Christine Pelosi out of the race and, by all accounts, deeply annoyed her mom, who felt disrespected by the rush to force her to step down. Before the June 2 primary, Nancy Pelosi decided to back a third candidate, San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, a more conventional liberal than either Chakrabarti or Wiener.

In the primary, the well-known Wiener finished first and Chan second with Chakrabarti being the odd candidate out. But the ensuing general election took on a whole new dimension when Wiener got some high-life money and backing from one faction of an AI industry that haunts San Francisco like a rich but demanding uncle.

Even as the Abundance Agenda was filled out by doers and thinkers who viewed Wiener as an inspiring figure, he had established a strong foothold in the AI-safety movement and its philosophical allies in the effective-altruism community, both closely associated with Anthropic. Wiener and New York legislator Alex Bores had become West and East Coast anchors of a group of state legislators committed to AI-safety measures who privately coordinated with each other on AI policy and how to handle pressure from industry lobbyists.

Bores’s congressional campaign in Manhattan became a national lightning rod and proxy war for battling schools of thought in the AI industry. An Anthropic-funded AI-safety-focused PAC (Public First Action) spent $12 million to back him, and a rival AI PAC opposing state regulation (Leading the Future, funded by big dogs representing OpenAI and the AI investor Andreessen Horowitz) spent $8 million to defeat him. In the end, Bores narrowly lost the Democratic primary to Micah Lasher. Restlessly looking for another champion in Congress, Public First Action decided to go big on Wiener, tossing $3 million into his campaign in mid-October. That gave the already well-funded legislator a crucial home-stretch advantage over Chan, who had lots of endorsements (from Pelosi, Senator Adam Schiff, and most unions) but not much dough.

As Wiener and Chan battled for votes, however, his relationship with AI firms became the campaign’s central issue with Wiener touting himself as an AI-safety watchdog of the industry and Chan and her allies labeling him a lapdog. Fortunately for Wiener, the Anthropic rivals who helped take down Bores did not get involved in the race; nor did Pelosi fix her candidate up with the resources necessary to win. Wiener ultimately defeated Chan by just over 6 percent of the vote.

Despite all the attacks on Wiener for both his up-zoning initiatives and his AI friends, he’d be considered a pretty rigorous progressive anywhere other than San Francisco. He was endorsed by the California Democratic Party, after all, and his actual campaign (rather than the shadow campaign that dwelled on his associations) focused on pledges to honor Pelosi’s legacy and fight Donald Trump tooth and nail. After Chan conceded the race, Pelosi pledged cooperation with Wiener, and in a final touch of irony, Christine Pelosi announced her candidacy for Wiener’s soon-to-be-vacated state-senate seat (though Wiener himself endorsed his Sacramento legislative ally Matt Haney).

Meanwhile, Nancy Pelosi’s successor is heading to Washington as an iconic figure in two separate movements that could be near and dear to the hearts of centrist Democrats going forward: the Abundance Agenda and the effort to thread the needle on AI via safety and guideline measures that regulate the industry without putting it down like the rabid beast so many progressives fear it has become.

That a man like Wiener will represent San Francisco in Congress is the product of both the perceived excesses of the city’s fractious progressive groups during their long dominance of the city’s political culture and the complex influence of the tech industry, which includes but transcends AI. More generally, San Francisco reflects California in its ambivalence toward the immensely powerful and wealthy spawn of Silicon Valley. Even as Wiener won the battle to succeed Pelosi with backing from some (but not all) tech titans, other tech titans massively funded the successful effort to defeat Proposition 40, the billionaire tax backed by Bernie Sanders and his allies but opposed by most of California’s leading Democrats. While the blue wave said a lot about what voters care about nationally, the upheaval that played out in San Francisco reflects the shifting tectonics of this Democratic-dominated but ideologically diverse state. It’s not entirely the Left Coast any more.
- The GOP Won’t Have a ‘Last Supper’ of Lawmaking
- GOP’s Vast 2026 Investment in Transphobia Went Bust
- Two Weeks Later, the Blue Midterms Wave Is Still Rising

items.title: Looking for a job you can dedicate yourself to? Be warned, the new world of work might scupper your dreams
items.description: I have not been very promiscuous. It might have been fun but I am just not that kind of guy. It means that in a career that now stretches across four decades, I have only had three places of work. The most recent of these, Monocle, has proved to be the longest
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: I have not been very promiscuous. It might have been fun but I am just not that kind of guy. It means that in a career that now stretches across four decades, I have only had three places of work. The most recent of these, Monocle, has proved to be the longest lasting. This week, LinkedIn informed me that I have just hit my 20th work anniversary in the business.

Now I am not going to make you accompany me all the way down memory lane just yet. That will happen this coming 14 February when we celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first issue of the magazine hitting newsstands. But do you mind if we head down the lane just a little way? I promise that you won’t even need your wellies.

While I was having dinner with Tyler, I asked for his advice about a couple of jobs that I had been offered. And that’s when he suggested that, before I made any hasty decisions, I should come see him the following morning. He wanted to show me a new magazine that he was working on with the working title, “Project Europa”. And it was a project that he would like me to edit. If I agreed, however, I would need to stay put at the newspaper where I was employed as he was still raising the start-up capital. The next morning, I went to see him and he showed me mocked-up covers and some poster-sized sheets created to show potential advertisers what was in store. I wanted to be part of this.

It took some months for the money to be raised but one day the CEO, Robyn Holt, phoned me and, in her great Aussie voice, said, “Doll, the money is in the bank. Resign.” I did. And just look at what has unfolded.

I have been lucky in many ways, including becoming friends with Tyler when we were both in our twenties (though he’s annoyingly younger than me). But also because I have been able to work on this magazine for so long. How rare will that be in the future?

This week I went to the launch of a report by Imperial Lifelong Learning – part of Imperial College London – called “Everyone but me: What UK employees told us about AI and skills”. Turns out that most people think that they have AI know-how but co-workers don’t. There was a panel of enthusiasts: all believers that AI has the potential to create efficiencies and aid creativity.

But as I listened, I also sensed that we were entering a world where staff will never be able to drop their guard. They will constantly need to look over their shoulders, fearing that they might become obsolete. How do we ensure that lifelong learning doesn’t become lifelong worry? And will people who don’t want numerous work partners be able to find a company where they are wanted, not for a quickie, but for something meaningful and long-lasting?

Last Saturday, on a perfect autumn day with trees ablaze with rich red leaves and the sun reflecting pools of mellow light off ancient windows, we went with friends from Madrid to the V&A. We drifted through rooms filled with bronze sculptures, Bauhaus silver and ecclesiastical treasures. It’s free to visit the V&A and the museum was full of people from every corner of the world. Then we headed to Soho for noodles and, later, dinner at Café Clement. The city was at its best, at ease, joyous.

As more places seek to dissuade tourists – unless they are rich – from clogging up their streets and as many European capitals hide behind boarded up shop windows, London is still rolling out the welcome mat. Tourists are welcome here. They add to the city. I like living in a place that’s gloriously cosmopolitan.
Oh, and one of those Madrid friends? I have now known him for almost 40 years. Seems that I am more reliable than I imagined.

items.title: Hit the right note with 12 fragrances and home scents to give this Christmas
items.description: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long winter evenings, here is Monocle’s pick of the best scents to gift this Christmas.
Discover a Homeric fragrance from To My Ships

Named after a line in Homer’s Iliad, To My Ships launched in what its founder, Daniel Bense, calls an “uninspiring” category: deodorant. The Aesop and Sunspel alumnus has since worked with celebrated nose Céline Barel to develop the brand’s bestselling Of the Gods perfume around polygonum, a herby ingredient that’s usually only used in trace amounts.
“It’s a fragrance discovered by those near the wearer, rather than announced to a room,” says Bense. Backed by 18 investors, the label has grown by word of mouth and will soon expand to Japan.
Toast the wool mill with Zegna’s Il Lanificio

For its latest foray into perfume, luxury menswear house Zegna drew inspiration from the life of founder Ermenegildo Zegna and his Italian Alpine homeland. The brand’s fragrance collection includes six scents and we’re particularly taken by Il Lanificio, which means “wool mill” in Italian.

The perfume’s heady mixture of suede, vanilla and sandalwood pays tribute to its namesake and is a celebration of Zegna’s ability to take raw material and transform it into something unique. Simultaneously urbane and rustic, this is a scent to savour.
Pair Italian fig with American cedar in Bottega Veneta’s Balliamo

Bottega Veneta expanded its fragrance offerings this year with Alta, a new collection of 10 scents. Each combines an ingredient from Italy with a far-flung counterpoint (think blood orange with North African neroli or plum with Spanish labdanum).
We’ll be wearing Balliamo – a heady combination of Italian white fig with American cedarwood – to the aperitivo.
Head into the woods with Documents’ Inter Cedar

Documents is one of a handful of Shanghai-based, high-end fragrance brands that is proving popular with Chinese consumers and poised to go global. Its premium scents are inspired by Eastern culture, featuring notes from ylang ylang and sichuan pepper to incense and black tea.
The brand operates more than 40 shops across 20 cities. We recommend its Inter Cedar eau de parfum, a tree-inspired scent with a woody profile and aromas of cypress, cardamom and mugwort.
Try Monocle and Claus Porto’s own Soleil Zeste

Crafted by French perfumer Daphné Bugey, this fragrance and body wash are the result of an exclusive collaboration between Portuguese beauty brand Claus Porto and Monocle, with packaging designed by our in-house art team.

The Soleil Zeste scent features notes of bergamot, lemon and lime, alongside green aromas of galbanum, petitgrain and cypress, and a refreshing base of white musk and lavender. Plus, the perfume bottles are made by Vista Alegre, an Aveiro-based heritage manufacturer of porcelain and crystal.
clausporto.com; monocle.com
Start a conversation with Jijide

Milan-based fragrance brand Jijide – meaning “positive” in Mandarin – emerged from a conversation between Italian and Chinese friends Adam James Cavallari, Andrea Alessandri and Fanqi Guan. Perfume, they decided, was the ideal language through which to explore their cultures.

The Riso scent layers notes of kumquat and rice with the salty intensity of soy sauce, while Dentro evokes an Italian morning through aromas of coffee and fig. It’s proof that perfume can be a talking point.
Count down to Christmas with Diptyque’s advent candle
The countdown to Christmas is celebrated in many ways. Some unwrap the gold foil of a small chocolate each morning or acknowledge Advent by fasting in advance of a seasonal feasting.

Parisian maison Diptyque has chosen to mark the days ahead with a Danish tradition. The kalenderlys candle burns down bit by bit, a simple reminder of coming festivities. This edition is scented with pine, cedar and moss, bringing the scents of the fir tree to warm the darker nights.
Bring the forest indoors with Deux Frères

Owners of gin distillery Deux Frères, Gian and Florian Grundböck, tend to think outside the box. Producing thousands of bottles of their signature gin in their Zürich-based distillery leaves several hundred litres of fragrant botanical remnants, known as tails.

“We wanted to turn the tails into something meaningful,” says founder Gian. Enter Forêt, a characterful room scent with notes of juniper, pink pepper and sandalwood. “For us, the fragrance is an example of how a by-product can become something distinctive in its own right,” says Gian. We’ll drink to that.
Escape to the Himalayas with Be Boundless

Beijinger Lydia Wang turned her personal interest in Tibetan medicine, meditation and yoga into a business in 2020 when she established incense brand Be Boundless. The label’s all-natural sticks are shorter than traditional incense from Lhasa, so they fit easily into a carry-on.

Wang tapped one of China’s leading graphic designers, Li Xibin, to create the branding, which features block colours and a bold typeface. A box set comes with 60 sticks in three scents, as well as a small, wooden pull-out tray. The Nighty Night scent – made from dong quai, clove, narra safflower and myrobalan – is a popular pick.
Light up winter evenings with Ffern

Somerset-based perfumer Ffern’s winter candle burns with comforting notes of coffee, frankincense and Peru balsam. Set into the lid of the attractive steel vessel is enamel artwork by South Korean-American illustrator Cory Feder.
Drawing from Scottish folklore, it depicts an ethereal woman swimming alongside a seal. The candle is both a covetable design object and an indulgent scent for the season.
Indulge in a slow burn from Astier de Villatte

Paris-based Astier de Villatte, a design house known for its elegant and lightweight ceramics, has found inspiration in the island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe for the latest addition to its incense line.

The new scent draws on São Tomé’s plentiful cocoa reserves, blending notes of roasted cocoa with Atlas cedar, labdanum, sandalwood and musk, making for a luxurious room filler to accompany the workshop’s delicate ceramics.
Channel the silversmith with Georg Jensen’s Home Scent

Seeking inspiration for its first foray into scent, Danish heritage design house Georg Jensen turned to its own silversmith. The result is a trio of candles that pays tribute to the materials found in the brand’s Copenhagen workshop: silver, steel and quartz.
As you might then expect, the candles emit scents with an intriguing metallic edge, balanced with olfactory layers taken from the Danish countryside – think moss, ivy leaf and pine.

items.title: Our ‘Design Directory’ 2026: The architects, studios and designers to know around the world
items.description: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the coun
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.
This Vorarlberg-based studio’s practice draws on the region’s timber-building traditions and exacting craftsmanship.
+43 5574 44440, bernardobader.com
Innsbruck architect behind light-filled houses, schools and rooftop extensions, with a gift for breathing new life into existing buildings.
Höttinger Auffahrt 11, Innsbruck
+43 5122 38601, fuegenschuh.at
Architecture studio known for designing markets, civic buildings and public spaces. Most recently, it completed Vienna’s Naschmarkt, a hybrid timber market hall and public green space.
Schottenfeldgasse 62/2/22, Vienna
+43 1 890 8921, mostlikely.at
Tapping into a storied heritage of art nouveau and Flemish urbanism, modern Belgian design is a leader in minimalist creativity.
Landscape architect who designs with the climate and microclimates in mind, working with prevailing conditions to create welcoming, self-sustaining environments.
Place Eugène Flagey 7, Brussels
+32 2 219 75 21, bassmets.be
Architecture and urbanism practice designing housing and mixed-use city blocks, including in the canalside City Dox district.
Square Eugène Plasky 92-94, Brussels
Architect and designer (and Molteni creative director) renowned for creating pared-back, material-rich homes and furniture.
+32 3 205 91 90, vincentvanduysen.com
Studio that fuses branding and identity work to create engaging, narrative-driven spaces.
Hessenstraatje 1G, Antwerp
+32 3 290 62 73, wewantmore.studio
From gothic towers to brutalist works, Czech architecture offers a wide range of styles. Today the nation is a pioneer in adaptive reuse.
Renowned for its thoughtful, community-minded approach to schools and civic infrastructure, including an extension to Prague’s Deutsche Schule.
Vaclavske namesti 828/23, Prague
Adept at marrying old and new, this studio has worked on heritage sites, transformed historic city gates and made gentle additions to civic spaces.
Hollarovo namesti 2275/2, Prague
Architecture studio that turns neglected urban spaces such as underpasses into sculptural skateparks and lively public areas.
+420 724 819 859, uustudio.cz
A new generation of designers is now standing on the shoulders of the country’s mid-century masters, ensuring that Denmark remains a leader in functional minimalism.
Cassandra Bradfield and Sofia Olsson’s studio for material-focused interiors and objects, spanning hospitality, retail and homes.
Sturlasgade 14, Copenhagen
Copenhagen studio that designs galleries, boutiques and furniture with crisp geometry and warm materials.
+45 22 25 65 47, atelier-axo.com
Designer making elegant utilitarian objects, from chairs and speakers to lamps and textiles.
+45 26 25 10 34, ceciliemanz.com
Danish-Italian duo fusing Nordic craft with Italian conceptual rigour, making furniture for the likes of Gubi, Koyori and Porro.
Vermundsgade 40B, Copenhagen
+45 51 90 01 17, gamfratesi.com
Founded in 1959, Henning Larsen is celebrated for light-filled civic buildings such as Reykjavik’s glittering Harpa concert hall.
Vesterbrogade 76, Copenhagen
Furniture designer winning awards for her sculptural contemporary updates to Denmark’s traditional design heritage.
+45 51 29 78 20, mariabruun.com
Danish practice with Japanese sensibilities creating pared-back furniture and restaurant, retail and hotel interiors.
Forbindelsesvej 12, Copenhagen
Nature-based studio of landscape architects and biologists creating biodiverse parks and urban spaces.
Njalsgade 17B, Pakhus 2, Copenhagen
Cross-disciplinary studio that specialises in world-building, combining architecture, scenography and furniture design.
The home of organic modernism, Finland has a contemporary scene that celebrates natural materials and human-centred design, while making room for new ideas and technological innovations too.
Helsinki practice that champions traditional construction materials and methods, such as the use of solid brick and natural ventilation.
Punavuorenkatu 1, Helsinki
Storied interiors firm that has completed more than 1,600 workplaces, schools and public spaces since its foundation in 1972.
Established by the late Yrjö Kukkapuro and run by his daughter, this Kauniainen-based museum continues to release colourful, playful archival designs.
+358 9 505 1080, studiokukkapuro.com
French design expands on centuries of haute-couture craftsmanship, pairing new technologies with exceptional handicrafts.
Design practice that plays with form and materiality to create sculptural, geometric architecture, interiors and furniture.
+33 1 71 20 31 01, corpus.studio
Dorothée Meilichzon’s studio weaves local history into cinematic hotels, bars, restaurants and lounges.
54 Rue Greneta, Paris, chzon.com
École Camondo-trained duo making lights and furniture in alabaster, plaster and cast glass in partnership with French ateliers.
22 Rue de l’Echiquier, Paris
+33 6 73 51 76 18, garnieretlinker.com
Young collective taking inspiration from Bauhaus design, the African and Arabic diasporas, and street culture to create bold furniture and scenography.
Paris-based practice creating climate-sensitive architecture through adaptive reuse, renovation and low-carbon architectural interventions.
+33 1 75 43 76 31, lateliersenzu.com
Beirut-born architect committed to paying tribute to place and shaping culture and communities through large-scale housing and civic projects.
75 Rue de la Fontaine au Roi, Paris
+33 1 43 38 12 47, linaghotmeh.com
Design house commissioning craft-made furniture and lighting by emerging European creatives.
102 Rue du Faubourg Poissonnière, Paris
+33 1 87 66 45 22, modernmetier.com
Designer who creates sculptural, shapely furniture and calming interior spaces.
+33 1 40 98 98 90, pierreyovanovitch.com
Art director helping luxury clients to understand and express their identity through narrative-led brand-development campaigns.
One of the most sought-after contemporary studios, Karl Fournier and Olivier Marty’s firm has a reputation for atmospheric, tactile interiors, furniture and architecture.
6 Bis Rue Gabriel Laumain, Paris
+33 1 42 71 13 92, studioko.fr
Creative agency with a sharp eye for emerging collectable design, connecting artists, designers and brands.
There’s more to German design than the Bauhaus and industrial precision. The country’s contemporary design scene is a respected leader in efficient architecture and savvy design.
Practice known for building tall towers with a sensitivity to place and human scale – showing that bigger can also be better.
Gubener Strasse 47 (Fabrik), Berlin
Pritzker Architecture Prize winner Francis Kéré’s Berlin studio has a focus on using regional materials and building capacity in communities.
+49 30 78952391, kerearchitecture.com
Industrial designer bringing raw materials and craft to contemporary industrial-production methods.
Ludwigstrasse 4, Offenbach am Main
+49 69 82368081, sebastianherkner.com
Classical antiquity and modern regionalism combine to define the contemporary Greek design scene.
Architecture studio known for making hotels, housing developments and cultural venues at scale.
Architecture practice focused on reworking historic buildings with Greek materials and a minimalist aesthetic, while displaying a sensitivity to context.
Objects of Common Interest
Split between Athens and New York, this studio is turning heads for its colour-shifting objects, furniture and installations that sit at the intersection of art and design.
+30 210 331 2860, objectsofcommoninterest.com
A studio creating sunny, contemporary residences with bright colours and raw materials.
Renaissance roots and postwar radical design continue to have an influence on contemporary Italian design, which now strikes a balance between industrial efficiency and elegant opulence.
Acclaimed architect Michele de Lucchi’s studio works at all scales, from well-designed desk chairs to community master plans.
+39 02 637 8681, amdlcircle.com
Furniture and interiors studio pairing Brianza craftsmanship with a commitment to promoting wellbeing, exploring the link between the mind, the body and the spaces that we inhabit.
Industrial-design studio that is a pioneer of modular and repairable furniture, as well as lighting for circular economies.
Via Sarson 185, Bassano del Grappa
Interiors and furniture studio creating moody, nostalgic works that mix mid-century traditions with contemporary influences.
+39 02 3653 7088, dimorestudio.eu
Industrial designer making clean-lined, organically curving furniture and objects for major design labels.
Via Privata Giovanni Ventura 5, Milan
+39 340 551 3672, federicabiasi.com
South Tyrolean designer whose studio is capable of distilling grand ideas down to singular forms and visions.
Milan-based Japanese designer constructing precise furniture and lighting.
Via Giuseppe Ripamonti 15, Milan
+39 02 3669 6624, keijitakeuchi.com
Research-led architecture practice responding to modern challenges such as resource shortages and environmental pressures.
Via Boncompagni 51/10, Milan
Designer creating sensual domestic objects spanning ceramics, furniture, lighting and appliances.

items.title: Issue 61 - Kinfolk
items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.
176 pages, offset-printed and perfect bound, full color on uncoated and coated paper. Printed in the United Kingdom.

items.title: Balming Tiger - Kinfolk
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously - Kinfolk
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.

items.title: Sofia Coppola's New 'Marie Antoinette' Merch
items.description: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
items.author: Douglas Greenwood
paragraphs: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
product photography COURTESY OF MACK

The merch-ification of the movies we love is a fairly recent development, brought on by cult studios who know we like our cinephilia to be seen at all times. But if you go back further than five years, then original, director-approved t-shirts, sweatshirts, anything, is much harder to find. Die-hards will scroll on eBay looking for scant objects made as wrap gifts or for crew. But that’s about it! For Sofia Coppola fans—a director whose lore-steeped, decadently formed, insular worlds are catnip for aesthetes—we’ve mostly had to rely on fan created or bootleg stuff. That’s all about to change.

This year, to mark the 20th anniversary of Marie Antoinette, Coppola has unveiled a trio of projects. There’s a remastered cut of the film, a documentary about the film’s creation directed by her late mother Eleanor Coppola titled Making Marie Antoinette (out now via MUBI), and the release of its hardback companion by MACK and Coppola’s own imprint Important Flowers, comprised of pictures shot by Coppola’s long-time collaborator Andrew Durham. Durham’s pictures have carried their own special stories for Coppola fans; now, you can wear them, or carry them slung over your shoulder with some new Marie Antoinette merch, available on MACK’s website now.

To celebrate the confectionary-sweet moment, Coppola spoke to us about the film’s modern reassessment, the merch, and the crew t-shirt she’d love to own from one of her favorite films. She also sent us polaroids taken of the new merch.

DOUGLAS GREENWOOD: Seeing Marie Antoinette’s new life—through the anniversary, the documentary, and the book—must have been so beautiful. Where has it sat for you in your own filmography since it was shot?

SOFIA COPPOLA: Oh, I don’t revisit my films much, but I did when working on my book. I’ve always loved my friend Andrew Durham’s set photos. It was really nice to put them all together in a book, revisit that shoot with Kirsten [Dunst] and Jason [Schwartzman] at Versailles, and see the restored film on a big screen again after so long. I’ve never done that before; it was nice to get to celebrate a film that didn’t have much of a release at the time, and wasn’t loved when it came out. It’s fun to share in the enjoyment of it.
I feel like people are excited about Andrew’s work in your world. What’s it been like to share this journey of the film with a friend like that?
I love Andrew’s photos and everyone likes when he visits my set. He’s fun and easy to be around, so he’s able to get photos that no one else could. I love his eye.

I love the life that your films live after they’ve been released, like here in this collection of merch you’ve made with MACK and Important Flowers. Can you talk me through how these pieces came together?

I just thought it would be fun to make some merch because I love the images, and there had been some counterfeit ones using Andrew’s photos, so I thought people might like to have them, and it would be nice for Andrew to benefit from his images (even if it’s a small run).
Is there a film you love that you’d love to own something from? Or to wear a t-shirt adorned with the visuals of?

I was really excited to get a New Order crew t-shirt from when they played at Versailles! I love crew t-shirts. I still have my kid crew t-shirt from Apocalypse Now! And it’s fun to see friends of my kids wearing a Bling Ring crew sweatshirt or something. I would like to have a crew shirt from The Hunger.

items.title: i-D X New Balance, Straight-Up!
items.description: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheeseca
items.author: Tiffany Lai
paragraphs: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheesecake before the party continued downstairs at the Knave of Clubs for pub drinks and a boogie.

At 8 p.m., a new billboard was unveiled outside the pub, celebrating version 7 of New Balance’s iconic 990 silhouette, set to release globally on November 6. Made in the USA, the 990 has been a proud “dad shoe” since 1982, so naturally, we had to ask our guests: who is your favorite American? And which celebrity dad has the best style?

Who is your favorite American? Kim Kardashian or Adam Sandler. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Rey Mysterio from WWE. What’s an album that’s on repeat right now? The new Worldpeace DMT album. What are you doing this weekend? Spreading optimism and premature Christmas cheer!

What do you do? I’m a stylist. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Ford Bronco cars. What are you wearing today? Mules, which aren’t very practical for walking in the rain, an old pair of Our Legacy jeans, a cashmere jumper to keep me warm, and a vintage bomber. My hat is made by my friend Biddyish. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Brad Pitt.

What’s an item of clothing you’d never part with? My 1960s vintage McGregor jacket that I picked up in Paris a few years ago. What are you drinking tonight? Guinness. Who’s your favorite American? Jim Carrey. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My granddad, actually. What’s your favorite form of exercise? Running, because of the mental clarity and the long and steady journey I’ve had with New Balance.

What do you do? I’m a photographer, director, and DJ. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? A secondhand leather jacket from a market in Paris. What album is on repeat right now? Choke Enough by Oklou. What’s a color that you’d love to wear more of? Green.

What do you do? I make music, but I like saying my job is just connecting the dots because there’s no laws or limits to art. Tell us about your outfit. My outfit’s steady but also flex-y, smart-casual. What are you doing this weekend? I’m always creating. I’m working on some new music, shooting cool videos, fun stuff. Who first taught you to tie your shoes? My mum. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? I’m in a black era right now.

What do you do? We’re freelance stylists. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Jacob: Jeff Goldblum. His personality is the style. If you had to run between two Tube stops, which ones would you choose? Jacob: Bethnal Green and Mile End because they’re the closest ones together. Lauren: Custom House to Canning Town. Nice scenic run. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? Lauren: A big fur coat.

Who’s your favorite American? Fred Hampton. He was one of the leaders of the Black Panther Party. What’s your side hustle? I’m rebranding my friend’s fashion brand. Doesn’t mean I give it less attention than a main hustle, but that’s the thing that I’m supporting right now! What’s your favorite form of exercise and why? Push-ups and pull-ups at home. I hate going to the gym. What are you doing this weekend? I’m seeing my friend who’s leaving for Australia. I’ve got to sort his Moonpig out ASAP!

What do you do? I’m the editor-in-chief of i-D Magazine. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Me. Which celebrity dad has the best style? My dad. He’s modeled in the Chopova Lowena show, he wears New Balance 990s, and he loves a Ralph Lauren polo. Best grail? This Prada scarf. Who’s your favorite TV dad? Michael Bluth from Arrested Development.

What do you do? I’m a fashion designer. What’s an item of clothing you’ll never part with? This pair of jeans that my boyfriend gave me. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? Gray. What’s your favorite form of exercise? I go to the gym, but I want to pick up tennis.

What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Black music. What are you wearing tonight? Made in the USA 2040 V5 New Balance shoes, Supreme Made in Japan denim, and a Bleue Burnham ring. What are you drinking tonight? Chili margarita, some red wine, Guinness, and water. Got to stay hydrated. What are you doing this weekend? This weekend, it’s the Amsterdam Dance Event where I live. My partner’s going clubbing, so I’m taking care of the kids.

What do you do? I’m a musician, and I play the harp. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? My 1800s Victorian body that is falling apart, but I’ll never let her go. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My dad. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a cemetery walk date with my girlfriend in Abney Park. Who’s your favorite American? Lana Del Rey.

What are you wearing? Hysteric Glamour boots with pink studs, a skirt that my ex-boyfriend gave me, a nice, warm Supreme jacket, and a Goldwin jumper. What are you drinking tonight? Two spicy margaritas, a glass of white wine, and a glass of red wine. Who’s your favorite American? Martine Syms. I like her exhibition at Sadie Coles. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a first date to a wine bar in Hoxton. Do you have a side hustle? Hustling!

What do you do? I work for Homer Jewellery and Louise Konrad Jewellery. Who’s your favorite American? The Tiger King. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? My sweatpants. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Zendaya’s Mugler outfit for the Dune premiere. What are you drinking tonight? Vodka soda.

items.title: The Story of Cécred
items.description: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
items.author: Eni Subair
paragraphs: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
hair NEAL FARINAH FOR CÉCRED
colour direction MASON POOLE

Haircare was always one of the many ways Beyoncé’s family expressed love. Watching her mother Ms. Tina Knowles care for everyone from doctors and judges to the unhoused in her now-famous Houston salon Headliners, Beyoncé saw firsthand how hair can empower and instill confidence in others—and in herself. It was in Ms. Tina’s salon chair, at just 9 years old, where Beyoncé’s appreciation for haircare began.

Decades and dozens of House of Deréon looks later, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina decided to bring their love and appreciation for haircare to the world. In 2024, they turned their lifelong shared passion into Cécred, with Beyoncé as the sole investor, founder, and Chairwoman and Ms. Tina as Vice Chairwoman. Years in the making, the brand was an endeavour worth perfecting—with Beyoncé and Ms. Tina personally testing every product.
Limited copies of the zine are available here.
The quality speaks for itself: Take the Restoring Hair and Edge Drops, which has become the number one hair product in the United States, driven by hair growth testimonials all over social media.

Meanwhile, a heartwarming Father’s Day short film of JAŸ-Z’s loc takedown process, using the brand’s signature Detangling Spray, has offered an intimate glimpse into the family. The love poured into the products only amplifies the scientific truths: These serums, shampoos, and gels really work for you.
This autumn, Cécred jumped across the pond from Los Angeles to London, offering its wide range of products for us Brits at Space NK stores.

To celebrate the UK launch, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina opened up about their hair and their lives. It’s a full-circle moment for the mother-daughter duo, who are sharing the lessons in hair confidence passed down through generations with a whole new audience. For Beyoncé, it’s about more than hair. It’s about continuing her mother’s legacy and making sure everyone feels their best in their hair.
ENI SUBAIR: What has been the most rewarding part of building Cécred?
BEYONCÉ: My mother and I poured decades of experience, tradition, and love into Cécred, so seeing our community grow across every ethnicity, texture, generation, and gender is so fulfilling.

In the beginning, it took some conditioning from the world’s perception of how to launch a brand founded by someone like me. I’m the founder, visionary, and sole investor—not the face or model for this brand. I had a vision to build something that solved real problems and performed so incredibly that the people who can’t stand my music still use Cécred, haaaa! … because it works.
Cécred has been years in the making, so why did 2024 finally feel like the right time to launch?

MS. TINA: Well, we tried to launch it two years earlier, and Beyoncé, you know, she’s a perfectionist. So, with the products, I thought they were amazing, but then I would give them to her, and she would test them on herself, her friends, and her daughters. Then, if one person didn’t have an excellent experience, she would give it back to me. She drove us crazy, and the team was like, “Oh my God!” But I’m so happy that she was so picky about it because it just got better and better. And our testing, research, and development is where we put a lot of money. I was like, this is so crazy expensive because we’re researching and testing so much. We’ve tested on three continents to get all types of hair textures, to make sure that it works on all hair. I had a salon in the ’80s, and what I was told all the time was that our hair was strong because they think that because our hair is coarser, it is stronger. But that is a myth surrounding Black hair. It’s just the opposite. Our hair is the weakest, most fragile hair, and the curlier your hair is, the more texture you have.

And I’ve always studied the science of hair: what it was made of and what it needed. Even making sure to reduce the molecular weight of products so that it can get through the cuticle and build and strengthen the hair.
What lessons have you learned from your mum that have helped you on this journey?

BEYONCÉ: Growing up I saw my mom pour love into others at her salon, and she still does this every day. I love that she trusts that the world is for her. She trusts God. She approaches things with humanity and love. I love my mother’s rebellious spirit. She can spark an idea and make it come to life. She’s fearless and I get that from her. It was in her salon that I witnessed stylists transforming women and helping them get their confidence back and see their beautiful potential. It was more than just getting their hair done, it became a sacred space where they were cared for. That impact resonated so deeply, and I wanted that to be reflected in Cécred and the community we’re building. Your heart carries energy and wisdom from your fingertips.

Recently my mom decided to surprise me by visiting a hair salon in the UK. No calls ahead, no warning. She packed a bag of Cécred, got into the car, and showed up without any pre-planning. Even though one of the managers told her she couldn’t be there, she stuck around and made the owner come. She was determined to build a relationship with the salon owners and clients and ended up spending almost a whole day doing hair there, ha!
What’s your first memory of experimenting with your hair?

BEYONCÉ: One day I decided to cut my own hair. I think I may have cut the whole ponytail off and also cut bangs! I walked in with my ponytail and said, “Mom, put this back on please.” And she was like, “I can’t.” But I thought she could, because I’d seen her be such a hair magician, especially when she would bond hair. Those crazy memories were the foundation of my childhood.
Both you and your mum love Tottenham—where do you like to go? What are your favourite spots?

BEYONCÉ: One of my favourite things about London is the drive to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and passing through Seven Sisters. I love seeing all the communities with their kids, the barber shops, and all the culturally diverse restaurants. As I get closer to the stadium, I start to see the fans who put so much effort into attending the show, either dressed in metallic silver, glistening in the streets and sunshine, or in full cowboy gear, boas, and boots. I can spot my Hive from miles away. When I’m onstage and see all the ethnicities, all the beautiful and fabulous outfits and families, there’s no other experience like it. The melting pot of beautiful diversity in London, particularly at my shows, is something magical to witness.

I love the music scene in the UK. I’ve watched Sienna Spiro grow up from a beautiful young girl to an extraordinarily talented young woman. I’ve known her family well for quite some time. I heard her sing when she was a kid discovering her voice and I can’t articulate the pride she brings me. What a God-given talent! I’m also so proud of Raye, who wrote some of the songs on The Gift. She has had such an anointing. You hear the vulnerability and wisdom in her voice. I also love and respect Olivia Dean. These beautiful women are all kind, have grace, and write and produce their own music. It gives me goosebumps. I just burst with pride when I see them.
Looking back, what was your favourite hairstyle during the B’DAY era, and your favourite look created by your mum?

BEYONCÉ: My favorite hair look was the B’DAY cover updo. That’s stood the test of time and has had such a renaissance this year. I love seeing everyone’s interpretations, and videos and the evolution of the early 2000s look.

My favourite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress—it was gorgeously simple and made with her love. We had a very small wedding in our home. We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends. Wearing a dress, she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress.

You recently re-wore a House of Deréon top that you wore back in 2006 to mark 20 years of B’DAY. What did you love about House of Deréon then that you still love now? What can we find in your archive?

BEYONCÉ: Yes, haaaa! I pulled out the Deréon archive for the Hive for the B’DAY 20th Anniversary re-release. I also had so much fun recreating some of my and my mother’s designs. We brought back the Deréon hoodies and metallic Freakum dresses. I’ll never forget calling my mum the day before the “Freakum Dress” shoot, asking her to make more dresses in more colours because I envisioned match-cutting the colours during the choreography. She was frustrated that I tasked her with making them so last minute, but she and Ty (Tyrone Hunter) got it done. I’m so very thankful for her. I’m so excited to pass all my archives to my kids, especially now that they’re all discovering their own personal style. I’m going to enjoy seeing how they pull from their parents’ carpets and tours if they’re ever interested. Rumi’s favourite place to shop right now is Ross and TJ Maxx these days.

items.title: Joe Biden Has a Lot of Unknown Unknowns
items.description: Good afternoon from Washington, where Party Animals has not forgotten the 5 a.m. wake-up required last Tuesday to attend Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first Pentagon press conference in six months. This was a peculiar one, arranged so Hegseth could brief
items.author: Aidan McLaughlin
paragraphs: Good afternoon from Washington, where Party Animals has not forgotten the 5 a.m. wake-up required last Tuesday to attend Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first Pentagon press conference in six months. This was a peculiar one, arranged so Hegseth could brief the public on his own personal battle for career survival.

The briefing kicked off at 8 a.m., but the press had to be at the Pentagon by 6 a.m. for an extensive security screening. I’d like to think that this cruel early start was a consequence of Hegseth’s self-proclaimed sobriety. What kind of drunk drags his sorry carcass before a crowd of jackals before noon? Not any I know.

But sources I spoke with for a new piece on Hegseth’s war inside the Pentagon told me there was a more Machiavellian motivation for the presser: Donald Trump loves to watch Fox & Friends at 8 a.m. And sure enough, soon after the conclusion of Hegseth’s performance, its intended audience of one offered a review on Truth Social.
Read on for my investigation into Hegseth’s turbulent tenure at the top of the Department of Defense, and what it means for his survival as Democrats take control of Congress in January.

The reviews are in for Joe Biden’s new book, Promise Me, America. The Atlantic calls the book “unrepentant.” The New York Times calls it a 400-page “cover letter.” The former president offers the fantastical opinion that he should have stayed in the race in 2024 and faced Trump, quite a position to maintain given he couldn’t voice his own audiobook and limited his press appearances for the release to a soft-focus People magazine story (his publisher did not respond to Party Animals’ multiple requests for an interview). According to the reviews, the former president dedicates scant attention to one of the biggest debacles of his presidency, the war in Gaza, which he abetted thanks to near-unwavering support for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu as 2,000-pound bombs rained down on the densely packed enclave, killing more than 70,000 people. As president, Biden publicly questioned the death toll numbers. “Too many innocent Palestinians were killed,” he now writes, as if possessed by the passive-voice ghost of Donald Rumsfeld. Mistakes were made, indeed.
