In contrast with his remarkably clinical view of dead Gazans, he writes movingly about his friendship with Netanyahu, recalling his farewell to the prime minister days before leaving the White House: “I still love you, pal.”
Elon Musk is Sorry About All That

Just five months ago, Elon Musk was promoting a movie in which a gunman goes on a mass murder rampage targeting supporters of immigration. That this was barely noticed is a sign of just how extreme Musk’s rhetoric has become over the years, as he devolved Xeet by Xeet into the online equivalent of a bum who yells at strangers on the street about race science. Then the midterms happened. After blowing nearly $500 million in an effort to get Republicans elected and falling short in key races, particularly in Texas, the octocentibillionaire seems to be seeking some kind of public rehabilitation. In a virtual appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk told Andrew Ross Sorkin that he is “not MAGA”—despite the many photos of Elon wearing a certain conspicuous hat—and that he is actually “a moderate.” Don’t take the hat’s word for it, though, here’s Musk on the record in October 2024: “I’m not just MAGA, I’m Dark MAGA.” Ah, well, nevertheless. He expressed hope for incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, and said he felt “foolish” for blowing so many millions to achieve very little. What’s the over/under on how long Moderate Elon will last?

Miller and Marco: The Wall Street Journal has a great report on the close relationship between Stephen Miller and Marco Rubio, who have forged an unlikely alliance despite their past clashes over policy like immigration. It’s a revealing look at how Rubio’s Republican Party lost to Miller’s Republican Party, and how Rubio then jettisoned his entire worldview to join the winning team.

Trump of Wall Street: The Washington Post reports that Trump’s financial disclosure revealed he held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August. That’s considerably higher than the $615,000 to $1.3 million he held at the end of 2024.

French, Toast: No one should know who “Bo” French is. No one really did until the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commission went viral for complaining about a group of college kids celebrating a touchdown at a University of Texas football game. (Some of the kids were not white; French objected to this). He became whatever the opposite of a sensation is and ended up losing his election to a Democrat. Now Politico reports French has taken another blow: River Crest Country Club, the Fort Worth members institution he frequented, has kicked him out.

Garcia’s Hit List: Robert Garcia, the House Democrat who is expected to lead the Oversight Committee in the new Congress, has begun mapping out his targets. Per The Atlantic: “Garcia this morning sent a dozen letters to high-ranking Trump-administration officials and members of the president’s family, providing the clearest signal yet of which topics—and which people—will likely face the greatest scrutiny once Democrats take control of the House.”
Oversight O’clock: New York Magazine’s Ben Terris went deep on the new era of Democratic oversight, everything from the war with Iran to Trump’s big beautiful ballroom.
No Longer Satire: Read Joe Bernstein, writing for The New York Times Magazine, on how America is becoming more and more like Grand Theft Auto.
Bye-Bye Boebert: Annie Karni writes for The New York Times about the rise and fall of the MAGA Mean Girl Caucus, as Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert, and Nancy Mace all exit Congress.

items.title: Kate Middleton Wore Matching Amethyst Necklace and Earrings for Her First Engagement in India
items.description: The Princess of Wales touched down in India this Monday for a whirlwind three-day visit to the country with her husband, Prince William.
items.author: Stephanie Bridger-Linning
paragraphs: The Princess of Wales touched down in India this Monday for a whirlwind three-day visit to the country with her husband, Prince William.
The couple visited Mumbai for the sixth Earthshot Prize Summit, which took place on Tuesday. It marked the Waleses’ first joint overseas visit since Catherine’s cancer diagnosis.

The busy schedule of engagements kicked off with a game of gully cricket—an informal version of the game played on the street. For the occasion, the Princess of Wales struck a balance between polished and casual, opting for crisp white Alexander McQueen trousers, paired with a white top layered under a pistachio blazer by Veronica Beard.

The finishing touch? A matching set of green amethyst earrings and a drop necklace from one of Catherine’s favorite jewelry labels, Kiki McDonough. Catherine has at least 20 pairs of earrings from the jeweler, ranging from the blue topaz drops she wore to Royal Ascot to the green tourmaline, green amethyst and diamond earrings set in gold, designed specially for her to mark Princess Charlotte’s birth.
The apple green amethysts, which she wore in Mumbai, are among the lesser-seen designs in her collection but proved the perfect accessory for this first engagement.

While in Mumbai, the prince’s program focused on The Earthshot Prize and its mission to accelerate solutions to the world’s most pressing environmental challenges. The princess joined the prince for a number of engagements during the visit.
During their time in Mumbai, the prince and princess also celebrated several of the deep cultural connections between the United Kingdom and India: cricket, fashion, and cinema.
Beginning with an engagement focused on the uniquely Indian passion of gully cricket and
concluding with a visit to the heart of Mumbai’s film industry, their royal highnesses
celebrated the creativity, talent, and cultural influence that continue to shape modern India and
strengthen ties between the two countries.

The highlight of the visit was the Earthshot Prize ceremony on Tuesday, November 17. Five Earthshot leaders were given 1 million euros (about $1.1 million USD) to accelerate the impact of their innovative solutions. Mumbai made perfect sense as the host city; India is home to more Earthshot Prize winners and finalists than any other country.

Since founding the prize in 2020, Prince William has attended all of the awards ceremonies: in London, Boston, Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro. Catherine joined the prince in London in 2021 and again in Boston the following year, but has missed recent editions in the further corners of the globe. This was partly due to the princess’s restricted work schedule while she underwent treatment for cancer and spent time in recovery.

It marked a return to the country for Prince William and Kate, who carried out a state visit in April 2016. The week-long tour saw the then Duke and Duchess of Cambridge explore Mumbai, New Delhi, Assam, and Bhutan, racking up a total of 22 engagements that saw them try their hand at cricket, meet Bollywood stars and royalty, and champion charitable causes close to their hearts.

It was one of four overseas trips taken by the couple that year. Although William and Kate still travel, it is with far less frequency as the couple prioritizes a stable family life. Their last major overseas tour was to the Caribbean in 2022.
Originally published by Tatler.

items.title: The Surprising History of the Royal Walkabout
items.description: “I have to be seen to be believed,” the late Queen Elizabeth II once said. And on Christmas Day, the royal family will be seen en masse during their annual walkabout on their way to services at St. Mary Magdalene Church on the Sandringham estate. For years, th
items.author: Hadley Hall Meares
paragraphs: “I have to be seen to be believed,” the late Queen Elizabeth II once said. And on Christmas Day, the royal family will be seen en masse during their annual walkabout on their way to services at St. Mary Magdalene Church on the Sandringham estate. For years, the holiday stroll, which features major and minor royals mingling with the public, has been a milestone event on the royal calendar.

But three controversial royals, the former Prince Andrew, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Duchess of Sussex, almost certainly will not be there. While Andrew has disappeared into his new life at Marsh Farm in Norfolk, Harry and Meghan have continued the tradition of the walkabout, reportedly infuriating the palace with a planned meet-and-greet with a small group of well-wishers in Nottingham. Although no longer working members of the royal family, it seems the couple knows the value and the power of this famous tradition, whose origins are far more recent than many believe.

For centuries, commoners were lucky to get a glimpse of royals riding a horse on a march across the country or nodding from a carriage on the way to the opening of parliament. The first Buckingham Palace balcony appearance was not until 1851, when Prince Albert came upon the idea of Queen Victoria appearing to celebrate the Great Exhibition of London.

The leading figure behind the idea of making the monarchy more visible to the public was a surprising one: the dour, but savvy George V, who ascended the throne in 1910. “I may be uninspiring,” he admitted, “but I’m damned if I’m an alien.”

These royal appearances ramped up significantly during the first World War, when the royal family came under scrutiny for their German lineage. George visited everyday soldiers on the Front, and Queen Mary and her children spent hours visiting the wounded in hospitals.

“George took ‘getting out and about’ to new levels. He visited industrial areas and poor housing, went down a coal mine and went on a relentless round of opening hospitals and inspecting regiments,” royal news website Royal Central notes. “Queen Mary once retorted to a princess complaining about yet another hospital visit: ‘We are the royal family—and we love hospitals.’”

However, these events were still carefully curated, with a distance maintained between the royal family and those they were visiting. It was not until 1939, that the first unofficial walkabout occurred, when King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (better known as the Queen Mother) went to tour Canada on a goodwill tour in the midst of the looming war. In May, the couple laid a wreath at Ottawa National War Memorial while an estimated 10,000 veterans looked on.

Overcome with emotion, the royal couple decided to go into the crowd to speak with onlookers. A CBC radio journalist watching the scene could hardly have sounded more in awe. “They all look most happy, most excited,” the reporter said. “One had the hand of the queen in one hand and the hand of the king in another. A delighted expression.”

George and Elizabeth were equally touched, and continued these meet-and-greets throughout the tour. “I lost my heart to Canada and to Canadians, and my feelings have not changed with the passage of time,” the Queen Mother recalled.

Known for her effusive personality and warmth, the Queen Mother became a pro at speaking with everyday subjects. During World War II, George and Elizabeth were praised for going among the people in bombed out areas devastated by the Blitz, listening to their woes and offering encouragement and strength.

But it was not until Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip toured Australia and New Zealand in 1970 that the modern walkabout was truly introduced into the British royal calendar. There are different origin stories about how the modern walkabout came to be. One version asserts that it was a spontaneous decision of the Queen to walk to her next stop in order to chat, shake hands and accept flowers from schoolchildren in New Zealand.

Others say that first walk was the brainchild of the modernizing Australian courtier William Heseltine, known as the “mastermind behind the monarchy.” A firm believer in making the family seem more approachable and normal, he was also behind the 1969 Royal Family documentary. But if that project proved to be controversial, the walkabout (a term coined as a result of the tour) was a smash hit.

According to Kitty Kelley, the first royal walkabout did not occur in London until 1972, during the celebration of Elizabeth and Philip’s 25th wedding anniversary. “People were agog; their sovereign had never been known to speak to ordinary people,” Kelley writes in The Royals. “This was the first royal walkabout London had ever seen, and flag-waving Britons cheered as the Queen, the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Charles, and Princess Anne melted into the crowd, greeting people and trying to make the royal family appear less remote.”

While the Queen reportedly enjoyed the intimacy of the walkabout, not every royal family member was quite as thrilled. “At nineteen years old suddenly being dropped in the middle of the street, suddenly being told to pick someone and talk to them,” Princess Anne said. “Fun? No, I don’t think so. A challenge.”

Soon, the walkabout was a major part of every royal’s schedule, and family members had to learn how to do them—like it or not. “I learnt the way a monkey learns—by watching its parents,” King Charles once said.

During international tours, the walkabouts made a packed schedule even more tiring, but Queen Elizabeth II never faltered. “On a tour of Canada, visiting Saskatchewan, the Canadian minister Alvin Hamilton was concerned that the Queen had been on her feet all day and had not even requested a ‘health break,’” Karen Dolby writes in The Wicked Wit of Queen Elizabeth II. “Her private secretary breezily replied that the Minister for Northern Affairs and National Resources need not worry, ‘Her Majesty is trained for eight hours.’ It’s impossible not to wonder about the training sessions.”

She also leaned upon her sense of humor when meeting folks of all different stripes. “On a walkabout in Scotland, a helpful observer commented that she looked just like the Queen, to which she quickly replied, ‘How reassuring,’” Dolby notes.

According to Dolby, the Queen also developed a system to communicate with her staff while talking with the public. If things were going well, she held her handbag in the crook of her left arm. If she wanted someone to relieve her so she could move on, the handbag was dropped to her side.

But the person who truly transformed the modern walkabout was Princess Diana, much to her husband Prince Charles’s chagrin. “Charles was smart enough to see what a stunning political asset Diana had become—but he was also deeply disturbed by all the adoration coming his young wife’s way,” Tina Brown writes in The Diana Chronicles.

From the start it was clear the young Princess had a connection with everyday people unlike any other royal. During a walkabout while touring Wales in 1981, Charles joked, “I seem to do nothing but collect flowers these days, I know my role.”

As Dianamania swept the world, the Princess became more and more comfortable with connecting with her often-rabid fans. Far from a stiff gloved handshake, she would clasp hands gloveless, hug well-wishers, kneel to speak with children. Frustrated that Diana constantly pulled focus, Charles delivered pithy one-liners with a forced smile. At one walkabout, the crowd openly groaned when they realized Charles was coming to their side, not Diana. “It’s not fair is it?” Charles quipped to the crowd. “You’d better ask for your money back.”

But despite Charles’s jealousy, he could not deny the impact Diana had during these walkabouts. “Everyone was really buoyed up to see her and she was making an effort to go along and speak to people and people appreciated the effort she put into meeting them,” one person she spoke with remembered. “I know it was her job but she gave that little bit extra to people that made her different and stand out.”
“She made people happy,” he noted. “It’s a rare gift.”

Catherine, Princess of Wales, has followed in her mother-in-law’s footsteps as a walkabout all-star. According to historian Robert Jobson, Catherine was initially scared during the walkabout, offering up the stiff refrain, “Thank you so much. We are so delighted to be here,” over and over. But she quickly acclimated and has become known for her chatty and warm ways. “There’s a real art to walkabouts,” she has said. “Everybody teases me in the family that I spend far too long chatting. I still have to learn a little bit more, and to pick up a few more tips, I suppose.”

In fact, it has become a sport for the press to catch Prince William subtly attempting to move Catherine along, often eventually giving up. During the Christmas Day walkabout in 2024, she was the last royal to leave the receiving line, quipping “I think I’ve lost my family!”

According to royal author Robert Hardman, King Charles can also be unusually chatty. No one quite wants to go up and go, ‘Sir, can you get a move on?’ he says. “Instead, Queen Camilla will nudge him in the small of his back with the corner of her handbag.”

But the predilection is one Camilla shares as well. On a walkabout in Wrexham, an irritated Charles was overheard telling an aide “Can we try to get [Camilla] back again? Please? We need to go! I was trying to wait for her, but she goes on!”

Learning the art of the walkabout—what to say, what not to say—is a lesson every royal must figure out, often on the job. When Meghan Markle married Prince Harry in 2018, she admitted her ignorance. “I never saw pictures or videos of a walkabout,” she claimed.

And with the advent of cell phones, the job has become much more difficult. “I’m glad that I’m not starting now because at least you had people to talk to. Now you don’t really. Phones are bad enough, but the iPads—you can’t even see their heads,” Princess Anne said.

And these engagements can occasionally go south. In 2018, the Duchess of Sussex was rushed out of a market in Fiji after the walkabout got out of hand. There are also the occasional overzealous fans, including recently when a woman attempted to kiss Prince William on the cheek. And who can forget the supremely uncomfortable walkabout at Windsor after the Queen’s death in 2022, when a warring William, Catherine, Harry and Meghan greeted public mourners. It was, Catherine reportedly said, “one of the hardest things she’d ever had to do.”

Walkabouts are also a logistical headache for royal protection officers. “You are always aware of who is in the crowd,” former royal bodyguard Simon Morgan explained to Hello! “That is one of the positives of our royal family, they always want to go and meet people and as a protection officer, you have to accept what their wishes are. The current trend of hugs, high fives and selfies, that’s going to continue, so the protection officer’s job is really brought to the front then, because the protection officer is constantly looking for what could go wrong, you are constantly working things through your mind for the ‘what if, what if, what if.’

But the walkabout shows no sign of disappearing anytime soon. And come Christmas Day, there will be cheers, hugs, and an enormous amount of quick, polite chats about the weather that citizens who wait and brave the winter cold will never forget.

items.title: Want to Smell Bisexual? A Hit Podcast Has the Perfume for You
items.description: You Must Remember This is a podcast dedicated, as its host Karina Longworth says in every intro, to exploring the secret and/or forgotten histories of Hollywood’s first century. Longworth, who is an LA–based writer and film preservationist, usually tells her s
items.author: Marisa Meltzer
paragraphs: You Must Remember This is a podcast dedicated, as its host Karina Longworth says in every intro, to exploring the secret and/or forgotten histories of Hollywood’s first century. Longworth, who is an LA–based writer and film preservationist, usually tells her stories in themed seasons. Those include Erotic 90’s, spanning the introduction of the NC-17 rating to Eyes Wide Shut; Dead Blondes (Marilyn Monroe, Jean Harlow, Veronica Lake); and a whole series exploring the web of connections Charles Manson had to Hollywood. It’s addictive, exhaustively researched, and narrated in a way that is both soothing and trancelike.

Longworth is a native Angeleno who has been writing about film for years. She was a film editor and critic at the LA Weekly for three years until 2012; wrote books on Al Pacino and Meryl Streep; and then started You Must Remember This is 2014. She’s also part of a film-loving couple: her husband of 8 years is the Knives Out writer and director Rian Johnson.

The latest season of the podcast is called The Bisexuals, spotlighting the stories of actors and actresses whose love lives were often much more diverse than anything sanctioned by a studio. One star that the season discusses is Libby Holman, a singer and socialite who married the tobacco heir Zachary Smith Reynolds in 1931. Not only did she have a fruitful sex life with Tallulah Bankhead and Montgomery Clift, but she was known for her signature scent called Jungle Gardenia.

In honor of that bombastic perfume that wafted off of her, Longworth, 46, collaborated with Joey Rosin, who formulated a fragrance, Bisexual. Vanity Fair spoke to Longworth about moviegoing in Los Angeles versus New York, what she smelled like as a teenager, being in grad school in your 40s, and her thoughts about Quentin Tarantino’s film programming.
The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.
Vanity Fair: What was the first perfume you remember wearing?

Karina Longworth: Coco Mademoiselle was really a big deal for me when I was 18, 19. It was one of the first perfumes that I ever knew about. I started with The Body Shop’s Tea Rose oil. I didn’t really have any female adult influences because my mom died when I was 11, and so I had to sort of figure out that whole world.
Have you always wanted to make a perfume? Are you a perfume nerd?

So I never had an ambition to make a perfume, but over the past 10 years, I’ve become really into perfume. I used to rent an office space in the same building as an independent perfumer, Jacqueline Ella Steele, whose brand was called Goest— which doesn’t exist anymore—but she made a perfume called Silent Films. She was the first person I contacted about trying to formulate this perfume. But she’s out of business. So that’s when I started asking around and I got led to Joey Rosin.
The idea came from your research?

I got the idea because, in reading and writing about Libby Holman, there are all these anecdotes of her walking into a room in a cloud of Jungle Gardenia, to the point where, people who were attracted to her were attracted to it, and people who didn’t like her found it so disgusting. I thought there was something really interesting about that, how the same scent could be either attractive or repellent, depending on how you felt about the person wearing it.
Personalities, voices and clothes all depend on who’s doing it.

There’s this really incredible anecdote in Patricia Bosworth’s Montgomery Clift biography about how one of Montgomery Clift’s friends was at a party at Treetops, Libby Holman’s estate, and she was looking for the bathroom, and accidentally walked into her bedroom, and the bed was a tangle of white satin sheets, and there’s a giant bottle of barbiturates on the nightstand and everything just reeked of Jungle Gardenia. She was grossed out, but then she also got the impression this is Libby and Monty’s sex lair.
Were you trying to recreate the smell?

We didn’t try to copy the exact old fragrance. Joey does his research, and he did research into what the original notes were. But we talked about not wanting it to be a slavish copy, and instead just trying to evoke for both of us what jungle would smell like with gardenia, and how that could evoke Libby’s story. And so we played around with adding different types of smoke to it.
Have you ever been in a jungle?

I’ve been to Tahiti. I’m trying to think if I’ve ever been to a jungle. We talked a lot about tropical plants and what the dirt would smell like, and the heat. It’s like hot weather almost has a smell. But then pairing that with this kind of old lady scent of gardenia. I went to visit his studio in Brooklyn a few times and he mailed some samples to me in Los Angeles. And by that point, it was like four iterations that were almost exactly the same. So it was just about what was giving me the best vibe.
You were living in LA for the process?
I was living alone in Rochester, N.Y. in a depressing situation because of the weather and being very alone, having no social life.
But you loved your grad school program, right? I forget the name but I know it’s long.

L. Jeffrey Selznick School of Film Preservation at the George Eastman Museum. I got so much out of the program, but it was grueling, physically, and mentally, and emotionally. It was really difficult to suddenly be living alone in a place where I felt like I had no one I could really talk to.
So you were in an entirely new, but temporary situation.

I started relying on scented candles to improve my mood and to change my mood. If I got home feeling terrible, the fragrance was helpful. I also had nowhere to wear perfume. At first I thought I would just make a candle, and then as I started learning more about fragrance, I learned that candles have to go through a much more rigorous process. And it takes a lot longer. We were not going to be able to get it done in time to have a presale like we have during the podcast season. But in the future, I would like to do a signature scent for You Must Remember This and have it available as a perfume and a candle.
What would that smell like?
It would be classic, but in a different way. I’m very inspired by the signature scent that they have at the Chateau [Marmont].
There has been a lot of talk about moviegoing being back. How has your tour been?
It has been great. In Savannah they sold 400 tickets to a very obscure, pre-code movie on a Friday night.
People must ask you a lot of podcast questions. What are your tips?
I say I don’t know what form yours is going to take, but mine takes the form of writing an extremely detailed script, and then sitting by myself in a room and reading it into a microphone.

I built a recording studio. I bought a little house in Laurel Canyon at the end of a private road, like at the end of a cul-de-sac, but you feel like you’re in the middle of the forest. I bought it from this woman who had lived there for 15 years and was kind of an all-purpose healer. She basically built a soundproof room with clay on the walls and crystals embedded into the clay, where she would do sound baths with them. When I saw this house, it was just perfect.
Which city has a better movie scene, New York or LA?
New York’s way better than LA, but LA is getting better.
Did someone buy the Vista? I loved that theater.

[Quentin] Tarantino owns the Vista. Because it’s Tarantino, he won’t let them show anything digital. It has to be a film print, and so he’ll show a new movie if there’s a print, like The Odyssey played there, Sinners played there. But when there isn’t a new movie out that is on a print, he programs whatever he wants to see. He also does a lot of like Saturday morning matinees of classical Hollywood cinema that is just his taste, you know. Sometimes it’s my taste, sometimes it’s not. It’s a lot of Jerry Lewis. But one thing I will say for Tarantino is that when he discovers a filmmaker or genre or something from the past, he shows. He’s been showing all these William Beaudine silent films, and I think that’s great because silent film has really fallen out of fashion in LA.
I was leaving to interview you today and someone said, “Oh, I love that podcast,” and was talking about the Manson series. Is that your most popular?
It changes. Increasingly, people are asking about the Polly Platt series.
Do you know what the next series is going to be?

I have two ideas that would involve talking to people or family members of subjects who have passed away, but who could give me access to sort of the family lore. I am in contact with both of those families, but I need to kind of do the legwork, talking to them more and figure out which story makes the most sense. I also sketched out a very long season about the three stars of Rebel Without a Cause. That is something that people have been asking me to do for years. But the thing that stops me from doing it is that we still don’t know exactly what happened to Natalie Wood. But that’s kind of in my back pocket.

items.title: THE BIRTH OF BOND | Vanity Fair
items.description: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered wh
items.author: David Kamp
paragraphs: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered when he first tried to take his hero to the screen. DAVID KAMP recalls the unlikely team—two small-time producers, a journeyman director, and a "rough diamond" of a star―behind 007's film debut, Dr. No,, the beginning of a $5 billion franchise
ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED IN OCTOBER 2012

nter Sean Connery, dark hair slicked with pomade, eyes locking hungrily upon a beautiful green-eyed girl. Her return glance leaves no doubt—the feeling is mutual. His slouch and casual banter exude languor and nonchalance, but there's an undercurrent of coiled menace to this man, as though he might, at any moment, spring into table-overturning, crockery-shattering action.

Except nothing of the sort happens. Instead, the other fellow in the scene cuts the tension by taking out his fiddle and favoring the room with a jaunty tune learned, he says in a stagy brogue, "in the old ruins on the top of Knocknasheega!"

This isn't a James Bond picture. It is 1959, and Connery is putting in time in a cornball live-action Disney feature called Darby O'Gill and the Little People. He's the second male lead, billed beneath not only Albert Sharpe, the elderly Irish character actor in the title role—a kindly farmhand who sees leprechauns—but also the greeneyed girl, the ingenue Janet Munro. Though verily pump-misting pheromonal musk into the air, to a degree unmatched before or since by any actor in a Disney family movie, Connery is still a jobbing scuffler, not a star. He has no idea of what lies in store for him.

The seventh of Ian Fleming's Bond novels, Goldfinger, has recently reached the shops. But there are no Bond pictures yet. In London, a Long Island-born film producer named Albert R. Broccoli, known as Cubby, is still lamenting that he blew his chance with Fleming. The previous year, Broccoli had set up a meeting with the English author and his representatives to talk about securing movie rights to the Bond series, only to miss the meeting to tend to his wife, who had recently been diagnosed with terminal cancer. In Broccoli's absence, his business partner, Irving Allen, let Fleming know that he didn't share his colleague's ardor. "In my opinion," Allen told Bond's creator, "these books are not even good enough for television."

This is an older, stiffer world, with Britain just five years removed from food rationing and America still in an era of Kramdens, Eisenhowers, and finned Caddies. It is a world unfamiliar with the catchphrases "Shaken, not stirred" and "Bond, James Bond," where no ears have ever heard Monty Norman's four-note Bond motif and no eyes have ever taken in Maurice Binder's amniotic credit sequences of lissome women undulating in silhouette to lavishly charted John Barry arrangements.

But it is also a world in transition. Transatlantic jet service is newly available to commercial passengers, thanks to the carriers B.O.A.C. and Pan American. G.D. Searle & Company, a pharmaceutical concern, is awaiting approval from the Food and Drug Administration to market one of its products, Enovid, as a birthcontrol pill for women. A scrubbed, fit group of U.S. military test pilots has just been introduced to the public as the Mercury Seven, America's first astronauts. And the undeclared Democratic frontrunner in the next presidential election is only 42 years old.

In March 1961, when he actually is the president, John F. Kennedy lists Fleming's fifth Bond novel, From Russia with Love, as one of his 10 current favorite reads in a Life magazine article. That same year, Broccoli, having parted ways with Allen and joined forces with another producer, a Canadian by the name of Harry Saltzman, finally gets the rights to turn Fleming's books into movies. After an arduous and seemingly fruitless search to find a lead actor mutually agreeable to the two producers and their studio benefactor, United Artists, Broccoli circles back to one of the lesser-knowns among the candidates: Sean Connery. To confirm his hunch that this tall, handsome Scotsman could be the guy, Broccoli, while in Hollywood, arranges for his new wife, Dana, to join him in a screening room at the Samuel Goldwyn Studio. There they watch the only Connery footage that Cubby has been able to rustle up: Darby OGill and the Little People. Dana Broccoli's response is instantaneous: "That's our Bond!"
And so on October 5,1962, at the London Pavilion theater, in Piccadilly Circus, Connery joins Fleming, Broccoli, and Saltzman on the red carpet for the world premiere of the first Bond film, Dr. No.

half-century later, even in an era inured to skin, gunplay, and wide-screen shots of tropical waterfalls, Dr. No remains exhilarating to watch. The azure brightness of Jamaica, with Connery striding purposefully through it; the seawater-salted flesh and ounces-light wardrobe of Ursula Andress; the modernist bachelor-pad fantasia that is the undersea lair of the titular doctor, played with cool reserve by Joseph Wiseman—it's all so fantastically stylish, racy, and forward-looking. So imagine what it must have been like for the people who actually saw the picture in a theater when it first came out.

Dr. No took just a few months in the U.K. to recoup its $1 million budget and ultimately made 20 times that amount in its initial release. Theater bookers in the U.S. hedged their bets at first, putting out the film "in the sticks," as a chagrined Broccoli noted, before allowing the sophisticates in New York and Los Angeles to see it. Nevertheless, the drumbeat had already begun, with North Carolina's Rocky Mount Telegram, for example, relishing how Connery "twists his supple body through a tiny aperture to potential freedom." The syndicated entertainment columnist Erskine Johnson suggested that "tawny 26-year-old Ursula Andress should have been billed not by her last name, but as 'Undress.' "

As it turned out, the coastal intelligentsia were pretty easily won over, too. "Oh, it was dazzling: Ursula coming out of the ocean, the brilliant art direction, straining your eyes to see the almost-nude women in the opening credits. They were cheap tricks, but good tricks," says Buck Henry, who, with Mel Brooks and the TV producer Daniel Melnick, was inspired in '65 to create the sitcom spoof Get Smart in homage. "It wasn't Brueghel," Henry says of the early Bond films, "but it was like the stuff that Lichtenstein and those other guys were doing—great Pop art carried into another medium."

Dr. No and its two follow-ups, From Russia with Love (1963) and Goldfinger (1964), are the cornerstones of Bond mania. Like the early Lennon-McCartney singles that spurred Beatlemania, they augured bigger, more elaborate things to come, but the sheer excitement they generated remains unsurpassable. Not only were these movies terrifically entertaining, they also delivered a sort of jet-age holodeck experience, granting regular folk an opportunity to glimpse the future awaiting them. As of 1960, fewer than 2 percent of all Americans had traveled internationally by air. So both Dr. No and From Russia with Love include what are essentially fetish shots of Pan Am jets landing on runways as air-traffic controllers announce their arrival. ("Hello, London, your flight PA1 just landed in Istanbul")

"It was a sense of 'Buy your ticket—we're going to take you places!' " says Guy Hamilton, the director of Goldfinger. He recalls the Broccoli-Saltzman attitude toward Bond transport as "Don't take a train when you can take a plane, and if you're going to take a plane, take the newest one around. And if you give Bond a car, don't show what's been seen—show what's not out yet." This is why, while Bond drives an Aston Martin DBIII in Goldfinger the novel, he drives a DB5 in Hamilton's movie, made five years later. It's also why, when Bond comes to after being knocked out with a tranquilizer gun in the same film, he is told, by no less than Honor Blackman's knockout aviatrix, Pussy Galore, that he is aboard "Mr. Goldfinger's Lockheed JetStar"—this at a time when the very concept of a private business jet was virtually unheard of. Even Bond's room-service breakfast order in From Russia with Love— "Green figs, yogurt, coffee, very black"—sounds ahead of its time.

Beyond the travelogue aspect, there was the sex aspect—another way, as it were, to hitch a ride with James Bond. "The actual film, to film, was sexy," says Shirley Eaton of her scenes with Connery in Goldfinger. Eaton is famous for being the blonde girl whose body is discovered nude, lifeless, and coated in gold paint—her death (by "skin suffocation," not a medical possibility in real life) a punishment by her boss, Auric Goldfinger, for switching to Bond's side.

But it's Eaton's first scene with Connery that packs the erotic wallop. Bond, poolside at Miami's Fontainebleau hotel, has worked out from which room Goldfinger's accomplice is spying on his opponent's cards, thereby allowing Goldfinger to cheat at his alfresco games of high-stakes gin rummy. Letting himself into the room, Bond discovers Eaton's Jill Masterson lying stomach-down in a black bikini on a balcony lounger, using binoculars and a radio set to convey the card info into Goldfinger's earpiece. Wearing a shorty jumpsuit of pale-blue terry cloth that only someone as masculine as Connery could pull off, Bond, grinning, simply lowers himself gently onto Jill, shrewdly opting for horizontal bodily contact rather than force to accomplish his mission.

Eaton, then 27, had been acting in movies since her teen years, "always playing the girl next door," she says, or a pretty thing to be ogled in one of Britain's low-budget Carry On comedies. "But this was entirely new," she says. "It was grown-up sexuality. Sean and I just fell into our natural sensuality without any rumpy-pumpy, and I think that's what made it so exciting."

Honor Blackman, likewise, had already established herself as the judo-chopping, leather-clad Dr. Cathy Gale on the British TV series The Avengers but found the Bond universe to have an altogether different dynamic. "Cathy Gale was a very proper lady, with collars up to the chin," she says, "whereas Pussy was supposed to match Bond's sexuality. She was a tough broad who also showed a fair amount of bosom." Johnny Carson, just a few years into hosting The Tonight Show, was so taken with the scene in which Pussy finally surrenders to Bond's charms (they trade martial-arts body flips in a hay-filled barn before falling into a love clutch) that "he badgered and badgered me—would I show him how it was done?" she says. Blackman feared injuring Carson, but she flew to New York to rehearse the bit with him, and when they performed it live "he passionately kissed me at the end, which wasn't planned. It was funny, but it also showed how much even someone like Johnny Carson wanted to be James Bond."

an Fleming had long been alert to the screen potential of his books, but realizing this potential proved to be something of a chore. Twice in the late '50s, Fleming worked with American networks to develop a TV series, first with NBC on a Bond-inspired spy show provisionally titled Commander Jamaica, and then with CBS on what would have been an explicitly Bond-based weekly drama. Neither show made it to the pilot phase. A little earlier, in 1954, CBS had aired an anemic one-off adaptation of Fleming's first Bond novel, Casino Royale, in which the character had been Americanized into "Jimmy Bond" and been played by a miscast, chipmunk-cheeked actor named Barry Nelson. Fleming then sold the book's movie rights to the actor Gregory Ratoff, who died before coming close to getting a movie produced. These rights, unbundled from rights to the other Bond books, eventually fell into the hands of Ratoff s agent, the Hollywood mcicher Charles Feldman, who, after Bond mania took off, produced the abominable meta-parodic version with David Niven, Peter Sellers, and Woody Allen that came out in 1967. (Only in the last decade was Casino Roy ale, the novel, reeled into the hands of the "official" Bond producers—Broccoli's heirs— the result being the 2006 franchise reboot starring Daniel Craig.)
"OH, DISASTER, DISASTER, DISASTER!" DIRECTOR TERENCE YOUNG SAID WHEN SEAN CONNERY WAS CAST.

Fleming had higher hopes for a treatment he worked on in 1959 for a film to be called James Bond, Secret Agent. It was not an adaptation but a new Bond story, and his collaborator was Kevin McClory, an up-and-coming Irish screenwriter. But this project, too, foundered. Fleming, unbowed, folded his ideas for the shelved movie into the next Bond novel. Not long before this book, Thunderball, came out, in 1961, McClory got hold of an advance copy and was angered by its resemblance to the story treatment he'd labored on with Fleming and another writer, Jack Whittingham. McClory filed suit, and, while the book's publication was allowed to go forward, the issue of its film rights would take another three years to resolve.

In the movie industry, Fleming had at last run into a thickety, double-dealing milieu that he, a suave operator his entire adult life, was ill-prepared to contend with. Before that, to all appearances, he had been Mr. Smooth. It has often been said that James Bond was Fleming's fantasy version of himself, while Fleming declared that Bond was "a compound of all the secret agents and commando types I met" during World War II, in which he served in Britain's Naval Intelligence Division. Whichever way it was, Fleming had certainly known Bondish people and lived through Bondish episodes of his own by the time he sat down in 1952 and created the character at his typewriter.

In his youth, Fleming, born in 1908, had been a rascally, athletic ne'er-do-well who attended but did not graduate from Eton and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, distinguishing himself more as a trainee roue than an officer candidate. In the '30s, he finally found some measure of professional fulfillment, first as a journalist working for Reuters, the news agency, and then, as war broke out, as an aide to Rear Admiral John Henry Godfrey, Britain's director of naval intelligence.

Godfrey, brusque and imperious, became the model for 007's superior, M. He took to Fleming, inviting the younger man to accompany him to overseas meetings with J. Edgar Hoover, the F.B.I. chief, and William J. "Wild Bill" Donovan, the founder of the Office of Strategic Services, the Central Intelligence Agency's precursor. Godfrey also granted Fleming significant leeway to conjure imaginative schemes to trip up the Nazis. One of these, Operation Mincemeat, is among the more celebrated in the annals of British espionage. In 1943, British intelligence officers took possession of the corpse of Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who had recently died by his own hand. After dressing Michael's body in the uniform of a major in the Royal Marines, stuffing his pockets with phony identification materials, and chaining to his wrist a briefcase containing a letter labeled PERSONAL AND MOST SECRET, they dumped him off the coast of Spain, creating the impression of an officer who had died in a plane crash. Spain was infested with Nazi spies, and the hope was that one of them would inevitably get his hands on the letter and pass it up the chain of command. It worked. Hitler was fooled by the documents, which indicated that the Allies were about to invade Greece, and hastily moved a division of 90,000 troops there. The Allies, with considerably less resistance than they would have encountered otherwise, proceeded to take their true target, Sicily.

A fter the war, Fleming landed a job as foreign-news manager for Kemsley Newspapers, which owned, among other publications, The Sunday Times—a assignment that allowed him to spend every winter season in Jamaica, a place he'd first visited during his naval-intelligence years. In 1946 he built a home on the island's north shore that he called Goldeneye, after the code name of an Allied plan to defend Gibraltar against seizure by the Axis powers. From '52 onward, Fleming used Goldeneye as his writing roost, banging out one Bond novel a year. Nevertheless, by the beginning of 1961, he had still had no luck with Hollywood, which he described to a friend as "a hell of a jungle" and full of "specious promises."

It was at this time that, for $50,000, he granted Harry Saltzman a six-month option to put a film deal in place for the Bond books. A stout, hedgehoggish man born in 1915 to Jewish immigrants living in Quebec, Saltzman had hustled his way into the American movie industry, eventually venturing to England to take advantage of the tax breaks the U.K. afforded filmmakers. On the face of it, Saltzman was a peculiar deal partner for Fleming. While he had achieved modest success producing film adaptations of John Osborne's table-thumping social-realist plays Look Back in Anger and The Entertainer, he was decidedly small-time compared with previous suitors. Saltzman's children have long puzzled over how their father, who died in 1994, managed to secure the option. One of his daughters, Hilary Saltzman, stumbled upon some revelatory clues when, in 2003, she decided to relocate with her children from Los Angeles to Quebec. Having let her Canadian passport expire, she ran into a hitch while getting her citizenship papers in order: The Canadian government required documentation of her father's reasons for immigrating to the United States. The next surprise she encountered was that her request to pull her father's U.S. records, a process she expected to be routine, set off alarms at the State Department. When, after more than two years of petitioning, Hilary finally received the documents she needed to satisfy the Canadian government, she also received a bonus: reams of material revealing that her father, who she knew had served in the Royal Canadian Air Force in the early years of World War II, had subsequently worked for the U.S. Office of War Information, specifically its Psychological Warfare Division. The senior Saltzman had never been forthright with his children about how he spent his war.
"SEAN AND I JUST FELL INTO OUR NATURAL SENSUALITY WITHOUT ANY RUMPYPUMPY," SAYS SHIRLEY EATON.

"I'm reading these letters of Robert E. Sherwood, the O.W.I.'s director of overseas operations, about my father," Hilary says. "The countries he was to visit overseas: 'Confidential.' Nature of business: 'Confidential war mission for O.W.I.' I'm stunned. It just blew me away that, finally, I understood what my father had done in the war. Finally, I understood his fascination with the spy genre of films." (In the '60s, Saltzman also produced a trilogy of films starring Michael Caine as Len Deighton's spy Harry Palmer, based on the Deighton novels The Ipcress File, Funeral in Berlin, and Billion Dollar Brain) One of Sherwood's unredacted letters, from 1943, informs G. Howland Shaw, assistant secretary of state, that "Mr. Saltzman will be assigned to the North African theater of war to serve on the staff of Mr. C.D. Jackson." Jackson was a noted psychologicalwarfare expert and propaganda mastermind who was then working for the O.S.S. and later served as a Cold War adviser to President Dwight Eisenhower. His base, Algiers, to which Saltzman was sent, was also one of Fleming's wartime destinations.

Hilary Saltzman and her brother, Steven, have yet to turn up evidence that their father and Fleming met before 1961; it's possible, even probable, that they did not. But Hilary posits that "because they had a similar background during the war, which was in confidential missions, they had a mutual understanding. Even though they couldn't publicize it, I really think Ian felt that this series was safe in my father's hands."

Yet by mid-1961 the Bond option was about to slip through Saltzman's fingers: He was five months into his six-month option and hadn't put together any backing. By happenstance, Cubby Broccoli was working with a screenwriter, Wolf Mankowitz, who not only knew Saltzman but was aware that he held the Bond option. Broccoli wasn't pleased with the script for an Arabian Nights-thcmcd movie that Mankowitz had pressed upon him, and when Mankowitz asked Broccoli what he'd rather be producing, Broccoli brought up his long-held desire to make films of Fleming's books. Mankowitz agreed to introduce Broccoli to Saltzman. Though Broccoli, having just shed his old partner, Irving Allen, hoped to buy the option in its entirety, Saltzman insisted on maintaining his piece of the action—and, in fact, had already drawn up a document for Broccoli to sign, affirming that "you and I have mutually agreed that we shall equally share" the film rights to all the Bond books save Casino Royale. And so, in June 1961, was born what Guy Hamilton calls "a wonderful double act": Broccoli, affable and teddy-bearish, serving as a tempering counterpoint to the volatile and argumentative Saltzman. They named their venture Eon Productions.

Broccoli was born in 1909 to an Italian-immigrant family from Calabria. His father, Giovanni Broccoli, and great-uncle Pasquale de Cicco were Long Island truck farmers who sold their goods in New York City and were actually instrumental in popularizing the vegetable broccoli in the United States. Notwithstanding his humble family roots, Cubby was better connected than Saltzman. In the '30s, through his sharpie cousin Pat de Cicco, Pasquale's son, a Hollywood playboy and the first husband of Gloria Vanderbilt, he had gained a toehold in the film industry, landing an assistant job on a Howard Hawks picture and later becoming close to Alan Ladd, the matinee-idol star of Shane and The Great Gatsby.

Taking advantage of the same tax breaks that had lured Saltzman to England, Broccoli and Allen had founded a British company, Warwick Films, that made its mark in the '50s with such war and adventure pictures as Paratrooper, Hell Below Zero, and The Cockleshell Heroes, the first two starring Ladd. In 1961, Broccoli worked his connections to secure a meeting in New York with Arthur Krim, the head of United Artists. Krim agreed to a budget of just over a million dollars for a James Bond movie. At last, a deal had been done.

Broccoli and Saltzman were keen to begin with the latest Bond novel, Thunderbolt. But in light of Kevin McClory's pending lawsuit, they opted instead for Fleming's sixth book, Doctor No, from 1958, which offered both a cinematically picturesque Jamaican setting and a sinister Eurasian villain who, on his private Caribbean island, Crab Key, plotted to sabotage U.S. rocket launches from Cape Canaveral—a story line that presciently anticipated the Cuban missile crisis, which unfolded the very month that Dr. No (as the film version was titled) was released in Britain. To ensure that things would run smoothly, Broccoli brought in a pair of trusted veterans from his Warwick days, the British director Terence Young and the American screenwriter Richard Maibaum. Maibaum was paired with Wolf Mankowitz to come up with a script.

Young, like Fleming, was a tall, rakish character of privileged background: educated at Cambridge, a tank commander in the Irish Guards during World War II. Maibaum, a native of the Bronx and frequent collaborator with Ladd, served in the war as director of the U.S. Army's Combat Films Division, handling footage both for classified use and for dissemination to the public through newsreels. The first screenplay he wrote after the war was for Ladd's film O.S.S.: a 1946 dramatization of the wartime work of the Office of Strategic Services that featured such proto-Bond touches as a clever espionage gadget (a Minox mini-camera) and a comely lady spy (Geraldine Fitzgerald).

In Young, Maibaum, and Saltzman, the Bond-movie team had a group of World War II vets who, like Fleming, were well versed in matters of military intelligence and would bring a level of verite and nuance to what were otherwise playfully escapist entertainments. In Broccoli, who did his wartime bit as an ensign in the navy and a wrangler of Hollywood talent for morale-boosting shows for the troops, the Bond pictures had their great showman and salesman.

Fleming's books are at once grittier and more preposterous than the Bond movies. His Bond registers fear and panic and has hangovers. But he's also something of a bizarre, half-mad sociopath, at times evoking Patrick Bateman, the vain, self-assured brand-name dropper of Bret Easton Ellis's American Psycho, and Jean des Esseintes, the debauched hyper-aesthete of J.K. Huysmans's A Rebours. Here is how Fleming, through Bond's eyes, rather creepily describes Vesper Lynd, the first Bond girl (in print, anyway), in Casino Royale: "Her medium-length dress was of grey soie sauvage with a square-cut bodice, lasciviously tight across her fine breasts. The skirt was closely pleated and flowered down from a narrow, but not a thin, waist. She wore a three-inch, handstitched black belt." In Goldfinger the novel, Bond, while tracking the villain through France, stops in Orleans—a place he dislikes, "a priest and myth ridden town without gaiety"—and takes in "one of his favourite meals: two oeufs cocotte a la creme, a large sole meuniere (Orleans was close enough to the sea. The fish of the Loire are inclined to be muddy) and an adequate Camembert. He drank a well-iced pint of Rose d'Anjou and had a Hennessy's Three Star with his coffee."

Clearly, the filmmakers were going to have to tamp down the soiesauvage-noting and muddy-fish-despising aspects of the character to make him more sympathetic and relatable to audiences. At the same time, Cinema Bond would have to maintain the man-of-action toughness that warranted his Double-Oh status—his license, as granted by M.I.6, Britain's foreign-intelligence service, to kill. This is why the casting of Connery was a masterstroke. Alone among actors, "Sean was able to suggest that dichotomy," said Maibaum in an interview with the film historian Patrick McGilligan. "Fleming thought David Niven would have made a great James Bond," Maibaum said, "but David Niven wasn't all that physical. Originally, Roger Moore was considered for Bond, you know. Then Cubby saw something in Sean which he thought was what they wanted. They took a gamble with Sean; they would have been much safer with Roger."

There is a phrase used almost universally by those involved in the early Bond films to describe Connery circa 1962: a "rough diamond." He was born in 1930 in Edinburgh to a truckdriver and a charwoman. As a young man he worked a variety of menial jobs in Scotland, including driving a milk truck—a detail that seems to captivate biographers and associates ("He was a blasted milkman!" says Honor Blackman)—before traveling to London to compete in a bodybuilding contest, in which he finished third. When he was 22, he landed his first acting job, an ensemble part in a London production of South Pacific.

Connery's looks and muscular build led to a middling early film career that showcased how attractive he was but little else. Moore, three years his senior, had the better track record and was on the verge of television stardom as the noble thief Simon Templar in The Saint. But Broccoli found Moore, at the time, to be "a shade too pretty" for Bond, and even when Moore finally assumed the role, in 1973's Live and Let Die, his light touch and fundamental lack of menace required a recalibration of the Bond character.

Connery's rough-hewn background served Cinema Bond well; it made him a more plausible creation than Fleming's Bond. Whereas the latter is a roguish posh boy, steeped in the finer things in life, who just happens to be a cold-blooded assassin, the former is not unlike Don Draper as portrayed by Jon Hamm in Mad Men: a mysterious self-creation whose virile good looks opened doors in his young adulthood and who seized upon these openings to learn the ropes as a gentleman, connoisseur, and lover, transforming himself into a convincing but dangerous facsimile of all of the above.

Not that anyone, Broccoli included, had any certainty of how well Connery would come off. Fleming was known to have his doubts, and Young, who had worked with Connery on one of the actor's uninspiring '50s films, Action of the Tiger, made no bones about his feelings when Broccoli told him that Connery had been signed. "Oh, disaster, disaster, disaster!" he said.

But Young overcame his initial misgivings, becoming, in fact, the man most readily credited with shaping Connery's Bond persona. It's a disservice to Connery's acting skills to say that he was simply doing his best Terence Young impression, but "Terence taught Sean, who was very basic in those days, a lot of good manners, and Terence felt himself like a James Bond-like person," says Ken Adam, the production designer on nearly all of the Conneryera Bond movies. Young, who died in 1994, took Connery out to restaurants in Mayfair and introduced him to his bespoke tailor, Anthony Sinclair. While the oft-told tale that Connery acclimated to his new handmade suits by sleeping in them is possibly apocryphal, Sinclair took pride in how his clothes functioned like a second skin on the star. "Any well-made suit," he told an ABC News interviewer in the '60s, "you should be able to take it, roll it into a ball, crush it, stamp on it, sleep in it, and then"—smoothing the narrow, impeccably draped lapels of the Sinclair suit he himself was wearing—"there you are, you're back again, you see?"
r. No's gestation was not without its problems. Sometimes a sentiment prevailed, perhaps as a hedge against failure and ridicule, that the movie was just a bit of nonsense, a B picture. Adam, whose w

items.title: Anthony Boyle and Lola Petticrew Are the Matt and Ben of West Belfast
items.description: Anthony Boyle and Lola Petticrew Are the Matt and Ben of West Belfast
items.author: Lola Petticrew
paragraphs: Anthony Boyle and Lola Petticrew Are the Matt and Ben of West Belfast

Anthony Boyle is on a generational run. Since his Tony-nominated turn as Scorpius Malfoy on Broadway, the West Belfast-born actor has become prestige TV’s go-to young lead, playing a WWII airman in Masters of the Air, John Wilkes Booth in Manhunt, IRA volunteer Brendan Hughes in Say Nothing, and Arthur Guinness in House of Guinness. Now, he transforms completely as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists, the Netflix limited series about the rise and fall of the crypto empire FTX and the volatile relationship at its center. Here, he talks about the role with his friend of 20 years, the actor Lola Petticrew, who has been his collaborator on screen, and who helps him run lines off it.
SATURDAY 1PM NOVEMBER 7, 2026 BELFAST
LOLA PETTICREW: We always knew this day would come and I’d be interviewing you.
ANTHONY BOYLE: Yeah, only I thought it would be me in a witness stand and you as a judge. So it’s good that it’s for an interview.
PETTICREW: [Laughs] We’ve been friends for 20 years on the dot. Does that make you sick to your stomach?
BOYLE: Jesus Christ. Is that true?
PETTICREW: Yeah. I’m 31 this year.
BOYLE: We’re old. 20 years is a long time. There’s been births, deaths, relationships, terrible hair. We’ve been through so much.
PETTICREW: When you say terrible haircuts, are you referencing when I got a crew cut when I was 14?
BOYLE: I’m thinking of that crew cut that was more of a bowl cut.
PETTICREW: [Laughs] Yeah. So I just want you to talk about our friendship a bit and say nice things about me, maybe for two minutes just to get into it.
BOYLE: Well, I think you’re my favorite actor to work with, my favorite actor to watch.
BOYLE: You got your nails done?
PETTICREW: Yeah, do you want to see them?
BOYLE: What’s that, a little Christmas sparkle we got going on there?
PETTICREW: Yeah. I also got my toes done.
BOYLE: Get the fucking toes out. Nice big black toe. Happy days. Do you want to say nice things about me for a couple of minutes?
PETTICREW: That’s what I’m about to do if you’d let me do my job. You’ve asked me to do this as if I don’t have enough on my plate.
PETTICREW: So you claim to be responsible for my career and we joke about it a lot, but that’s probably quite true if we were being honest.
BOYLE: Thank god this is going to be in print.

PETTICREW: I never would’ve got into drama school if it wasn’t for you because I actually just didn’t apply. And watching you actually go for it was the thing that made me actually go for it. So it’s been really lovely to have someone who’s like family to navigate everything with. There are not a lot of people that get to do that except for Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. So my question is, are we the Matt Damon and Ben Affleck of West Belfast? And if so, who’s Matt and who’s Ben?
BOYLE: I actually think we’re the Ant and Dec of West Belfast, maybe even Jedward. But if we’re going for Matt and Ben, I think…
PETTICREW: I know what I think.
PETTICREW: You’re Matt and I’m Ben.
BOYLE: Why do you think that?
PETTICREW: Because I too love—

PETTICREW: I too love J.Lo. I’m messy, because let’s be serious, Ben is a messy bitch, and I love looking sad and smoking and drinking the Dunkin Donuts coffee. And you’re Matt. You’re the movie star, bro.
BOYLE: Look, I’ll take Matt Damon. I think the Dunkin Donuts and cigarettes and looking sad is definitely your forte, and I’ll take Matt and run with it and be very proud to do so.
PETTICREW: Okay, so I want to talk about The Altruists. My first question is, did you know what altruists meant when you were auditioning or did you have to look?

BOYLE: No. I had to Google it and then I had to Google how to pronounce it. My mom said to me, “What the fuck does altruist mean? You should have just called it Crypto King.” Look, this interview is now a petition to change the name of The Altruists to Crypto King, and they’ll give my mom a bit of the cut. Did you know what altruists meant?
PETTICREW: Yes. So your mom is going to get a cut if we change the name to Crypto King. Do you think that I should get at least 5 percent for helping you with your audition?

BOYLE: Yes, I actually do. Although, do you think I should get 5 percent of all your income for getting you into drama school, getting you an agent, giving you inspiration, showing you what love truly is, showing you what friendship truly means?
PETTICREW: I’m not going to fight that.
BOYLE: Then yes, everyone’s getting paid.
PETTICREW: Everyone’s getting paid.
BOYLE: I can’t believe you’ve actually written questions down. I thought we were just going to talk shit.
PETTICREW: I think I thought if we talked shit, we would go way off, and I thought somebody had to steer the ship.
BOYLE: I will be your shipmate, you will be my captain.

PETTICREW: Great. So when we were shooting I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, you were auditioning for this role and I was helping with your lines, and I therefore was privy to the voice and the accent very early on. Was that something that immediately made you feel like when you dropped into the voice, you had a better hold on this guy?

BOYLE: Yeah, when you’re playing such a big character like this, you see all the YouTube clips and you see all these videos about him and immediately the first thing you start doing is a sort of impression, and then you get a little bit closer to it, and the voice really helps with someone like this because he’s so nervous. It’s two octaves higher than me. It sounds like I’m on fucking helium and he stutters a lot. I feel like he’s got a hundred computer tabs open at once and then when he clicks off one, five come up. So that’s reflected in the way he speaks. He’s going forward, going back, going back, going forward. He also has a Californian no and a Silibant S, those kids that have spent too long on a computer and they speak like this. It’s easy to drop into that and that then informs your physicality and your psyche too.
PETTICREW: It is also probably the only time you have played someone who isn’t conventionally hot. Do you want to speak on that as a conventionally hot guy?
BOYLE: I don’t think I’m conventionally hot.
PETTICREW: I think TikTok begs to differ.
BOYLE: I don’t think Arthur Guinness was conventionally hot.
PETTICREW: Okay. Maybe take out the word conventionally, it’s the first time you’re playing a character without being hot.
BOYLE: Look, beauty is in the eye of the beholder. To be honest, Lola, when you see the rest of the show, there’s something to him.

PETTICREW: Okay. This is not the first time that you’ve played a real person. Did this differ from playing somebody like Brendan Hughes [in Say Nothing] and maybe anxiety or nervousness that you had for portraying a real person?

BOYLE: I’ve played more real people than fictional people. I felt more nervous playing Brendan Hughes because he’s such a huge figure where we live in West Belfast. And because of the subject matter of Say Nothing, which we did together, that made me feel nervous because I wanted to get it right. Whereas this with Sam Bankman-Fried, I didn’t feel that much pressure. I don’t know why, I just thought it was really fun. The script was just really fun, the showrunner was really fun, the director was really fun, Julia [Garner] was really fun. I was like, “Oh, this is just a laugh.”

PETTICREW: Yeah, I remember when you were auditioning for it you were just so excited about the writing. It’s really nice because sometimes when you have an immediate excitement, that doesn’t always last the whole way through, but it seems like it has for you in this.
BOYLE: Yeah. And thank you for bringing up that you helped me with the audition again.
PETTICREW: I just want to make sure people realize that it’s really a team effort when it comes to you and I.
BOYLE: And me helping you with the Furious audition and with your Say Nothing audition.
BOYLE: Let’s talk about Furious, winning all the best reviews in the world and everyone’s saying that you’re the best actor ever. How does that feel?
PETTICREW: Save it for when you interview me for Interview.
PETTICREW: What was it like working with Julia Garner?

BOYLE: Julia is just phenomenal, an incredible artist, an amazing human being. She’s been creating these iconic characters for 10 years and everything’s just so different. She completely transforms and she’s so inventive, so free, but can be so intense. She’s like an athlete or something.
PETTICREW: And you shot it in Vancouver?
PETTICREW: How was Vancouver?
BOYLE: Vancouver is great craic. It’s class, a lot of Irish bars, and loads of Irish people. I didn’t really get much time off to explore because I was filming flat out, but I love Vancouver.

PETTICREW: I remember we found out that you were going to be filming in Vancouver and I was going to be filming in New York, and we thought we were going to be so close to each other that we could just hop across and see each other all the time, and it turns out they’re on two opposite ends.
BOYLE: Geography outside of Belfast and Derry, I’m not really great on, but hey, we got a couple FaceTimes in. It’s all good. What was it like working with Emmy Rossum?
PETTICREW: I’m going to need you to save it for when you interview me for Interview. Stop wasting the magic.
BOYLE: Precious time. Okay, go ahead.
PETTICREW: So I’m going to see you tonight.
BOYLE: Where are you? Give me your exact home address. Let’s dox you in the interview.
PETTICREW: I’m seeing you tonight because I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is closing the Belfast Film Festival.
BOYLE: So exciting. What a long title.
PETTICREW: It’s the longest title in the world, and I’d like people to know that Anthony and I petitioned to change it. Maybe we should call your mom.
BOYLE: It’s a long title and no one’s got it right. People keep saying, “I’m going to see your film, The Building’s on Fire and It’s Raining.”
PETTICREW: Doing I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning was the third time that we’ve worked together. Talk to me a bit about I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, and what drew you to that project?

BOYLE: Well, Clio [Barnard] and Enda [Walsh] wrote me a letter saying that they would love me to do it. Enda was one of my favorite playwrights, and has written some of my favorite films like Hunger. So getting that letter, it’s just a real pinch me moment. Clio was one of the best filmmakers working in England, I think. As soon as I started reading it, I just loved it. I loved the characters, I loved the world, and I was like, “I feel like I could do this role justice and be of service to their vision.”

PETTICREW: It very much felt like the type of film that we always wanted to make, and you and I were always the hugest fans of Enda. But then whenever I got the call, obviously, to ask me to read for it, I couldn’t quite believe that it was going to be Enda, Clio, and then yourself. And even though Say Nothing is set in Belfast and I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is set in Birmingham, it still felt really close to our community.

BOYLE: It’s funny, doing a role like I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, I didn’t have to do any research. Me and you just hung out in the community and got it immediately because it didn’t feel like a world away. Whereas when I’m doing House of Guinness or something, it feels like an anthropological study of who these people are who grew up in private schools. And then adding the element of you playing my wife in it was like I don’t really have to act in a way. Again, we’ve been friends for 20 years, so that means we’ve had ups and downs like in any friendship, and we’ve seen each other go through so much in our lives. I want to be doing a film with you when I’m 50, and I hope we will. That would be a great creative life.
PETTICREW: Yeah, I think there’s an inherent safety there. We have so much to fall back on that nothing that we do in a scene is ever going to be a lie.

PETTICREW: You have that ability that not a lot of actors have, which is that you can play roles that are very close to yourself and also really far from yourself. People are usually only good at one of those, and you have managed to make a career of being able to bounce between both. That’s class. And second of all, is there one of them that feels more exciting for you or more comfortable for you?
BOYLE: It’s so embarrassing to get a compliment from you for some reason. I don’t know why. I’m hiding behind my jumper like, “oh god.” What was the question? Which sort of work do I prefer?
PETTICREW: Not even that you prefer. Is there one that feels more comfortable? More exciting?

BOYLE: Honestly, it always feels like I want to do the opposite of what I’ve just done. I remember I’d done Say Nothing, which felt like an extension of me and everyone I’ve met who can tell a story in a bar in Belfast. And then doing House of Guinness immediately after, which is more of a character piece. It’s a completely different voice and body and psychology. So I guess I want to just do the opposite of what I’ve just done, and right now I’m doing a piece that was written for me and it’s me essentially, and I can’t wait to do a big character piece again. I really like when I get sent something and I’m like, “How the fuck am I going to do this? This is not me at all. How do I get into this?” That’s what really excites me.

PETTICREW: Okay. I would like to end the interview by having you describe to the people of Interview what Goodfellas is, because that’s where I’m going to meet you tonight before we go to the Belfast Film Festival.

BOYLE: Goodfellas is an amazing pizza place in West Belfast where you can bring your own beer. So Lola and I’ll be sat there with our big bottle of Glen’s Vodka on the table. Our mate CJ will bring some Buckfast [Tonic Wine] and we’re going to have some lovely pizza and we’re going to get on a party bus and go to the Belfast Film Festival.
PETTICREW: Can I ask what your Goodfellas order is?

BOYLE: Last night I went for pizza with my family and there was a thing on the menu called a piccante pizza and it was really spicy chicken salami. I’m going to see if I can get something similar tonight. I’ve had pizza three days in a row.
PETTICREW: Well, if you’re looking for a spicy pizza in Goodfellas, it’s going to be a Hot Sicilian.
BOYLE: Okay, then I’ll have a Hot Sicilian this evening.
PETTICREW: Well, I’m going to get a Hot Sicilian. I’m going to get half a pizza, get half Hot Sicilian, and then probably some of the garlic potatoes.
BOYLE: Well, I’ll have to join you on that. And if anyone in America is reading this and finds themself in Ireland, go to Goodfellas.
PETTICREW: Lovely people, lovely craic, great pizza.
BOYLE: I’m actually really excited, Lola, and I think it’s going to be great to screen it. How many people do you have coming? I have 700 people.
PETTICREW: I think your daddy has invited basically all of West Belfast.
BOYLE: Yeah, my dad’s invited everyone he’s ever met, so that’ll be a lot of fun.
PETTICREW: Well, thank you very much for talking to me. I’m going to go and get a shower, shave my legs, and get myself ready to see you in about two hours.
PETTICREW: I love you. Bye.
