items.title: These Espresso Machine Deals Give You Time to Practice Before Thanksgiving
items.description: Thanksgiving is coming, and so, possibly, is an audience. If you want to show your in-laws you know how to entertain in style with a postprandial espresso or cappuccino, don’t be fiddling with steam wands and the owner’s manual while Uncle Bob stands nearby an
items.author: Kat Merck
paragraphs: Thanksgiving is coming, and so, possibly, is an audience. If you want to show your in-laws you know how to entertain in style with a postprandial espresso or cappuccino, don’t be fiddling with steam wands and the owner’s manual while Uncle Bob stands nearby and offers his opinions (at full volume).

Luckily, there are plenty of early Black Friday espresso machine deals happening right now. If you take advantage, it will make you look smart both by not paying full price and by knowing how to pull a perfect shot, having had three weeks of practice.

Each deal below is on a machine a WIRED reviewer has tested—including a Breville that one colleague has used happily for seven years—and personally recommends. For more savings, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals, as well as early deals at Amazon and Home Depot.
Updated November 16: I’ve removed expired deals and added new deals on De’Longhi, Ninja, Nespresso, and Atlas Coffee Club.
Save $300 on a Stylish Meraki

This sleek, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing,” according to former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person, and it has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the 2nd Gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a new portafilter.

Formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried, with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos, and I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.
A Nespresso Machine for Under $100

The Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso, and the Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and new finishes, including this white one that’s on sale. (There’s also matte black-and-gold and a sort of gunmetal gray, but those are not as heavily discounted.)
Save $250 on a Slim-Profile De’Longhi

We appreciated this semiautomatic’s slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. The cold-brew setting is more of a gimmick than a way to make actual cold brew, and some design choices are a little quirky, but it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.
Score $100 off Ninja Luxe Cafe Premiere

Ninja sometimes has a reputation for doing too much, but this semiautomatic we liked is a beginner-friendly option that pulls some solid shots. It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, it also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for that alone. (Note the sale is on the “Gunmetal” color only.)
If You’d Rather Give Coffee

Maybe you or your recipient already has an espresso machine; in that case, they’ll need some quality beans. Our favorite coffee subscription, Atlas Coffee Club, has a new gift option on offer for Black Friday, which is a quarterly subscription of three bags of unique, globally sourced coffee every three months for $59. You can choose any roast you want, including espresso roast and even Nespresso pods. If you’d rather buy an ongoing subscription for yourself, your first bag is free with Atlas’ Black Friday sale.

items.title: Save $120 on the Mac Mini Ahead of Black Friday
items.description: All configurations of the Mac Mini are on sale today on Amazon, starting at $779 for the base M6 model. That's $120 off the full retail price that Apple charges.
items.author: Luke Larsen
paragraphs: All configurations of the Mac Mini are on sale today on Amazon, starting at $779 for the base M6 model. That's $120 off the full retail price that Apple charges.

For nearly half of this year, the Mac Mini was unavailable to buy; it was either sold out at retailers or subject to wait times that stretched up to three months long. But at the end of August, Apple launched a new model, which not only introduced the M6 (or M5 Pro) chip inside, but also restocked the Mac Mini so that you can actually just go out and buy one.

The sharp escalation in demand even took Apple by surprise, by its own admission. AI enthusiasts were buying these up for the quick and simple access to an always-on computer with enough memory to run models locally in an affordable package.

The M6 comes with 16 GB of RAM, which is barely enough to run some smaller models. Amazon also sells a 24-GB model (with 512 GB of storage) for $1,150. If you want to bump up the storage capability to 32 GB, you'll have to buy the machine directly from Apple. Either way, the extra storage will make your Mini quite a bit more expensive than the base model, but it's still $150 off the retail price. Best Buy is also selling the previous-gen M4 model for $649 if you're really trying to save cash—or just need a basic computer for work. The M6 does offer a substantial upgrade to GPU performance over the M4, though, so if you're planning to do any on-device AI work, it's worth the extra $120.

This isn't the lowest price I've seen the Mac Mini reach, but it's close. For one day in October, it dropped by an extra $10. I can't say for sure whether we'll see an additional price decrease during Black Friday. My gut says no, but if you're worried about it, you might want to put it in your shopping cart and wait before clicking Buy.
The best deal in the Mac world heading into Black Friday, however, is the M5 MacBook Air. It's currently $1,099, and that still gets you 16 GB of unified memory.

Updated November 14: I added new products on sale from Nothing, CMF, and Shokz, and removed products no longer on sale from Bose, Google, and Beats.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds not only for anyone with an iPhone—but also for anyone who wants to keep things simple. They sound great and have some of the best active-noise-canceling (ANC) and transparency modes on the market. They also seamlessly sync with all of your Apple devices. While 20 percent off isn't the best price I've seen for them, it's still a solid discount.

The Nothing Ear (3a) are one of our favorite pairs of earbuds under $100, and 30 percent off is the biggest discount I've ever seen for them so far. They have a semi-transparent design and bold colors that stand out from the crowd (particularly the yellow version). While the automated noise-canceling isn't the best, it's hard to fault them at this new low price.

The Shokz OpenFit open-ear headphones were one of my favorites before the newer clip-on open-earbud design started becoming more popular. This is the lowest price I've ever seen the Shokz model go for. They wrap around the top and back of your ear and rest there, leaving your inner ear clear to hear the outside world around you. The OpenFit 2+ have great sound quality (for open-ear headphones, that is), long battery life, and wireless charging support.
Best Over-Ear Headphone Deals

The more premium XM6 and the newly revived, cheaper XM4C have effectively replaced the Sony WH-1000XM5. But I am still seeing the blue colorway of these excellent headphones at the lowest price I've clocked for these sunsetting cans. When they launched in 2022, they were our top pick for over-ear headphones. They remain excellent and far outperform other options at this limited price.

The Nothing Headphone (1) are a home run in looks and sound, and they are at their lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday. They’re solid noise cancelers with a bold, transparent design on the ear cups that's somehow techy, retro, and futuristic-looking. Among their best features are the on-ear controls, namely the clicky wheel that adjusts volume and the flat rocker paddle that you can push back and forth to move to the previous track or skip ahead, respectively.
The budget Nothing Headphone (a) and premium Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are also on sale, but the Headphone (1) is the most appealing deal in my view.

Sony recently launched the WH-CN730N to replace these headphones, hence the rock-bottom price of 50 percent off. While these headphones can't compete with most specs of more premium options on this list, they're ultra-lightweight at just 192 grams. That and 35 hours of battery life with ANC on is nothing to scoff at.

Want to spend even less on headphones? CMF is Nothing's sub-brand focused on stylish designs at a lower price point, and this is the best deal I've seen on its Headphone Pro over-ear cans. Frankly, $49 is a steal for these headphones, considering they are comfortable, sound surprisingly good, and have noise canceling and long battery life.

Want the best ANC over-ear headphones? Look no further than the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). They are the benchmark to which I compare other ANC headphones. Plus, they are comfortable, premium, and sound excellent.

My top over-ear headphone pick, the best-in-class Sony WH-1000XM6 is matching the lowest price I've seen. These headphones are amazing across the board, with their high comfort, superior sound quality, and great noise-canceling capability.

AirPods Max 2 are excellent over-ear headphones for Apple fans, but the $550 sticker price is frankly absurd. Thankfully, they are almost always a little bit on sale, including now. This is far from the best deal I've seen on these headphones, and I do expect the price to dip further during Black Friday sales events, so I would add them to my cart and wait to pull the trigger.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI loves cheating
items.description: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthr
items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”
Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

items.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
items.description: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
items.author: Antonio Regalado
paragraphs: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

items.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
items.description: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
items.description: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up th
items.author: Amit Katwala
paragraphs: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack.

You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey. You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.title: The Joys of Wearing Your Mother’s Clothes
items.description: At the peak of quiet luxury and capsule wardrobes, a splash of vibrant color disrupted the endless beige void my TikTok algorithm had become. That color was Texas-based designer Carla Rockmore, whose diaphanous silhouettes, endless bangles, and Carrie Bradshaw
items.author: Rose Dommu
paragraphs: At the peak of quiet luxury and capsule wardrobes, a splash of vibrant color disrupted the endless beige void my TikTok algorithm had become. That color was Texas-based designer Carla Rockmore, whose diaphanous silhouettes, endless bangles, and Carrie Bradshaw curls captivated me. Rockmore now has more than 2 million followers across TikTok and Instagram as well as her own line of clothing sold on QVC.

While Rockmore’s signature style and bubbly disposition were what first intrigued me, her relationship with her daughter, Ivy, made me a die-hard fan. Early into her content career, Rockmore shared that her daughter had begun transitioning, and she started helping Ivy develop her fully embodied sense of style. Now a 22-year-old writer living in New York City, Ivy has become a fixture in Rockmore’s videos whenever she makes the trip back to Texas.

Asked to describe her mother’s style, Ivy calls it eccentric and colorful with a sense of history. “Everything she wears represents a different part of each era she has created for herself,” she says. Carla, meanwhile, finds her daughter’s style curious and effervescent: “It’s an exploration. It’s explorative. You’re just starting. I see a big change this year compared to last year, even, and a lot more confidence in her choices and her conviction.”

“If she’s saying ‘conviction’ for me, then I’m saying ‘devotion’ for her,” Ivy responds. That devotion is evident in their easy, warm banter as the three of us chat about their personal influences, clothing’s role in their relationship, and the ever-important distinction between style and fashion.
I want to know who the people were, real or fictional, who helped inform your sense of style?

Ivy Rockmore: Claire Danes in My So-Called Life was a big inspiration. And Mommy, you’ll be happy to know I’m in a video-production class, and for my final project, I used the Shalom Harlow McQueen video and the class loved it.

Carla Rockmore: My mother, she’s the first one. She’s the most iconic at the end of the day. She was never, ever afraid of standing apart but did it in such a classy way in the ’70s. That’s when she got a divorce and she was free. So 36 years old and in the ’70s, I mean, come on. I’m also a child of the ’80s into the ’90s, so there’s no way Annie Lennox isn’t in there. There’s no way Madonna isn’t in there, and the Cranberries. For me at that time, it was … There was grunge and there was … It’s called emo now, emu? What is it?
Emo, but let’s say emu. I like that better.
Carla: Then I’ve always been a character dresser, so Cher plus Edie Sedgwick from the Factory.

Ivy: I have two addendums. The first is, we did an interview with a Texas radio station four years ago when I was just transitioning, and we were asked the same question: Who are your style inspos? I said Jules from Euphoria. I look back at that and completely, like, I feel utter fascination that my 18-year-old self was so obsessed with this character and wanted to emulate her so badly. Now, my mom just watched the show, and she understands it finally in the past two months. I don’t dress like Jules anymore. I’m a woman. I’m 22 now. I’m a grown girl, and I don’t wear pleated miniskirts anymore, but she was the first I tried to copy. Before her, it would be silly for me not to say you, Mom, because my neurons were trained as a child in that red chair back there, seated, watching you try on everything. That was where I first understood the playground of clothing.

Carla: You had a language really early for it. It’s very funny, but we were on our way to the synagogue once with another family; a boy was with Ivy in the back seat. We all rolled out of the car, and Ivy said, “Don’t forget your clutch.” He said, “How do you even know that word?” I’ll never forget.
Ivy, how did you discover your personal style, specifically through transitioning, and what part did your mom play in that development?

Ivy: Four years in, it’s only starting. But now that I have the conviction, it has been the most fun thing in the world. But my mom is literally a godlike shepherd. Every Christmas break, Thanksgiving break, summer break, I’ll come home and there are three new pants, three skirts, three shirts on the bed for me to try on. There’s stuff she has pulled from her archives. Thank God I came out when I did because she has these racks of clothes that have been waiting. Getting dressed would not feel as playful without my mom in my life. It’s no longer about trying to dress super-femme; it’s about how I can be more like her in the way she approaches style. Not just the appearance of the clothes but layering, proportion — I’ve learned to think about that in ways I didn’t before.
Carla: I see the peeling away of the need to look femme and the interest in wrapping herself in the things that speak to her. She’s walking other paths of style and becoming a little more eclectic.

My grandma passed away this summer, and I picked a couple of pieces from her closet. Now, when I wear them, I feel surrounded by her and I feel her energy and confidence. Ivy, what is it like to wear not only your mom’s clothes but things she picked for you to wear?

Ivy: I’m sorry for your loss. I’m very close with my bubby. She’s my mom’s mom. She’s my best friend besides my mom. Today, I wore my mother’s leopard-print skirt and everyone’s like, “Where’d you get this? Where’d you get this?” And I was like, “My mom.” I wasn’t going to be like, “And she made it,” but it feels really freaking good knowing that, too, because there’s a sense of genealogy that lives in the piece. It feels like I am supposed to be wearing this. This piece was created in some way for me to be able to express myself or feel more like the form I’m now taking up.
Carla, on the flip side, what’s it like to see Ivy wearing something of yours or something you’ve picked out?

Carla: In the beginning, when she first started transitioning, it was very purposeful to bring her into the closet because it was not an easy time for her. In the first few weeks, we did a Get Ready With Me because it was super-important for me to show her the joy in it as a woman, but also I just wanted her to be okay. Now, when I see her wearing a piece of mine from the ’90s, first of all, I want to kill her because she always looks ten times better. It doesn’t matter what. I mean, my Rick Owens leather drawstring sleeveless jacket she got this season: She put it on and it looked so good I had to give it to her. It reminds me of when I bought it and what was going on in my life.
What are both of your personal philosophies about getting dressed every day or getting dressed for an occasion?

Ivy: If there’s an occasion, she makes sure I am dressed with a capital D. She’ll make me come two weeks in advance to show her what I’m wearing, and it’s amazing because she’ll give me a new bag, belt, and bracelet, and she’ll keep the core of what I was trying to do but it’ll look 20 million times better. She’s bad at math in the way I’m bad at math, but she’s very good at the math of clothes. There’s an equation you learn through repetition, and I think you repeat and you repeat and you repeat and you revise and you find your pattern. She’s good at that.

Carla: Everybody is born with something that is so joyful that they create. I don’t care if it’s a cupcake, an article, a painting, or a book. A plumber, maybe he puts together his tools in his truck in a way that makes sense for him, and that’s a creation. My clothing is a canvas, and my accessories are my paint and color. If you’re writing a poem, you’re not just throwing it out there, you think about the next line based on your thought process and the last line and where you want to go. I see Ivy doing that in her own passion, which is her writing. She doesn’t need to sit and curate her look for 20 minutes before she leaves the house because she’s already fulfilled. Her creative energy is ignited elsewhere. I just happen to be a one-trick pony.
Ivy: You have a lot of tricks up your sleeve — many, many a trick.
Is the difference between style and fashion important to you?

Carla: I’d argue you’re born with style. It’s a practice, and you hone in through that practice and fine-tune it. Fashion is what comes down the runway, and that’s where trends are born. When you have style, you can incorporate fashion into your wardrobe and still look like you. You still feel, as you walk through your day, very comfortable. When you’re looking only at fashion, there will be times for sure when you feel uncomfortable because maybe it doesn’t speak to your inner self.
Ivy: I wonder if we can make a Venn diagram with style and fashion, and in the middle is glamour because that’s what I think about when I think of my mom.
Carla: The pressure, Ivy, glamour!
What specific piece, look, or silhouette makes you feel the most yourself?

Carla: It’s more silhouette. For me, it’s long. It used to be micromini. I still have good legs, but it doesn’t matter. It’s not about the good legs; it’s about how the clothes make me feel, and I love something bottom-heavy. I gravitate toward the triangle silhouette — whether it’s a palazzo pant, a wider-leg pant with a heavy boot or a heavy shoe, or an A-line or maxi skirt — something a little heavier on the bottom with something shrunken on top. That’s where I feel most comfortable. On occasion, I’ll flip my triangle, but it has to be specific.

Ivy: I’m vice versa. I mean, I do love the maxi skirt. I’ve worn a maxi skirt the past three days. But when I’m going somewhere, I want to be in that black micromini dress, and I want to wear a statement belt with it.
Carla: As you should. When I used to go out, my father would say on my way out, “Is that a skirt or a belt?”
If you could raid the closet of anyone on earth, living or dead, who would it be?
Ivy: Answer’s easy, I would choose my mom.
To be fair, I would also choose your mom.
Carla: Definitely Iris Apfel. Cate Blanchett has perfect taste.
What advice do you have for anyone out there trying to develop their personal style?

Carla: Don’t start with that capsule wardrobe where you must have a black turtleneck sweater, trench coat, slim pants, and a loafer. You will not find your personal style. You need to listen to your gut, be adventurous, and be okay with making mistakes. Do you know how many mistakes I’ve made? Do you know how many photos of myself I look at and say, What the French was I wearing? Who let me out of the house? There were many times when I left the house feeling very uncomfortable, but that’s okay because then I knew not to repeat that thing. Don’t buy expensive things when you’re experimenting. Once you find something that suits you and you’ve worn the silhouette a number of times, then invest in one piece you think will last. Take advantage of lower prices in cool little markets, interesting artisanal shops, or maybe a smidgen of them all. I also give every person permission to buy the same thing over and over in every iteration and combination of fabric and color if it suits you because that means you’re starting. That’s a bread crumb of your personal style.

Ivy: Mine is to be the girl you wish to see in the world. If I’m on the subway, I’m looking around to gather what other people are wearing. But I can be the girl I would admire, and that’s pretty much all it is for me. To be more niche, be the doll you wish to see in the world. Inside and out.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: What Cut Editors Are Gifting This Holiday Season
items.description: ’Tis the season for our annual Cut editors’ picks. It’s your chance to see what people who test products and stay in the know for a living are actually gifting our loved ones this holiday season. We know what’s worth it (and what you can skip), and we’re shari
items.author: The Editors
paragraphs: ’Tis the season for our annual Cut editors’ picks. It’s your chance to see what people who test products and stay in the know for a living are actually gifting our loved ones this holiday season. We know what’s worth it (and what you can skip), and we’re sharing all of our recommendations.

Below, you’ll find a wide variety of gifts at every budget for everyone on your list — everything from a museum membership to a Christmas ornament. And if you still need more gift ideas, have no fear: We’ve already rounded up the best gifts for men, wellness gifts, travel gifts, K-beauty gifts, and so much more.
What Cut Editors Are Gifting This Holiday Season
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’m a big fan of J.Press and its sharp tailoring in general, and I think these rugby shirts would be great gifts for anyone in your life who has school spirit. There are the Made in USA triple-stripe shirts, which have a lot of school colors for the Ivies and such, and the regimental-stripe version comes in popular British school colors (London School of Economics, Royal Air Force, etc.). So if you know anyone who will be starting or just started school this fall, or just typically leans into a more preppy vibe, these are great — and the cotton is heavy enough to keep them warm if they layer correctly throughout the cold months. —Brooke Marine, deputy culture editor
New! You can now save this product for later.
New! You can now save this product for later.

This garment-and-shoe-bag set is the sort of gift you can give to someone who you think has everything already, because it’s something you’d never think about needing — until you find yourself packing a more formal outfit for a wedding or business trip and panicking because you don’t have a sturdy garment bag. The material can really take a beating (in the car, in the overhead compartment of an airplane) too. The perfect present for your man, brother, dad — or really anyone in your life who needs to travel a bunch and has a more rugged aesthetic. —B.M.
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the cinephile in your life, this survey of Black cinema by Ashley Clark (who also happens to be the Criterion Collection’s curatorial director) is a must. Clark explores a century of films — some you’ve heard of, many you haven’t — by Black artists across the globe. Get into it. —B.M.
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the art lover-slash-foodie-slash-general appreciator of holiday whimsy, Laila Gohar’s Advent calendar (with illustrations by Joana Avillez) is filled with chocolate goodies for each day of December — but the box, designed to reference the Art Deco style of the luxurious Prince de Galles hotel in Paris, is a treat in and of itself. —B.M.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Admittedly, not the sexiest of gifts. However, I told my family and friends that I’m going the practical route this year, which tends to land better than the “Oh, thanks. Another random trinket!” approach I usually opt for. My sister and her husband are expecting their first baby in the spring (yay!). While they will be receiving a boatload of adorable baby clothes from me — shout-out to Petit Sézane’s newborn-size cardigans — I’m also gifting them a Carepod humidifier to keep in their nursery. It’s small enough to hide in a corner but sleek enough that it’s not an eyesore if it is on display. Only the cleanest, crispest air for my baby nephew! —Emma Childs, fashion news writer
New! You can now save this product for later.

My Tekla towels from 2019 are still going strong. And so are my sheets. So, naturally, all that’s left to add to my home is its blanket. Yes, the price tag is quite hefty. However, knowing how well crafted the brand’s products are (and how cold my new apartment is, even with the heaters blasting), I’ll invest in this. —Bianca Nieves, senior style partnerships editor
New! You can now save this product for later.

Last year, I was gifted this set, and I loved it so much that this year I’m taking notes and gifting it to a friend who loves to host. Both bottles look great on the kitchen counter, and the quality is superb. —B.N.
New! You can now save this product for later.

My mom loves visiting me in NYC because she loves my Jolie shower filter. The one thing she always says is, “I wish it was handheld; then it would be perfect!” Lo and behold, the company has listened to my mom’s recommendation and just launched the handheld version of its beloved showerhead.
New! You can now save this product for later.

My brother has been dropping very obvious hints that he wants a pair of Thursday Cavalier boots. He keeps raving about how much he loves their construction and wants to “buy” a pair in each color, which means please, gift these to me, no matter the colorway! So this year he will be getting a pair. Shocker! —B.N.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I love gifting this every year. The stone makes it extremely convenient for those on your list who only travel with carry-ons, because they never have to worry about it being TSA-friendly. Your friend who loves wellness probably has everything they need but is missing a rich, moisturizing stone they can keep on their bedside table. —B.N.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’m a staunch believer that most clothing does not need to go to the dry cleaners. I want to free my loved ones from the shackles of their monthly dry-cleaning costs, which is why I want to introduce them to detergents specifically formulated to wash silk, wool, cashmere, and other delicate fabrics at home. —Carol Lee, beauty writer
New! You can now save this product for later.

The beauty community holds its breath each fall to see what Hourglass will come up with for its annual face palettes, and this year’s selection is one of my favorites. Not only are the powders beautiful, but the packaging — designed by French jewelry designer Lauren Rubinski — is exquisite. I’m gifting one to myself and one to a relative who collects an Unlocked palette every year. And once I’ve emptied the powder pans, I’m going to pop them out and use the outer shell as a clutch. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I have expensive taste, but so do some of my favorite family members. My aunt, for example, is addicted to Skinmedica products, which are, unfortunately, worth saving up for. She asked for a neck cream, so I’m getting this one. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’m hoping someone gets this for me, to be honest. I’m a white-sheet devotee, but I’ve been itching to mix things up a little. Adding this little coverlet on top (plus these matching shams) would bring just the right amount of coziness to my room. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Even if you’re not an influencer, you’re probably running out of storage on your phone and paying way too much for cloud storage. Sandisk created a MagSafe drive that attaches to the back of the phone so you can directly transfer photos and videos while you’re out and about. Don’t you wish you had this that one time when you were at your favorite artist’s concert and had to panic-delete a bunch of videos before they played your favorite song? The device also comes with a free month of Adobe Creative Cloud Pro for all you creatives out there. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

When I smell Rosie, I smell my sister. We both adore the floral musk, but it’s become a signature scent for my sibling. I can’t think of a more perfect gift for her than a solid version of the perfume, and I love that it’s also a beautiful object she can clip onto her bag. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I don’t believe in Advent calendars. Or I guess I should say that I don’t believe that most of them are worth buying. (Yes, I’m thinking about the Skims accessories Advent calendar right now.) But the ones Glasshouse produces each year are worth giving to the home-scent-obsessed person in my life. There are plenty of full-size and miniature products — including candles, hand washes, bodywashes, and perfumes — to try. And they’re not all holiday-themed scents, so whoever’s lucky enough to receive the calendar will be well stocked for all occasions for a long time — maybe even until next December. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Multiple women in my life are either expecting or postpartum, and much love to all the babies out there, but my first concern is always making sure the mothers are okay. I want them to have everything they need to feel good and cared for pre- and post-birth, and I find that they always appreciate fancy beauty treats that they wouldn’t necessarily buy themselves, like this belly-care duo from Hatch. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Our beauty editor, Asia Milia Ware, influenced me to start using oils to make my body glow for special occasions, and I’ve taught the trick to my friends too. Something else I appreciate about fragranced body oils is how their scent lingers, and Dime finally launched one that features 7 Summers, a fruity, woody gourmand a certain friend of mine loves.—C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Metallic lips are back! I can’t wait to whip them out for the holidays. Celebrity makeup artist Lisa Eldridge created her own, and of course they’re hydrating and long-lasting and make your lips look irresistible. Who needs mistletoe?—C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.
DedCool (maker of some of my favorite musky scents) and Emi Jay (creator of the best claw clips around) partnered to create a gift set any woman I know would be thrilled to receive. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I never know what to give my significant other’s father, but I found a solution early this year that’ll win me brownie points and address the backaches he experiences from standing all day at work. This wrap combines vibration, heat, and red-light therapy to relieve pain, and I can personally confirm that it feels incredible after a long day. —C.L.
New! You can now save this product for later.

This is the perfect special-occasion top or for when you just want to go out for a nice dinner. The draped material is so soft and flattering, and the snap buttons allow you to adjust it and customize how much or how little skin you want to show. I’m a sucker for items of clothing that you can wear in multiple ways; it always feels like a worthwhile investment. —Sofía Mareque, photo editor
New! You can now save this product for later.

For the outdoorsy people in your life who care about being dripped out and warm. Although it’ll break the bank a bit, a good jacket that will last a long time is always worth it, and I’m super-excited to gift this to my boyfriend (who is long overdue to replace the Lands’ End one he’s had for years). —S.M.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Speaking of tops that can be worn in multiple ways, I can wear this one to the office with a colorful tank layered underneath to have a pop of color in the back, or simply turn it around with a cute bralette underneath for a sexier occasion. —S.M.
New! You can now save this product for later.

My mom loves a beauty gift set (she thinks she’s getting several different gifts wrapped into one, and she’s not wrong), and I love gifting them during the holiday season. This limited-edition collaboration comes beautifully packaged in a box inspired by Erdem’s signature romantic florals and features four easy-to-use, natural-looking makeup products from Merit. I know my mom will get so much use out of the balm highlighter, blush, and eye shadow because she can apply them with her fingers for a soft wash of color. —Hanna Flanagan, senior shopping editor

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 19, 2026
items.description: Your patience will be tested today as conflict between the sun and Mars (in Scorpio and Leo, respectively) stirs up problems. Everyone around you will seem keen to show off, so you might feel you need to loudly assert yourself, too. But resist the impulse to g
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Your patience will be tested today as conflict between the sun and Mars (in Scorpio and Leo, respectively) stirs up problems. Everyone around you will seem keen to show off, so you might feel you need to loudly assert yourself, too. But resist the impulse to get needlessly combative. If someone is acting in a way that genuinely deserves a response, then by all means, push back. Otherwise, stepping away from everyone else’s drama, to the extent you can, will serve you well.

If you’re not careful today, you could waste your energy trying to justify yourself to the skeptics in your life. You’ll feel the need to convince everyone your goals aren’t unreasonable or you deserve to feel the way you do. But remind yourself that there will always be people who simply don’t understand you — and while that might not feel good, don’t let it hold you back.

You think of yourself as courageous and principled, and most of the time, you are. But sometimes you’re simply not in the mood to be brave — making a righteous stand is exhausting, and you don’t always feel up to it. If you’re feeling tired or fragile today, try to avoid putting yourself in situations where courage will be required of you. You can’t always control this, of course, but as much as possible, make things easy for yourself right now. There’s no shame in recognizing when you need a break.

Today, you’ll probably have big ideas and energy to spare. You’ll finally feel ready to tackle all the problems that have seemed too intimidating until now. Just be careful not to overestimate your capacity. Even if you feel like you could take on the whole world, it’s a good idea to pace yourself. If you make huge promises and take on too much right away, you’ll quickly burn out. Instead, start slow and gradually ramp up.

You might yearn to break new ground today and take on impressive projects. But there’s a difference between wanting the accolades you’ll get from achieving great things and actually wanting to do the work itself. Before you start any major projects, ask yourself whether you’re actually in the mood to challenge yourself or whether you just want positive attention. If it’s the latter, consider refraining from starting anything new for the time being. It won’t be worth the stress.

You could get the disheartening feeling today that nobody is as excited about your goals as you want them to be. Their support might seem disappointingly lukewarm. But consider the possibility that your expectations are too high: It’s unfair to ask others to be more devoted to your projects than you are. If you’re feeling a lack of enthusiasm right now, the answer isn’t to hope others will pick up the slack. Instead, give yourself time to rest, recharge, and reconnect with your passion and drive.

You sometimes imagine you need to earn the right to rest. But the reality is that if you’re tired, you’re tired. You can tell yourself all you like that you shouldn’t be, but that doesn’t change the fact of the matter. Today, stop worrying about whether you deserve to take a break and let your actual energy levels guide you. Pushing past your limits will only make everything harder in the long run, so take it easy when you need to. You’ll get better results that way.

It often falls to you to be the peacemaker in your social circle. You’re good at bringing people together, making sure gatherings run smoothly, and mediating the conflicts that inevitably arise. But just because you’re skilled at this doesn’t mean it’s effortless. You still have to work at resolving everyone else’s problems, and sometimes you get sick of it. Give yourself permission to take a break today. It’s not your job to ensure everyone else gets along. They have agency, so let them manage their own problems for now.

You care about doing the right thing, but sometimes, it’s challenging. Acting according to your principles is straightforward enough when it costs you nothing, but when it gets riskier, you get cold feet. You might try to justify opting for the path of least resistance. But today, it’s important you do what you think is right, even — maybe especially — if it’s hard. Sticking to your values will make more of a difference than you realize.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You’re already an independent person, but you’ll likely feel even more independent today. You have strong ideas about what you want to accomplish, and you’re not willing to wait around for anyone else to get on board. There’s nothing wrong with working alone, but take care not to isolate yourself too much. The bigger your ambitions, the more support you’ll need along the way. Even if you’re not in the mood to socialize right now, finding one or two people to confide in will make everything less daunting.

Today, remember that just because you are willing to take risks doesn’t mean the people around you are up for it. You might be tempted to brush off their concerns, imagining that they’re being dramatic, but consider the possibility that they have more to lose. You can (and should) be adventurous, but within reason, try to make sure your choices won’t negatively affect those around you.

You sometimes imagine that if you have to compromise to resolve a conflict, that means you’ve failed. You want to get exactly what you want, not some half-baked version of it. While this attitude can sometimes serve you well by encouraging you not to settle for less, today, it’ll only make it impossible for you to get anything done. Don’t be a pushover, but don’t be so stubborn that no progress can be made either. A compromise doesn’t have to mean you’re “losing”; it can also mean everyone is getting something they need.

You aren’t someone who needs to be practical at all times: You understand it’s important to let your imagination roam free, to dream about all the possibilities before you. But today, don’t get too lost in vague fantasies about the future. You’ll be happiest if you feel like you’re making yourself useful, so keep dreaming if you like, but find some tangible tasks to keep yourself busy, too.
