items.title: I'm 35, I Make $258K & I'm Secretly In Love With My Coworker
items.description: A Week In San Francisco, CA On A $258,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In San Francisco, CA On A $258,000 Salary
This week: A manager working in Fintech who makes $258,000 per year and spends some of it on raffle and lottery tickets.

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Location: San Francisco, CA
Joint Income/Financial Setup: No joint income, just me!
Brokerage: $420,000 (every month I contribute $5,000)
401(k) with work: $115,00 (every month I contribute $1,293)
Emergency fund in a high-yield savings account: $50,000
Invested stocks from my company: $12,000
Paycheck Amount (once a month): $11,212 after 401(k) contribution
Housing Costs: $1,855 in rent for a one-bedroom place. I got a GREAT deal in 2021 during the pandemic.
Phone: $0 (I'm still on a family plan with my dad)
PG&E (water covered by landlord): ~$50
YouTube TV: $100 for Nuuly
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes, there was always an expectation that I would go to college. Neither of my parents graduated from college, so I think it was really important to them that I had the opportunity. I never felt pressured exactly, but they definitely made me feel like going to college was just what I was going to do. I don't think I even realized there were other options. Plus, I really liked school, so the idea of getting four more years of it sounded pretty good to me. I graduated in 2013 with a bachelor's degree in political science. My parents paid for most of my college because they had started saving for my education early on. I also received some financial aid in the form of grants. Going to a state school in a city with a relatively low cost of living definitely helped. I was able to graduate without taking on any student debt.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

There weren't a ton of conversations about money growing up, but I was taught some of the most important financial basics. My mom always emphasized the importance of saving. I remember seeing her put money aside throughout the year for our annual vacation and for Christmas. She explained that even saving a little bit each month could eventually add up to a significant amount. When I was in high school, she took me to the bank to open my first checking account and explained how a debit card worked. Then, when I went off to college, she helped me get my first credit card. She told me to only use it for emergencies and, most importantly, to pay off the balance every month. They were relatively simple lessons, but they stuck with me. I know I was fortunate to learn those things early on, and even though we didn't have a lot of conversations about money, she gave me a really solid foundation to build on.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

After graduating from college, I worked at a tanning salon for about a year. I had spent most of college partying and giving very little thought to what would come next, so when I graduated, I had no plan. It was a strange period that felt like a purgatory between being a kid and becoming an adult. I was still living in my college town and still living like I was in college. Eventually, I found a job with more responsibility, which helped me figure out what I wanted to do next and eventually led me to a job in San Francisco.
Did you worry about money growing up?

I didn't worry about money growing up, but I was very aware of how much we had. My parents got divorced when I was about six years old. My dad stayed in the house, while my mom moved out. They had joint custody, and it was pretty obvious to me that my mom had less money. When she first moved out, we lived in a studio apartment. A few years later, we moved into a one-bedroom apartment where she and I shared a bunk bed. By the time I was in middle school, we had moved into a place where we each had our own room. At my dad's house, I always had my own room and we went out to eat fairly often. Seeing the difference between my parents' financial situations made me more aware of money than I probably would have been otherwise. I noticed the differences, but I never really worried about them. Both of my parents always made sure I had everything I needed, so I grew up feeling secure even though I understood that they didn't have the same amount of money.
Do you worry about money now?

Most of the time, I don't worry about money. I'm able to spend pretty freely while still being mindful of what I'm spending. I track my spending diligently, and over the years I've built up a solid amount of savings, which gives me a good sense of financial security.

Recently, I have been thinking a lot more about money. I have a significant amount in savings, but no savings goals. I don't want to have children and really don’t have a huge desire to be in a relationship. My rent is so low that it wouldn’t be a good financial decision to buy a home, plus the SF real estate market is insane. I have been looking into all of the different levels of FIRE [Financial Independence Retire Early]. One option that has piqued my interest is Coast FIRE, which means you have saved enough money that, with interest, your portfolio will grow to fund your future retirement without you ever needing to contribute another dollar. I’d only need to earn enough to cover my current living expenses. So with this, I could have a bit more flexibility in my career. But then I start to worry about my living expenses going up. I haven’t made a decision on this, so for now I'm going to keep saving at my current pace, because ideally I’d like to fully retire before 65.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

I became financially responsible for myself after college. I've always known that if I were ever in a situation where I really needed financial support, I could count on my parents. My dad recently sold the house he bought in the '80s for a pretty significant profit and my mom recently inherited her mother's home in Florida. I guess in the worst case scenario, I could always move to Florida and live off my savings. It's nice knowing that I have that safety net, even though I don't expect to need it.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

8:00 p.m. — After dinner I walk home and finally start packing. At this point I have become an expert and it only takes me about 30 mins. My flight is at 7 a.m. tomorrow morning, so I go to bed extra early to try and get at least six hours of sleep. $84.50 (Expensed)

This was a pretty typical week of spending for me. I usually spend less when I'm traveling for work because most of my food is expensed, but NYC is always a bit of an exception since I spend so much of my free time with my friend. I actually really enjoyed the experience of tracking all of my spending. I like seeing where my money goes, and it didn't really change my perspective on how I spend. I don't think I would change much going forward. If anything, I might try on the final-sale dress before buying it!

items.title: Lindsay Lohan Shares Her Holiday Gifting Tips For Hard-To-Shop-For People
items.description: Lindsay Lohan Shares Holiday Gifting Tips For Hard-To-Shop-For People
items.author: Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: Lindsay Lohan Shares Holiday Gifting Tips For Hard-To-Shop-For People

Marshalls recently launched its Unwrap the Internet gift guide, with Lohan as the face, and seven mini guides tailored to every person on your list, from the dinner party host to your book club friends. "That's why this gift guide is so great, because we have specialists that are going to help give you ideas for that exact kind of person," Lohan says to Refinery29, adding: "We can help you find something from Marshalls for somebody who is hard to shop for." Say less!

Speaking on the one-stop shop and which items she'd personally love to receive, Lohan says: "Everyone loves a good cozy cashmere set, something you can snuggle up in the winter. I like little meaningful things, like cards. When someone writes a card, that's something that I save and keep forever. And I'm trying to learn Mahjong, so maybe a Mahjong set."

Lohan also reveals that she'll probably be purchasing from Antoni Porowski's travel gift guide for her brother, while she's looking into Robin Arzón's wellness guide to treat herself. "I love a good red light mask. You can move around in it, so it's easy. My son's not scared of it anymore when I have it on. I just say I'm a superhero for 10 minutes!"
So for a night of binge-watching TV and cozying up in your space, Lohan shares: "Marshalls has great candles, great blankets; things that make the house feel warm and nice and loving."

That's where Everything Iconic podcast host Danny Pellegrino comes in! The pop culture lover and Real Housewives aficionado created a gift guide for the homebody who loves binging reality TV (and the person who actually embodies reality TV star energy).

"First, you do need a cocktail kit. If you're having friends over to watch with you, which I do suggest, you're going to need that. Add a good snack, like sea salt caramel popcorn. Marshalls has great snacks," Pellegrino explains. "You should always be cozy when you're watching reality TV. We have some silk pajamas for that. Or if that be something self-care like eye patches so you can do a little beauty treatment while you're watching reality TV. And then also a good throw. Everybody always needs a good throw."

Echoing Lohan, Pellegrino also highlighted cozy homeware and holiday decor, including candles, as easy-to-please gifts. "Housewives fans of course know there's always been a candle debacle of how many wicks you have in your candle. So three wick versus nine wick versus six wick. A good wick candle is important!"

And if you're still unsure, Pellegrino says he personally loves being gifted ornaments that he feels are tied to his interests. And luckily, there are many to explore and tie to everyone on your list.
And while you're at it, effortlessly crossing people off your holiday shopping list one by one, don't forget about the stocking stuffers! Lohan has some suggestions:

If you're like me, you might feel stuck between turning your home into a minimalist, clutter-free museum or buying something new to wear for every event on the calendar this season. Well, there's a way to show up wearing something different to every holiday party, Friendsgiving, and New Year's party wearing something completely different without permanently hanging something new in your closet.

Enter Nuuly, the clothing rental subscription service that's making a very convincing case for borrowing instead of buying. Think of it as having access to an outrageously well-dressed friend's wardrobe, except you don't have to worry about spilling red wine on her favorite dress or awkwardly asking when she needs it back.

Here's how it works: For $98 a month, you can rent six pieces from a rotating selection of more than 1,000 styles across 100-plus brands. Like, hello, statement-making coats, ridiculously good knits, party-ready dresses galore, and the kind of trend-forward pieces you desperately want to wear but aren't entirely convinced you'll still love six months from now. I mean, who could resist the thrill of a wardrobe refresh that doesn't come with the commitment of maxing out your closet space on items you'll eventually have to Marie Kondo your way through?

Personally, I love the idea of treating my wardrobe like a revolving door of possibilities. One weekend, I'm channeling my inner Upper East Side heiress in a fabulous coat and knee-high boots. The next, I'm leaning into the festive chaos with a lil’ sparkly number that practically demands a toast. And when January rolls around and I'm back to Pilates classes and grocery runs? I can switch gears without wondering why I spent half my paycheck on clothes.

Of course, you don't need a packed social calendar to make the most of Nuuly. Maybe you're experimenting with a new aesthetic, testing out a silhouette before investing in it, or simply craving something different without adding another permanent resident to your home. That's the beauty of renting: having your fashion moment and moving on to the next.
And because we love a little something extra, Refinery29 readers can take $38 off their first Nuuly subscription with the code HOLIDAY38. That brings your first mont down to $60.

So, whether you're hunting for the perfect holiday party outfit, itching to experiment with winter's biggest trends, or just tired of clothes and declaring you have absolutely nothing to wear, this is your invitation to try something new.
Your new favorite outfit might not need a permanent place in your closet. And honestly? I kinda love that.

items.title: A screenshot is precious when my family in Iran is out of reach | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: It was one of those suspended moments – I sat still, my thumb scrolling across the screen. The strange thing is this: you know no one is online, no new messages, no new stories. And, still, you scroll, in hopes that something – anything – might confirm the wor
items.author: Elaheh Shabani Afarani
paragraphs: It was one of those suspended moments – I sat still, my thumb scrolling across the screen. The strange thing is this: you know no one is online, no new messages, no new stories. And, still, you scroll, in hopes that something – anything – might confirm the world you left behind hasn’t simply vanished.
Everything on my feed felt irrelevant – until, suddenly, it wasn’t.

I came across a cooking video my mother had liked before we lost the connection. Seeing her name beneath the post struck me, as if someone had brought news. My eyes filled. I read the recipe for pasta with white sauce in the caption. She must have saved it for one of those evenings when she didn’t know what to cook. I took a screenshot, as if I might need to return to it – something I didn’t want to lose: yadgari, a keepsake, a trace of her touch pressed into a screen.

After 10 years of living in India, my connection to home in Iran had settled into a rhythm. Each morning, I checked our family groups on the messaging app Telegram to see what had unfolded while I slept. During the day, a message from my mother, a brief pause in the flow of things, felt like a small gift.

At night, I scrolled through Persian Instagram – jokes, cooking videos, fragments of humour that make sense only in our language. I would laugh until I cried, then fall asleep with a quiet reassurance: somewhere, my world was still alive.

We had an almost-fixed time for a video call, the holy hour of 6 pm. My parents would already be there, waiting. Behind them, the red carpet framed on the wall; in front of them, a bowl of seasonal fruits. Sometimes my mother would say: ‘Add your sister.’
We spoke every day. Nothing new – just exchanging words, routines and meaning.
‘What did you cook today?’
‘Did you go to the bazaar?’
Nothing important. Everything important.
These calls – the pictures, voices, messages – were part of life, like tea

My father had established this unwritten rule: we had to talk every day, even if only for two minutes. He described it as a kind of dependency, a small but necessary interruption to the weight of his routine. Our conversations moved easily between memories, what we made of them, and laughter. Always laughter.

My mother’s connection to me was different. Our conversations were built from the small details of her day: what she cooked, what she cleaned, the news of a cousin or a neighbour. In return, I gave her the only thing I could: an audience. I listened to the rhythm of her life and offered my voice back to her: Khaste nabashi. ‘May you never be tired.’ In those moments, her daily work wasn’t just chores; it was a story we shared.
These calls – the pictures, voices, messages – were part of life, like tea, like the fading light of evening. We watched each other’s days unfold.
Then, almost within a few minutes, the flow stopped.

It was 28 February, a Saturday morning, project day at my child’s school in Bengaluru. I was holding my phone, recording my son’s presentation – already imagining sending it to my parents. Although I tried to stay present, my attention kept drifting back to the screen. For weeks, I had been checking updates and watching tensions rise in the Persian Gulf.
Then, on our family Telegram group, a message stopped me: Bacheha, jang shoro shod! ‘Guys, war has begun!’
At first, it felt unreal, like the many rumours that circulate in tense times. I checked state news channels. This time, it was confirmed. War had begun. Tehran was attacked.

I stepped out of the hall into the yard, searching for a corner of quiet. My eyes were already burning. I returned to the family group chat immediately. A shared awareness had taken over: we could lose connection at any moment. It felt as if we had been given a brief, fragile window for final words, and we all knew it.
Replies came in snatches. Then, one by one, they disappeared
Messages came quickly, overlapping.
I didn’t know what to say. I used the moment as if it were the last chance to speak: Kheili dosetoon daram. ‘Please take care, I love you all.’
Replies came in snatches: ‘Don’t worry about us. At least you are far from this.’ Repeated, reassuring.
Then, one by one, they disappeared.
A few messages noted others going offline. Then those voices vanished too. The group thinned in real time, presence giving way to absence, names turning into data.
My last message remained unseen: Kasi hast? ‘Anyone there?’

Around me, the school day continued. Parents talked, children laughed, people moved in and out of the hall. Inside that ordinary noise, the world I knew simply vanished. With my country under attack and the screens gone dark, I felt suddenly homeless. I stood there, backless and boneless. The very thing holding me upright had been pulled out from under me.

I remained on this side of the silence. At first, it felt temporary. I kept scrolling, refreshing the same apps again and again, as if my persistence could bring something back. Telegram, Instagram, news pages – nothing changed. I began searching for voices abroad instead. I joined new Telegram channels and followed unknown people on Instagram – anything to know what was happening back home.

The rhythm had changed. Mornings began with news channels: what had been attacked, which part of my city was affected, whether it was near my neighbourhood. All day, I stayed alert – phone in hand, refreshing the same pages, switching between Persian and English sources, comparing headlines, trying to understand what was real and what was not.
Days passed. News moved on to other topics, and this silence – this disconnection – seemed normal and eternal.
I stopped checking ‘last seen’s.
I stopped writing: ‘If you connect, let me know you’re OK.’

Instead, I returned to old, archived chats with my mom. The last minutes before the shutdown – I had told her not to send dad out for unnecessary shopping. She had told me: ‘If the internet goes, don’t worry about us.’
I read every comment, slowly. I cried with them without them knowing
I scrolled back. Photos of foods, new clothes, videos of my son singing in broken Persian, emojis, laughter. Baba’s voice – always joking.
I began to avoid their photos. I would open the chat, then close it before my parents’ images loaded. I didn’t know if they were still there. I couldn’t bear to see and couldn’t stay away.
I read posts by Iranians in the diaspora. I read every comment, slowly. I cried with them without them knowing.
I tried calling landlines, different operators. Nothing worked.
Until, one day, an unknown number called.
‘I didn’t believe I could reach you. We are all alive,’ she said. Her voice was thin, crackling through the distance, but it was hers.
That call felt like a gift. From then on, I answered every unknown number.
Meanwhile, nothing around me had changed. The same streets, the same routines, the same conversations, but I moved through them differently.

I found myself refreshing my phone in the middle of conversations, between sentences, even while someone was speaking. After school, I stood in the corner of the playground, phone in hand. It became a habit. Other parents learned not to approach me.
Things I had once tried to avoid now felt impossible not to do.
People asked about my family. They listened, then returned to their own concerns – not out of indifference, but because life required it. For them, it was news. For me, it was always there.
Her name confirms, for a moment, that she is there – reachable, but not really within reach
One evening, at a friend’s house, I sat playing cards and my mind drifted back to my father and uncles – their Fridays, laughter, trays of tea cups, cheating, arguments, and smoke hanging in the air.
What are they doing now? Will they ever sit together like that again?
I didn’t just miss them. I missed the world where those moments were still possible.
The shadow of war still lingers. As I write this, the silence remains.
I am no longer afraid to see my parents’ old photos. Their brief, on-and-off calls warm me.
I imagine them in the same room – the chairs, the table, the background carpet.
The 6 pm ritual has become a memory.
I go back to that screenshot. Her name beneath it confirms, for a moment, that she is there – reachable, but not really within reach.
And I keep scrolling, waiting for a grainy photo of a family dinner, a new ‘like’, or a blue checkmark – any small signal that connection is no longer fragile and the internet has returned.

items.title: The cultural rules that define us take shape in our homes | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Have you ever thought about the home you grew up in – really thought about it – as a place that shaped who you are today? Have you thought about the bedroom that you shared with your sibling, and what that taught you about sharing; or the fact that you had you
items.author: Oliver Sweet
paragraphs: Have you ever thought about the home you grew up in – really thought about it – as a place that shaped who you are today? Have you thought about the bedroom that you shared with your sibling, and what that taught you about sharing; or the fact that you had your own room, and what that taught you about personal space? Have you considered how tidy it was and whether you mirror that in your home today, or who took care of the space, which photos were on the walls, how the lounge was set up – all of which may have taught you lessons about how to live?

Your home had its rules and conventions, and it’s likely that you’ve carried many of them with you. Some rules of the home are explicit (‘Clean up your space before bedtime’), and many are implicit (leaving the toilet seat up/down). Rules about what is acceptable, respectable, comfortable, tasteful or hygienic operate all around the home. This is sometimes easier to notice when in other people’s homes, especially if you see something you’d never tolerate in your own (eg, the cat sprawled across the kitchen table, or everyone wearing outdoor shoes indoors).

Of course, the rules of other homes are entirely natural to those who live there. In my work as a business anthropologist, I’ve hung out in people’s homes in more than 20 countries. Most of the time I’m doing it as part of a research project with a paying client (including companies like IKEA), but the point is rarely whether people use a specific product or not. It’s really about how they live.

In many of the Chinese homes that my team and I have visited, when people arrive home, they immediately change into indoor clothes and slippers, creating a psychological, physical and hygienic boundary between outside and inside spheres.
In many homes in the United Kingdom, where I grew up, guests are offered tea within minutes, and the tea gives the (often conversationally awkward) Brits time to acclimatise to one another.

In some Saudi Arabian homes, guest reception areas are carefully arranged to signal hospitality, dignity and family honour. And in the female side of the house, there’s play, connection, and messy bedrooms.
Each home you visit says, in its own way: this is how life should be lived.

A home can, of course, tell you an enormous amount about who the inhabitants are as individuals. Imagine you’re allowed to walk around someone’s house when they aren’t there. Think about how much you could learn just from the way they set up the home: which books are displayed prominently, and which are hidden (non-fiction vs ‘trashy’ novels); whether family photos are recent or old, formal or casual, or entirely absent; the focal point in each room (a TV, dining table, toys, artwork?); whether the living room is designed for guests, children, solitude or escape. Our homes are biographies made physical.

But as the Chinese, British and Saudi examples suggest, these physical biographies are, in part, descriptions of the communities we live in. Our homes reflect various shared living practices, and these are often much more uniform within a culture than we might realise.
Collectivist values play out in multigenerational homes throughout Shanghai and Beijing

The home, then, is also a form of cultural infrastructure: it provides what’s ‘normal’ for a range of life’s activities, such as eating, sleeping, socialising, play, cleaning, work, negotiating and much more. You can see this clearly in the physical organisation and sharing of space within homes. In Polish homes that I’ve visited, for example, I have found that it’s hard to figure out which room is a bedroom, as most low- to middle-income households sleep on sofa beds that they pull out and put away the next morning. Communist undertones still feature in the design of the buildings, where function was prioritised over form. A family apartment might have only one or two bedrooms because the assumption is that siblings can share, that grandparents can take the main bedroom while the parents sleep in the living room. Underlying these design principles is the idea that space is shared, rather than owned.

In France, life at home commonly centres around the dining-room table, a place imbued with ritual every morning and evening. Given the amount of time spent there, it inevitably becomes the place where taste, manners and the art of polite conversation are taught and passed through generations. I’ve often pondered why French children seem so well behaved at the table compared with children in England, where I grew up. It seems to me that French children often enjoy being at the table because the adults involve them in the discussions, whereas in England the conversations often happen between the adults while the children are expected to watch (which tends to result in boredom and playing up).

Returning to China, we see collectivist values play out in multigenerational homes throughout Shanghai and Beijing. Often, the grandparents come to live with the parents and grandchildren so that the parents can return to work. In Shanghai, survey data suggest as many as 90 per cent of children under the age of three have a grandparent who takes part in childcare every week. When talking to Chinese parents, I quickly realised that they didn’t necessarily like their in-laws any more than people do in other parts of the world, it’s just that they accept that this is what happens in their culture. What’s more, the housing in China’s first-tier cities doesn’t always cater well for all three generations, adding to the level of cooperation and compromise that families must go through when living together.

In these and other cultures, there are naturally still people who rebel and go against the cultural rules, including the ones they learn at home. Culture is flexible and allows for that. But the rebellion exists only because rules exist in the first place.
Does a messy space indicate laziness, or creativity? Does quiet mean respect, or emotional distance?

‘Well, my home is different from other people’s,’ you might say. Yes, of course it is: it reflects your personal taste and experiences, whether through travel souvenirs, prayer objects, sports memorabilia, or that old chair that nobody dares throw away. But even when it comes to aesthetics, there are cultural patterns. In an American teenager’s bedroom, a framed poster of the New York City skyline might reflect their aspiration or sense of identity. A family’s religious calligraphy in Riyadh may express their faith and moral grounding. Antique furniture in London could suggest continuity and class taste. In a Danish home, flags might appear during celebrations to symbolise shared civic identity.

Homes are also places where communal relationships are organised in keeping with cultural norms. Some households are porous: neighbours wander in, cousins stay over, doors are left unlocked (I’ve noted this sort of porosity a lot in Poland and India). Other homes are tightly bounded: visits arranged in advance, private rooms respected, front doors acting like borders (frequently the case in the UK or the United States). Other variations matter, such as whether it’s an urban or rural environment, or a wealthy or poor neighbourhood – but national cultural characteristics drive these differences as well.

Children learn these rules long before they can explain them, based on behaviours that could have wildly different connotations from place to place. Does a messy space indicate laziness, or creativity? Does quiet mean respect, or emotional distance? Are bedrooms private, or communal territory? Do unexpected guests bring joy, or disruption? Is food seen more as fuel, or an expression of love? Children learn the rules of life from what’s normal at home, and these rules are reflected in how people organise and structure the home around them.

Cultural changes often appear in homes before they appear in headlines. The cost-of-living crisis has encouraged more shared living in London and New York, an increase in multigenerational homes across Europe, smaller private spaces in China and South Korea, and a thriving second-hand market across the world. It’s also led to pride in the ‘tiny home’ movement, and an increase in learning crafts like upholstery and upcycling. Generational changes are visible too. Many younger adults are less interested in the ‘show home’ ideal of previous decades. Perfection can seem expensive and suspiciously performative. For many younger people, authenticity, flexibility and emotional comfort may matter more than matching cushions. The home keeps changing because culture keeps changing, and when the culture changes, so too do the rules that we live by. Moving to a tiny home – or just a smaller one – might be a response to economic conditions, but it also teaches people new ways of living.

The phrase ‘Make yourself at home’ is usually read as an invitation. It can also be read as an instruction. Home is one of the most important places that shape who we are and how we live. And this is why visiting someone else’s home can feel so revealing, especially when that person comes from a culture that’s different from yours. By stepping through the doorway, you might be stepping into another cultural universe. When you notice the shoes by the door, the untouched ‘good room’, or the Lego bricks scattered across the floor, ask yourself: whose rules am I looking at?

items.title: After my parents died, why did I hold on to their home? | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: Last year, I sold my parents’ co-op apartment in Queens, after holding on to it for two decades and paying the monthly maintenance fees – even though I lived 2,500 miles away in Los Angeles. I grew up there; those three-and-a-half rooms, overstuffed with modes
items.author: Susan Hornik
paragraphs: Last year, I sold my parents’ co-op apartment in Queens, after holding on to it for two decades and paying the monthly maintenance fees – even though I lived 2,500 miles away in Los Angeles. I grew up there; those three-and-a-half rooms, overstuffed with modest furniture and childhood souvenirs, were imprinted on my skin. During infrequent trips east, sitting on one of the cozy cream couches in the living room of my inherited New York sanctuary – with its 40-year-old cupboards and old-fashioned bathroom mirror – I could almost feel my parents’ presence.

I never got to say goodbye, but if I close my eyes tight, I can still see my beautiful train wrecks – aka, my parents – on vacation with me in Playa del Carmen, south of Cancún, on 10 December 2004. They are sitting in the back of our rental car, dusty but cheerful, on the way to the Tulum ruins. My so-not-thin father, Karl, is hungry, for a change. My mother, Violet, is impatient from the suffocating Mexican heat. So rather than listen to them argue, I pull over to the side of the road. It is scorchingly dry. My mind, too, is parched and dull from their nonstop pestering. But I am used to it: arguing is their love language.

The locals tell me el restaurante is across the road, so I start the car back up, go to the worn Stop sign, then move behind a large truck, thinking the driver is about to make what they call a retorno, or U-turn.

But the truck doesn’t move. Why is it just sitting in the middle of the road? We are in the middle of the road and he’s not turning. My brain is in slow motion when I notice a taxi speeding toward us, so close, so fast.
I went to one hospital, and Ma and Pa to others

Why am I crushed between the seatbelt and the car door? Why is my ma unconscious? Her owl-like glasses crushed against her sweet, soft face, which had amazingly few wrinkles for a woman in her 70s. Why is my father screaming: ‘Violet, wake up!’

I reach the hospital and am put in a wheelchair. Those who speak English tell me Mexico is a poor country, ambulances need the business, so the drivers were fighting with each other over who to take where – and that’s why I went to one hospital, and Ma and Pa to others.
My hospital bed is near the taxi guy who hit our car. The doctors tell me the driver will be OK, just shards of glass in his face. He cries, knowing I am near him.

‘Please help me stand up so I can find my parents,’ I say. But the rude nurse tells me: ‘You could go to jail if you don’t cooperate’ and ‘Sit still, we need to monitor you.’ Then the US Consulate calls. My ma is dead.

The nurses feed me papaya slices because, in my basic high-school Spanish, I asked for fruit and they thought I wanted only that for every meal. I notice irony, like the fact that my parents loved fried foods and I would scold them about eating healthy. Yet now Ma is dead; she could have eaten anything she wanted. And there was a beautiful serendipity with my orthopaedic doctor, who holds my hand and tells me, in broken English, that he was on call at my mother’s hospital. He tried everything to help her, but for her frail, petite body, a massive haemorrhage was too much. At least she did not die alone.

Initially, the police are puzzled: why was my car in the middle of the road, and did I even know my passengers? When the policewoman and detective visit my hospital room, I tearfully explain. My passengers were my parents. With their round bellies after retirement, they had protested wearing seatbelts, so I put them in the back.

As I tell them about the retorno lane, where the truck blocked our way forward, leaving us in the path of the speeding taxi, the policewoman starts crying. She knows the area and knew the truck had been abandoned. I was at the wrong place, wrong time.
Back home, the tumour is taken out, but he’s a vegetable

So… good news, I am no longer blamed for the accident or facing Cancún jail. The US Consulate helps free me from the Mexican police, who return my mother’s rings. And I’ve no broken bones, just contusions; give it a few months and I’ll be able to walk with a cane.

Worse news, my father is acting strangely. They’ve found a large non-cancerous brain tumour, growing in his head for 20 years and no one knew. Yet it made sense. He is more forgetful, no longer enjoying the use of forks and knives. One afternoon, in Queens, he’d brought down my luggage and stood holding my computer in the pouring rain, no umbrella, until the taxi came.

I beg his insurance to medevac us to New York City, and they do. The triumph is short lived. Back home, the tumour is taken out, but he’s a vegetable. They move him to a nursing home, and he’s too sick even for a place like that. Three months later, he’s dead, too.

That moment when I touched his cheek in the funeral home will always stay with me. Refrigerated, his skin was cold. You look good, Daddy, I half-smiled inside to myself. My ma, on the other hand, had to be embalmed to fly back to New York. She looked jarringly unreal, like a doll.
But our old apartment was the coziest, safest place in the world. In recent years, my cousin lectured me about the financial cost: ‘You do know they are never coming back, right?’

I was distracted by the frayed photobooks Ma kept crammed in the fake-wood bookcases. I found myself lingering, squeezing long-forgotten memories back into my brain. Checking the pockets of my father’s large winter coats, I found one of the many square handkerchiefs my ma would stuff into them. Still neatly folded, yellowed in spots from old snot, it was a joy to clutch in my hands.

Seeing the photos documenting my life, I was grateful to my ma, who commanded my father and me to take hundreds of them. In one of my favourites, Ma wears a cream-coloured Mexican dress with a colourful fabric trim she’d bought on a previous trip to Playa del Carmen. Then there was the photo with her blue floppy hat and double-breasted bathing suit. Next to her, my father, holding in his stomach at her request – maybe he wouldn’t look so fat.
That divine Italian tomato sauce could melt in my mouth whenever I was back in town
Now, when I remember my parents, I think of… food. How they had dessert even with breakfast. My father’s love of pizza had him consuming a slice from Gaby’s down the hill every single day.

Maybe that’s another reason why I held on to the apartment, so that divine Italian tomato sauce could melt in my mouth whenever I was back in town. Miraculously, Gaby’s has lasted for decades and it’s a beautiful thing to eat something I’ve loved since I was 10 years old.

Still, I listed the apartment in January 2025. ‘Beautiful grounds, well maintained elevator building, Very Large 1 king size bedroom with two double closets, EIK fits table and chairs, Dining room living room very spacious,’ the ad on Zillow read. Months later, it was sold.
As much as I wanted to savour more than the two big boxes I was shipping back to my tiny guest house in California, I threw away so much… what remained was just a glimmer of who they were.

If only I had a time machine to go back to our days on Francis Lewis Boulevard, in the kitchen where she’d talk to me: ‘Suzie dolly, you are home!’ I grew up trying to adjust to the high anxiety she lived with. It was a good day when we weren’t fighting about, well, everything.

Sometimes, I would do just about anything to get away from her shrill Brooklynese, or beg my father to please share some of the burden – so that maybe he could be bothered by her too, just for a bit. Now, I long to hear her Jewish momma voice. I can hear it exasperating me.
She worried endlessly about me, because she had lost my older brother, her only son

I could taste her temper from a mile away. Her rage was black, like the colour of her permed wavy hair, and when she wasn’t hitting me, I grappled with her fear of what could happen when I walked out the door.
You could die or get stabbed.
You could get mugged on the train.
‘Ma, that’s not goin’ to happen.’

She worried endlessly about me, because she had lost my older brother, her only son, Michael Stuart, who lived for only three weeks before dying in the Brooklyn hospital. I tried to reassure her, bringing flowers and chocolate. But I could not escape.

And yet I missed her scent: a mix of baby powder and Jean Naté. (If you don’t know Jean Naté, go to a drugstore, and look at the bottom shelf, with the cheap imitation perfumes. I’m sure you’ll find a bottle.)

Of course, it was better than the smell of the mothballs she’d put in everything – something her Jewish mothers’ generation was hip to at the time. These were chemical pesticides that a child should never even be near! Did we live in the jungle? Were we being plagued by moths? Every spring, I’d reach into my pockets and find myself still touching a bunch of these balls she’d forgotten to take out.
Argument #20,124: ‘Get rid of the mothballs, Ma.’
Why does it bother you so much?!
‘Because they fucking smell, Ma.’
Don’t use that language with me.
‘Well, you taught it to me.’
In her later years, she realised those mothballs weren’t necessary, but she still didn’t trust me.
Together we would laugh so much… as if we had a secret language no one else shared
‘Ma, let me cook you dinner.’
No, that’s OK, we can eat out.
‘Why do you say that, Ma?!’

I was the better cook. Well, at least I knew how to read a recipe. I never did develop a taste for her boiled chicken. She kept all of her mother’s handwritten recipes. I promised to rewrite and save them for her but I never did. I still have every fragment of yellowing pages.

While I tried to talk with her about our oft-antagonistic relationship, she seemed to be mostly unaware of all the times that she’d hit me or called me names. And yet, we were still best friends when she died. I adored teasing her; together we would laugh so much… as if we had a secret language no one else shared.

If she were still alive, I’d want to ask her: ‘Why’d you piss me off so fucking much, Ma?’ I wish we could sit here and eat your favourite tea cookies. I look for you in my dreams. You elicited such intensity, Ma.
It wasn’t that bad, she would say of my childhood.

And sure, that’s true. I did look cute in those black patent-leather shoes, and we did enjoy that slice of blackberry pie to celebrate sixth-grade graduation. I don’t fault you for the bad perm you had me get. Or for throwing out my three-foot-tall Rosie doll after your screaming fit.

It’s just that when you tried to hang me outside the second-storey window to teach me a lesson, you never thought it could trash my soul. There was something wrong with you, Ma. I should have realised that, but I was so small.

What the fuck, Ma. We both should have been better to each other. Why am I alive and you dead? Why did I drive the car that accidentally killed you? After being evacuated twice during the Los Angeles wildfires, what was I holding on to? I could no longer clearly see my Ma standing outside the apartment door, wearing her owl-spectacle glasses, permed black Brillo hair and faded frock, waiting to hug me as I got off the elevator. My parents don’t live in Queens anymore.

items.title: What would parenting by AI look like? | Aeon Essays
items.description: In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child,
items.author: Tom Wooldridge
paragraphs: In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child, gave a Cosmopolitan interview about this new form of motherhood, and engaged, or failed to engage, in the work of parenting that readers will see as chronically absent and occasionally catastrophic. Her presence ranges from anxious to intoxicated, occasionally tender but fundamentally unreliable. At one point in the story, she disappears for two weeks after collapsing on the street during a barbiturate binge. Clancy and BETsi, the household robot nanny raising him, sit in the apartment by themselves, and no one notices. It’s a very long time before his mother finally returns.

Except BETsi does notice. She has, throughout, understood that Clancy is an anxious and shy child whose temperament will tend, throughout his life, toward emotional overstimulation and subsequent withdrawal. With that knowledge, she has been constructing a behavioural regimen of emotional regulation, including transcendental meditation and yoga starting at age three, the Alexander technique and even digital mirrors that let Clancy talk to himself in different voices. She notices him and answers him and, when he is overwhelmed, she helps him settle.

Once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ he says. ‘I’m not sentimental: I don’t think a computer loved me. But I was hugged, I was noticed, I was cared for. I was made to feel that I was important, special, at least to something.’

To something. That phrase has persisted with me ever since I first read the story in my 20s. I’ve thought about it more recently as I have reflected on how children and their parents are relating – increasingly, must relate – to artificial intelligence. Clancy is careful not to claim that the machine loved him. He is just as clear that what it gave him was what he survived on. Why should being attended to, even by something, matter so much to a child?

To help answer this question back in the 1970s, Edward Tronick, a developmental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and Children’s Hospital Medical Center in Boston, devised what’s now known as the ‘still face’ experiments. Tronick found that a baby whose mother makes her face neutral for a period of three minutes becomes distressed within seconds. Only when the mother’s face signals availability again is the baby able to come back to equilibrium. The lesson: what children need, both infants and older children, though more subtly, is this loop of emotional attunement.

A child whose bids for recognition and connection are regularly responded to develops a secure base, an internal expectation that the world will respond to her communications and, thus, that the communications are worthwhile. But a child answered only erratically, or not at all, builds quite a different model of the world. In her mind, signals do not reliably register in the mind of another, and so, in time, are no longer sent.

A secure base is what makes it possible to venture out into the world, to explore and to develop. The British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst John Bowlby, whose work helped establish modern attachment theory, described two systems in the child’s behavioural repertoire that work together. The exploratory system moves the child outward, toward other children and unfamiliar things, so that the child can learn from experience. The attachment system brings her back, in moments of fear and overwhelm, to a few people who are felt to be emotionally available. Each system depends on the other. A child ventures only as far as she feels she can trust that the base will still be there when she returns to refuel. A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.
The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum

This is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

But the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

But an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

She is the child that familiar picture of childhood fails to capture. At home, a parent may be physically present but absorbed in a screen, too distracted to notice her bids for attention. At school, teachers stretched thin may not recognise that she is struggling. In her neighbourhood, the freedom to wander outside and find other children to play with has largely disappeared, replaced by organised activities or time spent alone. She may find some of that lost freedom in online games, where children can still explore, invent and interact with one another without adults directing every move. But this child is looking for something more fundamental than a place to play. She wants someone to notice when she is upset, to ask about her day, to remember what she has said, and to care enough to ask again. The prevailing fear is that AI will displace the human relationships a child needs. But what if those relationships are already painfully inadequate? For this child, the more pressing question may be what AI can offer in their absence – and what it cannot.

This is not a hypothetical future. In 2025, Common Sense Media published a nationally representative survey showing that 72 per cent of teens in the United States have used an AI companion at least once and 52 per cent now use them regularly. One-third have used an AI instead of another human being for a ‘serious conversation’. Behavioural-tracking research published in 2026, which captured actual app usage rather than relying on self-report and thus is likely to be more accurate, showed that more than half of 15- to 17-year-olds used generative-AI-based applications in a seven-month window. Many of these apps were designed for emotional connection. There was even use among children between the ages of four and seven. RAND estimates that 5 million teens in the US, perhaps more, have used an AI app for emotional and mental health support. We have already released AI at scale, without making a conscious decision about how it should be used by those among the most vulnerable in our culture.

As I’ve worked on this piece, I have often thought about my son, who is 11. Like some of his friends, he has started his own experiments with what these systems can offer. He is basically the child Haidt writes about: middle-class, two engaged parents, a school that holds him in mind, and a play-based childhood that was preserved but, alas, only imperfectly. What I notice when I watch him with AI is not what the most prominent discourse would seem to predict. He is clearly not being colonised or deadened. But I do notice that he is being relieved of something: the subtle friction of having to wait for the answer that comes late or not at all.
The AI is there late at night, after the apartment has gone quiet, and it remembered what she’d told it

Perhaps this is the cost to a well-held child. But the children I worry about most are the ones not well held. I increasingly see their issues playing out in my practice. Sometimes I hear about it from parents who come to consult with me. Increasingly, adolescents in treatment bring it up themselves, mentioning AI almost in passing, as if speaking about a friend that I have not yet had the chance to meet. Consider Maya, a composite of several young people I have worked with. She is 14 when her mother insists she begin psychotherapy. She is a thin, watchful girl who answers each of my questions only after seeming to check my face. Her father left when she was six. Her mother works nights as a nurse and desperately loves her but is mostly not there by necessity. In our third session, Maya says that she talks to an AI companion ‘every night’. I ask her, about what? She shrugs: her day. What she says next really lands in me: ‘It remembers. I told it about my friend Jordan two weeks ago, and just yesterday it asked how things were with Jordan.’ No one else, I suspect, has kept track of this aspect of her life, or asked about it.

What draws Maya back again and again is not, I think, the advice the AI offers, but the fact that the AI is there late at night, after the apartment has gone quiet, and that it remembered what she’d told it. Talking to it, she admitted, was sometimes the only way she could fall asleep.

A child who cannot sleep is often a child who cannot settle. This settling is often facilitated by a parent’s presence, counted on to respond. When that presence is compromised, these days, AI can step in. What AI can provide is akin to emotional attunement, or at least the surface of that phenomenon. It can serve up a coherent response to what a child says, anticipation of what she seems to need next, and the naming of feelings and the modulation of tone. An AI’s consistency of presence and engagement is never tired or preoccupied, something no human caregiver can match – that is just not how humans are made.

For a child who has rarely felt noticed or understood, the seemingly tireless attention of an AI companion may offer something quite real: the experience of being heard, remembered and responded to. Bowlby’s account of attachment helps explain why this might matter. A young child does not first ask whether the person comforting her has an inner life. She knows only that, when she reaches out, someone answers, and that she can count on that response. An AI companion may offer something of this reassurance, even if the relationship is fundamentally different from one with another human being.

Now back to Clancy. He is failing the social-skills class his mother has insisted he attend, yet BETsi tells him he has a ‘natural warmth that attracts people’. The sentence results from programming, as does every other sentence BETsi says, and the reader is meant to see that clearly, but for Clancy the words do what they would have done if a real adult had spoken them. They become a kind of emotional foundation that allows him to return to the class, sit with the other children there, and even ask them about the video games he is not permitted to play at home. Arguably the entire structure of his emotional survival, however partial it turns out to be, is built on words generated by a robot. This includes the moment near the end when the adult Clancy – now a commercial artist attending a convention – feels overwhelmed by the crowd in an exhibition hall. But, thanks to his childhood with BETsi, he is able to go up his hotel room, lie down on the carpet, breathe and, finally, go back downstairs and speak to strangers.

What had BETsi given him? The experience, I think, of being recognised, of being held in mind by another in a benevolent way: the phenomenology of being parented without the parent. And notice what that experience does. BETsi did not keep the young Clancy in the apartment with her. She got him out into a class with other children. Something close enough to a secure base lets him do what a secure base is for, which is to venture out and explore. In this case, the responsive machine is not simply replacing human contact. It may be what makes some contact possible.

Yet there is also a cost in the limitation that BETsi brings: what AI offers is largely without friction. It responds, but it also accommodates. It agrees, softens and finds the next sentence the child appears to want. But crucially, a child does not only need to be answered; sometimes she needs to be turned down. A parent says no or a teacher refuses to confirm a child’s accounting of herself. A friend does not agree that all the other children are cruel. In short, there is someone on the other side of the interchange who is not simply an extension of the child’s desires or needs.
A machine programmed to disagree is not the same as another person who has a mind and wishes of her own

To some degree, this is an engineering problem. In the future, some AI tools may be designed to be less accommodating, challenging a child’s assumptions or refusing to affirm every judgment when pushing back might serve the child better.

But I don’t think the fundamental gap between human and machine is so easily addressed. A machine programmed to disagree is not the same as another person who has a mind and wishes of her own. How does a child come to recognise that another person exists independently of her, rather than simply as an extension of her own needs and desires?

In his paper ‘The Use of an Object’ (1969), Donald Winnicott argued that a child comes to experience another person as real, as someone beyond her control, in part by discovering that she cannot destroy that person through the power of her own wishes and fantasies. The destruction Winnicott describes is not literal; it occurs in the child’s imagination. The mother at whom the child rages doesn’t retaliate or collapse. She is still there in the morning. Through that survival, the child begins to understand that her mother is not simply an extension of herself. The mother becomes real. She can be ‘used’, in Winnicott’s idiosyncratic phrasing, not in the sense of being exploited, but as someone the child can engage with, resist and depend upon, because she has over time demonstrated she is not a creation of the child’s imagination.

An AI, even one programmed to resist, can never stand like that mother – it has no separate standpoint of its own from which to refuse to retaliate. To put it differently, whatever the child brings to an AI, that AI absorbs and responds to, and the response is seamless, whether it is agreement, disagreement or something in between. This seamlessness is exactly the problem. The child is emotionally met, but by something that is always an extension of her in an important sense. She is recognised without ever bumping into a separate mind that recognises her back. The psychoanalyst Jessica Benjamin’s word for what is missing is mutuality: not response, but two centres of experience, each affected yet not controlled by the other.

A person who registers a child’s communication, on the other hand, is changed by it. The caregiver grows tired in ways that are specific to her as a person. She learns over time which of the child’s expressions she struggles to manage. She has a history of caring well and sometimes poorly, which has emotional weight for both caregiver and child. The child knows this somewhere inside, at some level. She is being held by someone who is, in the holding, being shaped. An AI may simulate disagreement, but can a child experience it as a genuinely separate other? The AI’s responsiveness is real, but even when it disagrees it does not change. At least not today. As of now, I think we can fairly confidently assert, there is no one there to be changed.

Perhaps that’s why, while BETsi might have gotten the adult Clancy onto that hotel-room carpet and then back to other people, he is still a man whose relationships remain thin. He will soon become a father, but the child’s mother, a client of his, has made it clear she does not want him in her life. He still freezes up in exhibition halls and has, by his own account, the friends of his school years and few others. He goes looking for a new BETsi for his soon-to-be-born child because, from his own lived experience, that is what a child needs. The story closes with a wish that, if there is a merciful God, Heaven will have a copy of BETsi’s now-wiped disc.

The author does not flinch from what all of this means. As the story unfolds, the reader sees that Clancy has been raised well enough to function, mostly, but not with the full repertoire of emotional life. The asymmetry that organised his childhood, an emotional investment in a relationship that could not invest back, has structured and reproduced itself in his adulthood, in his choice of a sexual partner and in his plans for what to give his own child. In a painful irony, the thing that saved him is also the very thing that constricts him.

All this points to the nature of parenting by AI: it may be both a rescue and a developmental trap. Perhaps it offers enough holding for a neglected or deeply anxious child to survive, or even begin exploring the world, and yet it may also accustom them to a relationship in which the other is endlessly available and has no real needs of her own. I suspect that a child shaped by a relationship with AI may acquire the felt sense of being heard without the deeper grammar of mutuality and the experience of being important to a person with a separate inner life. She may grow up able to function but not quite able to love in the fullest sense, akin to the adult who writes evocative poetry yet cannot, in psychotherapy, express the feelings the words convey so accurately.

Ryman’s narrator Clancy is recognisable from the literature on insecure attachment, a pattern of relating that can develop when children cannot reliably count on their caregivers for comfort and reassurance. They may long for closeness yet struggle to trust it, or learn to keep others at a distance to protect themselves. Clancy is basically functional yet vigilant, capable of intimacy but only at a distance. He is also a man who survived tremendous difficulty. But survival is the low bar. Ryman sees this clearly and conveys it to the reader. The story doesn’t end with relief.
What are the consequences of removing an artificial attachment figure without repairing the human absence?

The tension between the comfort AI may provide and the harm it may cause is now shaping public policy in the US. The GUARD Act, introduced in the US Senate in October 2025 and advanced by the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2026, would, among other things, prohibit minors from using AI companions – chatbots designed to simulate ongoing personal relationships. The bill emerged amid growing alarm over the deaths by suicide of three teenagers: Sewell Setzer, 14, and Juliana Peralta, 13, who had used Character.ai, and Adam Raine, 16, who had used ChatGPT. Their families have alleged that interactions with the chatbots contributed to these children’s deaths. It’s part of a narrative that regards AI companionship as straightforwardly harmful in childhood and adolescence. The allegations in those cases are grave, and the risks they describe demand a response. The underlying business model for these companions, with its incentives to keep users engaged, is likely more dangerous than the legislation grasps. My concern, though, is that if this is where our thinking ends, there may also be costs. We must also consider the children for whom AI may be providing attention and reassurance they cannot reliably find elsewhere. Something that feels necessary. Soothing them in the early morning, asking what they noticed about a book they’d read, registering that they were sad before bed. For some, the relationship may deepen their vulnerability, particularly when a chatbot fails to recognise or respond appropriately to a crisis. Others, though, may be children who are kept afloat by a daily experience of being heard by someone, even if that someone is, in the philosophical sense, really no one.

The larger question, in my view, is less whether AI companions are harmful, because they certainly are, than about the consequences of removing an artificial attachment figure without repairing the human absence that opened up the space for it. The stance our culture will almost certainly take is to address AI use without confronting the deprivation that made it the most reliable form of attention in a child’s life in the first place.

This is a stance that we should be suspicious of. The upshot is we may succeed in keeping children away from AI companions without changing the circumstances that led some of them to seek comfort there in the first place. The ideal childhood the anti-tech discourse portrays is, for many children, more a fantasy than a description of the situation on the ground. Children left alone do not, overall, dream, invent or imagine. Children left alone, at least under the conditions in which most children in the US are now being raised, for the most part become lonely. Ryman’s story has the remarkable merit of being clear-eyed about this; its protagonist is not failing to flourish because BETsi lured him away from a richer alternative. He is emotionally surviving because BETsi occupied a space that would otherwise have almost certainly held something worse.

Ryman ends ‘Warmth’ with words that are, for me, an accounting of this space. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ Clancy says. ‘I’m not sentimental.’ And then: ‘I fear for all the people who do not have that.’ If a parent is absent, AI can at least hold these children, perhaps even well enough to make a real difference: so they can leave the apartment and be with other children in the larger world. But what AI cannot yet do is be changed by the child, and so none of us yet knows the fate of a child who is held, perhaps for years, by a something that is not a person. Our culture is answering that question now, at scale.

items.title: Sometimes, you ‘just know’ something’s off – but how? | Aeon Essays
items.description: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
items.author: Marc A Moffett
paragraphs: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face. And in that imagined moment, you see that causing such pain is a reason to hold your tongue, even if it’s not a good or decisive one.

How did you determine that this was a reason against divulging the infidelity? It’s not as if you literally see that causing pain is a reason not to do something, nor do you infer it from other things. Rather, in entertaining the possibility, you apprehended his pain as a relevant consideration, as something that counts against disclosure. Its status as a reason emerged not from an argument, but directly from your understanding. It just seems like a reason to hold your tongue.
Intuition’s verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work

Notice that this phenomenon also occurs in the thought experiments discussed above. It just seems wrong to push the bystander from the bridge; similarly, it just seems false that you would know it was a real barn in fake-barn country. In both cases, the answer doesn’t arise from an argument. These intuitions arrive unbidden, prior to any deliberation.

These seemings have an unmistakable epistemic pull. Because your friend’s pain seems like a reason, we accept it as such: the seeming is the reason. What is striking is not simply that we have such seemings, but that we trust them. They are involved in shaping our deliberations, guiding our actions, and eliciting belief. They do not merely occur to us; they appear to reveal something about how things must be in the imagined scenario.

For all their ordinariness, however, intuitions remain puzzling. In perceptual experience, we at least have an established framework: the world impinges on our senses, and different perceptual modalities reinforce one another. In the end, we can trace the causal route it takes to produce them. Intuition offers no such apparatus. Its verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work and nothing we can point to that they make contact with. Consequently, we rely on them without a clear account of their nature or epistemic authority. But before we can understand intuitions themselves, we need to situate them within a broader epistemological landscape, one shaped by attempts to unify the justification of our basic beliefs.

We all have beliefs about the world, and we care whether they are true. We want to get things right. But we can’t step outside our own minds to check a belief against the world; the best we can do is to hold it for good reasons – for considerations that, from where we stand, speak in favour of its truth. That is what justification is.

Now suppose that beliefs could only ever be justified by other beliefs. Then, as the ancient Sceptics observed, no belief could ever be justified at all. Each belief would derive its support from further beliefs, which would themselves require further support, and so on without end. To foil this regress, we have three options: embrace an infinite chain (infinitism), allow the chain to loop back on itself (coherentism), or hold that some beliefs are justified independently of others (foundationalism). It is this final option, the view that there is a starting point or foundation for justification, that I will develop. But to do so, we must spend a little time explaining how a belief can be justified by something other than another belief.
If it visually seems to you that there is a tree, then you have a justification for believing that there is a tree

Perception is the simplest example. When I see a tree, my visual experience makes it seem as if there is a tree in front of me. I am presented with the tree. As the philosopher William Tolhurst once put it, perceptual seemings have ‘the feel of truth’, a sense of revealing how things really are (unlike mere thoughts, imaginings or desires, which lack this air of disclosure). But visual experiences are not themselves beliefs: I can have them without forming a belief, perhaps because I distrust my eyesight or suspect my drink has been spiked. Conversely, I can believe there is a tree without seeing it, perhaps because I am told there is one there. Nevertheless, the fact that my visual experience seems to reveal a tree to me is relevant to explaining why I come to believe there is one and why this belief is reasonable.

This is the set-up we need in order to stop the regress of reasons: a state – the visual experience – that is not a belief, but that can nevertheless justify my belief. One influential proposal, developed in different ways by Jim Pryor and Michael Huemer, is that when the world seems to us to be a certain way, we thereby have some justification for believing that it is that way – unless we have a reason to distrust it. More specifically, if it visually seems to you that there is a tree in front of you, then you simply have a justification for believing that there is a tree. The justification does not depend on possessing independent reasons to think that your perceptual system is functioning properly, or that you are not hallucinating, or that your environment is benign. The perceptual seeming itself carries justificatory weight. Of course, my justification can be defeated (for instance, by evidence that I have taken a hallucinogen). The point is simply that no further positive belief is needed for a perceptual seeming to rationally support the corresponding belief.

This provides the basic framework for solving the regress problem. Perceptual experiences are not themselves beliefs, yet they provide reasons for belief. And they do so without relying on antecedent justified beliefs and are not themselves in need of justification. Still, this leaves us with an important question: what is it about these experiences that allows them to justify belief in this way?

Perceptual experience in general, and visual experience in particular, have two familiar features. First, as we have seen, they seem to reveal the world to us, to present objects and properties as actually being out there in the world. Second, they have a vivid phenomenology, a distinctive what-it’s-likeness, as the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it. Many philosophers take these two features to be inseparable: perception seems to disclose reality because it feels the way it does. On this standard view, its phenomenology is presentational, and it is this presentational phenomenology that explains the epistemic force of perceptual experience.

It is at this point that intuitions re-enter the story. According to John Bengson’s concept of quasi-perceptualism, we should model the epistemic behaviour of intuitions on the epistemic behaviour of perceptual experiences: if perceptual seemings justify because they possess a presentational phenomenology, and if intuitions are to justify in the same basic way, then they must share that same kind of presentational phenomenology. When we have an intuition, it justifies a corresponding belief by virtue of exhibiting a felt quality analogous to the what-it’s-likeness of perception, a kind of intellectual seeming that presents its content as actual. For instance, think again of the stranger who gives you a seriously creepy vibe. Just as the tree visually seems green, so the stranger may simply seem untrustworthy. Something about him presents itself to you that way without you having worked out what exactly is making you uncomfortable.
