items.title: ‘GTA 6’ Earns Rave Reviews and Lands 99 Metacritic Score, Tying for Highest-Rated Game of All Time
items.description: The review embargo on “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally lifted and the game, which on Tuesday was nominated for Game of the Year ahead of its launch, is considered Rockstar Games’ latest masterpiece.
items.author: Jennifer Maas
paragraphs: The review embargo on “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally lifted and the game, which on Tuesday was nominated for Game of the Year ahead of its launch, is considered Rockstar Games’ latest masterpiece.

“GTA 6” currently holds a score of 99 on Metacritic, which ties it with the original 1998 Nintendo 64 version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” for the highest-rated video game of all time on the platform. (The recently released remake of “Ocarina of Time” for Switch 2 has a score of 96 on Metacritic and is also a 2026 Game of the Year contender.)

“Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around ‘Grand Theft Auto VI‘ – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself,” Game Informer’s Matt Miller wrote in his review, which gave the game a perfect score of 10.

Thirteen years in the making, “GTA 6” is a massive open-world game that follows protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino (voiced by Manni L. Perez) who find themselves stuck in the midst of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida after a score goes wrong.

“Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are an interesting pair of playable characters, and unlike any leads that have come before them in the series,” Luke Reilly wrote for IGN. “Their motivations and goals are very different from the main characters of previous ‘GTA’ games, and their priority is really about escape rather than revenge or empire building. They’re not angels, and it is invariably their recklessness as small-time crooks that puts them in the wrong place at the wrong time, but the overall sliminess of their far more powerful antagonists does make the couple easy to root for throughout their story – which unfolds like four or five seasons of a prestige TV show.”

“GTA 6” officially launches Thursday in the U.S. but has begun rolling out worldwide as the clock strikes midnight on Nov. 19 in different territories, starting with New Zealand, which got access to the game Wednesday at 6 a.m. ET. While fans had been waiting to see if and when “GTA 6” reviews would drop before the game did (with several debating The Game Awards nominations being revealed before “GTA 6” was out), Rockstar Games chose to set the embargo in line with the game’s public release.
The game costs $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version and reportedly offers approximately 80 hours of gameplay to complete its main storyline alone.

“Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please,” The Guardian’s Keza MacDonald wrote. “There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.”

“I have quibbles about some clunky controls and some story pacing problems in the game’s later chapters, but like crappy cupholders in a million-dollar supercar, they don’t really get in the way of what’s here. Instead, they’re minor issues to point at as I hit the gas and go 200 MPH with the radio blasting,” Kotaku’s Zack Zwiezen wrote.

items.title: Warner Bros. TV, Paramount TV Studios to Combine as a Single Mega-Studio
items.description: Skydance is making a big move with its TV studios, combining Warner Bros. Television and Paramount Television Studios into a single entity that will have more than 100 productions under its umbrella.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: Skydance is making a big move with its TV studios, combining Warner Bros. Television and Paramount Television Studios into a single entity that will have more than 100 productions under its umbrella.

The combined studio will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, a nod to the larger of the two current units. The new organization will officially launch early next year, with each group operating as usual until then. WBTV chief Channing Dungey and PTVS head Matt Thunell will be presidents of the combined studio, reporting to Skydance TV co-chair and chief content officer George Cheeks. Dungey also continues to lead Skydance’s cable portfolio.

CBS Studios, headed by David Stapf, will keep operating as its own entity. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and nonfiction unit See It Now Studios fall under CBS Studios. BET Studios will become part of Warner Bros. TV Studios.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level,” Cheeks said in a statement. “With Channing and Matt at the helm, we have two exceptional leaders who understand what it takes to empower creative talent, foster bold ideas and deliver programming that resonates with audiences everywhere. Alongside CBS Studios, led by the incomparable David Stapf, Warner Bros. Television Studios gives us two world-class studios, with the breadth, depth and creative ambition to deliver for Skydance platforms and third-party partners across the industry.”
Dungey and Thunell — who previously worked together at Netflix — offered praise for their soon-to-be partnership in statements of their own.

“Matt has extraordinary creative instincts, and a deep understanding of great storytelling. I couldn’t ask for a better partner as we bring these storied studios together,” said Dungey. “We have a unique opportunity to create something truly special for our creative partners and audiences around the world. I’m very excited to begin this new chapter.”

Added Thunell, “Channing is one of the most accomplished and respected executives in our industry, with an extraordinary track record of building successful businesses, developing enduring partnerships and delivering some of television’s most acclaimed programming. Ever since our time together at Netflix, I’ve hoped we’d have the opportunity to work together again, and I’m thrilled that day has finally come.”

Skydance combining the two TV studios follows a similar playbook to other big media mergers in the past decade. After Disney took over 21st Century Fox’s entertainment assets, four TV studios eventually became three, then two and now just one (20th Television). A year before its own 2025 merger with Skydance, Paramount shut down Paramount TV Studios, then revived the name under as it combined Skydance TV and Showtime/MTV Entertainment under Thunell.

It’s also worth noting that the antitrust lawsuit settlement that paved the way for the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger did not explicitly mention TV studio operations, even as it set benchmarks for the number of feature film releases from the Warner Bros. and Paramount movie studios. The primary TV provisions in the settlement concern carriage agreements with cable and satellite operators and the editorial independence of CBS News and CNN. Even though the combined Warner Bros. TV Studios and CBS Studios produce some 150 series, including international co-productions, that side of the business went unremarked on.

The combination of the two studios will also likely result in layoffs. “We know there will be questions about what this means for individual teams,” Cheeks wrote in a memo to staff Wednesday (read it in full, below). “HR will share more information as plans are finalized.” It will also mean one fewer place for writers and producers to pitch and sell series projects.
The text of Cheeks’ memo outlining the changes is below.

Today, I’m sharing an important next step for how our television studios will serve the creative community. We are combining the Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios into one studio, which will operate as Warner Bros. Television Studios, beginning in early 2027. Until then, both studios will continue to operate independently.

This move aligns our leadership, resources and creative focus for two studios with considerable success producing for streaming, as well as broadcast. By bringing these teams together, we can build on their strengths and create an even stronger home for great talent and great storytelling.

Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell will be Presidents of Warner Bros. Television Studios, jointly leading the combined studio and reporting to me, with oversight of its creative departments and an expansive and growing portfolio of scripted and unscripted programming. They are exceptional creative leaders who understand how to support talent, champion bold ideas and build strong partnerships across our industry. Channing and Matt will also oversee BET Studios and Warner Bros. International Television Production studios around the world.

David Stapf continues in his role as President of CBS Studios, reporting to me, building on the studio’s strength as one of the industry’s leading global studios. Home to many of the Network’s biggest franchises and hits, David and his team remain a critical supplier to our broadcast business while continuing to grow their streaming footprint. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will operate under the CBS Studios umbrella.

Collectively, Warner Bros. Television Studios and CBS Studios present two powerful creative engines with extraordinary talent, award-winning programming, hit franchises and the global scale to serve Skydance platforms and third-party partners across the industry. Add to that, CBS Entertainment, led by Amy Reisenbach, and the Global Cable Media team under Channing, Skydance TV is a creative force in entertainment across scripted, unscripted and live events.

Channing, Matt and David will be connecting with teams in the coming weeks to talk more about the new structure. We know there will be questions about what this means for individual teams. HR will share more information as plans are finalized.

I’m excited about what we’re building. We have extraordinary creative talent, an unmatched portfolio and tremendous opportunity ahead. Bringing these teams together gives us an even stronger foundation to support storytellers, champion great ideas and bring exceptional television to audiences around the world.

items.title: Will the Kennedy Center Honors Go Full Trump?
items.description: Never mind who’s onstage at this year’s Kennedy Center Honors. Keep an eye on the banners.
items.author: Benjamin Svetkey; Julian Sancton Editors
paragraphs: Never mind who’s onstage at this year’s Kennedy Center Honors. Keep an eye on the banners.

Donald Trump’s efforts to put his name on the performing arts institution continue to be thwarted by a federal court. But this year, while the Kennedy Center’s main building is closed for renovations — and still, after five months, remains shrouded by a tarp hiding the building’s original signage — the Dec. 7 honors ceremony is moving to Washington’s Capital One Arena, where the judge’s no-name-changing order may not apply.

“The injunction may only block Trump from affixing his name to the physical building that’s owned by the federal government,” says a source familiar with the Kennedy Center’s inner workings, noting that it remains “a very good question” as to whether there will be “Trump-Kennedy Center” branding at the Capital One event. After all, we know how much the president loves top billing.

If Trump’s name does end up on posters and programs, it’s unlikely the recipients will object too strenuously. This year’s crop of honorees — David Mamet, Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia and Barbara Mandrell — ranges from outspoken Trump admirers to, at least publicly, Trump agnostics. Mamet has enthusiastically championed the president; Anka performed a modified version of “My Way” at Mar-a-Lago (“When we vote your way”); and Foster hosted a fund-raiser for Trump-backed L.A. mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt.
“In normal times, the board was 50-50 Democrat and Republicans,” says the source. “But Trump is now chairman of the board, so he’s making the final decisions.”

Also in normal times, honorees were traditionally announced in midsummer. But this year, like last, they came months later. The holdup in 2025 was apparently because of Tom Cruise, who kept the board dangling while considering the invitation before finally deciding he had “scheduling conflicts.” It’s unknown who, if anyone, kept the board hanging this year, but they still haven’t announced a lineup of presenters and performers. Those names could provide an even more revealing measure of Hollywood’s willingness to participate in the Trump-Kennedy Center Honors — or whatever they end up being called.
Also in Rambling Reporter:

Taz F. Stark used to run the hottest club in London. Today, he’s a first-time director whose harrowing short film is wowing folks like Al Pacino, Bill Nighy and Rufus Swell; The 4DX seat-shaking theater tech is supposed to make audiences feel part of the action. But then came Wicker.

items.title: Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul
items.description: Keeping up with Alix Earle is beyond the capacity of most mere mortals. Over the past year alone, Earle could be found delivering a perfect foxtrot on Dancing With the Stars weeks before shimmying alongside Pedro Pascal and Cardi B on Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Ha
items.author: Chris Gardner
paragraphs: Keeping up with Alix Earle is beyond the capacity of most mere mortals. Over the past year alone, Earle could be found delivering a perfect foxtrot on Dancing With the Stars weeks before shimmying alongside Pedro Pascal and Cardi B on Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Halftime Show; vibing to Lady Gaga’s Coachella set and hours later lecturing a Harvard Business School class about the creator economy; falling in sky-high platforms at Kendall Jenner’s L.A. Halloween party, then strolling New York’s CFDA Awards red carpet (bruises hidden) in a gown styled by Law Roach. For weeks this summer, she cruised in a yacht along the Sardinia coast with Kylie Jenner BFF Stassie Karanikolaou, flying to Los Angeles for the Sept. 1 premiere of her Netflix reality series Earle Meets World (a global top 10 debut just renewed for a second season), all while weathering headlines about a rumored fling with Tom Brady and the messy fallout of a business rift with Call Her Daddy‘s Alex Cooper.

The quickest way to locate this 25-year-old jet-set influencer is, of course, on TikTok, where her videos have attracted 8.7 million followers, with each post garnering view counts in the millions (not to mention 1.7 billion likes) for documenting all of the above in real time. Her meteoric rise on social media kicked off during the pandemic, filming “get ready with me” makeup tutorials in between marketing classes, wild party nights, battles with anxiety and a breast-implant “boobaversary,” while she attended the University of Miami. She reads as a sorority girl, but IRL, her vibe is more tough-cookie-from-a-Jersey-construction-family who exudes the kind of warmth that might have you bellied to the bar, sipping margs and having a kiki.
At the moment, though, seated in a sunny conference room inside Reale Actives’ Beverly Hills office, she’s taking her magnetic energy and putting it to work on keeping her winning streak alive.

Less than eight months ago, on March 31, Earle launched Reale Actives, a skin care brand formulated in collaboration with dermatologist Kiran Mian and tailored for sensitive and acne-prone skin. Developed in secret for two years, the four-product launch drew a record-breaking response from Earle’s online community — a fiercely supportive tribe, particularly after she shared a years-long, psychologically debilitating struggle with cystic acne. It generated $1 million in sales in less than five minutes. By midday, sales hit $5 million, and by 4 p.m., all products and sets had sold out completely.

It’s nearly lunchtime on a late-October day, and Earle, at the head of the table, is introducing five members of her team: CEO Andrea Blieden, director of influencer marketing and partnerships Katie Clementi, brand director Brianna Ellis-Mitchell, social director Logan Reynolds and, on Zoom, chief marketing officer Amanda Goetz. By year’s end, there will be 23 full-time employees across two office floors.

The brain trust is gathered to evaluate a top-secret item that will hit Reale Actives’ site in March to mark the brand’s one-year anniversary. Will it fit in with the rest of the product line, including the recently launched Go Calm serum? Is it giving REI? Does it need more branding? Maybe a free gift with purchase or a fun slogan? (“Zit girl” could work, but men buy the products, too, so maybe “dirty thoughts, clean skin”?) Do we like the shape?

Everyone weighs in. “Yes, I have my own opinions,” Earle says after the meeting ends, “but I trust their points of view. We all want the same thing: Everything we put our name on and ask our community to purchase with their hard-earned money must be the best product with the best quality.”

Blieden, whose résumé includes executive posts at Kiehl’s and The Body Shop, says Earle is totally dialed in and personally tests samples nonstop. “We have nine different text channels that include Alix,” she says. “She’s not like other celebrity or influencer founders. She is truly involved.” True to form, Earle connects directly with her consumers whenever she can. “I’ve seen her in every situation when people approach her, and she always stops to talk, introduce herself and get names. She gets addresses and sends product,” says the CEO. Once, when a user was having a hard time with breakouts, Earle had the company fly the fan to New York for a consultation with the Reale Actives dermatologist. All this while assiduously keeping up her prolific content creation, often with multiple posts daily. The day I visited, Earle posted a GRWM video that featured her putting on makeup and selecting an office fit for our interview: a gray cashmere sweater and pants, Saint Laurent Brigitte patent pumps and a Mombasa purse. It has since been viewed 1.3 million times.

“If you were to ask me, at any point before I was doing anything on social media, what I would want my career or end goal to be, I would have said having a brand of my own,” says Earle. “My dad and his brothers have a construction company together, and seeing how passionate they are about it has always been inspiring. I didn’t know exactly what kind of company I wanted or that it would come so early for me. The second I got this massive opportunity online, it was great — but I also understood that it can be fleeting. You have relevancy one moment, and it’s gone the next.”

Earle’s father, Thomas “TJ” Earle, says he never doubted his daughter’s ability to achieve a goal. “In her youth, she was a terrible basketball player, but she didn’t care. She was really small, but she went out there and gave it 100 percent. It didn’t matter that people thought she wasn’t good at it,” says TJ, who heads up Earle construction while managing the careers of Alix and her influencer sister, Ashtin. (Alix is repped by a powerful team that also includes senior agents at UTA and attorney Kevin Yorn.) “She did the same on TikTok. She was always giving the camera to somebody and asking them to take videos of her wherever we went. We all made fun of her and gave her the nickname ‘TikTok.’ She knew she wanted to do it and just kept powering through.”

TJ recalls Alix, while still in college, calling home excitedly to say that brands were offering her $250 for sponsored posts. These days, she reportedly commands between $250,000 and $500,000 per post for a one-off brand collab. While TJ won’t confirm exact figures, he says all her deals have one common denominator: “It always comes down to whether or not she truly likes it.” If she really likes it, he says she may “even do it for free.” Recently, Earle agreed to a deal to promote what she later said on TikTok was a foundation, but after trying the product, she realized she couldn’t in good faith endorse it. She told her agent to cancel the contract. “In some way, it feels so silly to be throwing away insane amounts of money,” she says, “but I really do just believe in longevity and maintaining that trust with my audience.” (Earle endorses and backs Cymbiotika supplements, GORGIE energy drink, SipMargs margaritas and was an early investor in Poppi, which sold to PepsiCo for $1.95 billion.)

Before launching Reale Actives, Earle fielded offers to become the face of several brands, deals that came with the freedom to claim she “did everything” to build it but meant she didn’t have to lift a finger beyond signing her checks. It never interested her. “This started as a concept in my head, and I want to be a part of every single little decision and detail,” Earle says. “The team does a great job of taking some of the front load off so that when we get in here, there are already different directions we can choose to go in.”

Earle does the hiring interviews herself. “The first two roles I interviewed were for a CEO and dermatologist. I’d just graduated college, so I was trying to find people who would share the same passion for the brand because I didn’t know how to rate their experience since I didn’t have any.” Blieden says she interviewed with Earle four times, put together a project presentation and underwent a surprise test. “It had come down to me and another candidate, and on a Saturday, Alix sent us each a text message that said, ‘Hey, I’ve been thinking about some stuff about the brand. Would love to discuss it with you,’ ” recalls Blieden. “I responded in 1.2 seconds because I was so excited. I guess the other person responded Monday.”

The hustle culture may not be for everyone, but there are no days off on social media. “She is lovely to work with, but she’s a beast and doesn’t mess around,” says the CEO. Adds TJ: “If you look at her calendar, it’s filled seven days a week, crisscrossing the country, meetings, events, photo shoots. Nobody could keep up with her pace. She’s just an animal.”

Earle describes scrapping the launch video they’d “spent so much time and budget on.” The clip was just “vibes,” nothing memorable. They jettisoned it for a nearly nude video featuring Earle dripping wet, unretouched — as all Reale Actives imagery has been since — to normalize imperfect skin. “I wanted people to think that two things can coexist: The line can be efficacious for your skin, but it can also be daring, fun and sexy. Skin care doesn’t have to be clinical and boring.”

The rollout ran on Earle’s knack for turning fans into co-conspirators, beginning with an Instagram account, @wtfisalixdoing, that dropped hints about the launch and continuing with influencers receiving locked suitcases containing a single puzzle piece, and a blank billboard in New York’s SoHo that put the pieces together one by one until the puzzle was completed, at which time creators received codes for unlocking the Reale Actives swag inside their suitcases. The award-winning campaign spanned a week, after having been fueled for weeks prior by Easter eggs on Earle’s social accounts.

Nick Brown, co-founder of venture capital firm Imaginary, which backs the brand and has also invested in Kim Kardashian’s Skims, Glossier, Farfetch and Tom Holland’s Bero, explains what has become known as “the Alix Earle Effect.” “You can count on a very small number of hands the number of times a creator has been able to move product at such a force that you start to realize it as an investor,” he says. “It’s seismic and not one-off. I kept seeing her do this — for mass brands, masstige brands, luxury brands, in beauty and in apparel. She really has a deep understanding for the brands she connects with and, more specifically, the connection between her own passion and what her audience will respond to. That’s why it’s organic and works so well.” Brands that enjoyed the boom included Giorgio Armani Beauty, Drunk Elephant, Patrick Ta Beauty, Charlotte Tilbury, Mielle Organics and NYX Makeup. Now that she’s applied her magic touch to Reale Actives, Brown confirms the business is already “very profitable” less than a year in and, he forecasts, is well on its way to becoming “a multi-hundred-million-dollar net revenue business.” Likening Reale Actives to Hailey Bieber’s Rhode and Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty, he says, “She is constantly thinking about how to turn left, create an element of surprise and do something that’s a slightly different riff on what’s been done, enough to make people stop and say, ‘That was really cool.’ She is otherworldly when it comes to that.”

Despite what may seem like a charmed path to a reported $20 million net worth (so far), Earle has hit some speed bumps, facing criticism that it was her several rounds of Accutane, long considered a silver bullet, and not Reale Actives that cleared her skin. “I knew that was coming,” she says matter-of-factly. “But [the criticism] was not something I was afraid of because the truth is the truth. After I finished Accutane for the third time, my skin went back to being a mess and was probably worse than ever before. The moment that people started talking about it, I made a video and I showed my skin journey and was like, ‘Here’s before I did Accutane, here’s after I did Accutane, here’s before I started the products and here’s after I started the products.’ I have nothing to hide. I’m not lying. I actually use these products and nothing else.”

Earle also bore the brunt of the “negativity bandwagon” when she surfaced videos of her long (by American standards) European summer holiday. “Things got so negative this summer that it really helped me thicken my skin and gain a little bit more confidence in myself, knowing that you’re not going to be able to correct every narrative out there,” she says. “As a female founder, people want to put you into this box of ‘you can’t have.’ But you can let loose and have fun and share the human moments that we all have.”

Jumping from the phone screen to the small screen for Earle Meets World was also an adjustment. The series featured her divorced parents, TJ and Alisa Earle; her stepmom, Ashley (as in Dupré, the woman at the center of a 2008 sex scandal involving former New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer); four siblings and mom Alisa’s boyfriend, Todd. “I was worried going into it because I wasn’t sure if I would be able to connect with people in a different way than on socials,” she says. “But it gave people a completely different perspective on my life. As scary and embarrassing as those moments are, I really, really loved doing it.” Earle, who works with an acting coach, has passed on all scripts that have come her way, more out of fear of getting it wrong than anything else: “I only want to do something if it’s the right fit or I could be good at embodying that character.”

The season ended with Earle’s first on-camera comments about the falling-out with Cooper. Back in 2023, Earle and her podcast, Hot Mess, became the first creators signed to Cooper’s media network, Unwell. The deal lasted 18 months, at which point Earle found out she’d been dropped from Unwell when it broke in the media. “I constantly felt taken advantage of and used and mistreated and manipulated,” Earle said on her reality show, with her father adding that the podcast wasn’t given basic resources like video crews. Cooper has yet to comment on the drama.

Earle also recently faced a wave of criticism when she told a magazine that she’s never read a book. “Let’s clear the air: I have definitely read a book,” Earle tells me with a smile. “But no, I don’t actively read. I’m not reading anything right now.” (Other than — wink, wink — Daddy Issues, by Sofia Franklyn, who also had beef with Cooper; Earle posted a clip of herself perusing the title on TikTok overlayed with audio from Barstool Sports podcast hosts Dan Katz and Eric Sollenberger criticizing her admission. The clip had drawn 9.3 million views as of press time.)

A big teachable moment came in the form of her evolving relationship with her father as manager (dad-ager?): “She would not respond to emails, answer my calls or would roll her eyes at me in a meeting, which is typical stuff for a 20-something to do to their dad, but not someone you work with. Finally, I said, ‘Alix, listen, I’ve been doing this a long time with family, and here’s how it needs to work. There’s Dad, and then when it’s business, you treat me no differently than you would treat anybody else on the team.’ She’s super respectful to everyone, so that was easy for her.”

Running a business with multiple revenue streams and being smart about money were modeled by her dad, after all. She says, “I’m saving a lot, so some goes into a retirement fund, and I’ve invested in different stocks and bonds beyond the company investments. I always have the understanding that this can go away at any time, so I always keep that at the back of my mind.”
This story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: From Book Club to Netflix: How Katherine Center’s ‘The Bodyguard’ Became ‘Guarding Stars’
items.description: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
items.author: Lexy Perez
paragraphs: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

When director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum first scrolled through BookTok, she had an epiphany. The Purple Hearts director, whose credits also include Aquamarine, the upcoming Aquamarine pilot for Disney and Ramona and Beezus, kept finding fan-made lists of the romance tropes readers love most: enemies to lovers, forced proximity and only one bed. She recognized some from her own work.
“Oh my God, I’ve been called out. I’m a cliché,” she remembers thinking. Then she started taking notes.

By the time she was developing the Netflix romance film Guarding Stars, those notes had become a working checklist. “Any time there wasn’t enough enemies-to-lovers in the script, I’d say, ‘We need more enemy here! Where’s the enemy?’” Rosenbaum tells The Hollywood Reporter.

Those notes and being attuned to what fans of the book and romance readers want ended up shaping her new film Guarding Stars, Netflix’s adaptation of Katherine Center’s 2022 novel The Bodyguard, which premieres on the streamer on Nov. 18. Leighton Meester stars as Hannah Brooks, a bodyguard assigned to protect movie star Jack Stapleton (Jared Padalecki) and ends up posing as his girlfriend while staying with him at his family’s Montana ranch over the holidays. But just as readers were top of mind for Rosenbaum, the film’s road to the screen started with that audience too. Producer Genevieve Padalecki selected Center‘s book for her Instagram book club, which led to an Instagram Live with the author and, months later, an option.

As studios and streamers turn to romance novels for their built-in audiences, the people who made Guarding Stars say they kept Center’s fans in mind at every step, from the script to the Easter eggs. In separate conversations with THR, members of the creative team behind the film detail how the new holiday romance came together.
Author Katherine Center and Genevieve Padelecki first bonded after Padelecki selected The Bodyguard as her online book club pick. The kinship led to interest in adapting it.

KATHERINE CENTER (AUTHOR): Gen got in touch and said she wanted to feature The Bodyguard in her online book club. Back then it was just Instagram. Of course I said yes, and we did an Instagram Live together, and I instantly fell madly in love with Genevieve Padalecki, because she’s a book person. She had the best possible book-person, English-major energy. When you’re a writer and you talk to a lot of readers, you can tell when somebody genuinely loves books for all the right reasons, people who just love getting lost in stories. The minute I met her, I thought, “Oh, she loves stories.” I could have gone for 10 hours.

I thought that would be that. What a lovely treat. Then, maybe six months later they circled back about wanting to option it. I said, yes, please, no pressure. And I don’t know how we got here, but here we are.

GENEVIEVE PADALECKI (PRODUCER): One thing I love about Katherine’s books is that they have strong female leads who aren’t wilting flowers. They’re women with a struggle, a backstory. They’re not crippled by the chips in their armor; it actually reinforces them. And then on top of that, you have the flip side of the bodyguard story: a tiny, petite, Lilliputian female bodyguard guarding a male celebrity.

I immediately thought, this would be so fun for Jared [Padalecki]. The book has all the wonderful tropes we love in a rom-com, the things we come back to and watch on repeat. So I turned to Jared and said, “We have to find a way to partner with Katherine and bring this to life.”
“We Have to Do This Movie!”
After finding a home at Netflix, a team was assembled including director Liz Allen Rosenbaum and producers and co-writers Gina Matthews, Grant Scharbo, Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith.
PADALECKI: When we came to Netflix with this story, they got it immediately. They loved this story so much, and it just became a natural fit.

GINA MATTHEWS (PRODUCER/WRITER): Netflix reached out to us [herself and producer-husband Grant Scharbo] when they were considering the book. Jared and Gen had brought it to them, and they were looking for people who had produced and written a lot in the rom-com and holiday space, because Gen and Jared were new to that as producers. I produced What Women Want, 13 Going on 30 and Isn’t It Romantic. It’s a genre that’s really close to our hearts, and it’s hard to do well.

We loved Katherine’s book because of the way she writes characters, and she’s not afraid to go to emotional places. It’s funny, and it’s high-concept; it has everything that makes a book a solid, strong movie adaptation. But what we also loved is that there’s real heart and real trauma these characters have to get over on this journey, inside a big, fun holiday romantic comedy with action. We love movies that take audiences on that ride, where you’re laughing, and then you’re crying, and you’re like, “Oh my God, I was literally laughing 20 minutes ago, and now I’m in tears.”

RICHARD KEITH (WRITER): Gina sent it to us [himself and co-writer Erin Cardillo] to see if we were interested. I put the audiobook on [while] leaving L.A., and about two hours in, I had to pull over to charge the car. I texted Gina: “Oh my God, we have to do this movie. I’m obsessed with this book!“ Erin and I are both huge fans of old-school, Richard Curtis-style rom-coms, and there are very few where the two leads get to spend most of the movie together.
ERIN CARDILLO (WRITER): I just loved it! She’s a delightful writer: whimsical and funny, with characters so specifically drawn. We both fell in love with it.

ELIZABETH ALLEN ROSENBAUM (DIRECTOR): It came to me as a director-for-hire project, and I’d been really choosy about those, because I was developing my own material. But my agent said, “It’s a go movie. You should really take it seriously.” So I read it, and the moment Hannah flips Jack on that tarmac, I thought, “Oh! I’ve actually never seen anything like this” where the woman was the strong one. I’ve only done female-oriented projects my whole career, and I’d never seen anything where the woman was the strong one. I had to put everything else aside for a minute and make this.
“Everybody Shared the Same North Star” — Putting Readers First
With a built-in audience already for Center’s bestseller, the creative team always had readers at top of mind when sorting out how to bring it to life onscreen.

ROSENBAUM: Believe it or not, almost every movie and pilot I’ve done has been based on a book. But Purple Hearts [which Rosenbaum directed] came as BookTok was taking off, and I wasn’t really acquainted with it. It had a very small budget and no big marketing campaign, and when it started to take off, I was like, “What’s happening?” We knocked The Gray Man, a $200 million movie, right off the top spot, and it was because of that grassroots groundswell of well-read, cool women. So I started spending all this time on BookTok accounts, trying to understand it.

They kept talking about tropes, and I grew up thinking those were bad. They make lists of the tropes they love [including] “enemies to lovers,“ “there’s only one bed“ and you’ve got to have “forced proximity.“ These are all words I’ve learned. The first time I said one, I’d have died of embarrassment: “Oh my God, I’ve been called out. I’m a cliché.” But then I started taking notes. And I realized tropes are good, and I love tropes!

So on Guarding Stars, any time there wasn’t enough enemies-to-lovers in the script, I’d say, “We need more enemy here! Where’s the enemy?” We did a few drafts after I came on board, and there are plenty of things in this movie that I learned from what people enjoy and want. I’m feeding off the audience too, and I love them.
MATTHEWS: We love that enemies-to-lovers trope. We really do. That conflict, getting under each other’s skin, is one of our most fun things to write.

MATTHEWS: For Gen, with her book club, she really knows the emotional core of what’s going to resonate with those fans. And ironically, those fans are movie fans. Book fans and movie fans are the same in this genre.

PADALECKI: Katherine’s fans in the book world are akin to the Supernatural fans. She has a very loud, excited audience. What was so fun was making sure we reached out to that audience. We did a thing about the title, and we made sure there were Easter eggs throughout that are very important to the story. Katherine’s input in keeping us on track was integral to making this film.
GRANT SCHARBO (PRODUCER/WRITER): Having a built-in audience definitely does not make it easier. You have this fear of disappointment.

MATTHEWS: Everybody shared the same North Star: What are the most important things in the book that Katherine’s readers care about? The parts you found so emotional you cried? Or the part where she flips him at the opening of the movie, which is in the trailer? We wanted to keep those touchstones, especially because we weren’t able to use the title The Bodyguard. Of course we all wanted to, but there’s only one Bodyguard movie!

ROSENBAUM: Katherine knows her audience so well. I don’t just mean psychologically. I mean she actually knows them. She makes a point of it and does so many things in person. Jared and Genevieve do that too. It’s this cyclical, beautiful circle that keeps feeding itself. And Katherine guided me through that. She knows what readers love about her book, and it’s been really helpful to have her blessing and her guidance.
“They Brought Those Scenes to Life”
Casting Jared Padalecki, “a rat-a-tat-tat, Bogart-and-Bacall romantic lead,“ and Leighton Meester, the “rom-com heroine we’ve all been waiting for” as the film’s leads.

PADALECKI: I said, “Jared, you have to read this book. It’s so fun.” At the time he was filming Walker; we were juggling three kids, and we were just coming out of the pandemic. He read it and was so excited. I don’t want to speak for him, but I think initially he was a little nervous. He’d never played a very confident, swaggering character like Jack Stapleton. But he was a pretty easy sell.

ROSENBAUM: Jared was already attached when I came on board. It felt like a perfect fit. Before I signed on the dotted line, I watched a lot of his material. What hooked me was all his behind-the-scenes footage, because his character on Supernatural wasn’t a flirty, bantery character. But there’s an enormous amount of BTS on the internet with his co-star, and they’re so funny together. He’s a born rat-a-tat-tat, Bogart-and-Bacall romantic lead. I mean, part of the reason he hadn’t done a movie in a long time is because he’d been so busy and sought after for 20-some-odd years. I mean, who has that streak? He happened to be available. I was like, this is just perfect.
CENTER: Jared Padalecki was born to play Jack! He totally nailed everything about that character. And can I also say he should just be in every rom-com ever?

KEITH: He was instrumental in the development of the script. He and Gen loved the book, and he was adamant that we stay true to who Jack was. But in the book, Jack is pretty wonderful. His flaws are few and far between. To Jared’s credit, and some actors shy away from this, he really wanted to find some flaws in this man so we could give him room to grow. It was awesome to see him do that, especially in the scenes with Noah LaLonde. They’re really moving. The love story between the two brothers is just as integral to the plot as the love story between Leighton and Jared’s characters.

MATTHEWS: Jared had a lot to do, because Jack is kind of a jerk. It’s the same as Mel Gibson in What Women Want. He could get away with so much because he was so charming. You’re like, “I want to smack you, but I kind of want to kiss you!“

ROSENBAUM: Leighton’s a queen. She doesn’t have to audition anymore. I’d worked with her on Gossip Girl, just one episode, way back when it was getting started, but you learn enough in a few weeks to see the depth of somebody. She was so sharp with her comedy as Blair Waldorf. And apparently she had made a wish, or a New Year’s resolution, that action comedy would come her way, and then we sent her the script.

CARDILLO: When her name came up in the casting process, we were both like, “Oh my God, yes, that would be so great.” She’s unsuspecting as a bodyguard. You don’t think of her that way, but she really is tough in this movie, and it’s something we haven’t seen her do before.

KEITH: It needs to be someone unassuming enough to be Jared’s bodyguard without the parents suspecting but with that innate strength. I’d like to think we wrote a lot of funny lines for her, but she was never playing at being a bodyguard. She never acted like she was aware of the jokes.

PADALECKI: I remember in some of our first meetings, her descriptions of how she saw the characters brought so much depth and humor that I didn’t even know was in Hannah. She’s truly one of the hardest-working humans I’ve ever met.

CENTER: She’s the rom-com heroine we’ve all been waiting for. She does this perfect balance of tough but vulnerable. You want somebody you can admire, with a lot of moxie. But I also want her to break my heart a little bit. Yes, in real life she’s a movie star. But in this movie, she’s me. She can take Jared Padalecki and flip him over like that, but there are also things that scare her.

MATTHEWS: You can write that crackle on the page, but you don’t know how it’s going to be. Neither of them comes at it from a place that feels false or disingenuous. It was really about character for both of them, and they brought those scenes to life in a way we couldn’t have dreamed of.
The team shifted the story to become a holiday film that serves as a “love story to families.”

SCHARBO: We made it a Christmas movie. In the book, it was Thanksgiving. It’s a beloved book, and we know we have to make changes to adapt it, so it’s a lot of pressure to adapt something people love. We ran a lot of things by Katherine. “How do you feel about this?” And she would say, “I think they’ll be OK with that.”

CENTER: My books are emotionally cozy. I want them to feel like a hug in story form. When you’re telling a story in visuals, and you have the contrast between very cold, snowy stuff outside and fireplaces and twinkle lights and candles inside, it helps you tell that story. This is a story about people who are out in the cold at the start, and then they find a way to reconnect with their families and themselves. You don’t just understand it intellectually; you feel it.

CARDILLO: The book takes place over a longer period, and for a feature, condensing the time frame made a lot of sense. It makes it a little bigger for a movie, more fun to play with those holiday tropes. The stakes of spending Christmas with your family, versus just a stretch of time with them, were really appealing.

KEITH: In movies, you want those scenes where you go, “Here’s where the movie really starts.” Andie MacDowell lying in a bed saying, “Well, you guys are going to stay for Christmas, right?” is such a concrete way into the concept that it was a no-brainer.

ROSENBAUM: The story is really a love story to families. [Hannah]’s not only falling in love with [Jack]; she’s falling in love with the family, and she never knew she needed that. With movies, you have to turbocharge things. To me, Christmas is everything family is about. It’s the one time a year I see my whole extended family. You need a bigger holiday, where everybody’s home, people fly in and there’s magic. When I came on board, I had a big meeting with Netflix about making it even more about family.

KEITH: We really loved the parents’ relationship being aspirational for the two leads. It has obviously informed the sons’ opinions of what love should be, but we wanted that for Leighton’s character as well. She grew up with a broken picture of what love could or should be. We really loved that in the book she’s not just falling in love with this guy, but with this family, and with the understanding that she deserves to be loved. It’s a love story on many levels.
“This Is Better Than the Book”
Slight creative liberties were taken when adapting the book, in particular with the family dynamic. One change even made the author prefer it over her original take.

PADALECKI: This is Katherine’s baby. She worked on this for a long time to put these words, these ideas and these characters onto the page. As a producer, taking it into a new medium, where we have to take the scalpel and dissect it and put it back together, means making sure the integrity is still there and that we’re honoring Katherine’s words.

MATTHEWS: In the book, Hank is the older brother, but in the movie he’s Jack’s younger brother. And there were no kids in the book. That came when Liz came on. She thought there should be a family that represents the life Jack didn’t have. If it’s a younger brother who got left behind, there’s such an emotional feeling of abandonment. Hank is still angry. He still has all this resentment. But it’s grounded in feeling abandoned by the brother who should have been there to take care of him. I think fans will understand why and feel it’s a layered choice that still stays true to the book.

We also wanted to see [Hannah] do her job. In the book, once they got to the ranch, they mostly stayed there, and it was about the relationship. She’s a female bodyguard who is underestimated by everyone. No one sees her coming, which is her superpower. So we asked, how can we create sequences that are cinematic and show her doing her job? At our test screenings, people who had read the book loved that. They got to see it in action and connected to her character even more.

CENTER: The moment when Jared Padalecki gets out of the helicopter is not in the book. This is better than the book. In the book, she meets him at the house he’s renting, and it’s fine. I have no beef with my own scene. But the movie makes so much more of that moment: he’s getting out of a helicopter, he’s got aviators on, slow motion through the snow. I’m like, “This is so much better!”
“A Family Event in Every Way”
During filming, the cast’s families were always present with even Padalecki‘s son acting in a scene while Walker Hayes’ wife was present for an onscreen kiss.

ROSENBAUM: For about four months of prep, Jared and Gen were in every Zoom meeting. I was up in Calgary and they were in Austin, working out of their house, so I got to know their family. The kids would pop in and say hi. I thought, this movie’s about family, so you need your whole family in it. One of his sons plays the young version of him. He auditioned, because I didn’t want to put someone in who’d flounder, and he did a fantastic job! Jared had a grueling schedule, and it was so cold, and he stayed the whole time his son was shooting. In one scene, with the safety rules for little kids, it was Gen’s hands in an oven mitt, puppeteering it as if they were the kids’ hands. It was a family event in every way.

Walker Hayes had auditioned for Hank. All of his kids helped him with that audition, giving him notes offscreen. I thought, “He’s interested in acting. Why don’t I make him the sheriff?“ The sheriff was written as about 65, and everyone said, “We can’t have a singing hot sheriff.” Yes, we can!

[Hayes] and his wife met doing Little Shop of Horrors in high school, and the sheriff is supposed to kiss someone for the kiss cam. He said, “I can’t kiss anyone unless it’s my wife.” We had to appeal to the Canadian government to fly her up. It’s their onscreen debut together.

CENTER: My novel-writing life is very isolated. I drive down to Galveston Island and spend four or five days alone with my imaginary friends. It’s me and the dog. So when I visited the set, I was blinking back tears the whole time, because everywhere I went there were people 100 percent invested in this story. Their whole month was about how to bring it to life, and the project just happened to be my book. I got to take my mother, and we spent a full day bebopping around the set. I’m the middle of three girls, and we’re always in a light competition over who our mother loves most. I got some street cred in that fight that I may never have to give up.
“Books Are Leading the Charge”
With the film coming amid a time when romance adaptations are continuing to make their way onscreen, the creative team says love stories are a “force to be reckoned with.”

ROSENBAUM: The largely female audience reading the books is strong and vocal, so they’re guiding the studios toward what they like and what to make. I think that’s so democratic. When I started in this industry 25 years ago, that was not the case. It was really hard, first, to get directing gigs as a woman, and second, to get taken seriously with female content.

SCHARBO: If you asked most people what they want more than anything in the world, the answer would be love. And books are leading the charge. It actually never went away in books. What happened is that movies took a pause from these stories. They got replaced by comic books, dark or action or genre, on the thinking that you need big spectacle to bring people to theaters. That’s not how movies originated, and it’s not how they are today.

KEITH: Growing up in the ’90s, there were so many [love stories]. People our age who grew up with those movies were starved for them, and we want our kids to see love put on a pedestal. People were ready to see characters who weren’t in latex or didn’t have a superpower find each other.

CARDILLO: The world feels a little dark and isolating for a lot of people right now. There’s something about reading about connection and love, and watching it on screen, that gives people a feeling of connectedness, hope and escape from what they’re dealing with.

CENTER: Love stories are being treated more like a force to be reckoned with these days, which I love. Broadly speaking, it’s the most eye-rolled-at genre. For years I’ve been asking, why is people falling in love more ridiculous than zombies? This happens every day. Why do we believe in zombies but not humans? The fact that people are watching movies like this and reading books like this and standing up for love in this new way allows more stories like this to be told. It feels a little bit like a movement.
Guarding Stars releases on Netflix on Nov. 18.
A previous version of this story misidentified Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith as producers. They are credited as screenwriters.

items.title: Matt Damon on the Oscars, Tarantino, and the Roles That Got Away
items.description: In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollyw
items.author: Frazier Tharpe; Richard Burbridge
paragraphs: In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollywood, and specifically on a year that will go down as one of that career’s most challenging and rewarding passages.

Damon set 2026 off with The Rip, a throwback pulp thriller that reteamed him with his lifetime BFF Ben Affleck. He then went on to dominate the summer to a degree most actors crossing the other side of 55 wouldn’t dream of, with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey—a noisy, thrilling, engrossing feat of big-budget moviemaking that wouldn’t have worked without an Odysseus compelling enough to command audiences to take the 20-year journey with him. The role demanded everything in Damon’s toolbox, and then some, but the result was a cultural and commercial run that only Spider-Man himself could top.

This is rare air, and Damon knows it. Lightning struck once for him, with Good Will Hunting in 1997—he never thought he’d see that happen again, much less 29 years later. If exhaustion is the price of beating those odds, then so be it. Still readjusting to life on dry land, Damon sat down to unpack the most unlikely filmmaking experience of his career—and begin working out where he might want to go next.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
Matt Damon: That is amazing coming from him. Yes, I did hear about it.

Yeah, I think if you talk to any actor my age, any of the usual suspects, they’d probably say the same thing. I think the more you do it, if you’re working with really good people, you’re always improving, you’re getting better. And then you’re living more life and you have your family dynamics, all of your primary relationships kind of fill up your reservoir. I’ve talked to other actors my age about it, Ben included—I think there’s a tendency to push when you’re younger, a little bit, to try to work yourself up, and the older you get, the more available a lot of this stuff is. These very, very, very big emotions are kind of just sitting [near the surface]. And so you can really relax into the work, and it can be very full without being forced.
I think so, yeah. I mean, I’ve never been a part of a movie like The Odyssey that was…. Well, I guess Oppenheimer, to an extent, was somewhat of a phenomenon as well.

My workload was a lot heavier on this one, and everybody’s was, and that was kind of the joy of it. We knew we were the first ones to ever try to do a full film in IMAX [70 mm], and that comes with a whole host of challenges for every single department. We were all, I think, very patient with each other because we knew what was being asked of the other people. So in terms of the acting department—the IMAX load is two and a half minutes or three minutes. And so these big, heavy emotional scenes—you couldn’t play them all the way through. You’d have to cut them up. And the crew was just awesome, very patient with us. It felt like we were explorers, in a way. We got to be the first ones to do it, and that really bonded us.

I never would have expected it. And also, to play a role that’s so physical and, at my age, to even have a role that’s available on a scale like this. I’d always wanted to make a David Lean movie. To have it come at this point in my life, I felt incredibly lucky, not only to be able to do it, but also to be able to contextualize it. I don’t think I would’ve appreciated it as much 20 years ago.

No, I just don’t think I would’ve been able to understand and to hold as much gratitude as I am and as I did throughout the process. It’s all about how you look at things. And in retrospect, yeah, we were probably cold and wet. There was a lot of physical discomfort that was temporary. But because I felt so grateful to be there, I was just so excited. I was just so joyful the whole time that I didn’t really notice any of that.
[Laughs] There are no sure things, man. I think that’s where you get into trouble, being like, Well, this is a surefire hit. I’ve heard that before.

I felt it when I saw it. There is that thing that can happen where you make a movie, and you feel like it’s really good, and it just doesn’t connect, and there’s just nothing you can do about that. But as the audience reactions started to come in and the critical reactions were great as well, it was like, Okay….

Chris [Nolan], the most nervous he is in the entire process, from the very beginning to the very end, is the eve of the film coming out. He’s genuinely nervous. He talks openly about it, because that is the moment that you put it out into the world and you have to live with the reaction. Ultimately, the audience decides. Once it opened and the responses were what they were, I think I felt like, We’re going to be okay. It was a big bet in the sense that it was a big budget. I’m not used to playing in that arena. The numbers that movies have to get to just to break even at that level are just so beyond the movies that I’m known for.

A few of them. But The Martian, which I think is the biggest movie that I’ve ever headlined—I think The Odyssey made three times what that made. And that was a real hit for me. But there’s this other league of these kinds of movies that are in the billions that I’ve just never….
[Laughs] It’s just, like, What?

Well, the thing about a role like that is every single day I was paired with an unbelievable scene partner. One day I’d be working with Annie [Hathaway], and then the next day I’d be working with Himesh [Patel]. It’s following this character through all these different stages of his life and people who are close to him. So every day was a different, exciting little challenge, a little puzzle to figure out. I’ve always said that when you’re working with a great actor, they’re so good that they’re good enough for both of you. And it’s almost like this wave comes and you just stand up on your board and ride it. Then you have Samantha Morton, who literally just picks you up and shoulder-carries you.

It’s very hard to come in and do really intense things in a very short time frame. [Morton’s scenes]—that was under a week of shooting. Each day being incredibly intense. And that was what was so incredible about these actors who would come in. They’re under a lot of pressure. Nobody says that, but we all know the deal. These are critical scenes, and everybody just came in and killed it. It just got more and more exciting as we were going.

I agree. She’s incredible. She’s always been incredible. We had a near-miss working together in 2003—and I got to know her then—in a movie with Heath Ledger. I just think the world of her as an actress, and I was excited when we did the scene. I was like, This one’s going to really work. And I hope—it doesn’t always happen right away, but hopefully it’s lodged her back in the minds of people who are making those decisions, because she’s just extraordinary.

That’s the emotional spine of the movie. A lot of that monologue that I have at the end is in voiceover, but I wrote it all out and I had it on my phone and I would just carry it with me off set. I would just revisit it and run through it a few times, and I was doing that for months and months. Firstly, I thought it was just so beautifully written, but also because I knew that scene had to land. If that lands, then the movie works.

And that also means setting them up as a young couple before he leaves. There’s a lot of engineering that goes into getting to a scene like that and then you have to execute it. I spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about that one.

Well, at that point, the audience has been on the journey with you, and it’s been a hell of a journey, so you don’t have to tell them that. We were tired. That scene I shot with Samantha, oddly, we had come from Iceland, but we were shooting nights, and we came to Scotland, and I had it happen two or three times on this movie where I just didn’t sleep. I was tired and I went to bed, and I’m sure everyone’s had that feeling where you’ve got to get up the next day and you have something that you have to do and you can’t fall asleep and you’re kicking the blanket around and you’re staring at the ceiling. By the time I got to work to do the scene with Sam, I hadn’t slept in 24 hours, and by the end of the day it was 36 or whatever. I remember thinking the great thing about this character is he probably didn’t sleep last night. Don’t worry about it. So the weariness was very real for a lot of the movie.
It’s all in there because it’s what I’m actually feeling. As I was saying before, it’s very easy to relax into what’s real and available and to have access to it.

This was the biggest one that we’ve ever done, and we’ve always had a two-week rule. I think the first stretch [on The Odyssey], I was away for three and a half weeks. The first half of the movie was the hardest because the kids were still in school. And then once the summer hit, they could come to set and we could be together. But that first stretch—luckily they’re huge Chris Nolan fans and they knew that it was this incredible role, so they were really supportive, and it was a sacrifice for them, and they were awesome about it.

He’s turned down a lot of work. And in fact, he really wanted to take on the CEO role at [Damon and Affleck’s production company] Artists Equity because it would keep him home. So when he directs—for instance, Animals, that was all shot in LA. He said to me when we started the company—he’s got joint custody, which means he gets to be with the kids half the time. And he said, “If I go to Estonia and do a movie, it’s not like I get that time back.” So that for him means he’s got to stay in LA.
It’s all downhill from here.

I felt that way when I did Air with Ben. It was such a joyful experience, and we had so much fun, and we really loved the movie we made. We had this discussion about how I don’t want to do [a project] unless it’s joyful and unless it’s really right for my life. So much of being a young actor is you’re afraid it’s going to go away. You’re very much still in touch with that feeling of being unemployed. And so when Ben and I got famous, we both really worked. Buried ourselves in work. Partly because people are suddenly offering you things and you can’t imagine turning anything down, right? It just seems counter to everything you’ve been trying so hard to do for your entire life.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Absolutely.

The first time was before The Bourne Identity came out. I had done The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will [Smith] and Charlize [Theron], and that movie didn’t do well. And Will was, as he is now, the biggest star. And so it’s like, it’s not Will’s fault. [Laughs] And then I did All the Pretty Horses with Billy Bob [Thornton], and that was a whole fraught experience. There were different ideas between the studio and between Billy Bob about what the movie should be, and so it ended up getting cut in a way that wasn’t to Billy’s liking and it didn’t do well. And so I had had these misses. And so there was this stretch where the phone just didn’t ring. The silence was…. It was a real rose-colored lenses coming off.

Well, the other thing was that The Bourne Identity was delayed something like a year. And so the word was, That’s going to be a stinker. But in that time, I went right from [filming] Bourne to Ocean’s Eleven. Then there was this whole period of time where nobody was calling, except for Steven Soderbergh, who called and offered me the movie The Informant! And I was so confused. I asked him, “Are you asking me to write it?” Because I couldn’t imagine he was asking me to be in it, because nobody else was calling. He goes, “What? No, Scott Burns is writing it. I want you to be the lead.” And I’ve never forgotten that. He just paid no attention to what everyone else was saying. But anyway, leaving that aside, nobody else was calling. And then The Bourne Identity came out, and it was a big hit.

It’s not personal. It’s business. And people can’t really go out of their way to help you. It’s really a pretty cold calculus that determines whether or not you’re on the list or off the list. And you never know who’s on the list. And the list can be different for different studios, who they’ll greenlight a movie with.

No, no. There’s very, very frank conversations between agents and studio people going like, “I can’t greenlight the movie with X, but I can with Y.” And that list is always changing, and I know that sometimes I’m on it and sometimes I’m not. I just have to remember it’s not personal, but you can feel it if you’re on the list or not.

Yeah. And [the] quality of projects [you’re offered]. I’m sure I’ve worked my way off that list a number of times. I’ve had some movies that didn’t work, and then you got to pay attention. I remember 2012 to 2014-ish, maybe, Patrick [Whitesell], my agent for 35 years, said I was taking a lot of supporting roles—because again, I’m not strategizing at all. I’m just like, Oh, True Grit. I want to work with the Coen brothers. Great.

Yup, George [Clooney directing], great. So there was this string of movies like that. Patrick called me and he said, “You’ll become a supporting actor. We got to think about this next one.” And then what happened to come along was The Martian. But that’s about as much strategizing as we’ve ever done.

Interstellar was in there too. I’m so happy that I’m in that movie. I love the role, even though it’s a tiny part. When Chris offered me [the role], we hadn’t worked together, and [when] he offered me the part in Interstellar, he said, “Do you know that saying ‘There are no small parts, there are only small actors’ ? This is a small part.” But I think he undersold it, because it’s a really kind of pivotal role, and I had a ball doing it.

Yeah, I think I was on a Bourne movie or about to go do Green Zone with Paul Greengrass. That and Milk. I was supposed to play the Dan White part. And I was really excited about it. I’d spoken to Sean [Penn], and I’d started the research. I’d been watching the documentaries about him. Then Sean’s schedule changed and the movie had to push three months, which meant that it was going to conflict with the movie I was going to do with Paul. So I had to bow out, and I just loved that script so much. And I love Gus [Van Sant], obviously. And so that was a bummer. But having said that, they got Josh Brolin, and Josh is absolutely brilliant in the movie. That helped a lot, I think, with this feeling that I have, that I do believe that the right actor gets the part.

I never like to say that, because I don’t want to live with the regret, but I can tell you that I passed on Ted, and I’ve never had this experience where I laughed so hard reading a script. I literally took it to dinner and was reading parts of it out to my friends at dinner. And then I just got too clever by half. I don’t know what I was thinking. I was like, Well, maybe the teddy bear’s actually the best part.…

So I overthought it and I talked myself out of it. And because it shot in Boston, it would’ve been a chance for me to be home—my father’s passed away now, and I look back and I go, Man, that would’ve been six months back [home].
But, again, the right actor got the part. Mark [Wahlberg’s] great, and the movie’s great, and I wouldn’t have made it any better.

They’re really hard to do. And I don’t read a lot [of them]. I don’t think people think of me for comedies a lot. But I love them, and I love watching them, and I love doing them if I can get my hands on one. But they’re few and far between. I think because they don’t travel well. They’re harder to get made because you really have to get all your money back in America. Comedy is so cultural. So the margin for error, I think, is smaller, which is what’s so great when you see a great one.

Anthony [Minghella], I think, was the first, with Talented Mr. Ripley. And he talked openly about it. A lot of these directors do. They want to use whatever it is that you have to offer in a new way and in a fun way and in an unexpected way. Some of those roles are the best roles that I’ve ever had a chance to play. Really interesting, complex people, and I love that.

I shot a scene in a movie theater with [Jack Nicholson], and Jack was working with an earwig. It was just the three of us before the crew came in, and we were just rehearsing. Marty [Scorsese] goes, “Let’s run this and see how we think it’s going to go.” And Jack took the earpiece out and we rehearsed the scene a few times and Jack was letter-perfect with his dialogue. And so Marty went to get the crew, and as people were coming in I said, “Hey, man, what’s the deal with the earwig? You obviously know all your lines—you’re writing stuff.” And it was really interesting because, he goes, “The older you get, the harder it is to remember your lines.” And that feeling of going up on a line, that panic, that surge of adrenaline that you get—he goes, “It just makes me so uncomfortable.” It’s a fail-safe. And if he knows [the earpiece is] there, his body stays in that relaxed state. People might think it was laziness. It was the opposite. He was a grinder. He worked really, really hard. It was more about just protecting himself.

No, no, no, no, no. I think everybody was really focused on Marty. And I remember I was shooting second unit for The Bourne Ultimatum during that Oscars, so I didn’t go. I was living in Miami at the time, and I had an infant. [My wife] Lucy and I were laying in bed watching it and so nervous for Marty. And then when he won, I was jumping up and down in the bedroom and I remember being really excited. And then the next category was best picture, and The Departed won. And I realized in that moment I hadn’t even considered that that could happen. And I turned to Lucy and I was like, “Shit, we should be there!” And then the next few weeks, I got all these calls from all the cast and the studio, like, “Hey, where were you, man?” I totally blew it. And then the next time that that happened was on Oppenheimer, and we had this whole scary thing happen where my wife had a brain aneurysm.

She’s totally fine, thank God, but [she] had this brain surgery the week before the Oscars. But it was the first night she felt good enough to get up and had her energy back. And she surprised me and got a dress and we went out to the after-party, because she remembered that the last time it happened, I didn’t do it. And she was like, “This time we’re going out.” And it was pretty fucking heroic of her to do that and really meaningful.

It’s not something you can control. You got to just do the work, and that’s got to be the reward. Because it’s like, then if you don’t win, do you feel bad about something that was really positive? Don’t turn this into something bad. It’s a tricky one. I always think about old movies when I look at them and it says, “So-and-so won an Oscar, so-and-so didn’t.” You’re judging it in a totally different way. It’s not attached to that anymore. I think the real way they should do them, really, is 20 or 25 years later. You’ll have a really good idea of which movies really endured and really still matter to you. There can be hype in the moment, or it can be a zeitgeist thing, but it doesn’t hold up. The goal for me is to make as many of those movies that are around 20 years later. That’s a cool thing. People come up [to me] about Good Will Hunting and I realize they weren’t born when the movie came out. It’s just very cool for Ben and me to have a new generation of people actually see it.

I don’t know what that means. I live in Brooklyn. [Laughs] If the trail is in that area, yeah. I don’t know what that entails. I will say, the technical side of this movie—I think of someone like Willie Burton, our sound guy, who’s in his 80s and he is a legend in the business.

And I did not loop a line in this movie, which is incredible. And I did not loop a line in Oppenheimer, which is incredible. Willie and Doug [Shamburger], his boom operator, are so good. Every scene on the ship, Willie is down below in the hold mixing in storms. The fact that he salvages all of that dialogue is nothing short of amazing. The technical achievement of our heads of department and their teams were really special. And I just hope that people realize that, realize what it took to do what they did, because from a technical standpoint, I hope they all get their flowers.

I didn’t think I was going to work. And then the Daniels called me and they had this project that was so out there, and it was such a Daniels movie and it’s so different from anything I’ve ever been able to do that I couldn’t pass it up. They’re really good people, and this movie’s like a cosmic love bomb for the world. So it felt like the right place to put my energy, but we’re almost done shooting it, and yeah, I’m going to take a long time off.

I haven’t thought about it. There are a lot of great performances. Paul Newman had some great ones at the end. We have the studio now with Artists Equity, and I feel like we’re just going to do stuff we really want to do, because it’s a very time-consuming job, and if you’re not 100 percent in, it’s just not worth doing. You have to really let it take over your life. I think that was one of the joys of The Odyssey—it dominated our lives.

There was a funny thing that happened on The Odyssey. We were in Scotland. I was with my kids. They’d just come over and gotten out of school, and we were eating dinner in this tiny hotel in this tiny town. And so there was one little dining room, which had 10 little tables in it, and the crew had watched dailies and so they were shuffling in, and I was already eating with my kids—I had jeans and a flannel shirt and a baseball hat on. And Chris came in and he walked by the table and I said, “Hey, Chris.” And he turned and he goes, “Oh, hey, Matt. I didn’t recognize you with the beard.” Chris doesn’t say stupid things—it was definitely the stupidest thing he’s ever said, because we’d been next to each other for six months.

He had just walked out of dailies watching close-ups of me, I’m sure with this giant beard. And I looked at him and he immediately realized what he’d said and he just looked at his shoes and then he looked up, like, Can we just agree that this never happened? And he shuffled off, and my kids go, “Dad, does Chris Nolan not know who you are?” I was like, “No, guys, he’s just exhausted.” He was that tired. He hadn’t seen me out of wardrobe in a while, you know what I mean? We were so tired by the end of that movie.
Well, he should write us a movie. We would be very happy if he did that.

Who knows? I have no right to expect it, let’s put it that way. I don’t want to sound like a broken record, but I have such gratitude for the fact that this came along my path at this point. I have no right to expect anything like that to happen again. But in the meantime, I just want to make good stuff and definitely keep working with Ben, because we’re at that point in our life where we’re like, “Fuck it, why not?” This was our dream as kids, as boys. We got to honor those boys and keep working together if we can. ✦
