items.title: Dressing ‘Horny’ in My 40s
items.description: A few weeks ago, as I was getting ready to head out for dinner with some girlfriends, I caught my husband staring at me. Nearby, our two young daughters were playing “family,” the 6-year-old tucking the 4-year-old into a bed they’d made from a cardboard box. H
items.author: Meghan Nesmith
paragraphs: A few weeks ago, as I was getting ready to head out for dinner with some girlfriends, I caught my husband staring at me. Nearby, our two young daughters were playing “family,” the 6-year-old tucking the 4-year-old into a bed they’d made from a cardboard box. His brow was furrowed in an expression of mild confusion. I stared back at him.
He cleared his throat. “You look hot,” he said.

I was wearing a vintage dress I’d thrifted at Curator Consignment earlier this year on a girls trip to Maine: a silk floral with a drop waist and tiny buttons up the back; entirely sheer, underwear glaringly visible.
“Are you …” he said carefully, then trailed off. He tried again. “Are you going to wear a jacket?”
“I … no reason,” he said. He chewed his lip. Then, in a rush: “I’m not sure you should go out like that.”

It was cute, his feminism warring with whatever mammalian instincts a 45-year-old professor of moral philosophy possesses. I felt the way I had as a teenager, my mom’s eyes trailing me through the house, assessing my hemline, the cut of my shirt, fearing for — what, exactly? My safety? My virtue? “No one is looking at me,” I reassured my husband as I left the house, which is mostly true. At 42, I am largely invisible, my postpartum and perimenopausal body absolutely no one’s sexual ideal. I made it home without anyone giving me a second glance. (My girlfriends, though, thought I looked great.)

Twenty years ago, this layer of invisibility would’ve been crushing; a decade ago, looking “inappropriate” for my age would have left me feeling, as my mother often says, “like mutton dressed as lamb” (Britspeak for embarrassing yourself by dressing younger than your age). But my previous body disappeared somewhere between my two pregnancies, and when I stopped nursing just over a year ago, I confronted my now-unrecognizable body as an explorer discovering a new land. How to shop for this form? What clothing could possibly communicate the enormity of what I had done?

Focusing on how clothing feels, rather than looks, seemed the natural place to start. Sensual, after all, literally means the gratification of the senses. There’s a kind of forced bodily engagement that comes with pregnancy and nursing, and with this acute understanding of what my body had been through, I was unwilling to give it anything but the best.

I purged anything that felt too tight or low-cut, anything that reminded me of the way I used to move through the world: carefully, nearly unbearably self-conscious. I committed to thrifting most of my clothing, which forced me to pay attention to fabrics and feel. To get into my body, even when I might not know how. Gradually, a new wardrobe began to emerge: crop tops paired with vintage white bloomers. A ’90s Betsey Johnson butterfly skirt, just this side of translucent. Rachel Comey snakeskin platforms I scored for a steal on Poshmark. A tissue-thin lace shirt I might have worn to a rave as a teen, if I ever went to raves as a teen. These are clothes that display my body, all two kids’ worth of it. Clothes that express an unfocused feverish desire, albeit weirdly and slightly askew.

It isn’t what others might think of as sexy, not skintight or cleavage baring. It’s combative and aggressive, demanding attention long after society has deemed you worthy of it. Refusing, as a friend recently said, to go gently into that good night. I dress the way I often wish I could behave: I want things, and I want them now.

Laurel Pantin, owner of the L.A. boutique Earl IRL and author of the forthcoming What to Wear Every Day, calls it “horny dressing,” a term I read in her newsletter that rang clear as a bell. Horny dressing, first and foremost, “has nothing at all to do with sex.” This is a key, if slippery, distinction. Pantin, who is 40, has a very clear understanding of what makes her horny: her girlfriends; ordering (and eating) the plate of fries; being called “a broad”; clothing with a purpose that moves as though it was made for her. “I look for clothes that show my clavicles, that you can scrunch up around your arms, that have a tactile quality,” she tells me. These are clothes that you can throw on, wrap up, tie around your waist, and forget about.
“I want the fabrics to feel good, my skin to feel good, for everything to just make me feel really good in my body,” Pantin says. “It’s like a little kitty purr.”

I’ve seen a similar shift with my friends, too. My friend Eva piles gold necklaces under men’s silk shirts she leaves unbuttoned; Brook let her hair go gray and cut it into a severe bob that she pairs with feverish red lipstick. We’re stretching our wings, letting things go fuzzy around the edges. We’re meant to be heading into our Talbots era; instead, we’re dressing like the teens we didn’t have the courage to be.

“I want my clothes to push me a little past where I think I ‘should’ be dressing as an early 40s doctor and mom,” Carolyn says. The 42-year-old — who went through a “second puberty” at 40, getting a tattoo and nose piercing — sends me mirror selfies in her olive-green velvet minidress with fringed sleeves, braless in a black-and-white shift, a sheer polka-dot dress worn over bike shorts. “Divorcing really unlocked giving no fucks,” she tells me. “I’m an eldest daughter raised Catholic in the ’90s in the Midwest. I did everything right and my life still imploded. So that approach clearly didn’t work.” Whatever version of herself she thought she might be at her age had to go. “I was never going to be a Lululemon mom, but I’m thrilled not to want to or let myself disappear anymore. I’m horny for life.”

When she was younger, Justine, now 39 and the mother of two boys, imagined that at this age she’d look “a bit like Lily van der Woodsen.” Instead, she left her abusive partner and gave up the outfits that signified maturity and control. She’s since broken up with a man who once asked her, derisively, “Is that what you wore to drop your kids off?” and recently flew to Paris on a whim wearing a trench coat and lace stay-ups to meet her new lover. These days, she’s leaning into oversize men’s button-downs with boots and no bra. “I want to feel French,” she says — emphasis very much hers.

The deeper I get into my 40s, the more fascinated I am by this decade, the strange interregnum between postpartum and perimenopause, young enough to desire, too old to be categorically desirable. I know there’s an expiration date on this feeling, and that there will come a time when I feel less inclined to expose anything at all, let alone my entire midriff. At my age, my mom was wearing oversize skirt suits. I hope she felt powerful, but I can categorically say she didn’t feel horny.

For now, like Pantin, I’m reveling in pleasure. “Horny dressing has less to do with the clothes themselves than how my body feels in the clothes,” she says. It’s about “being out in the world,” which gives her the most pleasure of all. I’m doing the same, pairing a tiny sequined miniskirt and a One Direction tee with red jelly sandals for a Harry Styles concert where I danced harder than anyone with a 42-year-old pelvic floor really should. Choosing pleasure, as a woman, can often be a difficult and radical act. What’s hornier than that?

items.title: I Want Anne Hathaway’s Brown Velvet Baby Carrier
items.description: Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway. Yesterday, the Oscar-winning actress confirmed the birth of her third child via a very cute pap walk wearing a baseball cap, oversize wool coat, and a little sweetie tucked into a baby carrier on her chest. I, to
items.author: Marisa Carroll
paragraphs: Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway. Yesterday, the Oscar-winning actress confirmed the birth of her third child via a very cute pap walk wearing a baseball cap, oversize wool coat, and a little sweetie tucked into a baby carrier on her chest. I, too, became a New York mom of three this fall. I, too, wear a baseball cap, oversize wool coat, and little sweetie tucked into a baby carrier underneath. I, too, am an Oscar winn— nevermind, but I am interested in Hathaway’s approach to street style this fall and winter, when we’ll both be dragged to big-kid activities while holding wee babes. I was curious about the attractive brown velvet carrier Hathaway was wearing in the photos.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I was never into babywearing with my oldest. I registered for the black Ergobaby Omni Classic carrier that everyone swears by, but (for reasons that could be user error) it strained my back. Plus he was my only child, and I carried him around like a prince on a tuffet at all times. I ended up giving the Ergobaby to a friend. Since then, the baby-gear market has exploded. For my second son, we used a Ciel-colored Happy Baby Original baby carrier in a linen blend, which I bought at the lovely shop Nesting House in Philadelphia. It was snug on my over-six-foot-tall husband and I could never get the fit quite right, either, but it was functional and we wore it to literal pieces. This time around, I needed a new carrier. With our 2- and 5-year-olds running around, there’s really no other option than wearing our daughter much of the time. Babywearing promotes bonding, and how else is anybody going to make dinner or put away the laundry? But I didn’t want just any carrier. I wanted the Artipoppe Zeitgeist in Denim.

I know: It’s influencer-y. It’s expensive. But, as my husband will be quick to point out, the cost per wear has proven to be low. It’s the most comfortable baby carrier we have ever used. We share it and use it every single day. With the Artipoppe, we experience zero back pain. I actually look forward to wearing it. And sorry, but it’s cute! I don’t carry a purse (with what free hands?); this is my primary accessory for the next year plus. When I’m done, I will give it to a friend. We regret not buying it five years ago when our first child was born.

So when I saw Anne Hathaway’s brown velvet one, I guessed that it was a new Artipoppe colorway and reached out to the brand to confirm. Turns out, it’s the Zeitgeist Java in organic velvet, on preorder now. I desperately want to wear this baby carrier to Thanksgiving and holiday gatherings this winter. You can dress it up or down, and, best of all, it looks like it would keep my baby warm. And velvet is surprisingly easy to clean spit-up and other questionable liquids off of. Thank you for the inspo, Anne.

Another great, more affordable option: Tula just redesigned its carriers with style in mind. The brand sent me the cotton Explore baby carrier in the Sahara Stripe print. Though I prefer the Artipoppe, I do like this one — I’ve worn it to a dozen school pickups and for an evening of trick-or-treating — and the brown tones mimic the one Hathaway wore, and it’s less than half the price of the Artipoppe. Even better: Tula offers a Cocoa Brown linen option that looks nearly identical to Hathaway’s, minus the velvet.
New! You can now save this product for later.
We reached out to a rep for Hathaway and will report back if we hear more.

items.title: Yes, It Takes An Entire Book To Explain A Friendship Breakup
items.description: The Impossible Task Of Explaining A Friendship Breakup
items.author: Madeleine Frank Reeves
paragraphs: The Impossible Task Of Explaining A Friendship Breakup
Reading Sofia Franklyn’s Daddy Issues is like watching a falling out in slow motion through a VR headset. And I mean that as a compliment.

Anyone who’s been through a friendship breakup — whether it’s as public as Sofia Franklyn and Alex Cooper’s or only of interest to the approximately five people who know you both — has been faced with the obvious question: What happened?

In my experience, I tend to answer in one of three ways. The first, when I’m feeling like my highest self (or fear I’m in enemy territory), is a simple “Ah, we just grew apart! But I’m always cheering for her!” followed by a swift subject change.

The second approach is less magnanimous and includes such bangers as “Oh, it turns out she’s actually a horrible person” or “I learned the hard way that you should never be friends with a toxic narcissist.” I might add an ominous “I hope she gets the help she needs.” I try to avoid responding this way, since it can kind of just seem like you’re talking sh*t and name-calling.

The last and perhaps most regrettable way I respond begins with a deep inhale and “Well, you see…” followed by a rambling soliloquy starting from the day we met. Here, I like to include an excruciating level of detail about the most seemingly insignificant of perceived slights. I can see in the other person’s eyes that they don’t care, that they lost interest four tangents ago, and that they regret asking. No matter how many times I’m asked, I still haven’t found a satisfying way to answer the question. The first feels dishonest, the second feels unfair, and the third is still somehow insufficient.

The problem is that explaining the truth — the actual events and why the relationship was meaningful enough for its demise to be so brutally destabilizing — takes far more than a single conversation. A friendship breakup is rarely about one inciting incident. It’s death by a thousand tiny cuts, most of which don’t even register until you look down and realize you’re bleeding out.

Perhaps nothing illustrates this better than Franklyn’s new memoir, Daddy Issues, in which she finally answers the question audiences and media outlets have been asking since her very public 2020 falling-out with former best friend and Call Her Daddy co-host Cooper. In the aftermath, Cooper walked away with sole ownership of the podcast, signed multimillion-dollar deals, and became one of the biggest names in media, while Franklyn was largely cast as the villain.

Since Daddy Issues came out last week, much of the coverage has been of the “We Read Sofia Franklyn’s ‘Daddy Issues’ Memoir So You Don’t Have To: Here Are the 6 Biggest Bombshells” variety. In other words: What happened?! But reducing this book to a handful of shocking revelations misses its greatest achievement: how it mimics the experience of a life-altering friendship breakup with someone you genuinely loved.

Franklyn recounts incident after incident, some seemingly insignificant at the time, others that were impossible for her to ignore, until the accumulation reveals a relationship that looks almost unrecognizable in retrospect. What happened when, from Sofia’s point of view, Alex seemingly discouraged her from hanging out with her childhood best friend Mia, made sure Sofia couldn’t get too close to their other roommate Lauren, kept Sofia away from her creative calls with Muji Fricke, or met with Barstool executives behind her back? Of course, Alex might tell a very different version of some of these stories. Was she deliberately trying to isolate Sofia from her other friends, or is Sofia assigning motives to interactions that only look suspicious in hindsight? That’s the tricky thing about revisiting a relationship after it ends: The more patterns you recognize, the harder it can become to distinguish what actually happened from what you’ve come to believe it meant. And yet, reading Sofia’s account, by the time we arrive at the dissolution of their partnership, it almost feels inevitable.
Am I finally seeing this relationship for what it was, or am I rewriting pieces of history to make sense of how it ended?

There's something particularly disorienting about realizing you’ve been an unreliable narrator of your own experience. In my friendship breakup, I found myself reconsidering things I’d barely registered at the time: the nights she’d ignore me at group dinners, the way she expected me to drop everything whenever she was free, the times she’d talk to me like I worked for her, or accusatorily ask why she’d never heard me laugh with her the way I did with another friend. But even as the patterns become clearer, there’s another uncomfortable question lurking in the background: Am I finally seeing this relationship for what it was, or am I rewriting pieces of history to make sense of how it ended? After all, the other person has a version of this story, too.

Central to this, too, is how good memories complicate everything. There can be a particular layer of grief that comes with the end of a female friendship, because there’s often such extraordinary intimacy and joy in these relationships. The conversations that go deeper than any you’ve had before, nights curled up on the sectional splitting a bottle of wine and dissecting each other’s romantic woes for hours, laughing until your stomachs hurt. The way this person alone seemed to hold the keys to unlocking parts of your personality that you didn’t even know existed. You can look back and recognize all the ways the relationship was unhealthy without wanting to erase the wonderful memories. And you can’t tell the story accurately if you leave out the parts that made you want to stay.

As Franklyn said in an interview with The New York Times, writing the memoir actually made her miss her former friend, a realization she described as “crazy.” But perhaps it isn’t so crazy. You can’t make someone understand why losing a friendship was devastating without first explaining why having that person was extraordinary.

This nuance is hard to convey, whether it’s in a headline about a celebrity feud or a text about a falling-out in your friend group. It’s simpler to just dub a villain. What happened is another way of asking: Whose fault is it? Whose side should I be on?

People want to take vague, media-trained statements, anonymous-source allegations, cryptic Instagram stories, and secondhand gossip and piece together a tidy black-and-white narrative. There’s something addictive about playing detective in this way, perhaps because it lets us mentally absolve ourselves of fault in our own failed relationships. I’d never do that, so this friendship breakup wasn’t my fault. That’s why people dissect Taylor Swift lyrics for Easter eggs about Karlie Kloss and lose their collective minds when they’re seen together in the year 2026. It’s why, when the Internet seems to agree on whose “fault” something was, they come hard and fast for the person. They’re bad, and I’d never do something like that, so I’m a good person.

When Cooper and Franklyn’s partnership imploded, the Internet quickly aligned with Cooper’s 52-minute “The Truth About Call Her Daddy” video, in which she called Franklyn a “liability.” Franklyn was painted as greedy, disloyal, and willing to throw away her friendship and career for a man, with people coming hard for her on Reddit and social media. Barstool even released “Cancel Suitman” merch aimed at Franklyn’s boyfriend.
But the trouble with reducing a friendship breakup to a question of who’s the villain is that you’re applying binary logic to a complicated, nuanced narrative.
The most revealing part of telling the entire tale might be recognizing that you aren’t always the hero of your own story.

Franklyn’s memoir shows how the verdict isn’t the point; the point is the story. And crucially, she doesn’t let herself off the hook in telling it. She examines her own role in the relationship, the consequences of her issues with drinking, the warning signs she ignored to keep the peace, and the ways she contributed to the dynamics of shutting out other friends.

That doesn’t mean Daddy Issues represents the one and only definitive truth about what happened between Franklyn and Cooper. One could argue that there’s actually no such thing in a relationship between two people. But that’s precisely what makes it so valuable. The most revealing part of telling the entire tale might be recognizing that you aren’t always the hero of your own story. The incidents, the traumatic experiences, the moments of extraordinary intimacy and excitement all add up to something much bigger than an explanation of why two people stopped speaking. By the end, you don’t just understand how the friendship fell apart. You have a sense of what it felt like to be inside it and why losing it was so devastating.
And perhaps that’s why I found the book so satisfying. Franklyn did what I’ve been trying, unsuccessfully, to do every time someone asks the dreaded question. She got us to understand.
What happened? Next time, I’m going to try a new response on for size: “You’ll just have to read about it in my book.”

items.title: Would You Pay An Etsy Witch To Cast A Spell For Your Favorite Sports Team?
items.description: Some Sports Fans Wear Lucky Jerseys, Others Hire Etsy Witches
items.author: Frankie de la Cretaz
paragraphs: Some Sports Fans Wear Lucky Jerseys, Others Hire Etsy Witches
From tarot readings to victory spells, people are turning to mystical rituals to help their favorite teams and athletes succeed.

Last winter, Megan Ryder got very close to hiring an Etsy witch. She was rooting for her favorite figure skater, Japan’s Wakaba Higuchi, to make the Olympic team for the 2026 Winter Games in Milano Cortina. Ultimately, Ryder got cold feet and didn’t end up going through with the spell — and Higuchi didn’t make the team. The thought of what could have happened if she had sought mystical help plagued her. The regret only intensified when she saw someone post on social media that they had hired an Etsy witch to successfully lift a hockey player out of a scoring drought.

So when her beloved Golden State Valkyries faltered during this fall’s WNBA Finals, losing Game 3 to the Atlanta Dream by nearly 30 points, she didn’t want to make the same mistake twice. Ryder, 32, doesn’t describe herself as particularly witchy. She owns a tarot deck and some crystals, but she doesn’t cast spells or perform rituals on her own. Still, she didn’t want to leave anything up to chance. She decided to commission an Etsy witch named Melinda Spells to try helping her team win the championship. For less than $10, Spells promised “extreme” results. (Her prices vary by delivery time and strength; “extreme and permanent” magic can run up to $20.)

“I initially went into it thinking, ‘This might be fun and it can’t hurt,’ but not really believing that it could help,” Ryder says. Regardless of its impact on the court, though, the purchase had another effect.

“I genuinely felt five times lighter and more hopeful,” she says. “Describing what I wanted for the team in the Etsy personalization field actually felt very grounding. I articulated the problems I was seeing on the court and asked for help removing any mental, emotional, or spiritual blockages that were preventing the Valks from playing like the connected, driven, and joyful team I know they can be.”
Eight days later, Golden State took home the title.

Ryder is not alone in seeking out esoteric mediums or New Age spiritual rituals to support her favorite sports team. When she posted in a Valkyries fan Discord about the spell, another community member said that an Etsy witch had helped the NWSL’s Seattle Reign achieve their longest-scoring streak in team history. A Seattle Mariners fan famously sought mystical help online to help get them out of a slump — and it worked. Beyond spells, some people make altars or use prayer candles, while others pull tarot cards to predict what might happen in a game or series.

“Athletes and sports fans are a superstitious crowd,” says astrologer Sam Manzella. “For the average fan, there isn’t actually much you can do to support their performance. I imagine that esoteric mediums like witchcraft, tarot, and astrology can give fans a sense of agency.”

Almost a third (30%) of Americans say they consult astrology, tarot cards, or a fortune teller at least once a year, according to a 2024 study from Pew Research. These interests are especially popular among millennial and Gen Z women, as well as LGBTQ+ people — the groups who are also most likely to be passionate about women’s sports. Part of the appeal is that they are accessible in ways that many organized religions are not, as they don’t require a house of worship or an ordained leader. Many of these practices actively de-center the leadership and influence of men, encouraging practitioners to instead connect with the Earth, the planets, and the energy of the universe.

This accessibility is what drew Robin Yang to a tarot practice. Yang, 39, was at a leadership retreat in Tuscany this fall, where participants used tarot and journaling for self-reflection. Surrounded by rolling hills, cypress trees, and delicious food, the diehard Valkyries fan was getting up at 3 a.m. to watch playoff games on laggy WiFi. She felt “so much FOMO” about not attending the playoffs, so she decided to turn to a medium that has brought her comfort in the past: tarot.

When she shared her reading with a Valkyries fan group on Discord, the response was positive and immediate. Like sports fandom, spirituality is often a collective experience. She decided to continue pulling cards before tipoff and created a new account, Courtside Tarot, where she answers questions such as “Who will be the most impactful player in Game 5?” She says, “I love when people message me after a game and share how they felt the readings ended up connecting to what happened.”

Though she still considers herself a tarot skeptic, she says, “There are times when the cards feel super on the nose.” Ahead of Game 7, for example, she asked her deck about each team’s journey. For the Dream, she got The Star, which she interprets as “celebrating what you’ve accomplished thus far but taking a short rest to reflect before climbing the last hill.” For the Valkyries, she pulled The World, the final card of the Major Arcana, which symbolizes the successful completion of a cycle. So Yang keeps coming back.

Tarot isn’t limited to just predictions. Snatch Magazine, an independent print magazine run by artist Sophia Mitropoulos, recently released cards for Connecticut Sun fans — fittingly, a Sun-inspired version of the sun tarot card. The team is moving to Houston,, so this card pays homage to the historic franchise before it rebrands as the Comets.

Even Manzella, the astrologer, acknowledges that spiritual effort has its limitations. “In my experience, doing magic alone won't change your life; you need to meet the energy halfway by taking aligned actions,” she says.

This, of course, isn’t possible for fans watching from the stands or afar. But spellwork, tarot, and other esoteric mediums let people channel their passion into something tangible. It’s a way to engage with a game, even if they can’t control it.

That surge of excitement may make difference in the arena. After Gabby Williams led the Valkyries to victory in the championships, she told SFGate, “There were moments when I was like, ‘How am I going to play through all of this?’ And then I would walk into Ballhalla and be like, ‘That’s how.’”

items.title: What Playing Moms Has Taught Ruthie Ann Miles About Parenthood
items.description: What Playing Moms Has Taught Ruthie Ann Miles About Parenthood
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: What Playing Moms Has Taught Ruthie Ann Miles About Parenthood
The Tony-winning actor on The Fantasticks and why theater is great for pondering your life choices: “It’s dark, it’s quiet, and [there’s no] exit exam.”

In the original off-Broadway production of The Fantasticks, which ran for 42 years, two dads pretend to feud, employing reverse psychology to get their son and daughter to fall in love. Now the long-running musical is making its Broadway debut — with a few updates: The revisal has been reimagined as a gay love story centered on two men, Matt and Lewis, with two benevolently scheming mothers replacing the father roles.

“Everyone’s included now — mothers and sons, daughters and same-sex couples… we’re all here now and welcome to the table,” Tony winner Ruthie Ann Miles says of The Fantasticks, which opens tonight and runs at the Hayes Theater through Feb 7. “To me, it only makes sense with moms, but I’m sure somebody who watched it 60 years ago [thought], ‘Of course, it has to be dads. I can’t imagine it with moms.’”

Miles, who plays Lewis’ mother, Bessie, says she’s “really lucky to play mothers,” having also portrayed matriarchs in shows ranging from The Light in the Piazza to The Seat of Our Pants to The King and I, for which she won the 2015 Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Musical. They’re roles with rich territory to mine, she says — and ones that she never tires of.
“I think I have the rest of my life to continue to play a mother onstage,” she says, “and I would be happy if I get to play a mother forever.”
On the roles she’s drawn to now:

It’s always fun to find what I have in common with these people and also the ways that we’re different: What can I learn from this person? What mistakes are they making in their life that I can do better in mine?

Theater is maybe the ultimate safe space. It’s dark, it’s quiet, and no one’s making you answer an exit exam afterward. People can reflect on themselves, on their own lives: “Oh, that’s terrible.” “I don’t agree.” “That person should do that instead.” That’s something that I really love about the characters that I’ve been fortunate enough to play — they all teach me something.

There’s so much that the world needs to see represented about parents onstage and the choices they make: different survival tactics, different strategies, different ways that we care for our children — because we want the best for them, despite it maybe not coming across that way.

In The Fantasticks, the mothers realize when they manipulate their children, it’s not the happy ending that they thought they would get if everything went their way. Instead, they have to love, and they have to lose. They have to let their children make those mistakes. And only then do they get the kind of ending that perhaps they didn’t see coming in. When I watch these mothers and the mistakes that they make, it makes me think about my relationship to my child. I have to be the disciplinarian because my daughter needs that boundary to thrive. But also, in what ways can I just be lenient? Can I just let her, you know, run and make a mistake and fall down, and then come to me when she’s ready for Mama to hold her?
On her college Fantasticks encounter:

The Fantasticks came up in a musical theater history class, and it was in a big textbook. And it just happened to be the story that I picked for my final paper, our character analysis — I chose El Gallo [the mysterious narrator]. I was really fascinated by this character who would choose to hurt somebody for their own good. I was repulsed but also captivated by that idea. It drew me in, because I didn’t understand it.
On getting into character:

I really just like to take my time. I assess my voice if she’s a little tired. I have all manner of teas and ginger powder and manuka — anything that I could possibly want to wake my voice up and make sure my body feels cozy. But really, when it comes to character work, putting on the wig and the makeup and the costume marks a shift in my brain — we’re not Ruthie anymore.

Leslie [Rodriguez Kritzer, who plays Mildred] and I share a room here, so it’s lovely to be able to take care of each other in the hour before we get to go onstage. We listen to each other really well and trust each other really deeply — like, “Hey, I’m having a rough day” or “I didn’t sleep well” or “I need this,” and then responding, “How can I support you in that?” We’re always checking and doing that with each other. To work so closely onstage with somebody and also get to share a dressing room with them together — you get that quiet moment together before the show.
On touching stage-door anecdotes:

I love when people tell us that they have a history with The Fantasticks. There was a mother who saw The Fantasticks with her husband 40-some-odd years ago and brought her daughter to see The Fantasticks now — a new generation. People say, “You know, we went on our blind date to The Fantasticks, and now my wife and I have been married for 40 years, and we flew from out of state to come and see the first preview.” We have dozens and dozens and dozens and dozens of stories like that: “We walked down the aisle to one of the songs — ‘Try to Remember,’ ‘You Are Love.’” “He proposed to me at The Fantasticks.” It’s just another reminder of how special it is to get to play this today, and how special it is that families get to share this now.

items.title: Exclusive: The New 'Hunger Games' Stars React To Jennifer Lawrence's Return
items.description: Joseph Zada & Whitney Peak Fanned Out Over The OG Hunger Games Cast
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Joseph Zada & Whitney Peak Fanned Out Over The OG Hunger Games Cast
The Sunrise on the Reaping stars and director Francis Lawrence open up about the reunion.
Spoilers ahead for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Katniss Everdeen is back, and I’m not crying, you are. Scratch that — everybody was crying.

In an exclusive interview with Bustle, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping stars Joseph Zada and Whitney Peak, and director Francis Lawrence, opened up about having the original actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson return for the prequel, with the new cast revealing they were on set as the OGs reunited.

“We were there for that one day,” Peak tells Bustle, calling it “such a trip,” with Zada agreeing. “It was the trippiest thing ever, being on the other side of the monitor, watching that happen, seeing those two,” he says. “It was like...” Peak quickly finished his sentence: “What is happening? And they all look the same. Talk about aging gracefully.”

Aside from not aging a day since the original movies, Zada describes the trio as “the coolest in the entire world,” and says their presence on set made the entire experience surreal. “It made it really feel like we were in a Hunger Games movie, which still doesn't feel too real. On that day especially, it was like, they were in this franchise, and we’re in this franchise. That’s crazy. It’s still a lot to process,” he says, with Peak adding that it’s “so bizarre.”

While the two said they “were just talking” to Lawrence, Hutcherson, and Harrelson like normal people, Peak admitted to feeling totally starstruck. “I was very sheepishly introduced, and then I immediately ran away,” she says. “But I did chat to Woody a little bit. He was lovely.”

Zada, however, was also aware that the trio was reuniting with the director and the film’s crew for the first time in over a decade. “Also, they had done three films with this entire team,” he says. “So it was just lovely to see them interact with our family now as well.”
The director tells Bustle that “it was not hard” to convince the trio to return, saying they remain a “family” to this day, even as he went on to helm Hunger Games prequels without them.

“I’ve stayed close with Jen for years. I’ve done four movies, three of them Hunger Games, with her,” he explains. “She and Woody are really close, and Josh has also been close to all of us. These are good movies that are really about something. We all had a lot of fun making them. This is not a series that's an embarrassment to them. They were like, ‘Yeah, I'll be back in a second.’”

He knew seeing the OG trio would be an emotional day on set just by reading Sunrise on the Reaping, long before asking them to return. “This is a very tragic story. It's very emotional,” he says. “But reading the epilogue, sitting in Suzanne [Collins’] agent’s backyard, I cried when I read it. And I wasn't crying because I was sad. I was crying because of how hopeful the story ends up being.”

As a result, the director was determined to let their reunion serve as a hopeful ending, especially after his last film. “I didn't want people leaving the theater going, ‘Well, that's a bummer,’” he says. “I just did that with The Long Walk, where I was pretty nihilistic with the ending, which is staying true to the spirit of the book. I wanted there to be a purpose to the tragedy so you knew [Haymitch] did not go through all of this for nothing.”

items.title: Mckenna Grace & Other Gen Z Style Stars Can’t Stop Wearing This $500 Coach Bag
items.description: Gen Z It Girls Can’t Stop Wearing This $500 Coach Bag
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Gen Z It Girls Can’t Stop Wearing This $500 Coach Bag
From Mckenna Grace to Elle Fanning, Hollywood’s coolest young stars are all in on the same iconic silhouette.

While millennials have been taking accessory cues from Carrie Bradshaw for the better part of three decades — still keeping Fendi Baguettes and Dior Saddle bags at the top of their wishlists — Gen Z’s most stylish have seemingly crowned their own generation-defining arm candy: the Coach Tabby.

Mckenna Grace, Elle Fanning, and other young fashion icons have been repping the reimagined ’70s bag in recent months, making a strong case for the Tabby as the must-have plus-one this season. Not only does the style have a luxury look without the four-figure designer price tag, it’s also endlessly versatile. It can be the perfect topper for a casual daytime outing or a statement-maker at a more glam night out. All you need are a few styling tweaks.
The Perfect Arm Candy From Day...

On Sunday, Nov. 15, Grace traded her recent ethereal press-tour looks — full of delicate 3D floral and butterfly appliqués — for something decidedly edgier during a Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping outing in New York. Taking cues from Katniss Everdeen’s iconic hunting jacket, the actor paired a vintage-style black leather piece with brown trim, a lighter brown miniskirt, and matching knee-high boots, anchored by a chocolate suede Coach Tabby.
The bag, which retails for $575, took the ensemble from Panem cosplay to street-style chic (and marks at least her second Tabby sighting this year, following a black version she carried in February).

Last week, Madelyn Cline got a similar memo. She nailed the model-off-duty aesthetic during a coffee run, pairing a classic white tee and jeans with a cropped trench coat, pointed-toe pumps, and a dark brown Tabby — proving that even your most basic errand-day uniform can benefit from a sleek finishing touch.

Of course, the Tabby’s potential doesn’t stop in broad daylight. The bag is also a front-row fave. At Coach’s Spring/Summer 2027 New York Fashion Week show, Fanning embraced maximalism in a bra-baring button-down, a bright red pencil skirt, and a leopard print coat. To add even more drama, she accessorized with a beret and a studded Coach Tabby.

The bag has been spotted on red carpets, too. At the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards earlier this month, Lola Tung, Fanning, and PinkPantheress all made the case for pairing their evening gowns with Tabbys. The Summer I Turned Pretty star gave her sleeveless floor-length black leather gown a bit of shine with a metallic silver Tabby, while PinkPantheress went the gold-on-gold route, pairing her gilded bag with a crop top and skirt in the same golden sheen.

As for Fanning, she opted for a playful spin on the silhouette. She carried a black Tabby sprinkled with shimmering metallic pink confetti, adding a bit more edge to her delicate dusty rose slip dress.

If you’ve been meaning to invest in a new bag, consider this your sign to put the Tabby in the running. Grab one in a solid neutral color to give casual outings a sleek, put-together look, or opt for one with hardware like Fanning for a more maximalist approach. Need one that’s holiday-themed? A fuzzy-trimmed bag in Santa Red is totally festive, while one in a deep merlot hue will take you seamlessly from fall into winter.
