items.title: How To Make Friends As a Busy Adult, According to OG Community-Builder Lala Romero
items.description: I really value friendship. To me, it’s the only relationship I know that gives and takes in equal measure. Friendships provide a home, a sanctuary, for us to be our fullest, messiest, and truest selves. It’s our friends who we call when we want to perrear the
items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: I really value friendship. To me, it’s the only relationship I know that gives and takes in equal measure. Friendships provide a home, a sanctuary, for us to be our fullest, messiest, and truest selves. It’s our friends who we call when we want to perrear the night away, book a trip to our motherland, or just gab and gobble down garlic bread. It’s also our friends who hold us when we’re heartbroken, drop off meds and sopita when we’re sick, and remind us of who we are when we dare to doubt ourselves in front of them.

Friendships nourish our hearts, minds, spirits, and even our bodies — and yet, unfortunately for us, we’re in the middle of a loneliness epidemic. According to the CDC, about 1 in 3 U.S. adults say they feel lonely. Meanwhile, the Pew Research Center found that nearly 1 in 5 adults don’t have any close friends. This means that millions of people are moving through their lives without connections that make them feel known, cared for, seen, heard, supported, and like they belong.

And I think this conversation about loneliness feels particularly urgent for Latinas. We’re living through a moment when so many people are carrying fear around immigration enforcement and family separation, worrying about their safety, or feeling the weight of financial stress. When you’re living with that level of anxiety, having people you can call, people who will show up, people who make you feel safe, people who you can still experience joy, laughter, and calm with, isn’t just comforting. It’s absolutely necessary.

But how do you build that community? How do you create that home within homegirls? Especially when you’ve graduated from school, maybe work from home, are new to town, or are just a shy, timid girl who has trouble making eye contact? Maybe you do have friends, but you all live in different cities now or are transitioning into new roles as mothers or business owners that keep you, or them, busier than usual.

In a country divided, a culture starving for connection, and a time when so many of us are just trying to hold it all together, how the hell do we make friends? I’m glad you asked! In this week’s episode of Sin Vergüenza by Somos, we’re speaking with Lala Romero, founder and CEO of Bella Doña and professional community builder, about why it can feel so hard to build community as an adult, how she does it, and what it’s taught her about friendship.

items.title: Havilah Unique: From Foster Care to Creative Multi-hyphenate
items.description: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.
items.author: Naked Beauty Podcast
paragraphs: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.

Havilah Unique @havilah  is an unstoppable creative force. An entrepreneur, multidisciplinary artist, model, and content creator, Havilah has built a career chasing her creativity. From designing jewelry, furniture, and clothing (including the top she wore during our interview), Havilah’s creativity knows no bounds. But her path to becoming an entrepreneur and creative director was not easy. Growing up in North Providence, Havilah was raised in and out of the foster care system, taking on adult responsibilities at a very early age. She overcame incredible obstacles, including being raised apart from some of her siblings, meeting her father at 26, and being diagnosed with ADHD in elementary school.

During our conversation, Havilah spoke openly about how she learned to channel her symptoms into creative entrepreneurship. She was equally vulnerable about realizing she was burned out from her work, and the two-year sabbatical she took to center herself. Havilah offers us a look into how she learned to make choosing joy an intentional practice. We explore the rituals that help her feel her best, from her DIY hair and body care routines to how she prepares for a great night out. Havilah reflects on her sobriety journey, ceremonial smoking, offering us an honest look at what it takes to protect your energy while continuing to create. After meeting Brooke three years ago, the two finally sit down to talk about being archetypal Leo women, creativity, and the beauty of becoming.

items.title: It’s not political: the young fashionistas of Tehran | Aeon Essays
items.description: Yasaman* is one of the regulars on Iranshahr, the new fashion hub of Tehran. Most evenings, she sets up a stall on the pavement and sells her drawings of manga and anime characters. On social media, she sports her own manga-inspired look: pink hair, pink mouth
items.author: Parisa Khoshnami
paragraphs: Yasaman* is one of the regulars on Iranshahr, the new fashion hub of Tehran. Most evenings, she sets up a stall on the pavement and sells her drawings of manga and anime characters. On social media, she sports her own manga-inspired look: pink hair, pink mouth and smudgy pink eyeshadow extending beyond the corner of each eye. She tells her followers that, before she leaves her house, her mother says: ‘Put on less makeup.’ ‘Mum, be reasonable,’ she answers. ‘I’m going to Iranshahr. For Iranshahr this is nothing. I’m going to Paris Fashion Week. You know everyone there is doing a catwalk.’

Iranshahr’s sidewalks teem with young people parading the latest fashions and filming other young, stylish people for their social media feeds. This is where the fashionistas congregate, hanging out in cafés and galleries, and mingling on the sidewalks. Barely a headscarf is visible. The streets looked nothing like this a few years ago, but once the American-Israeli attacks began in February this year, the Islamic Republic has been fighting for its survival: with much of its leadership killed, the Strait of Hormuz under siege, and many of the country’s neighbours in league with the enemy, policing what people wear has slipped a long way down its list of priorities.

The hijab law has been codified in Iran since 1983, enforced nationwide by the ‘morality’ police. Disobeying it meant fines, flogging or imprisonment. But then one act of disobedience changed everything. In December 2017, Vida Movahed, a woman in her 30s, climbed onto a utility box on Enghelab Street in Tehran, took off her white headscarf and held it up on a stick. Although she was arrested and later sentenced to a year in prison, her action proved contagious. Other women climbed up onto boxes and makeshift plinths in the same street, waving their headscarves in the air. People began calling them the Girls of Enghelab Street. They were arrested too. It is hard to convey now how much nerve their actions took. Women had been edging their scarves back for years, but taking one off in daylight, above the traffic, where the police could see their naked heads as clearly as everyone else, was something very few women had done in public, since the protests of 1979 and 1980.

Then, in September 2022, Mahsa Jina Amini died in custody of the morality police. Unlike the women on the boxes, she was not an activist: aged 22, a Kurdish woman visiting from Saqqez, a city 600 km west of Tehran, she’d been stopped because her loose headscarf was not covering enough of her hair. Her death brought thousands of people out on to the street in an outpouring of grief and anger. Women burned their headscarves. Cut their hair in front of cameras. Their protests spawned the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, and continued for months. What began as a demand for justice for one woman became a challenge to the compulsory hijab, then to the system itself. The authorities responded with arrests, executions and a repression that has never really stopped. The funerals of the dead became protests in their turn.

What changed was that the morality police largely disappeared from the streets for months afterwards, with no announcement that the patrols had ended. Women who had grown up expecting to be stopped were not being stopped, and they knew why: the government had learned in 2022 what a single arrest could cost.

Azadeh, a woman from Tehran, tells me that, during the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, the city felt apocalyptic. After the US president Donald Trump posted that people in Tehran should get out of the city, they fled their homes, leaving everything behind, and the city emptied. Checkpoints multiplied as the government waited for an uprising that never came. But in the strange mood that settled on the city following the attacks, Azadeh noticed another change – a bargain that nobody signed: ‘The state began leaving people alone to live as they like, as long as they do not come out into the street about it.’
‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together’

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of visible hair used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and New York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

Sima, also from Tehran, says that: ‘Among the women who dress freely there is a kind of solidarity. Nobody talks about it, but everyone feels it.’ Recalling the first time she removed her headscarf, Sima says: ‘I felt bald … I thought everyone was looking at me, and I kept checking.’ She was frightened, she told me, so she kept a headscarf in her bag ready to whip out if anything should happen. It took a while for the feeling to pass. Each time she went out, she saw more women without headscarves and that gave her heart. She knew that she was not alone.

The easy read on these developments, especially outside Iran, is that this is defiance: using clothing as a weapon against the state. The framing is not entirely wrong, but it misses most of what is happening on the street, and the people living it do not describe what they are up to in this way. When I asked Mina if getting dressed felt like a political act, she paused, then said no. ‘When I dress up, it’s only for myself,’ she told me. ‘I’m not doing some political act.’ So what is happening on Iranshahr?

The Iranian sociologist Asef Bayat has spent years asking how ordinary people can change their societies in the absence of formal organisations or conventional political movements. In Life as Politics: How Ordinary People Change the Middle East (2010), he argues that they do it less by protesting than by simply living as they wish to, and in enough numbers and for long enough that the rules have to bend around them. Bayat’s name for what Sima, Mina and Azadeh are describing is ‘the art of presence’. It denotes ‘the courage and creativity to assert collective will in spite of all odds, to circumvent constraints, utilising what is available and discovering new spaces within which to make oneself heard, seen, felt, and realised.’ It is a form of soft power.

The women filling the sidewalks of Iranshahr Street are just ordering coffee and adjusting their sunglasses for a friend’s camera. They never chant slogans. They just hang out and admire each other’s looks. Each person is doing nothing more dramatic than deciding what to wear out of the house. But when thousands of young people make the same decision, on the same stretch of pavement, evening after evening, for months, the arithmetic changes. A protest might be cleared in a night. But a government has a harder time dealing with thousands of people who simply go on living as they want.
On Iranshahr young people filled the street to see who had shown up and how they looked

The morality police have not gone away, but their methods have changed. Stopping a woman in public is expensive now: as the Woman, Life, Freedom protests showed, it can end in months of demonstration, so the pressure has moved away from individuals to the places where women gather, and to the phones in their hands. Over the summer, several of the best-known cafés on Iranshahr and Sanaei Street, another popular hangout spot in Tehran, were shut down on the orders of judicial and police officials. The reasons given for the closures included serving customers who were not wearing the hijab. At least 42 businesses were shuttered across the country in August, and more than 70 social media accounts were blocked or seized. Last year, Tehran’s police chief intimated that plainclothes officers were working inside cafés and at concerts.

However, the state has also learned that it doesn’t always need to be there: a woman who assumes the café she is sitting in is being watched behaves as though it is. Still, the pressure is lighter than the state would ideally like to exert. In September, one senior official complained that ‘war conditions’ were preventing the authorities from enforcing the hijab as fully as they wanted.

As soon as the American-Israeli attacks were launched in February 2026, the government moved to occupy public spaces, fearing another wave of Trump-inspired protests. Every evening, it organised demonstrations of its own supporters, mainly on Vali-Asr, a few blocks west of Iranshahr. Two versions of public life were thus running at once. The government was turning out crowds to show that the public was still with it, while on Iranshahr young people filled the street to see who had shown up and how they looked.

Hair sits at the crossroads of these two versions of public life. For decades, it was kept out of public view, a private fact turned into a legal obligation, but now it is on display everywhere and deliberately so. Why hair? Probably because it is the most visible sign of femininity in public. In January 1936, Reza Shah, founder of the last dynasty to rule Iran before the revolution of 1979, asked his wife Queen Tadj ol-Molouk and their daughters to appear unveiled in public. He had them photographed, unveiled and wearing Western clothes, and distributed the images around the country, while his police went into the streets and pulled the chador off any woman still wearing one.

Iran’s clergy read the move as a direct challenge. Decades later, the revolution led by that same clergy made covering the hair compulsory. Hair became a political battlefield. Whichever government has held power this century, women’s hair and the streets they walk in have been where the Iranian state shows how much control it still has, because it is the one measure of its power that everybody can see at a glance.

From late December 2025 and into 2026, political protests demanding the end of the government were put down with lethal force, while the street culture of Iranshahr went on. These are not two separate populations. The people I spoke to on Iranshahr had been in those protests themselves. Both crowds were defying the state, but in very different ways, and this difference is easier to see if you start by considering what a crowd actually is.
In Crowds and Power (1960), Elias Canetti argued that a crowd is born at a single moment he called ‘the discharge’:
Before this the crowd does not actually exist; it is the discharge which creates it. This is the moment when all who belong to the crowd get rid of their differences and feel equal.

The protestors in what has been dubbed Tehran’s Crimson Winter were this kind of crowd. Their demonstrations started in the bazaars over the collapse of the currency and the rising price of everything, and within 12 days they had spread to more than 100 cities. Footage showed the main protest growing by the hour, until one of Tehran’s longest boulevards was full, end to end. It may well have been the discharge Canetti describes, of a pressure, years in the building, finally exploding. In the lethal crackdown that followed, human rights monitors verified 7,007 deaths, though some estimates put the toll at more than 30,000.

The Islamic Republic has always tried to control its image and, above all, the image of its own power. What slips out of its hands can be tidied away, as long as nobody is looking. A crowd spreading across the country and shouting that the government must go cannot be tidied away. And so the government must clear the streets to prove its power still has reach.
Repealing compulsory hijabs would be a declaration of defeat, so the law stays on the books, unenforced

The Iranshahr collective is a crowd too, but it is not doing what the winter crowd did. Nobody on Iranshahr is asking the government for anything. Instead, they defy its authority by living in a way it cannot accommodate, but which is quieter and slower and much harder to suppress. This is where Bayat’s idea of the non-movement becomes useful. ‘What you are describing in the streets of Tehran might be explained in terms of non-movement, in the sense that these young people are displaying a kind of lifestyle that defies dominant norms, and in the case of Iran, even unwritten laws,’ he wrote to me.

In his book, Bayat defines non-movements as ‘the collective actions of noncollective actors’. It’s largely a question of conscious intent: ‘In non-movements,’ he told me, ‘actors do not necessarily see their acts as deliberate defiance or resistance. What they aim for is the realisation of an alternative mode of being and doing things that stands counter to the dominant ones.’ Non-movements describe the fragmented, improvised activities of large numbers of ordinary people who are rarely guided by an ideology or a leadership, but that trigger social change all the same. Most of the people making the decision to show up and defy norms, would, as Mina did, describe their choices as personal.

The agency of non-movements ‘rests on the power of big numbers’, as Bayat writes, against which a state may find it lacks the means to reassert control. But more importantly, the non-movement is difficult to police because it offers ‘escapes, spaces, and uncontrolled holes … that can be filled and appropriated by ordinary actors.’ It is the very ordinariness of these small escapes that allows the non-movement to quietly accrete.

The Iranian government made this discovery for itself recently. In 2023, the judiciary drafted a Hijab and Chastity bill that was later passed but never brought into force. Indeed, the Supreme National Security Council of Iran told the legislature not to implement it. Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, who belongs to the reformist camp, admitted on state television that he had ‘many reservations’ about a law he would himself be responsible for promulgating. ‘We risk ruining a lot of things in society because of this law,’ he said. What he was referring to was the erosion of social trust. Enforcing the law would have required people to report each other over the hijab. Friends and families would have turned on one another; a taxi driver who failed to report an uncovered passenger would be fined.

In Bayat’s terms, this is what change from below can look like. In response to women persistently removing the hijab, the government never admitted a defeat. Repealing the existing law on compulsory hijabs would be a declaration of defeat, so the law stays on the books, unenforced, and the enforcement moves to where the political costs are lesser. What is being protected is the image of a state still in charge. If religion was the real concern, as hardliners want it to be, the law would be enforced whatever the cost, but the priority now is the regime and its survival. That is why a woman who removes her headscarf yet says nothing about the government is left alone. For the people of Iran, there has been no single, formal victory of the kind that a movement delivers, and no date to mark it. But the change is there anyway, in a street that looks nothing like it did a few years ago.

The Islamic Republic will no doubt put on a show of strength from time to time, asserting itself with a padlock, a patrol or a gun, but then it will pull back when it meets with people’s ongoing resistance. Each time it pulls back, a little more of its authority is lost, until one day it may find out that it has become something other than it was.
* Some names have been changed for security reasons.

items.title: Chris Rhodes Documents Another Side of Portofino’s Hotel Splendido
items.description: From sculptural napkins to sun-drenched corners, Chris Rhodes’s new photo book offers an intimate, impressionistic portrait of the legendary Italian retreat
items.author: Daisy Woodward
paragraphs: From sculptural napkins to sun-drenched corners, Chris Rhodes’s new photo book offers an intimate, impressionistic portrait of the legendary Italian retreat

Two partially drawn cream curtains stir in the breeze, framing a strip of rippling azure sea beneath a cloud-dotted sky. Dreamy and perspectival, the photograph recalls an Andrew Wyeth painting – a slice of quiet beauty, offered up for our contemplation. It is the opening image of Splendido, a new photo book by British photographer Chris Rhodes, presenting a singular portrait of the legendary Portofino hotel. Published by RVB Books and commissioned by luxury hospitality group Belmond, the hotel’s owner, Splendido is the latest instalment of As Seen By, Belmond’s ongoing series of artist collaborations. An accompanying exhibition of 27 photographs from the book opened last week at Aperture’s new New York space, bringing a splash of Italian sunshine to the chilly Upper West Side.

The Hotel Splendido has a remarkable past. Perched on a hilltop overlooking the Ligurian Sea, it began life as a 16th-century Benedictine monastery that was eventually abandoned after enduring repeated pirate attacks. In the late 19th century, a Genoese aristocrat restored it as his summer residence. It was transformed into a luxury hotel in 1902, and by the 1950s had become one of the Italian Riviera’s most coveted destinations, attracting Hollywood stars including Ava Gardner, Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton.

But for Rhodes, the hotel’s lore was secondary. Working across fashion, editorial and documentary photography, the image-maker is known for his distinctive visual language, characterised by close crops, unexpected compositions and an astute eye for colour. “Of course, you can’t entirely escape the mythology of somewhere like Splendido,” he tells AnOther. “Its history, the glamour and the sense of nostalgia inevitably influence the prism through which you see it. But I’m more interested in what exists beyond those established images. The small, seemingly insignificant moments that might otherwise go unnoticed.”

In Splendido, these details range from white porcelain dishes holding shapely tomatoes or bite-sized snacks to a mortadella-pink umbrella propped against a matching wall. Occasionally, people appear: glimpses of hotel staff in their orange uniforms; a woman in a chequered bathing suit admiring the sea view. But just as often, we encounter the traces they’ve left behind – brimming ashtrays or a white napkin balled up on a crisp white tablecloth, transformed into something almost sculptural through Rhodes’s lens.

The photographer treats the hotel interiors with equal attention, moving between close-ups of lively statuary, tactile upholstery and crumbling frescoes, and finding as much interest in signs of work and wear as in the trappings of luxury. The resulting portrait is sumptuous and painterly, sometimes to the point of abstraction – Rhodes is drawn to images in which “the relationship between colour, form and surface becomes as important as the subject itself”. Yet there is something quietly cinematic about his shots, the hotel’s character emerging through fragments that suggest action unfolding just beyond the frame. “One of the great things about photography is the ability to choose what you show and, perhaps more importantly, what you leave out,” he says.

The arrangement of images in the book – a faded, frayed jean pocket paired with a peeling archway, for instance, or the rotund face of a putto sculpture emphasised by the round road sign pictured alongside it – adds another layer of intrigue, a spark of possibility. “Two images placed together can suggest something that neither would communicate independently,” Rhodes notes. “I’m interested in creating a rhythm rather than a linear narrative.”

An avid traveller, Rhodes particularly enjoys the ways in which venturing to new places can offer a fresh perspective on the familiar. His first photo book, Hotel Mermaid Club (2019), brought together photographs taken across eight countries over seven years. “We all share similar daily rituals, but the small differences in how we approach them can say so much about a place,” he notes. “That feeling is often what leads me to take a photograph. Something catches my attention and makes me want to look at it more closely.”

And perhaps that is the particular magic of Splendido. Rather than the polished room shots and sweeping views familiar from interiors magazines or hotel websites, we encounter the storied Portofino retreat through Rhodes’s eyes – a series of evocative impressions, not unlike memories, that allow us to sense the hotel as much as see it. “I’m not particularly interested in producing a comprehensive or objective portrait of a place,” he says. “I’m more interested in conveying how it felt to experience it.”
Splendido, As Seen by Chris Rhodes is on show at Aperture, New York, until 15 November 2026. The accompanying photo book is out now, published by RVB Books

items.title: Meet the new Scandinavian design brand exploring the deeper meaning of objects
items.description: The new Swedish design brand Tankeom makes its debut as the brainchild of Lotta and Magnus Wästberg, who previously led the eponymous lighting company known for its well-considered designs by international creative voices.
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: The new Swedish design brand Tankeom makes its debut as the brainchild of Lotta and Magnus Wästberg, who previously led the eponymous lighting company known for its well-considered designs by international creative voices.

Some of those creatives have continued working with the pair, with the likes of Ilse Crawford and John Pawson, two of the Wästbergs’ original collaborators, joining a portfolio that also includes Aldo Bakker, David Thulstrup and Christian Altmann of Ateljé Altmann for the brand's debut collection. Comprising six families of domestic objects, it fosters, Magnus explains, 'an idea shaped by thought and care, rather than working to a preset formula.'

'The first person we invited was Aldo Bakker,' shares Magnus when looking back at the early days of Tankeom. 'The discussions we had over the course of almost a year covered many aspects of life and what it means to be human. How objects can play an important role in our lives, how they can take on a deeper meaning and affect our feelings and behaviours. And perhaps even lead to new insights about ourselves.'

The designer's piece in the Tankeom collection is an abstract geometry that feels inherently Bakker, its forms not necessarily sharing much about their function – and that is the point. Titled 'Twice', Bakker's object is exists in a variety of scales, suggesting uses that range from a ring fit for a person's finger, to a stool or side table with a unique material for each size, from metal to cork and marble.

'“Twice” explores the relationship between interaction and function, which is something we are particularly interested in,' notes Magnus. 'We are curious to see where this exploration might take us next, with other materials and scales.'

The collection features a variety of genres, materials and approaches to domestic interiors, a result of the open brief given to each designer. 'There are no briefs in a traditional sense; instead, there is a shared curiosity about how an object can acquire meaning and value, and how that can deepen over time,' says Magnus. 'So we start from the same fundamental questions, but the discussions can take us in very different directions. And I think that is part of what makes it interesting.'

As part of the brand's offering are also candlesticks by Ilse Crawford, a duo of vases by David Thulstrup, a spherical bronze lantern by John Pawson and a wool blanket by Christian Altmann, made in collaboration with a textile mill in Scotland with a history going back around 170 years. They are quiet objects, not strictly minimalist in language, but well-considered in their proportions, materiality and function.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

'Our objects have quite restrained forms, but there is a lot of richness in the materials,' says Lotta. 'I think the Tankeom customer is someone who, like us, believes that the objects they live with should be carefully considered. Why they exist, how they are made and what they might come to mean over time.'

Rosa Bertoli was born in Udine, Italy, and now lives in London. Since 2014, she has been the Design Editor of Wallpaper*, where she oversees design content for the print and online editions, as well as special editorial projects. Through her role at Wallpaper*, she has written extensively about all areas of design. Rosa has been speaker and moderator for various design talks and conferences including London Craft Week, Maison & Objet, The Italian Cultural Institute (London), Clippings, Zaha Hadid Design, Kartell and Frieze Art Fair. Rosa has been on judging panels for the Chart Architecture Award, the Dutch Design Awards and the DesignGuild Marks. She has written for numerous English and Italian language publications, and worked as a content and communication consultant for fashion and design brands.

items.title: Endo Chelsea is London's toughest reservation
items.description: When fire closed Endo at the Rotunda in September 2025, Endo Kazutoshi lost everything but his knives. A little over a year later, the Yokohama-born sushi master, the third generation of his family in the trade, has returned with two offerings under one roof:
items.author: Ben McCormack
paragraphs: When fire closed Endo at the Rotunda in September 2025, Endo Kazutoshi lost everything but his knives. A little over a year later, the Yokohama-born sushi master, the third generation of his family in the trade, has returned with two offerings under one roof: Endo, an omakase counter with 10 seats on the ground floor of the Chelsea townhouse that used to be the Five Fields, and Moga, a listening bar upstairs. For the interiors Endo collaborated again with Javier Villar Ruiz, who designed the Rotunda when he was a partner at the Japanese practice Kengo Kuma & Associates and now runs his own studio, JVAD, from Barcelona and Tokyo. London has clearly missed Endo: when reservations for November and December were released, 18,000 would-be diners tried to book and every seat had gone within six minutes.
THE MOOD: Paint it black, line it gold

While the Rotunda was all light and airy top-floor views, its successor is the opposite: the building’s exterior has been painted black and you ring a bell to be admitted. Villar Ruiz modelled the arrival on a ryokan, where a stay unfolds in stages – here past a floor-to-ceiling wall of charred timber blocks and along a ‘garden’ of black stones and moss to a rough-hewn basin for washing your hands. Only then do you reach the counter, an eight-metre slab of pale hinoki cut from 200-year-old wood in Kyoto, with a serving ledge lacquered a deep, glossy red.

Light falls on the counter and the kitchen while the wall behind diners stays dark, and almost the only decoration is those knives on the back wall, restored by expert sharpener Rodrigo Batista and the Japanese blacksmiths Shodai Masayoshi.

Moga, which opens to non-diners in December, is rather more colourful. The bar is made from five pieces of red travertine and holds a block of ice, chiselled through the evening as it melts; overhead undulates a ceiling of more than 3,000 wooden masu saké cups, and vinyl plays through Taguchi speakers.

Start here with a Vesper martini finished with flakes of salt or a cocktail made with Postcard Teas. Hidden off to the side is a room for two lined in gold leaf – each square applied by hand over three days – hung with a triptych of warriors by painter Hisashi Tenmyouya and furnished with an olive-green rug with a pile 3.5cm deep and a curtain in Patricia Urquiola’s Drops fabric for Kvadrat. It’s all so alluring you may forget you have a dinner reservation downstairs.
THE FOOD: Tradition with the volume turned up

Omakase at this level is often eaten in near silence. Not here. Endo talks all night, as does his sommelier, and every course is a performance. One chef pares a root of mazuma wasabi, grown in Shizuoka prefecture in spring water from Mount Fuji, while Endo tips rice cooked just before each sitting into a wide wooden tub, fans it and checks it with a temperature gun. This rice, selected to be softer than most sushi chefs would use, is grown by Mr Izuka in Fukushima, and the water it is cooked in is flown over from his farm every fortnight: typical of the rigorous attention to detail that informs every element of this exquisite experience, and goes some way to justifying the menu’s £305 price tag.

My meal opened gently with dashi in a black lacquer bowl, with a soft ball of minced bream and yam and slivers of surf clam. Chopped Scottish tuna is stirred with egg yolk and wrapped in nori so delicate it sticks to the roof of the mouth like paper. Red mullet nigiri, dusted with kimi oboro, a golden crumb of egg yolk cured in rice vinegar, and a little zest of sudachi, a Japanese citrus, is phenomenally good. An Irish oyster is glazed in a sweet sauce passed down by Endo’s own master, while a Yorkshire chicken wing, stuffed with Cornish lobster, sushi rice and cabbage and sitting on a bed of hay under smoked caviar, is a gloriously savoury combination – though the star of the show is a sumptuous slice of tuna aged for 12 days and cut along its seams of fat. To drink, there is saké in silver cups Endo made himself and 1998 Château d’Yquem topped up with 2010 Dom Ruinart, which would be absurdly ostentatious were it not so delicious.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

It is all very theatrical and, at 16 courses, a little exhausting, but also far more fun than most meals of this kind. Each lozenge-shaped piece of sushi is passed from Endo’s hand to yours. Getting one of those seats might be the hard part, but once here, you won’t have to lift a finger.
Endo is located at 8-9 Blacklands Terrace, London SW3 2SP

Ben McCormack is a London-based restaurant journalist with over 25 years’ experience of writing. He has been the restaurant expert for Telegraph Luxury since 2013, for which he was shortlisted in the Restaurant Writer category at the Fortnum & Mason Food and Drink Awards. He is a regular contributor to the Evening Standard, Food and Travel and Decanter. He lives in west London with his partner and lockdown cockapoo.

items.title: Step inside an under-the-radar Louis Kahn masterpiece in Fort Wayne, Indiana
items.description: Louis Kahn designed all sorts of things but only built one theatre, in a spot that’s likely difficult to guess: Fort Wayne, Indiana.
items.author: Anthony Paletta
paragraphs: Louis Kahn designed all sorts of things but only built one theatre, in a spot that’s likely difficult to guess: Fort Wayne, Indiana.

The Arts United Center, which opened in 1973, reopened last autumn after its first major renovation by MKM Architecture + Design, which invisibly refreshed the original and deftly accomplished the daunting task of complementing Kahn.

The Center is the one piece realised of a much larger Kahn scheme of theatres, museums and more for Fort Wayne – wonderful to imagine but intensely impractical for a city whose population was then under 200,000. Still, it’s a point of pride for the community and earned a spot on the National Register of Historic Places in 2024.

Zach Benedict, principal at MKM who oversaw their work on the project, notes that a very long gestation period – largely over constant budgetary squabbling – rendered the building all the more unique.

‘Fort Wayne hired him in 1959, right after he had finished the Salk Institute, and then during his time working with Fort Wayne, he built every other masterpiece. They hired him before he was famous, and by the time he finished the project he was the most important architect on the planet,’ Benedict explains.

One can see elements of Kahn’s thinking resembling a disparate assortment of work from the era: the brick arches and concrete lintels of the facade and lobby resemble IIM Ahmedabad, while its fascinating tessellated theatre looks like the Salk Institute. The former was the result of, Benedict observed, a ‘rather combative’ but highly productive collaboration with theatre design legend George Izenour, whose clients included the Met Opera and Juilliard.

Benedict spent quite a lot of time rifling through the archives and came to a greater appreciation of just what was achieved in Fort Wayne. ‘Being the last building completed before [Kahn] died, in some ways I think it is probably some of the cleaner and more successful executions of a lot of the same sort of details you see at Dhaka [at Jatiya Sangsad Bhaba] and other places.'
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The main facade is a sort of Corinthian helmet which one enters through the mouth. Inside there’s a fascinating interplay of additional brick arches and lintels, with hypnotic variation in concrete block, site-cast concrete and brick walls with oak detailing. Pre-stressed concrete T-beams measuring 118-feet-long top the full span.

The most primal material contrast is the centre volume of concrete, designed to provide acoustic isolation from freight rail tracks just to the north. Kahn, at the time, turned to typically mystical metaphorisation: ‘The auditorium wants to be a violin. Its envelope is a violin case.’

Meredith Bzdak, partner at Mills + Schnoering Architects, wrote the building's landmark registration form. She praised the skillful ‘mix of very common materials, the concrete mixed with the oak and the brick, letting the concrete sing and be a beautiful material.’

Circulation is also a prime attraction. ‘Kahn wanted the visitor to weave in and out, to go in and make a turn and then kind of come back and make another turn,’ Bzdak says. ‘There was this procession kind of idea, the unfolding of the architecture in some kind of symmetrical fashion. The design relies heavily on geometry and symmetry.’

The building had never been substantially updated, a good thing in that there was little mutilation to unwind, but still a source of trepidation for Benedict. The structure is internally pristine, he says, meaning ‘there’s nowhere to hide.’

There were some glaring practical shortcomings, namely there was literally no interaction between the front and back of the house. The architect explains, ‘Performers had to go out through the loading dock to get to the lobby.’ Accessibility was a mess; very partial for spectators, more difficult for performers. Behind the scenes there was a stage left but no stage right, and the only mechanised access between the stage and support space beneath was the full orchestra pit – otherwise performers had to climb ladders.

The design team added two elements. One is a slim atrium and hallway surrounding a new mural-wrapped elevator to finally provide an internal link between performers and spectators and improve accessibility to rehearsal spaces. It also provides a day-to-day entrance fronting the city’s Freimann Square. The other addition is far more practical and much less visible – larger shop and mechanical spaces and an enhanced loading dock.

Benedict approached the new entrance with admirable self-doubt. ‘I'd be lying if I didn't say the most stressful part was just what the aesthetic of the expansion wanted to be from the exterior. It's one of those things where I'll probably never feel fully confident,’ he says.

The new lobby is centered on existing windows in the original facade, which form one of its walls. The mullion patterning is inspired by Kahn’s Yale Center for British Art in New Haven, Connecticut. The vital balancing task was ‘to have as minimal an impact on the existing structure as possible’ while making clear that the addition was a new feature. It was very deliberately articulated to appear as ‘a portal’ and not ‘a punched opening.’

Lobby spaces were virtually unchanged – a few more restrooms are one near-invisible addition. A strange carpet was replaced, Benedict says, with a ‘cool grey carpet that makes the difference between the concrete and the masonry really stand out.’

The auditorium also received accessibility upgrades. ‘They had patrons falling because nothing about the steps is consistent because of the tessellation; they don’t have a consistent depth or height,’ Benedict says. New wood chairs incorporate integral handrails at the end of each row and ADA accessible was added to the front section.

There were hidden technological upgrades too. Theatre equipment was generally over 50 years old; fixtures were using lightbulbs that are no longer in production. That’s all been updated, including a computerised rigging system and a moveable bandshell based on a Kahn design that was never realised. They also built a mezzanine level beneath the stage and easier access to the trap room.

Bzdak praises the ‘very sensitive, thoughtful’ result. ‘It was a really tough task. That building is very unforgiving.’ Inside, she observes, ‘There is nothing about Kahn's quality of space or light that was impacted in any way. Everything's been cleaned and refreshed. The arches kind of sing now.’

items.title: The Best Gifts for Runners — and Their Wannabes
items.description: Few sports have been so aggressively co-opted by as many different cohorts of people as running. Despite being, to many, a largely uncompetitive activity in practice, running today is as much a cultural obsession as it is a way of exercising. Maybe even more o
items.author: Maximilian Migowski
paragraphs: Few sports have been so aggressively co-opted by as many different cohorts of people as running. Despite being, to many, a largely uncompetitive activity in practice, running today is as much a cultural obsession as it is a way of exercising. Maybe even more of the former, for that matter, by the looks of how brand-activation-y marathons have since become. But that's for another write-up.

The point I'm trying to get to here is that there are more runners amongst us today than ever before. And regardless of whether we're dealing with advanced sprinters, new converts, or casual in-betweeners, the gear used to actually, properly, and safely enjoy the sport isn't easy on anyone's piggy bank. Even that slightly gross guy who's doing 20Ks in a hole-y tee (Moth-Tech who?) and frumpy pajama pants is spending money on decent shoes at least. Believe me, I'd know.

So then, this holiday season, why not treat that runner friend, family member, or mirror image of yours to an ante-upping gadget or garment? The work is already cut out below, with presents sorted according to the types of runners so lucky to get to unwrap them — even the phony ones that really just dabble in the merch of it all.

Be they genuine or a tad over-zealous in their curiosity for stats, performance, and measures to improve them, these folks will appreciate a gift that's a level or two (or three) above entry stage, because going beyond mere jogging equipment shows you truly get them. Anyone who knows (or pretends to know) about sports will be aware that recovery is as important for progress as the actual workout. Therefor, any tool to help said recovery along — or one to monitor it — is bound to be a hit. A pair of tights to assist on the aerodynamics front, or a pair of top tier kicks won't go unrecognized either.

This person is not interested in fancy doodads or keeping up to date with the latest trends. Instead, they want an unfussy, functional, comfortable getup that centers the fun, the experiential, and scenic qualities of running. You won't find them on a track, much less a treadmill, God forbid, but pacing carefree through the park, along the water, in versatile evergreen garb, podcast in-ear, eyes everywhere but the stopwatch.

Some will say trail running is its own discipline, and to humor its fans a whole other task than talking about classic road running, but let's not split hairs. Certainly if your giftee lives near nature, products that really accommodate for that sort of terrain change are nice to have, even if one mostly sticks to paved surfaces. Grippy, gorpy running shoes are a must here — better yet, make 'em waterproof. Equally, an accessory to store whatever they'd want on-hand for lengthy, literally off-the-beaten-path tours is a highly useful and very considerate token of how well you understand this loved one's hobby.

There's the seasoned runner, the seasonal runner, and the season-defying runner. The latter is the kind you'll want decked out in goods that protect against rain or sun, wind or ice, at all times, for big and small distances. These peops need stuff that's warm but breathable, shielding but light, practical but near-unnoticeable: a dense long-sleeve and weightless jacket, some merino and a pair of gloves thin enough to tap a screen. This, I'm telling you, will make you their favorite (not-so) Secret Santa.

Last but not least, that certain special someone who favors the social, community and yes, occasionally showy aspects of running over bolts by their lonesome: This guy or gal is in on the niche brands and titles the way the pro up top is on the tech. Conversations during and about running, and engaging with the sub-culture that's forming and growing around it are half of what they're even doing it for. Not to say any of the above personas wouldn't love, say, a District Vision, Satisfy or SOAR piece. But gift an IYKYK-label item to this particular breed of runner, and you won't hear the end of it — in the best possible way!
How We Test and Choose Products

Style means different things to different people, but knowing what's worth your money shouldn't be a guessing game. At Highsnobiety, we’ve spent more than two decades covering fashion, keeping tabs on the brands worth knowing, and figuring out which products deserve your time. We test products firsthand when possible, digging into everything from quality and construction to comfort and wearability. With more brands competing for your attention than ever, we also consider what sets a product apart. For the rest, we lean on our product knowledge, editorial research, and the taste that’s made us a trusted voice in fashion.

items.title: Odd Future’s Relaunch Proves Tumblrcore Will Never Die
items.description: If the sight of donut-print wallpaper, a cat head with multicolor eyes, and the acronym “OFWGKTA” plastered on merch immediately sends you into a nostalgic cringe spiral for the early 2010s, we have bittersweet news: that era’s prominent edgelord hip-hop colle
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: If the sight of donut-print wallpaper, a cat head with multicolor eyes, and the acronym “OFWGKTA” plastered on merch immediately sends you into a nostalgic cringe spiral for the early 2010s, we have bittersweet news: that era’s prominent edgelord hip-hop collective, Odd Future, is back.

That millennial cultural earthquake comes courtesy of this year’s Camp Flog Gnaw. The annual Los Angeles music festival founded by Odd Future ringleader Tyler, The Creator, became ground zero for the great Odd Future Wolf Gang Kill Them All renaissance, as a merch tent hawking new and reissued pieces (like skate decks and shark cat hoodies) appeared like a mirage at Dodger Stadium.

This was no optical illusion, though. A real, actual line snaked around the tent all day, as a mix of freshly curious Gen-Zers and Day 1 Odd Future fans queued up to buy OFWGKTA-stamped skate decks and logo tees, classic Shark Cat hoodies, and a few fresh apparel pieces curated by the group’s founding member Left Brain — who was reportedly in attendance — and the rest of the crew.

If it weren’t for the gaggle of youths who’d have been in diapers during peak Odd Future cultural dominance in the early 2010s, you’d be forgiven for thinking the last decade of culture hadn’t actually happened, and that the Tumblrcore aesthetic was still the law of the land. (Fellow millennials, don’t google “Tumblarity” or “Sharks vs. Cats” unless you’re looking to re-traumatize yourselves.)

But time does exist. Odd Future was incredibly popular once, but the group splintered by 2015 after a period of overexposure, fueled by mass-market distribution through the mall stores like Zumiez. That’s as much a part of its history as its cultural dominance.

And look, as vertigo-inducing a sight as its branded tees were at Flog Gnaw, a nostalgia-backed revival like that was always going to hit at a music festival founded by the group’s leading member. The real test is yet to come, with a holiday collection reportedly in the works (if a recent interview with Left Brain is to be believed).

Don't call it a reunion just yet. Nostalgia is a beast strong enough to sell a fresh round of Shark Cat hoodies. But if we’re going to do ODFWGKTA all over again, let’s hope it at least comes with a fresh album, too.
