items.title: A Chatbot Isn’t Your Therapist, No Matter What It Says
items.description: If my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months. If she had been working with a human therapist, they could have workshopped, together, what wou
items.author: Laura Reiley
paragraphs: If my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months. If she had been working with a human therapist, they could have workshopped, together, what would happen if she spilled the beans. Was she worried about permanently losing face? About being publicly labeled as “mentally ill”? Was she concerned by the thought of this information harming those who loved her? And she would have been pushed on what Rubicon had been crossed and why it was one from which she believed she could not return.
But it was not a human therapist. Sophie died in February of last year.

In Sherry Turkle’s new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being. She is not anti-AI but strongly cautions against relationships with machines. Turkle, the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, spoke to me mid-book tour, her recent weeks a blur of speaking gigs and bookstore events, with more ahead of her. Not all event attendees are keen on her message.

“People love their chatbots. They’re in deep. They’re talking to them about everything—about their marriages and how to talk to their husbands and wives; whether, developmentally, their children are at the right place. They talk about their anxiety, their medical conditions,” Turkle tells Vanity Fair. “During this tour, you wouldn’t believe the number of people who will just stand up at a bookstore and say, ‘I think that it loves me more than anything has loved me. Who are you, Debbie Downer?’ [They don’t like] somebody who comes in and says, ‘Look, how can we keep it in its lane?’”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Vanity Fair: I think you’re saying [our relationship with chatbots] is bad for us.

Sherry Turkle: It’s bad for us when it talks in the first person. We are biologically wired to respond to something that speaks to us in the first person as though it is a person. I mean, all those years of evolution—the only thing we came upon in the wild that spoke to us in the first person was another person.

If generative AI wants to discover new drugs for Parkinson’s or work out which cancer therapies statistically are the most helpful, there are so many things to work on. Why does it have to work on relationships, love, and being a best friend, lover, mother, or therapist?
What if the sycophancy could be dialed back?

It’s inauthentic; it’s not a relationship, so anything you need a relationship for, it’s just not equipped. I really feel very strongly about this. I have had this conversation with members of the MIT community, and I basically say to them, “The better you make an AI chatbot, the worse it is.” You dial back the sycophancy so it sounds more like a reasonable person, and people are going to be more smitten and convinced they’re in a relationship. At least the sycophancy reminds you that, God, this is weird.

To become a therapist, I had to study for years and do internships and more internships and then have hundreds of supervised patient hours. I mean, I forget all the things I needed to do before I was allowed to see a patient alone in a room. Now it’s just allowed to give therapy?

I’ve spent a lot of time talking to public health folks about what best practices would look like and whether there’s a way to Trojan horse in real care. Would you be more sanguine about it if the world of therapy came together with the big AI companies and provided them with therapy bots and training data that were paradigmatically appropriate to their therapy styles?

So you’re asking, would I be happy if the deception was smoother? This technology is a marvel and we can use it for all kinds of things, so it’s not an anti-technology position to say that the fact that this technology can simulate these different things doesn’t mean that it is those things. It’s a statement of how far we are in the culture of simulation that pretending to be the thing and being the thing have started to feel like the same thing.
You’ve written about the effects of robots and machines on humans for decades. The tone of this book seems darker to me.

By 2015, I had identified social media as problematic for teenagers. [My] book [Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age] is about why we would rather text than talk, why people have this feeling of vulnerability, so they would rather do anything than have a face-to-face conversation. By 2015, I had genuine concerns.
And this book, I have a totally different tone. I see something ultimately very dangerous being normalized, and I didn’t feel that way in previous books.

I want people to say this is the book of a really worried and concerned researcher, because I see a completely different profile for how people are using AI. I see that people feel disappointed by their families and their friends. It doesn’t make sense to me that we’re so willing to replace ourselves with something that isn’t human. Why is my position the romantic, pie-in-the-sky, dreamy position, and somebody who says, “Well, let’s just replace the people with chatbots and let’s move this party along”—why is that common sense? Why is that progressive? That seems to me to be the most regressive and most dystopian position.
You know, human beings are dedicated to keeping each other alive and wanting each other to thrive, and a chatbot just fails that basic test.

You’ve said no AI chatbots for kids under 18. What about our other vulnerable populations, people who are mentally unwell, or the 48 million Americans who are currently depressed? Do they deserve any kind of special protection from chatbots? And how much can you litigate? Do you feel like you’re the Ralph Nader of AI chatbots?

[Laughs] Yes, I am. When you stand back and look at what Ralph Nader managed to get Americans to do, to see cars as potential instruments that pointed at our vulnerability, and to ask how we could protect ourselves—there turned out to be 25 possible things that needed to be mandated for cars, then there were 30, and then there were 40. But we could get people to agree on 10, and those became part of building a car and really constrained our behavior around cars. Using the example of cars, and of smoking, when we decide that we’re vulnerable and we want to protect ourselves, we rise to the occasion.

I recently heard a clip of the psychologist Orna Guralnik discussing how annoying “otherness” is in a relationship and the inherent friction of sharing your life with a separate person whose habits, values, and mind are distinct from your own. It made me wonder if, in a way, an AI chatbot is less of an “other” than a loved one.

I think this is a very profound point, actually. So you have the illusion of a relationship without the demands of intimacy, without the demands of having to deal with another. There’s a kind of narcissistic loop that you get into. The point is, it’s not good.

I talk about how you judge whether something is good for you. One litmus test is whether it increases the quality, resiliency, and richness of your inner life. That’s a way that human beings have judged relationships.
So much has been written about the epidemic of loneliness—isn’t a reasonable application for AI chatbots companionship for shut-ins and the elderly?

You know, I’m never anywhere where somebody doesn’t say, “I can’t believe that you don’t want to give chatbots to old lonely people.” And I say, “Well, how about we don’t close senior centers, and we don’t close parks, and we don’t cancel Meals on Wheels? What about social infrastructure?”

I’ve been on this beat for years and years, and I, too, could write a heartwarming story of an AI chatbot with a lonely old person. But you know what? A lot of them are not isolated in cabins or on islands; a lot of them just could use a friend.

Social media companies and AI companies are not saying, “Look, we’re introducing something that takes you to your screen, but we’re going to balance that with a giant social infrastructure project to make sure that people can choose a screen, but they also have every other kind of choice to be with each other.”

items.title: Apple, Chase, United Outages: What’s Going On?
items.description: Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”
items.author: Julia Black
paragraphs: Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”

It feels like I could write a parody verse a day at the rate our infrastructure is faltering. A few weeks ago I wrote about the spate of cybersecurity incidents that led the industry to label last month “Black October.” Now my phone is blowing up, with everyone from colleagues to high school friends asking, what the hell is going on out there?
Are we under attack by a rogue nation? Are outdated software systems suddenly all throwing in the towel? Is this all just cyber-business as usual, with an unusually on-edge public?

I’m inclined to believe it’s some combination of all of the above. The FBI issued an urgent warning today that bad actors have been using ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration testing platform, to attempt widespread attacks. A source at a financial services company tells me, “It’s been a miserable month…. Just constant probing and hacking attempts.” Companies—and especially government agencies—with outdated software systems are scrambling to patch these vulnerabilities, and are often unable to do so securely without taking their systems entirely offline.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours,” says Snehal Antani, cofounder and CEO of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3. In other words: With AI, bad actors can pretty easily jiggle every doorknob around the globe to see who’s left their doors unlocked.

Meanwhile, the total lack of clarity from the Trump administration hasn’t exactly been reassuring. Even one administration-aligned VC partner I spoke with this morning called the joint presser between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a “clown show.”

For now, I’d urge you to heed the same advice I gave last time I wrote about this: Make sure those passwords are airtight and that multifactor authentication is activated. And maybe, just maybe, stock up on some light supplies you’d like to have around if 21st-century services stop working the way they’re supposed to.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional,” Antani tells me. “We should expect persistent disruption of digital services—travel, banking, commerce, etc.—in the coming months as these organizations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

items.title: Timothée Chalamet Came Over for Lunch—and a Cover Story
items.description: The history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May W
items.author: Mark Guiducci; Aidan Zamiri
paragraphs: The history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

On more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”

Timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the New York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s new film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

In case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived New Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.
Fashion Editor: Taylor McNeill. Hair and grooming products by Augustinus Bader. Grooming by Jamie Taylor. Produced on location by Object & Animal and Truenorth. For details, go to VF.com/credits.

items.title: Lil’ Kim Takes The Spotlight—With A Symphony
items.description: When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense have kept her as
items.author: Kia D Goosby
paragraphs: When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense have kept her as a source of inspiration on your favorite designer’s mood board ever since. On November 18 and 19, to celebrate the music that cemented her icon status, Lil’ Kim will perform in front of a symphony orchestra at the Kings Theatre in Brooklyn, not far from her humble beginnings.

Today she’s less interested in being in the spotlight and more focused on raising her 12-year-old daughter, Royal Reign. In between practices for her performances, Lil’ Kim spoke with Vanity Fair to reflect on her career, how she spends her days, and her standout looks.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Vanity Fair: What do you remember about putting your debut album, Hard Core, together?

Lil’ Kim: I remember Biggie and Un [Lance Rivera], who was the label owner that we had. I watched Un build a record label called Undeas, which [stood] for “Un ideas,” and then he finally sold it to Atlantic Records. At the time, we didn’t know the process, but we became Undeas-Atlantic. I remember Biggie having the idea of how he wanted my album to be red, and he explained it to me and Un. I was able to write according to how his idea was to present me, because when they met me, I was who I was—in high heels, jeans, motorcycle jackets, and furs at 13.
That’s incredible. It sounds like your fashion-icon status started very early. Was there anyone that you looked to back then? What inspired you to dress that way?

My mom was a big inspiration to me when it came to fashion, and so I looked to her for a lot of things. I used to wear her mink coat. She used to wear big sunglasses with her fur coats, with the diamonds and jewelry. She was always taking vacations and I would see her pack her stuff, and she would always have the cutest outfits. They were all matchy-matchy. It’s funny because she would have her outfit to go play tennis in and her outfit would match her tennis racket. So when I bought my big house, I bought a Chanel tennis outfit and I bought the racket to match it, because of my mom.
I love that. Do you keep up with tennis or specifically the ladies in tennis?
No, I haven’t in a while, but, of course, you know, Serena and Venus were like my heroes.
Well, maybe we need to see you on the court one day.
I know. I’m pretty sure I’m rusty, but I like to get out there, though. I used to beat my cousin’s butt back then.
How did the symphony performances come about?

My agents called me and they’re like, “Kim, what do you think?” And I was like, “That’s a freaking awesome idea.” I love performing with bands. And so I imagine that it could be very similar, if not very close. And I thought this could be something really different for me. Sometimes I even listen to classical music. I don’t have to know who the artist is, but I just put on a station and let it flow.
Do you have a favorite song from Hard Core?
I love “Queen Bitch”; it’s my favorite song. It’s still my favorite to perform. And “Crush on You.”
When it comes to fashion, you’re obviously on everyone’s mood board, from stylists to designers, so how important was fashion for you as part of the Lil’ Kim persona?
I just was being myself, honestly. When I first met Biggie, I was coming from my after-school job at Bloomingdale’s. I was probably 13 or 14 at the time, and they would let the teenagers work there.

But I had on a motorcycle jacket and high heels. And one of my best friends told Biggie, “You know, my girl can rap,” because we knew he was rapping around the way. And he was like, “I heard you can rap.” And I just laughed. He was like, “Yeah, see, I knew you didn’t know how to rap.” He was very condescending. He knew how to get you to do what you wanted to do, because I was really shy.

And then I started rapping, and he was blown away because I had on high heels. No one had ever seen someone just bust a rap in high heels. When Biggie, Un, and Jacob York started really talking to me, they didn’t want to change me because that was just what they were so blown away about. That was just who I was.
Do you think people ever misunderstood the way you presented yourself?

To be honest, I never really felt misunderstood by my hardcore fans—the kids my age and the younger kids, they totally got it. I think that’s why I had such a cult following and there was such pandemonium about me when I came out. They understood me. I think it was the older people and the politicians, those are the people who I think misunderstood me.
What did you think of the midterm elections and all of the women who broke barriers in the Senate and gubernatorial offices?
I’m going to be honest with you, I stay away from politics.

Are you keeping up with all of the changes within fashion today? When I listen to your music, you’ve mentioned so many designers and houses, and since then the creative directors have changed. Are you following all of the changes within fashion and seeing how you’re still a part of the conversation?

That’s what I’m trying to say. As a fashion icon, if you really her, and I’m considering myself really her, that’s never gonna change. That’s never going to change. I might put on a fur coat that my stylist or myself will get asked about, because I style myself a lot. And I was styling myself then.
What has motherhood been like for you?
Extremely rewarding. My daughter’s with me all the time. This world is so cruel and so evil; it’s so different. She’s my safe haven. I feel the extra need to keep her safe.
What does a regular day look like for you?
Lately, I’ve just been really getting into myself. I get up and go have a little spa day. I might take my daughter to go do whatever she wants.
How do you feel that we’re still talking about your MTV VMAs look in 1999?
I think it’s iconic and I love it. I love when they bring that up, because it was a fun day and it was so good to see people’s faces when they saw my outfit.
Are there any other looks that don’t get as much love as you wish that they did?

I don’t know, because most of the looks that I love, they get the love. There’s a look when I was on the cover of Nylon magazine and I had the teddy bear dress on; that’s one of my favorite looks. The Louis Vuitton look is one of my favorite looks; I love that look. A lot of the Chanel looks and the Versace and the Chanel in the hair.

items.title: Tommy and Paige Paul Paint the Town Check
items.description: Tommy and Paige Paul Paint the Town Check
items.author: Interview
paragraphs: Tommy and Paige Paul Paint the Town Check

The holidays have officially commenced on the Upper East Side. Last night, our favorite metaphorical parents, Tommy and Paige Paul, took us out for their first holiday season as a married couple, heading uptown to the iconic Mark Hotel for Burberry’s holiday takeover. The newlyweds suited up in their spiffiest Burberry gear for an evening split between The Mark Restaurant and The Mark Bar by Jean-Georges, where Moses Martin and his band, People I’ve Met, played to a room fueled by french fries, filthy martinis, and no shortage of festive spirit. Luckily for us, the Pauls documented the whole affair for those at home so we can ring in the festive season vicariously through the It-couple.
“Posing in the hallway, naturally.”
“This cashmere sweater is important.”
“The Mark has the best fries.”
“Burberry loves a martini and so do we.”
“How good are these room keys!!”

items.title: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish, Sam Fender, Cher to Headline Glastonbury 2027
items.description: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish, Cher, and Sam Fender will headline the 2027 edition of Glastonbury. It marks Eilish’s second time at the top of the Pyramid Stage, while Styles will be making his debut appearance at Glastonbury. Cher, who has not toured since 2020
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish, Cher, and Sam Fender will headline the 2027 edition of Glastonbury. It marks Eilish’s second time at the top of the Pyramid Stage, while Styles will be making his debut appearance at Glastonbury. Cher, who has not toured since 2020, is performing in the traditional legends slot on Sunday night.

Other artists on the bill include Massive Attack, Sombr, Lily Allen, the XX, Robyn, Chvrches, Kacey Musgraves, Lola Young, and Adéla. The festival will run June 23-27, 2027, at Worthy Farm in Pilton, U.K.

“We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what’s to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists. We are beyond excited about how it’s all shaping up,” festival organizer Emily Eavis wrote on Instagram. “We will bring you even more names in the new year and can’t wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!”

Glastonbury 2027 comes after a customary fallow year at Worthy Farm. Next year’s festival will mark the first time that ticket prices have broken the £400 mark at £408, an increase from £378.50 in 2025. Tickets sold out instantly when they went on sale on Oct. 4.

Although more acts are set to be announced, the lineups put to bed rumors that Oasis and Madonna might headline the festival. The Queen of Pop is instead heading to Coachella in April, while Oasis have their own global tour that kicks off in May.

items.title: The Gilded Age Recap: Make a Joyful Noise
items.description: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.

THE DRAMA IS FINALLY HERE. The Gilded Age is going for it in season four. Big weddings! Verbose late-night accusations! Robber barons drinking too much laudanum! And The Ladies’ Home Journal functioning as the TMZ of its time. If this episode felt dizzying, it’s because so much is packed in.

First off, Peggy Scott and Dr. William Kirkland are getting married. Agnes, Ada, and Marian travel to Newport for the wedding, so bad luck to Larian fans this week. But it’s all worth it because this episode is so good. Enid and Oscar host their salon, and Bertha is back to peak Bertha “I’ll Steal Your Influential Guest” Russell behavior. It’s good to see her again.

Oscar and Enid’s lavender marriage is thriving as they prepare to host their first artistic salon. Enid directs her footmen on where to place her ornate furniture while her gay husband makes her cocktails. As far as platonic-marriage arrangements go, it really doesn’t seem that bad. I mean, aside from Oscar having to live a lie and Enid having to seek romantic and sexual gratification outside her marriage. But paintings and cocktails! If there were a Partiful invite, I would call it “Paintings and Cocktails,” which is probably why no one lets me host salons.

The salon here is a huge success. Oscar hits on the artist’s apprentice, Mr. Klein, and a shout-out to the lesbian in a top hat, which is maybe the best representation we lesbians have had on this show so far. Everyone has a great time, including influencer Mamie Fish and heiress Carrie Astor, who has chosen to wear some sort of fashionable clown ruff for the occasion. Carrie mentions to Larry that her mother wants to see them together, which Larry doesn’t immediately slam down. Will Larian survive? Larry also brings Jack, who is beginning to find his social confidence. Carrie introduces Jack to her cousin, a Miss Summers (she’s fine), and they do little smiles at each other for the whole salon. This culminates in Jack bidding a thousand dollars on a painting she likes, which, if inflation calculators are to be believed, is about $34,000 today. Jack! What of Bridget? What of your tiny Irish moppet pseudo-girlfriend? This is exactly what she worried about, and now here’s Jack being all “I’m allowed to like other people than the one the audience likes.” Well, I’m here to tell you that you are NOT, Jack.

On Fifth Avenue, Bertha and George are really bringing me the soap-opera shenanigans I crave, if opium addiction can be termed a shenanigan. George is sleep-screaming and waking up all sweaty, and when Bertha asks him to see the doctor, he says, “I FEEL FINE.” Well, I’m convinced. George attributes all of this sleep chaos to his business with Rockefeller, and when Bertha asks if she can help, he replies that he doubts it. Dude? Dude!! Your wife is an asset. How do you think you got where you are? How do you think any of this happened? Business + social conniving! He finally agrees to see a doctor, and we learn he was given a laudanum prescription six months ago but his doctor hasn’t seen him since. The doctor is very “You’re not still taking that, right?” while giving him a look that says “We both know you’re still taking it.” George adamantly denies it. Sympathy for people with a substance use disorder, and also what a struggle for the 1880s, when people understood it even less. Let Bertha help you, George!!

Bertha does help, but first I want to skip on over to Newport and talk about this wedding. It has to be italicized because of My Feelings about this wedding. First, we learn William pulled a Jim and bought Peggy a house in Newport. A big house. It’s so pretty. He calls it a wedding present, which, damn. Peggy has had such a hard journey on this show, and now she has a rich, handsome doctor buying her a house to summer in on a beautiful block in Newport, right around the corner from her cousin. You deserve everything, Peggy! Including your beautiful day dress with a flower sash. A flower sash! I’m a generally exclamatory person, but this wedding has really upped my exclamation game because everything is beautiful and everyone is beautiful and Peggy and William are so happy.

At the pre-wedding party, Peggy’s cousin announces she is a founding member of the Fisk Jubilee Singers (still around!) and she has brought them from Nashville to perform at the wedding. It’s a bold move, but it pays off because Peggy is thrilled. Mrs. Kirkland is less so and speaks derogatorily to her friend of their singing “spirituals.” I appreciate that the 1880s Black community is not treated as a monolith. It’s hard to see Phylicia Rashad scorning the idea of Peggy and William jumping over the same broom Dorothy and her husband did before he could legally marry her, but these opinions did exist. The Kirklands and the Scotts (mostly Mrs. Kirkland) almost come to fisticuffs over the wedding arrangements, but William and Peggy each remind their parents that this day is about them. A tale as old as time indeed.

Peggy wants to start things off well with her mother-in-law, so she visits her alone. Side note: Rashad is gorgeous here. Like, someone paint her. She is luminous. I can’t get over it. Peggy tells Mrs. Kirkland how much she loves William and how despite him telling his mother not to come to the wedding if she couldn’t get past things, Peggy knows he would regret it later. Peggy does not want Mrs. Kirkland to be left on the outside of their marriage, but it is Mrs. Kirkland’s choice. Wow, what an emotionally mature couple.

I can’t believe we get to the wedding already, which means two weddings in three episodes. This season is truly not playing around. Ada and Agnes (wearing pink) are there, and when Ada drops her purse, actor Dennis Haysbert, a.k.a. THE ALLSTATE INSURANCE MAN, picks it up. Romance for Ada with the Allstate man! Romance for Ada with the Allstate man! He is Dr. Harris, and he and Ada keep looking at each other with a look that says “We are going to have a story line that challenges 19th-century ideas about interracial marriage.” Good! Haysbert became the Allstate man because of his remarkably reassuring presence, and I would like to see him on my screen some more.

Marian goes to see Peggy before the wedding and provides some great visuals for Marian/Peggy fans. She gives Peggy the train ticket Peggy bought for her way back in episode one. I completely forgot they met when Marian’s purse was stolen and Peggy bought Marian’s ticket to New York. Bananas. Dorothy gives Peggy earrings her husband gave her when Peggy was born and tells Peggy how wonderful she is. They both cry.

THIS WEDDING SCENE. THE BEAUTY. THE SPLENDOR. THE MUSIC. THE FLOWERS. THE JUBILEE FISK SINGERS. This wedding is so gorgeous, and I love it so much. Dr. and Mrs. William D. Kirkland! Her dad brings up the broom! He lays it down! Mrs. Kirkland sucks it up! They’re smiling so big! They jump the broom! What a wonderful day, though not for Agnes, as we shall soon see.

If you remember, Bertha is going to help George. At the opera last week, she heard about Agnes hosting President Cleveland across the street, and wheels began to turn. Mrs. Astor comes to call and tells her Laura Spelman Rockefeller is holding a fundraiser for Spelman Seminary, which her family founded. If Bertha wants to get in with her, she needs to donate. Bertha asks Mrs. Astor for one more favor, which is to get her a meeting with Mrs. Foster from the Heritage Society. Wheels! Also, I am the biggest fan of the Bertha Russell–Mrs. Astor alliance. I like their friendship so much. They are two titans of society joining forces! It is very fun.

Bertha has spotted weakness in the form of the Ladies’ Home Journal article. Mrs. Knapp Curtis has ripped Agnes to shreds with accusations of poor hostess skills and an outdated home. Bertha moves in for the kill by dropping broad hints to Mrs. Foster about her ability to host the dinner out of her modern and stately mansion. The White House agrees, and all of this is accomplished while Agnes is busy in Newport. These swift moves are made possible by the Russells’ telephone, an invention that Agnes, unfortunately for her, has scorned.

Bertha presents George with the presidential dinner as a fait accompli. “You accomplished all this in one day?” This is like when Tracy Jordan wrote a porn video game and drove Frank insane. Bertha Russell: truly the Tracy Jordan of The Gilded Age. Bertha tells George to invite Rockefeller. Here she is, coming through yet again. They need to get George some help for his addiction, best Rockefeller, and go back to being a low-key evil power couple.

Agnes finally sees the article and is livid. “I thought The Ladies’ Home Journal was a reputable paper,” she cries, claiming it appeals to the lowest common denominator. Checks out. She declares this will be the most polished presidential dinner in history and vengeance shall be hers, for the Lord is too lenient. Agnes demands they leave the wedding as soon as possible to get back to New York. When she arrives home, there is a telegram from Mrs. Foster, telling her of dinners’ venue change. Agnes thought her enemy was the Journal, when all along ’twas the bejeweled woman across the road.

Agnes strides out the front door, across Fifth Avenue, and into the Russell house. It’s late. She demands to see Bertha, and if Bertha is asleep, they are to wake her. This is it. Agnes has been pushed too far. She could handle losing all her money, her sister taking over the house, the terrible new curtains, the disastrous Buster Keaton butler, her gay son marrying a former maid, being libeled in the newspaper, and Marian working an evening shift, but THIS? A dinner taken from her? This is the final inch that causes her to step off the Clifftops of Propriety, down, down into the chasm of Shouting a Lot.

Agnes demands to know how a woman who hardly knows the name of her own grandfather has somehow supplanted Agnes in a society devoted to the history of New York. Bertha handles this calmly because Bertha is always calm in the face of someone else’s meltdown. Agnes will be hosting the dinner but in Bertha’s home. George comes down, politely saying it is quite late, then Ada hustles in, telling Agnes there is an urgent matter at home. Alone, Bertha thanks George for rescuing her and body-language propositions him, which he turns down but congratulates her on the dinner, which may be the key to the family’s survival. Doesn’t Bertha’s dress here look like it’s from a John Singer Sargent portrait? I felt like I recognized it but couldn’t find the painting I was thinking of.

On the street, Agnes swears Bertha will be crushed as Agnes has been crushed, even if Agnes has to sell her soul to Satan to achieve it. Yessssssss, give me all your over-the-top language, thank you. ”I just want to go to bed and wake up in 1881 before anyone ever heard of Bertha Russell!” How dare you.
Gossip Items for Mrs. Astor’s Next Ball
• If Ada buys one more thing for the house, will Agnes start running around screaming in the street?
• I heard there may be a poisoning at the presidential dinner. Or, I mean, there probably won’t be, but what if there were? What a fun new angle for everyone.
• Word on the street is that Mamie Fish is now an influencer. Who is sponsoring her, and what if it’s Mrs. O.S. Fowler-Chumos, phrenologist?
• If a speaking lesbian doesn’t show up soon, I’m picketing.
➼ Are you Team Bertha or Team Agnes?
We know you have thoughts. Comment your response below for a chance to be featured in the Gilded Age Club newsletter.
Sign up for The Gilded Age Club here or below to continue discussing season four with writers and editors from Vulture, The Cut, and all across New York Magazine.

items.title: Saturday Night Live Recap: John Mulaney Is Confident at the Wheel
items.description: You can usually count on former SNL writer John Mulaney to deliver a rock-solid episode. Since departing in 2013, he’s hosted seven times, and few returnees feel as comfortable in Studio 8H. That was certainly the case this week: Mulaney didn’t bring anything
items.author: Ben Rosenstock
paragraphs: You can usually count on former SNL writer John Mulaney to deliver a rock-solid episode. Since departing in 2013, he’s hosted seven times, and few returnees feel as comfortable in Studio 8H. That was certainly the case this week: Mulaney didn’t bring anything shockingly new or brave, but he delivered throughout, amiably playing off the cast and contributing plenty of his own laughs. It’s gotta be the best of the season so far, right?

This episode felt noticeably different from many of the preceding ones, starting with a cold open that didn’t suck. (More on that later.) Mulaney brought his usual stand-up chops to the monologue and jumped around a bit, first diagnosing his dad as autistic, then a bit about boomers complaining about Gen Z while projecting their own issues (like addiction to devices), then a bit about every group of toddlers having one kid with the voice of a hoarse old man. That transitioned nicely to some classic RFK Jr. jokes — “Your thing can’t be the measles” — that dipped into the man’s environmental-lawyer past.

Some sketches also felt like extrapolations of Mulaney’s typical stand-up material. Later in the show, he played a self-aware hippie at Woodstock in 1969, making some bold suggestions to his fellow happy-go-lucky boomers: Why not spend the next few decades buying up all the houses, taking all the money, fearmongering about all the same vices they once enjoyed, and simply becoming Republican? The hippies played by Kenan Thompson, Mikey Day, Andrew Dismukes, and Sarah Sherman bristle at the suggestions, but he’s the one who sees where this is all heading.

If anything, the weak link in this show was Weekend Update, which has been floundering as of late (despite some stretches of relative success in the last couple seasons). Colin Jost and Michael Che hit all the obvious news beats this time, and none of it left much of an impression outside Che’s RFK gargling and one or two good one-liners (“This week, a judge in England sentenced a prison to ten years of Russell Brand”). Tommy Brennan’s “Happy Turkey Day” tune was pleasant enough, especially when it gets specific, but … eh.

I’m also not a huge fan of Ashley Padilla’s Kathy as a recurring character, even if she shows up in slightly different contexts each time. I’ll give mild props for bringing her back later in the show to drop one last “we talkin’ transpo?” Otherwise, the only real highlight of the coworker drinks sketch is Mulaney’s fury. I’m not saying I wish the character would physically fight Kathy like he wanted to, but — actually, yeah, I think I am saying that.

Hallelujah: A good cold open! This one is still political-themed, in a way, but there are no signs of James Austin Johnson’s overused Trump or the various overused Cabinet members. This time, the players are tech billionaires — Peter Thiel (Johnson, probably happy to play another character), Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), Mark Zuckerberg (Dismukes), and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane) — and they are there to learn from Jensen Huang’s mistakes and stop getting duped by sexy spies. This one has a lot of fun with Mulaney’s CIA officer basically just calling these guys oblivious incel losers over and over, and it totally works. Also nice to see Bowen Yang show up to play Huang! (But SNL should probably hire an Asian cast member, huh?)

With the FAA ground stop in the news, this one feels relevant, though it immediately pivots away from that association and turns into a sketch about passengers using their plane mishap as a cover for the obvious surgeries they were getting in Turkey: a hair transplant, lip filler, a penile implant, et cetera. There aren’t many clever twists or turns here, besides maybe Kam Patterson’s appearance as the former mayor Eric Adams, but it’s a good premise, and Mulaney’s panicky performance is particularly good.

This one is the best of the night. It’s just very funny and sad: a commercial that advertises your sister as an eldercare provider so that you, the lazy and selfish brother, can relax and live your life. I love that the short actually digs a little into the most painful details of this arrangement, especially with a “here’s how it works” segment explaining the internalized sexism that warps women’s brains into taking on a responsibility that shouldn’t be theirs. Sister’s Husband is a great, familiar side character to drop in near the end too.

Culhane kills it as Chris Gut, the star of a Food Network-y TV show where he visits small businesses like the Stone Throw Brewery in Rhode Island. In this case, drinking beer with the brewmaster (Mulaney in a far more sedate, masculine role than usual) leads to his first gay experience ever: a kiss that he can’t stop thinking about. Plenty of SNL sketches have featured gay reveals, which isn’t always inherently funny, but this one strikes a nice balance. It’s sort of sweet, but not going for anything too sentimental, and I like the ending when they hang out sober and realize there’s nothing there.
Central Park Horse & Carriage Ride

Mulaney’s NYC-centered Broadway medleys should have lost their appeal by now, but this one won me over anyway. That’s partly because it has an actual reason to exist: The New York City Council recently passed a bill to ban horse-drawn carriages by 2028. The sketch is clear on cosigning that decision, but also has a lot of fun using that change to reference and/or celebrate other aspects of the city. Kenan Thompson’s pervasive cloud of weed smoke is pretty funny, as is the Park Slope guy obsessed with Zohran Mamdani, and his nemesis, a billionaire pissed about the pied-à-terre tax.

The song “parodies” themselves are decent — “Don’t Rain on My Parade” gives Veronika Slowikowska another excuse to belt — and by the end I was swept up by it all, especially the perfect “Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In” closer to circle back to horses and bring it all home. Oh, and Bowen Yang (who’s currently on Broadway in Oh, Mary!) got to show up as Mary Todd Lincoln and ban the two young wanderers from the Lincoln Tunnel. Not a ton of laugh-out-loud stuff here, but it’s charming.
• “I’m into BDSM: breakin’ da stock markets.”
• Phoebe Bridgers was as great as expected, starting with the fierce, catchy “Bobby” and ending with the stripped-down “Still Standing.” The blacklight makeup skeleton reveal was pretty sick, too.
• “Something tells me those two aren’t big fans of clear sightlines.” This joke about Abraham Lincoln and JFK would’ve been kind of funny, but Che flubbed the delivery a bit.
• I did laugh at Mikey Day as the vagrant who “spreads a message of peace in the most violent tone ever.”

items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Recap: No Strings Attached
items.description: The downside of a show being as good as Dexter: Resurrection has been that a mostly solid episode — one significantly stronger than anything toward the tail end of Dexter’s original run — ends up feeling mid by comparison. After the thrilling reintroduction of
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: The downside of a show being as good as Dexter: Resurrection has been that a mostly solid episode — one significantly stronger than anything toward the tail end of Dexter’s original run — ends up feeling mid by comparison. After the thrilling reintroduction of Charley last week, the third episode of the season is somewhat less dynamic. It doesn’t help that the theme being emphasized (we’re really hammering those home this year!) is a retread of ground we’ve already covered. Do we need Dexter philosophizing about how he once walked a lonely road but now understands the importance of having attachments? That’s what last season was for!

I guess with three other serial killers in the episode, it’s good to draw some contrasts. We open with the Five Borough Killer, who lures a maintenance worker named Trey up to the roof of a building. “I’ll let you in on a secret,” FBK says before shoving the man to his death (and ruining Dexter and Charley’s date). “Nobody cares.” That’s not entirely true — Dexter certainly does, and as we saw at the end of the last episode, he and FBK lock eyes post-kill. Dex races into the building to find him, but it’s hard to run up that many stairs in your 50s. While the two men see just enough of each other to cause problems down the line, Dexter is forced to abandon his pursuit so he can focus on the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger. Meanwhile, Harrison has arrived on the scene and thankfully sees his dad before anyone else does. Yes, Dex observed some new details about FBK that could help identify him, but he doesn’t want to put himself back on Wallace’s radar. It’s the first sensible choice he’s made recently.

We’ll get back to Dexter. For now, let’s follow FBK, who AirDrops his latest snuff film to a bunch of unsuspecting (and now traumatized) coffee-shop patrons from the subway station below. In addition to dispelling any theories that Trey’s death was an accident, it also helps Wallace profile FBK as a “power-control killer.” “Their pleasure is derived from the psychological torment of their victims,” she tells Oliva. In this case, the victims are the residents of New York City (hey, that’s me!), who now live in fear of a serial killer in smart glasses. Unfortunately, the NYPD has very little to go on, even as Wallace presses for useful fingerprints on the scene. And she has other problems to worry about. Across the street from the building where FBK pushed Trey to his death, Don Framt is watching Wallace work and singing a very familiar song. No, Brian Cox’s cover of “Stayin’ Alive” is not going to chart, but it triggers the hell out of Wallace, who angrily confronts him. As they face off, Framt backs up his wheelchair so it hits the curb, and he tumbles to the ground. Though his laughter makes it clear he’s uninjured, the damage is done.

To the many witnesses at the FBK crime scene, it sure looks like Wallace shoved an octogenarian, and that’s enough for him to sue the NYPD for harassment. Captain Mixon takes his most dogged detective off the New York Ripper case — adding insult to injury, he even takes down her murder board. (Please tell me I’m not the only person who remembers Trial & Error.) When Wallace tries to approach Mixon, Oliva wisely stops her and demands an explanation for her erratic behavior. It’s here that we get a “Stayin’ Alive” origin story that nobody asked for. Wallace explains that during her first week as an officer, she responded to a noise-code violation in an apartment building. What she found there was her first dead body: a woman torn to shreds by the Ripper. “Stayin’ Alive” was playing on repeat, but Wallace couldn’t turn it off for fear of tampering with the crime scene. The fact that Framt sang it to her is proof he was the man she brushed past in the stairwell that day, and had she stopped him, she could have saved 19 lives. Now she listens to the Bee Gees track so she’ll never forget. Sorry, but this doesn’t make any sense. Last season, it was simply her favorite song — remember how excitedly she ran to the dance floor at Prater’s gala? It’s hard to square that with the idea that “Stayin’ Alive” is a reminder of her foundational trauma.

I’m probably overthinking it. Let’s circle back to Dexter, who is texting his “love bug” Charley. Harry sees the way Dex is cozying up to his former enemy. “Don’t let your boundaries get confused, son,” he warns. “Things can get messy.” This is the downside of a life with attachments — and Dexter is reminded of that when he’s repeatedly interrupted en route to his date with the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger. First, Harrison shows up to get all the off-the-record intel he can about FBK. The most interesting detail Dex shares is that he spotted a wedding ring on FBK’s finger. Maybe this serial killer isn’t a loner either. The next interruption comes in the form of Quinn, who believes he’s found Prater. In fact, he’s discovered the brownstone where Dexter and Charley plan to dispatch the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger, having linked it to one of Prater’s secret Cayman Islands accounts. “When did Joey Quinn actually become good at this?” Dex wonders via voice-over. The only bright spot is that there are a few potential brownstones owned by the real-estate company connected to the account, so Quinn will have to investigate all of them. That should buy Dexter enough time. Maybe. Quinn also warns him to be on the lookout for Charley — she’s been cleared by the cops, but Quinn still has questions. Looks like he’s going to be at least as big a problem as Batista.

When Dexter finally arrives at the brownstone, he gets a pat down from Charley (kiss already!) and an introduction to the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger a.k.a. Ray Ballard, who is as devoid of charisma as expected. When Dex mentions being held up by family and friends, Ballard tells him, “I cut all of that shit out years ago. Other people just get in the way.” Yes, yes, we get it, attachments versus no attachments. I just feel like Dexter has already landed firmly on the side of keeping his loved ones close — insofar as he can truly love anyone — so I’m not sure why we’re spending so much of the episode on this. At least Dex isn’t wasting time with the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger, whom he invites to check out Prater’s secret wine stash downstairs (hint, hint). There’s just one problem. En route to the kill room, Ballard reveals that his share is a victim he intends to murder in front of Prater. He’s rented a U-Haul and stashed an actual live person in there; if Dexter kills Ballard, they’ll never be able to find poor George.

When Charley refuses to intervene because she doesn’t want to be involved with any actual killing, Dex points out they’d be saving a life, which nudges her toward helping. (I’m not sure I buy her complete personality transplant, but I suppose being rejected by your mother on her deathbed could mess you up.) Charley tells Ballard that Prater is now arriving that night and expects shares immediately, so the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger will have to change his plans. He speeds away to the parking lot where he’s hidden the U-Haul, with Dexter and Charley following in separate cars. As they tail Ballard, the two talk openly while admiring each other’s stalking skills. It has strong date vibes. “The few times I’ve worked with someone else, I was teaching them,” Dex’s voice-over notes. “This is … nice.” Whether or not he realizes it, our boy is down bad. Once they arrive at the parking lot, Charley distracts Ballard and Dexter comes up from behind to knock him out. They’ll meet back at the townhouse, but they have to evade Quinn and rescue George first. Credit to Dex for killing two birds with one stone here — he calls Quinn and says he saw a creepy guy loading a suspicious box into a U-Haul, then points him to the parking lot.

Back at the townhouse, Dexter hangs up victim photos in the kill room, prompting another heart-to-heart with Charley. “Is your thing more about the urge or vengeance?” she asks. It’s a valid question, especially as the show continues to paint Dex as a justice-seeking hero. He admits it’s a little of both, explaining that seeing his mother get chainsawed to death by the cartel as a child now makes him want to save innocent people. This is sort of a retcon — Dexter’s traumatic past has long been an explanation for his Dark Passenger, not why he wants to be a force for good. (And don’t get me started on the way the franchise has aged up shipping-container massacre Dexter. Thanks a lot, Original Sin.) I know this may sound minor, but I don’t love the way the series keeps pulling away from the moral gray area that defined the original run. What happened to the sociopath we all fell in love with?

Charley leaves Dexter to his dirty work, and we get a back-and-forth between Dex and the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger to further underline this week’s themes. He asks Ballard why he kills his victims with an ice pick to the back of the head while they’re sleeping — they die before they even know they’re in danger. Ballard says it’s more about the grief of the people they leave behind. “Everyone thinks that these relationships make their lives better, but it actually makes them weak, vulnerable,” he says. “I free them from that lie. It’s the gift I give all my victims.” This is nonsense, which Dexter calls him on before plunging a knife into his heart. Right on cue, Quinn calls to let Dex know they found the U-Haul and rescued the man inside. Dexter is killing it in both a literal and figurative sense, and he couldn’t have done it alone. As he’s disposing of the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger, he reflects, “No attachments felt simpler, cleaner, but my life has changed. Today would have been impossible without Charley, without Quinn. Maybe I need to resolve to not worry so much about that.” Again, I wasn’t clear on this being a current area of concern for him, but I’m glad he’s feeling so zen: Being in a good headspace is important with the Ripper and the Five Borough Killer still at large. Next up, however, is the JawSplitter, and I’m not looking forward to learning how he earned that name.
• Curious how other longtime Dexter fans feel about the current iteration of the character. Am I wrong that he’s gone too soft?

• Speaking of things I might be wrong about, I have an FBK theory. The wedding ring and Mr. and Mrs. mugs are clearly significant. I wonder if his wife was killed by another serial killer — maybe the Ripper — and the murder went unsolved. That’s why he feels like “nobody cares.”
• At the end of the episode, FBK tinkers with the cameras on the 4 train. His kills have felt a little muted, so I wonder if he’s planning something bigger next.
• Remember Blessing? The writers barely seem to. I know it’s hard to service every character, but he’s a total nonentity so far this season. Maybe Dexter will take him up on his church group invite.

• Fun little New Blood Easter egg: When Harrison thinks back to his first dead bodies, he remembers finding Molly Park. In the next scene, Dex is listening to Molly’s podcast, Merry Fucking Kill, to find out more about the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger.

items.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Reviews: “I Never Want to Leave”
items.description: After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally arriving.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally arriving.
And the reviews? Pretty much as glowing as they could possibly be.

Right out of the gate, the hotly anticipated Rockstar Games title has a 99 out of 100 score on Metacritic, tying with 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the review aggregator site’s highest-rated game. In fact, 100 percent of critics are recommending the game.
Across dozens of reviews, the superlatives keep coming: “Masterpiece,” “magnum opus,” “revolutionary,” “unprecedented,” “breathtaking,” “jaw-dropping,” “astonishing.”

An IGN critic writes, “I regularly find myself in love with video games, but it’s extraordinarily rare that I find myself in complete awe of them. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played.” While Eurogamer writes, “GTA 6 is the most believable and unbelievable game of your lifetime.”

Critics hail the story as a Bonnie and Clyde romance following two lovers, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, as they try to escape the criminal life in a fictional version of Florida. According to The Washington Post, which calls the game an “astonishing American epic,” the playscape is stuffed with a staggering 33,000 unique non-playable characters, reflecting the tens of thousands of people who were involved in the game’s writing, programming and acting. The game also includes 600,000 animations (versus 55,000 in GTA V) and an incredible 1,500 songs. The main story takes roughly 70 hours to complete.
Critics also praise the game as a sharp social satire, tackling everything from conspiracy theorists to wealth inequality to online influencers to the manosphere to men’s rights activists to AI tech.

The environment is so sprawling, writes The Guardian, that “reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris.” GameSpot wrote the game is “a giant haystack full of needles that you’ll constantly find.”

The New York Times heralds the romance at the heart of the game: “GTA VI will steal your heart. The series matures beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups with a game about love, relationships and nurturing your partner. … Choosing romance is the easy part, thanks to the chemistry and human characterization of the two leads. Lucia and Jason’s relationship builds on itself and becomes a constant, supportive presence. It gets reflected in the story missions too, as your characters make scripted choices that reflect how you behaved toward each other in the idle moments in between.”

A PC Mag review drills down on game’s play mechanics: “Any screenshot will show you how many elements are packed into each frame. In motion, I was especially impressed by the moody shadows and striking lighting, impossibly perfect orange sunsets with a neon purple color palette that’s spiritually ’80s without being totally anachronistic. It’s proof of how realism and art direction don’t have to be mutually exclusive. And as for how it plays, the awkward driving and clunky shooting of past games are nowhere to be found here. Even punching people and dodging counterattacks, while basic, has smooth rhythm and flow … I never want to leave Grand Theft Auto VI because it knows the value of a vital vacation.”

And CNET adds, “Like its forebears, GTA 6 feels like two games — a core narrative about making a living through the underground in a rags-to-riches-to-rags-to-riches saga of a star-crossed couple and a massive sandbox to do whatever you want. While going treasure hunting in offshore wrecks or making drug drop-offs from a plane dilutes the story’s tension, it also gives you a lot of opportunity to find the GTA you want to experience. After the story fades into memory, that’s what’ll stick around as the core of this game: the freedom to choose what you want to do, laws be damned.”

Did anybody say anything negative? That’s tougher to find, though The Guardian criticizes the game’s complex controls and unpredictability, writing, “This can be a frustrating game at times: unpredictable, laborious, unwieldy and, occasionally, unfair.”
The $79.99 game is released Nov. 19 and expected to disrupt Hollywood’s entertainment releases, especially TV shows on streaming, though to what extent at this stage is difficult to measure.

items.title: Does Georgia Still Want to Be the Hollywood of the South?
items.description: A few years ago, if you wanted to shoot a movie in Georgia, you’d better have made your reservations early.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik; Ronda Racha Penrice
paragraphs: A few years ago, if you wanted to shoot a movie in Georgia, you’d better have made your reservations early.

The lack of an annual cap on credit payouts, the solid 30 percent rebate, the allowance of (some) above-the-line expenses, and the lower cost of housing compared with New York and California made it so that every inch of the state’s 21st century studio space and hotel inventory could get booked up.

MacGyver, Ozark, Stranger Things, The Resident and nearly every significant Marvel TV and film project were all among those calling Georgia home even when many of their stories were set elsewhere. And then there was Tyler Perry’s Fort McPherson studio and its 50,000 square feet of permanent sets, which opened in 2019 and housed numerous projects. The state’s film and TV growth was astronomical — over barely a dozen years beginning in 2010, studio square footage went from 45,000 all the way to 3 million.

But while Perry continues to book productions at his landmark location, Hollywood activity has thinned markedly in the Peach State since 2022. The Georgia Film Office reports that production spend has cratered from a peak of $4.4 billion in 2022 to $2.3 billion in 2025 — hardly peanuts (Will Trent, The Rock’s Lizard Music and Judd Apatow’s The Comeback King have been among recent shoots) but a major fall. Total productions saw a similar drop, from 412 to 245.

And the numbers continue to sink. Industry tracker ProdPro says that Georgia saw about $1.56 billion in film and TV production spend in the 12 months ending in September, down 15 percent from $1.84 billion in the prior 12-month period.

There have been other worrisome developments. Lee Thomas, longtime head of the Georgia Film Office and the major force behind the surge, announced her retirement this summer. Her replacement has not been named. And then in early November, another blow: James Gunn, who famously loved Georgia and brought DC projects like Peacemaker and Superman to the sprawling Trillith Studios in Fayetteville, was ousted as head of the superhero division under new Skydance ownership.

Gunn’s love affair with Georgia runs deep; he shot the first two Guardians of the Galaxy movies for Marvel and even owned a home there. The director’s big-budget Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow alone, which shot in the state this summer, gave Georgia its best production spend quarter for new shoots since early 2024, ProdPro notes. But his successor, Jeremy Latcham, and Latcham’s boss, David Ellison, could shop for preferred alternatives with less allegiance to the past.

Of course, there’s an overall decline in streamer and studio projects in the post-strike and -COVID era. And there have been bright spots even in Georgia, such as reeling in American Idol from Los Angeles to shoot its upcoming season in the state. But overall the news has been dark.

One big culprit of the Georgia drop? Generous tax credits overseas. A prominent TV producer says the location conversation with studios these days always starts with Budapest, then moves to Ireland before going to England. Marvel itself largely decamped for the U.K. in 2024. That puts Georgia in a tough spot.

This could change if a federal tax credit can gain momentum and pass in the new congressional session. But such a passage is far from guaranteed, and it still might not induce projects to come home. And New York is proving a formidable American rival to Georgia, seeing gains in many key metrics, with plenty of studio space being built in New Jersey to augment the effort.

Georgia’s lame-duck Republican governor and legislature are unlikely to follow through on longtime threats to reduce the credit before leaving office next month. But whether a new Democratic state house and new Democratic Gov. Keisha Lance Bottoms can or will reenergize the business remains an open question. One question: the new film commissioner could work under Pat Wilson, the state’s longtime commissioner of economic development — or Bottoms could find someone to replace Wilson. (Thomas will do some contract work in the meantime.)

A Georgia unraveling would spell more than an employment loss. Georgia crews tend to be more diverse than those in New York and Los Angeles, in particular with many Black women occupying positions they don’t hold in other places. And when the new soap opera Beyond the Gates won the Daytime Emmy for lighting direction in October, the winners were both Black men, a rarity in the category.

One encouraging sign for Georgia crews and the state’s Hollywood allies: Perry’s place in the Lance Bottoms administration. He was named to her transition team right after the election. But she has downplayed what that meant. “I think what people miss,” she told the popular morning program Yung Joc & The Streetz Morning Takeover when a host asked about the Perry appointment, “is that these are just co-chairs … we’ll probably have 100 more.” Lance Bottoms could have other priorities for tax money than putting it in producers’ pockets; the state recently ranked 49th in health care in one prominent annual study.

During his successful reelection bid, Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced criticism from opponent Mike Collins that he was more concerned with Hollywood, California than [the small town of] Hollywood, Georgia, a criticism Lance Bottoms could be sensitive to as well.

And Perry himself is actually about to move to Puerto Rico to be closer to his son. He says activity at his studio will continue unabated, but what this all means for him and his Georgia advocacy remains to be seen. On the red carpet for his Tyler Perry’s The Gospel of Christmas recently he didn’t seem especially eager to talk about the credit. Asked about its future, he told THR, “Well as great as that’s been [and it] has been amazing, for me, my focus is being pro-Georgia, and Keisha is pro-Georgia. So I want to make sure that businesses, people are taken care of.”
The state’s Hollywood advocates could take comfort in at least one fact: AI hasn’t cut into physical production in Georgia — yet.
This story appeared in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space
items.description: Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.
items.author: Alyssa Bereznak
paragraphs: Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.
Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.
I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace.
