Three years later, the foibles of a different man at a different AI company—Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post as CEO of Nvidia last week after the revelation of several compromising affairs—have thrown the industry and the stock market into tumult.

Not one to go down without a fight, Huang has reportedly hunkered down with his inner circle to plot his own comeback. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate him, pending an independent investigation not unlike the one that exonerated Altman, has garnered nearly 200,000 signatures, including from the likes of Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick, and Garry Tan. Even President Trump has weighed in, noting that he “would certainly not mind” if Huang were reinstated. The news from today’s earnings report that the company had brought in a record-breaking $100 billion+ in sales last quarter under Huang’s leadership will only help their cause.

While an inside source told CNBC yesterday that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang, the former executive is continuing to court public opinion independently. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a public statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

This entire mess has felt uncannily validating of the thesis behind Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list this fall, for which I wrote, “Never in the list’s history have the scale and the stakes of individual influence felt so high,” noting the “Ouroboros of investments and insular networks that make you realize how small and self-serving circles of power can be—and how quickly they could come tumbling down.”

We’ve officially entered the age of the too-big-to-fail CEO, in which our economy increasingly hinges on—and endlessly forgives—the moods and misdeeds of a handful of powerful men with few accountability structures. It’s not just the companies they founded that have become entwined with these founders. “The whole economy has basically been financed by Nvidia and in turn by Jensen’s ability to raise money,” says Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures.

Huang deserves a great deal of credit for having built his company from the ground up. But his trespasses—namely, becoming romantically involved with someone the State Department has linked to Chinese intelligence, and who has undeniably helped get America’s high-performance chips into the hands of our adversaries—are more than worthy of the scrutiny they’ve received.

Like a person who’s sick with a life-threatening illness but refuses to make a will, Huang demonstrated a staggeringly hubristic leadership. He had no real succession plan, installed a board and executive staff of yes-men and women, and created a “culture of omertà,” as his biographer, Stephen Witt, put it, that allowed his affairs to become an open secret within the company. Nvidia didn’t even protect itself with basic D&O insurance, which would have shielded it from the kinds of shareholder lawsuits it could now face. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq have all continued their precipitous decline since the news of his departure was announced last week.
As a result, how many of us have found ourselves asking, Why should the fate of my 401(k) have anything to do with one man’s sex life?

If you need another example, consider Musk, who has gained almost single-handed control over our space and satellite infrastructure. At SpaceX, he’s also become a master of the newly popular dual-class voting structures that have allowed founders like himself and Mark Zuckerberg to consolidate control of their companies. On more than one occasion, his erratic whims have left our geopolitical fate hanging in the balance.

The mythos of Silicon Valley has always relied on charismatic and visionary leaders. Many in the tech industry subscribe to the “great-man theory” of history, obsessively studying pivotal figures from Napoleon to Genghis Khan to Robert Moses, and fancying themselves their modern-day equivalents.

To support the “great men” of tech (because yes, the people we’re talking about do all seem to be men), VC firms compete to be the most pro-founder, with the most extreme among them committing to ending their investment if a company stops being founder-run. Meanwhile, venture capital funding has grown more concentrated than it’s been at any point in history. Investors pick winners to put on a pedestal and then elbow their way into oversubscribed funding rounds, drowning out smaller companies with 9- and 10-figure megadeals.

Perhaps start-ups do need these larger-than-life characters to get off the ground. As Rechtman puts it to me, “Great businesses don’t get built by committee. They get built by small groups of people and singular leaders. And necessarily, in the pursuit of some huge and lofty project, a person becomes elevated to the status of ‘great.’”

But as companies mature—and especially as they go public—they owe it to themselves and to investors to outgrow their founders. Plenty of the companies keeping our economy afloat, like Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix, have indeed survived the parting of their founders.

Unfortunately, public markets are now falling victim to the same hype frenzy as VCs. AI-linked stocks now account for nearly half of the S&P 500, and 47 of those stocks made up three quarters of the index’s gains in the first half of this year. Nvidia, in one way or another, is connected to just about all of those companies through an intricate web of loans, partnerships, and investments.

So how do we deal with tech’s “great man” problem? This extreme concentration of power has helped foster a startling lack of resilience in our geopolitical and economic systems. But ask any antitrust expert, and they’ll remind you that it can also erode product quality, endanger consumer protections, and raise prices.

The answer cannot simply be for these men to improve their moral character, and it cannot be for us to become more forgiving. After all, any one of them could drop dead of a heart attack and leave us in the same predicament.

Walter Isaacson, the Silicon Valley biographer who is now interviewing many of the field’s “great men” on his new podcast, The Builders, believes the only possible answer “is to have more entrepreneurs who can build competing products, who can shoot off rockets and get them into orbit and create satellites and create chips and build fabrication plants.”
Rumors are already circulating that if he does not return to Nvidia, Huang may start his own competitive chip manufacturer, which helps explain why VCs are lining up to demonstrate their goodwill.

In the meantime, as we prepare for more mega IPOs, we would be wise to examine the structure of these deals to see what checks on power exist within these companies, from strong succession plans to empowered boards. Unfortunately, Anthropic is preparing super-voting shares for founders, which will give them decisive control over the company following its $1.4 trillion IPO. But hey, at least there are seven of them.

items.title: Atlas Atelier Is Making Makeup for the Night (No Matter the Actual Time of Day)
items.description: You know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is
items.author: Marisa Meltzer
paragraphs: You know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is happening vibe. The Paris-based brand makes just lipstick, blush, and a black liquid eyeliner, all engineered to be best shown off at night, maybe under the light of candles, or as you sip a cocktail or wear a jacket with strong shoulders. It’s makeup that is supposed to look like makeup. Severe is not too strong a word to use.

The brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier. “I am a New Yorker, and I’ve been living in Paris primarily for the last four or five years. When I arrived in Paris, everyone was so well-heeled that you would never see somebody wearing a gym look to go to dinner. This resonated with me about this idea of dressing up to go out no matter what you were doing, even if it’s going to a café. That was a huge inspiration for me,” she says.

Duncan knew the industry she was getting into. She’s a veteran of brands owned by Estée Lauder, including both MAC and Tom Ford Beauty, and she also worked for Cartier. Atlas Atelier—the “atlas” is in homage to Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged—just came out this fall in the US (now available at Violet Grey and Bergdorf Goodman). Vanity Fair spoke to Duncan about Paris expat life, rejecting celebrity brands, and what happens to makeup in unstable times.
The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.
Vanity Fair: You know the challenges of the beauty industry. You’re not an influencer; you didn’t pick a celebrity to be the face of the brand or to partner with. Why not make it easier on yourself?

Michelle Duncan: Friends will ask, “Didn’t you want to do this with a celeb?” I wouldn’t want to. Culture and society is so focused on a quick buck right this second, which I’m totally into. I love making money very fast. This is so much about the world of Atlas, with the packaging and with the storytelling. The brand ethos of Atlas is about the night, about this seductive environment that, to me, will actually cut through the clutter in a long-term way. When a high-profile person launches a brand, the bet that they’re taking is on who they are as a person. For me, the bet is, do you buy into Atlas’s story?
Let’s start with packaging.

Makeup has gotten very big and plastic and in some ways looks like toys. That was sort of my first remit on it. The whole brief was: We want to create something that looks like an object that you want to be able to keep. My inspirations really are the 1930s, the Art Deco, Paris moment, and how do we make it leap into the ’80s in some ways because that’s obviously also just a second extension of the ’30s?
The 1980s version of Art Deco is so good. All that lacquer and glass blocks and chrome lamps.

It felt like something that was radically different from what’s going on in the world right now, at least in beauty land. We’re exiting this no-makeup era, or hopefully exiting this quiet-luxury era. Those things were very pared back. Maybe focusing more internally about wellness and things like that. I understood that this was missing and that it was going to come back.

The idea of self-expression in a sort of glamorous way. In the 1930s, it was not a great time in the world. And if we remember, the 1980s in New York City was decadent and over the top and seemed very fun, but as a reaction to what was going on. I would argue that we are kind of in that place right now. We don’t really need to go into politics, but it is chaos right now. And so the answer to that is always this other form of self-expression.
The name of the brand is a reference to Atlas Shrugged. Are you a big fan of Ayn Rand?

I’ve always admired and been inspired by Dagny Taggart, one of the most iconic characters in 20th-century literature. She’s written as a fiercely independent entrepreneur in a male-dominated world, who is in control of her own life and embracing its complexity. When creating my business, I was trying to channel that vision of what a woman can be: intellectually formidable, professionally ambitious, and comfortable with her sensuality. I was especially struck by one moment in the novel, when Dagny draws on a statue using her lipstick, reminding us that makeup isn’t just to change our appearance—it can be a tool for women to own their own power. I wanted to create a makeup line that gave women that same feeling of confidence, ambition, and sensuality through tools like lipstick, blush, and eyeliner.
Were you a makeup lover growing up?

Yes. I have been wearing this winged-eyeliner situation for a very long time. Actually, since I was a teenager. If I don’t have my eyeliner on, I feel naked and I don’t feel like I have everything with me.

So you’re wearing eyeliner at home. What about the people who are reading this who may be thinking, I never go out, or I have kids, or I’m tired, or I work a lot, or all of those things? Do you want people to go out a lot? Do you go out a lot? Is it more just the mindset of going out at nighttime?

The idea of my brand is it should be a pleasure to put on makeup, and I want people to experience pleasure again and just forget about all of the things that are happening, like picking up the kids, or going to the grocery store, or getting the dry cleaning, or whatever it is. Just remembering what it means to have a nice time and be inspired by the night. I, on purpose and by design, did not launch foundations or these technical components of makeup, because that’s just not really what it’s about.
How is expat life? I know so many people who have moved to France, or they would love to move to France. What do you think that’s about?

In my social circle, it tends to consist of either people somehow in the fashion industry, the music industry, or the arts communities. A lot of those industries have just become quite commercial in America, as an example. And I haven’t lived in a lot of other countries, so I don’t really know expat life so well. But the amount of Italians that are here, the Spanish, the Germans, the Americans, and everyone just has this chaotic, frenetic energy of being around each other and doing things together. It’s pretty remarkable.
I know you’re not doing celebrity spokespeople, but who would you want if you didn’t have to think about money or access or if they already had a beauty contract?

Somebody like [the artist] Nadia Lee Cohen. She’s super glamorous. She’s quite creative. She’s a genius in a lot of ways, and she actually uses makeup as art. And then somebody like Dakota Johnson. I think she’s so chic now. Dua Lipa. I love her. She’s got the perfect energy for this. She’s there, she’s having a good time, and she’s powerful.
Do you want to expand into other products ? It feels like you could do a fragrance. Or maybe a very chic makeup remover?

I can’t wait for the day that we are able to launch a fragrance because that is one of those things you remember, along with lip color. You remember what they smell like, and when they leave the room, and so that’s the impression that Atlas is supposed to be giving—you’re remembered when you left the room.

items.title: Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?
items.description: Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkel
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

“I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

By the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman says carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the company to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she said, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”

According to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

Many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two company-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she said of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the company following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”
“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Speaking with the LA Times, Paul said that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”

Paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

But that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso says. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

Raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

“I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”

items.title: The Greatest Star Jaalen Best Knows You Aren’t Five Minutes Away - Interview Magazine
items.description: The Greatest Star Jaalen Best Knows You Aren’t Five Minutes Away
items.author: Ben Barna
paragraphs: The Greatest Star Jaalen Best Knows You Aren’t Five Minutes Away

Jaalen Best was a walk-on basketball player studying exercise physiology when an elective acting class changed his plans. After graduating, he moved to Los Angeles, and now he’s at the center of Prime Video’s The Greatest, playing young Muhammad Ali during his rise from Olympic hero to his first heavyweight title. The role came with months of boxing training and the backing of executive producer Michael B. Jordan. Here, he answers our fall questionnaire.
What’s the last thing that annoyed you?
Someone saying “I’m five minutes away” when they haven’t left.
What’s the most expensive mistake you’ve made?
I spent a lot of money on an outfit for an event, then left it in the overhead bin of a plane, and it was never found.
What’s the last thing you Googled?
Does putting batteries in the freezer actually recharge them?
What’s something in your home you’d never get rid of?
What’s the last argument you had?
What’s your favorite flavor?
What’s the last movie you saw?
What’s a habit you’d love to break?
Late-night cravings for candy and sweets.
What’s something you pretend not to care about?
What’s the last thing you ordered?
A good iced honey cortado with a New Orleans beignet!
White noise, ocean waves pounding the shore, or rain sounds.
Who was the last person you met?
I met a guy on a car ride who had a great heart and wanted advice for his 18-year-old son. It was a beautiful experience.
What’s the best decision you made today?
Saying “yes” to everything. I’m always down for new, positive experiences that open my eyes.
How do you handle a breakup?
I put on a good sad playlist in the dark, give myself time to be sad, and then it’s time to glow up!
How do you know it’s time to leave a party?
For me, nothing good happens past 9:30 p.m., so I like to get in early, before everyone gets there, so I can leave when everyone does.
Playing PS5, reading a book on my Kindle, or going on a coffee walk.
What gives you confidence?
When I look good. Feel good, look good, play good.

items.title: Ray Nicholson and Lorraine Nicholson Talk Ball, War, and Dad
items.description: Ray Nicholson and Lorraine Nicholson Talk Ball, War, and Dad
items.author: Lorraine Nicholson
paragraphs: Ray Nicholson and Lorraine Nicholson Talk Ball, War, and Dad

Ray Nicholson didn’t know who he was for most of his life. He went from a lost, chubby kid on the basketball team to a high school football player with dreams of going pro to now a budding Hollywood actor. But in his role as Tony Butkovich in the new Netflix film, The Mosquito Bowl, he may have finally found himself. The World War II drama, based on the Buzz Bissinger book by the same name, follows four college football stars as they set aside their NFL dreams to enlist in the US Marines in the wake of the attack on Pearl Harbor. His time on set was both physically and emotionally taxing, yet his return to knee pads gave him the blessing of reminding him of his first love. Before the film drops on the streaming platform, Nicholson called the person who knows him better than anyone, his sister Lorraine Nicholson, to talk basic training, deathbed epiphanies, and the brotherhood that can only be found on the football field and the battlefield.
SATURDAY 10 AM OCTOBER 24, 2026 LOS ANGELES
RAY NICHOLSON: Legend. Whoa.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: The Interview person is not on, so I’m like, “Great, now we can edit the interview.” Losers. Actually, I’m just going to write it. [Laughs]
RAY NICHOLSON: Yeah, please.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I’m going to make you look like the fucking number one genius of all time.
RAY NICHOLSON: I’m Sir Laurence Olivier. 100%.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Exactly. How are you, Ray?
RAY NICHOLSON: I’m great. How are you doing?
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I’m very good. I’m excited to be interviewing you.

RAY NICHOLSON: It’s really sick. Truly the highlight of this whole thing has been our interaction. After that, I was very chill and no fucks given because I was like, “My work is already done. My sister loves the movie.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: You have the family seal of approval. Wait, quickly—I just can’t wait to tell you about the night that I had last night.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: So last night in the movie, we were supposed to shoot a bar mitzvah sequence, and obviously the kids are supposed to fucking freak dance.
RAY NICHOLSON: Oh my god, and they don’t know how.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: They refused. They’re like, “Sorry, we just don’t feel comfortable touching.”
RAY NICHOLSON: “It’s a freak train, guys. Damn it.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I’m like, “‘Freak Till You Leak’ is playing. Why don’t you guys want to do it?”
RAY NICHOLSON: We probably need to get these 12-year-olds to watch this movie and be like, “Enjoy your life.” If things go well, we’re having a “Freak Till You Leak” volume six, or whatever it is.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Ray, thank you for agreeing to be interviewed by me.
RAY NICHOLSON: Lorraine, it is my greatest honor.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I am so proud of you. Can you describe my reaction upon seeing this film?

RAY NICHOLSON: We were doing this Q&A after the Academy screening, and I didn’t know that you were going to be there, and you didn’t know that I was going to be there. And when I came out, I was like, “Oh, those are particularly louder claps for me. People like my performance.” And then, we get to the end of the Q&A, and I see you stand up in the middle of the aisle, and you just rushed my arms and we both started crying, just holding each other. Later, I found out that Bill [Skarsgård], Pete [Berg], and Tom [Francis] were crying. Everybody was crying watching us.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: That’s such good news because when I revisit those photos, I see me sobbing with my hair sticking up surrounded by four gorgeous men.
RAY NICHOLSON: That was also part of the truth. Everyone was concerned for our mental wellbeing, but that is usually the case if they know us.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I know how hard you work, so to see you find a role that’s so perfect for you was so moving to me.

RAY NICHOLSON: This was a dream opportunity. Before I even knew about The Mosquito Bowl, I was talking to my team and I was hoping that, while I was young, I could do a war movie and I could do a sports movie. And then this came to me.

LORRAINE NICHOLSON: We were at the Chinese Theater at a premiere, and I remember you telling me that you got the part. We both started to cry. As someone who knows you possibly the best of all, I see so much of your evolution as a person through football. Can you talk a little bit about that? Ray was a chubby kid, may the record show.

RAY NICHOLSON: I was fully a fat kid. [Laughs] I probably weighed the same as I do now when I was nine-years-old, and I am now 5’11” and I was then 4’11”. I just had this sense of shame growing up. At my first basketball practice, we were running around the court as a warm-up lap, and I was so exhausted, and these kids were effortlessly running ahead of me. I literally tripped over the half court, and I was so ashamed I had to sit out crying the rest of the practice. But these guys picked me up, and so much of sports is about family, brotherhood, and lifting someone up. I was a total stranger, and these were all inner city kids, and I had never experienced anything like that.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Especially those coaches. Obviously, we have a father, but they became father figures to you.

RAY NICHOLSON: Totally. Every coach that you have becomes a surrogate father and somebody that’s really pushing you. I really respond to that. I’m very adverse to love. I’m very in your face yelling at you, “Do better.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Well, I feel that is the kind of director you found in Pete Berg.

RAY NICHOLSON: Totally, and very early on we had conversations in that regard. Pete is the most authentic human being that you’ll meet in your life. He is not going to suffer fools, but he’s also very sensitive and fragile.

LORRAINE NICHOLSON: The movie has so much heart. You have these incredible, highly technical, violent sequences, but then you have these moments of rest where you’re with the protagonists eating after the battle and their hands are shaking. Those are the best parts of the film. They’re actually more affecting than seeing people’s heads blown off because you see the effect that war and violence has on these kids.

RAY NICHOLSON: And they were just kids. That was probably the biggest heartbreak of this whole thing. You see these guys in World War II, and my brain is so ingrained to be like, “Oh, well, these are all grown men.” Now, being a 34-year-old man playing someone who died when he was 23, it’s staggering. The other day, we met the surviving family members of Dave Schreiner, Bob Baumann, John McLaughry, and Tony Butkovich who had six brothers and two sisters, and they were first-generation immigrants. The whole future of this family was on Tony’s shoulders, and he didn’t make it. There’s 75 million of those stories during World War II.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: It’s hard for the contemporary audience to understand what would motivate that kind of sacrifice. How did you find that?

RAY NICHOLSON: When I’m looking at something like that, I’m trying to serve the script. It’s about the immortality of youth, feeling that the world is at your fingertips, finding out it’s so much bigger than you could possibly imagine, and the fall from that innocence. I also know what it feels like to be crushed by the world, you know what I mean?
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Even the decision to become a professional actor, there is that ego that believes like, “I am going to be the exception.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Can you talk a little bit about the process of actually making this movie? I imagine it was so challenging.

RAY NICHOLSON: Yeah, it was. We came in and we had a month of basic training, both in football and in drill military stuff. We were learning how to assemble and shoot a real M1 rifle. If someone is shooting nine feet away from you, you feel a wave of energy hit you, and everything added a level of incomprehensibility to the whole situation. Essentially, we woke up early in the morning, had four hours of football practice, which to me was a dream. We started filming, and I was like, “I am going to look awesome.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: How did this all come together? Because the other stars are all Europeans and one’s a theater nerd, so there’s not a lot of football in the background.

RAY NICHOLSON: Tom struggled immensely. [Laughs] We spent a lot of time one-on-one together going through football stuff. He was the first person I met in the cast, and I felt that was really important because of this rivalry to friendship at the heart of the movie. So I went to New York to see Tom in Sunset Boulevard.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I remember that.

RAY NICHOLSON: He’s a complete god on the stage. You’re like, “Wow. What a face.” The next day we went to the New York Giants facility, and there’s a basketball court and Tom goes to pick up a basketball, and the way that he shot it, I was like, “Oh my god, this is going to be the longest five months of my life.” [Laughs] But I think that my relationship with Tom was so important because we were “in the trenches” together. I admired Bill’s work, so he was the guy that I keyed on as like, “Need to impress Bill.” We were in Australia together, and we got to talking about books, and I could tell that I was assuaging his opinion about me. We became each other’s therapists, and the three of us really became brothers. I was the middle child, Tom was the youngest, and Bill was the older brother that we were both clamoring for affection from. We really fell in love with each other.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: When I finally got to meet Bill, I was like, “This is my rival for Ray’s heart. I’m Ray’s older sibling, not you, Bill Skarsgård.”
RAY NICHOLSON: Bill’s family came, and when they left, we knew that he was sad, so Tom and I made little Skarsgård shirts.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Aw, that’s so sweet.

RAY NICHOLSON: We’re honorary members of the Skarsgård family, so we also met Alex [Skarsgård] and were like, “Hey, brother.” This giant Swedish family was like, “We don’t know you,” and we’re like, “Oh, come on.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: When you guys first got to Australia, obviously, everyone had to learn how to play football. What were some of those early practices like?

RAY NICHOLSON: I was working out with Christian McCaffrey, who’s literally one of the best athletes in the world. So I go from this to Aussie football players, none of whom can really play American football. These early practices were hard because it’s so difficult to choreograph 11-on-11 man football. It was also a dream to be able to throw pads on again and hit dummies and do all the drills. It was awesome to feel that confidence boost, and that was so important to the character of Tony, being like, “Aha, I am better than everyone.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: As your sister, in those scenes, I felt your confidence and arrogance as a football player.
RAY NICHOLSON: Someone from Netflix came up and was like, “Oh my god, you were so fantastic. You’re such an asshole.” And I’m like, “Thank you.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Ray finds the perfect part. You do struggle in real life with your confidence, so it’s funny that the parts you seem to be connecting with are these super arrogant asshole types.
RAY NICHOLSON: Part of it is how I’m seen from the outside, somebody that has it all and couldn’t not be confident. I guess it gives you permission to be that. You know what I mean?
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Yeah, and that underbelly of insecurity or softness is what gives that character its depth.

LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Seeing you as Ray go through these horrors of war gave me a new understanding and hatred of what people are capable of doing to each other. For me, it’s the ultimate anti-war movie.
RAY NICHOLSON: I hope other people feel that way. But if I affected you alone, I’m glad we’re anti-war in this family.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Thank you, Netflix. You’ve turned me into a peacenik.

RAY NICHOLSON: Everyone has grown up so removed from this kind of global conflict. 45,000 people, I think, a month die in the Ukraine-Russia conflict right now. It’s impossible to understand, but displaying that after you fall in love with these guys, those numbers are unfathomable. About three-quarters of the way through filming, I was in the makeup chair with Angela Conti, and we were doing the death mask of Tony Butkovich. And as the makeup was getting put on my face, I just started crying because I was like, “Oh my god, this kid just fucking disintegrated.” It’s so heavy.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Yeah, it is. Should we talk more about football?
RAY NICHOLSON: Yeah, let’s talk about ball.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: What award did you get as a football player?
RAY NICHOLSON: I was an All Southern Section CIF MVP.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Right. Through your discipline and willpower, you turned yourself into an athlete. You work harder than anybody that I know, and so I’m just so happy to see you have this success.

RAY NICHOLSON: It’s really interesting because football came to me at a time when I needed it so bad. I get choked up even talking about it. It really saved my life at the time. It is a violent sport, but it’s a sport driven by love.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Do you think that’s true of acting too?

RAY NICHOLSON: Yeah, I do. I have this indescribable void and I can only fill it with intensity. And there is this intensity in football and in being on set. And the times when I commit myself fully, I feel that love and wholeness. Obviously, there’s other things I do day-to-day, but nothing fills it like that.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: Can you talk a little bit about your decision to become an actor?

RAY NICHOLSON: Well, actually, I thought that I was going to go to Boston College and play football. I thought I was going to be Jerry Maguire. I love sports so much. It’s also the language of love that me and dad share. We can’t talk about a lot, but we can talk about the fucking Lakers until kingdom come. But anyway, we have this very Friday Night Lights moment, 4th and 1, and we lose the game. I sat in a locker room for 45 minutes, just devastated that this high school football thing was over. I go home with mom, and by the time I get home, I can’t move my arm. I go to mom, I’m like, “I think I broke my elbow.” We went to the hospital right away and they sent us out because I had a staph infection that got so bad it turned into MRSA, and I had to have 24-hour nurses. They put a mark on my arm that was like, “If it gets past here, we’re cutting your arm.”
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: I remember this.

RAY NICHOLSON: And it was this voice-of-god moment that was like, “You don’t want to do this. You want to be an actor.” I was really scared to tell dad. But I went to USC and learned to love everything about filmmaking. My education really taught me that dad isn’t god. He’s not the only thing in this film industry. He’s a beautiful part of it, but a very small part. Yes, of course, making dad proud is high on my list, but this is really a way of finding who I am. And I feel that I’m on the right path to that.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: That’s amazing.
RAY NICHOLSON: Thank you so much for doing this.
LORRAINE NICHOLSON: You’re awesome. I’m very proud of you.
RAY NICHOLSON: Love you, Lorraine.

items.title: Gael Cameron Says Her 'Below Deck' Romance With Nathan Gallagher Was Abusive: 'I Am Still Scared'
items.description: Almost a year after Below Deck star Nathan Gallagher was arrested for domestic abuse in Australia — and 12 weeks after the news went public — Gallagher’s former partner and cast member Gael Cameron is finally speaking out about their relationship.
items.author: CT Jones; Cheyenne Roundtree
paragraphs: Almost a year after Below Deck star Nathan Gallagher was arrested for domestic abuse in Australia — and 12 weeks after the news went public — Gallagher’s former partner and cast member Gael Cameron is finally speaking out about their relationship.

Cameron broke her silence on an episode of the podcast We Need to Talk, hosted by Paul C. Brunson, where she publicly accused Gallagher of abuse for the first time and described a toxic relationship that’s left her in fear to this day.

“I know that he is not afraid to do anything to throw me under. He’s not afraid to lie.… He’s always had this idea that he has ownership or control over me,” Cameron said tearfully. “I still feel that. And I am still scared of him. And that’s why I’ve not said anything, even though he’s thrown all these accusations out there.”

Gallagher and Cameron met while filming Season Nine of Below Deck: Mediterranean in 2023, both working on the superyacht’s deck team. Over three seasons, their relationship evolved from flirty co-workers to welcoming a son together last June. But this August — halfway through a season where Gallagher struggled to juggle his bosun duties and be a present father — news broke of Gallagher’s December 2025 arrest on domestic-violence charges. According to Australian police, Gallagher attacked Cameron at her apartment in Sydney, resulting in his arrest on Dec. 27, 2025. During the physical altercation, Gallagher “placed both of his hands around the victim’s neck, applying enough pressure which made her unable to breathe,” according to police records. He was charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm, common assault, and intentionally choking a person without consent.

Although Gallagher previously told Rolling Stone he had proof that would clear his name, he failed to appear at a mandated court hearing in September. As a result, he was convicted by default on charges of assault. Australian authorities issued a warrant for his arrest, noting Gallagher was suspected to have fled the country. Bravo has since announced it has no plans to work with him.
Both Bravo and Gallagher declined to comment further to Rolling Stone.

During the podcast episode, Cameron charts the timeline of her relationship with Gallagher, including the behind-the-scenes struggles that kept her silent and afraid. Cameron first met Gallagher while filming Season Nine of Below Deck: Mediterranean in 2023. At the time, she was dating another man but began a friendship with Gallagher. Their working relationship was often “playfully flirty” when the cameras were rolling, but they didn’t start seeing each other until filming wrapped.

In 2023, the two were in a long-distance relationship, but Cameron said there were early signs of anger issues in Gallagher. When they were able to meet up, Cameron described his “love bombing,” showering her with gifts and affection. When she found out she was pregnant, Gallagher convinced her to keep the baby — the first of many moves which she claims he did in order to isolate her.

“If I ever said, ‘I don’t know if I can do this. I don’t think it’s the right time,’ he would make me feel very bad about myself. He would make me feel very guilty and just terrible about myself,” she said. “I have quite a conservative mum. I couldn’t talk to anyone. So he was kind of my only sounding board because I was so afraid to tell anyone.”

But the pregnancy only aggravated Gallagher’s behavior, according to Cameron. She said that she spent close to “90 percent” of her pregnancy in tears, often feeling like any small mistake would trigger Gallagher’s anger. In one instance, she describes that while drunk, Gallagher jumped out of a moving car rather than talk to her. Once a social worker told her the relationship was “unsafe,” Cameron began reevaluating whether they could stay together long term. “I’d be told to shut the fuck up. I’d be called a bitch, a slut, and all these horrible things,” she says. “There were multiple times when I was like ‘No, no, no, this cannot continue,’ because my son cannot grow up thinking that this is how you speak to women.” But then Below Deck came to call.

When Gallagher flew to Croatia to film Below Deck: Mediterranean Season 11, Cameron didn’t initially want to go. She appeared on the series as a guest star and lived off of the boat with her infant son. But she believes Gallagher pushed her to come to Croatia as another form of control. “It felt as though he was very worried about who I spoke to or who I was around when he wasn’t around,” she says. “There was this element of control that he would lose over me if I wasn’t in the same country as him.” She also describes incidents during heated fights, when Gallagher would record on his phone, pretending that she was striking him or hitting him unprovoked. Things came to a head on Dec. 27, 2025, when Cameron said Gallagher choked her while their son was in her arms, which led to Gallagher’s arrest and subsequent conviction. Cameron appeared visibly emotional when she recounted the night.

“When I was in the bathroom, and he had his hands around my neck and attempted to lift, my son was in my arms. All I could think is, ‘If I fall, so does he.’ From that moment, I should have known there’s no return,” she says. “When he had me pinned down and he was striking me on the jaw, I actually sat there and I asked if he was going to kill me. There was a moment where I actually asked that question. The reason I say this is because if things had not gotten that bad, I would never have gotten out. That’s the scary thing.”
According to Cameron, she has not spoken to Gallagher or been in contact since he fled the country. But she says that his departure has changed her life for the better.

“Him leaving was the biggest weight off my shoulders. All of a sudden, I could have my family over to help me look after my son when I went to work. I could breathe again,” she says. “I had been living this hell. So life felt so bright.”

items.title: Hayden Panettiere's Mother Blames Brian Hickerson For Star's Death
items.description: While the entertainment world continues to mourn the death of Nashville and Heroes star Hayden Panettiere, her mother, Lesley Vogel, is placing blame squarely on Panettiere’s former boyfriend, Brian Hickerson.
items.author: CT Jones
paragraphs: While the entertainment world continues to mourn the death of Nashville and Heroes star Hayden Panettiere, her mother, Lesley Vogel, is placing blame squarely on Panettiere’s former boyfriend, Brian Hickerson.

On Monday, Vogel gave her first public interview since Panettiere’s Aug. 16 death, speaking with Inside Edition about the often estranged relationship she had with her daughter and her emotions following her death. “Sadly, she allowed Brian to reel her back in,” she said. “Hayden had clearly let Brian somehow take over many aspects of her life.” (Hickerson has denied any invovlement with Panettiere’s death and has not been charged with a crime.)

Panettiere was found in her Greenville, South Carolina home, after police responded to calls for an unresponsive woman. She was 36 years old. In a public statement provided by her representatives, her father Skip Panettiere called her an “incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” In Sept., the Greenville County Coroner’s Office revealed her cause of death as the “toxic effects” of fentanyl and other drugs. Tests found traces of Xanax, the muscle relaxant Methocarbamol, and Quetiapine, a drug that is prescribed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or depression, but the coroner said there were no signs of trauma or foul play. On Oct. 28, the Greenville Police Department closed their investigation, ruling Panettiere’s death as “accidental.”

Throughout her time in the spotlight, Panettiere was open about her struggles with mental health; including postpartum depression following the birth of her daughter but also anxiety and substance abuse issues tied to her early brushes with fame. She also had a publicly contentious relationship with Hickerson, who remained her on-again-off-again boyfriend until the time of her death. In 2020, she requested a restraining order against him. And in her May memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning, Panettiere described their relationship being fraught with emotional abuse and physical violence.

At the time of her death, Panettiere had recently finished a stint in a rehab facility. And according to a police report obtained by NBC News, Hickerson and his brother Zach were both in the home at the time of the actresses’ death. (Brian Hickerson’s lawyer declined to comment on Vogel’s claims. Zach Hickerson did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone’s request for comment.)

When news of Panettiere’s death was first released, Vogel told NBC News that she had been extremely concerned about her daughter’s relationship with Hickerson. “This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death, and that was Brian Hickerson,” she said at the time. “There is a lot of history in the past that Brian has enabled Hayden many times, and this is why her father and I had been concerned for a long time about him.”

But in her most recent interview with Inside Edition, Vogel placed the blame firmly on Hickerson. When she was asked if Hickerson was responsible for Panettiere’s death, she responded, “Absolutely. There’s no doubt in my mind. And I think that he knows that.”

Vogel claims Panettiere’s treatment for substance abuse was “going well,” but blamed Hickerson for their estranged relationship. She also claimed that Hickerson sent “harassing emails” to her after Panettiere’s death, threatening “action” if she kept making statements.

During the interview, Vogel also dismissed rumors that she was not invited to Panettiere’s celebration of life, instead saying she chose not to attend to keep the peace. ”I knew that some of the people there wanted to believe that I’m the horrible mother because Hayden was angry and made statements,” she said. “I just didn’t want to rock the boat either. It was probably for the best.”

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: Do You Caramel
items.description: Do you remember the Warrant song “Cherry Pie?” I honestly hope that you don’t, but there’s a lyric from it that I think about all the time: “Tastes so good it makes a grown man cry. Sweet cherry pie.” He’s not, you know, actually talking about cherry pie. He’s
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Do you remember the Warrant song “Cherry Pie?” I honestly hope that you don’t, but there’s a lyric from it that I think about all the time: “Tastes so good it makes a grown man cry. Sweet cherry pie.” He’s not, you know, actually talking about cherry pie. He’s talking about something else, but this episode reminded me of it. Not because they made cherry pie. In fact, it was Caramel Week, which has very little to do with cherries or pies, but because this episode was so delicious, it made a grown man cry. That grown man is me, and maybe you if you are a man. It also definitely made Moyin cry, and I think maybe, just maybe, we got a little drop melting out of Paul Hollywood’s icicle blue eyes.

Caramel Week starts with the bakers having to make a treacle tart, but the catch is that they have to make the golden syrup themselves. Treacle, where the tart gets its name from, is very similar to molasses, a by-product of the sugar-making process that was repurposed for other foods. (However, there was never a Great Treacle Flood.) Golden syrup, which is now used to make the dessert, doesn’t really have an American corollary, just like you can’t find construction paper in any store in the U.K. (How do English kids make birthday cards for their nans? Do they use paper plates?) It’s kind of like Karo corn syrup, but it’s not made out of corn; it’s made out of boiling sugar and water for a really long time, as the bakers demonstrate. While I like the idea of making a very traditional dessert, particularly because it plays to the strengths of more mature bakers like Connie, asking them to make the syrup is kinda silly. Everyone just buys it in the store. What’s next? Making them grow their own baking powder? Is that how you make baking powder? No clue. I’ve only ever bought it in the store. I guess, like Mo preparing for this challenge, I’ll just watch two (2) TikToks about it and call it a day.

A treacle tart, as Mo says, is the kind of medieval food that is a British staple from when they were known for having the most terrible cuisine on the planet, but they stick by it anyway. It combines breadcrumbs and golden syrup and, honestly, I’ve never eaten one because I think I would rather lick the underside of a boot. Most of the bakers do a great job. Tom turns his into a PB&J treacle tart, even though he eats his PB&Js with cherry conserve. I’m sorry. The PB&J Council of America specifies that our national delicacy should be made only with grape, raspberry, or strawberry jelly and never the kind where the peanut butter and the jelly come in the same jar. Paul says it tastes great and like something totally different. Yeah, that’s probably why they like it. Mo makes an apple crumble tart, and Nigella says that the apple flavor combines well with the traditional treacle, though his pastry is a bit too thin. Moyin made a sticky toffee pudding tart that combines Mary Berry and Paul Hollywood’s recipes, so it’s no wonder Paul loves it.

But Gabe and our girl Connie struggle. Gabe’s is orange and almond flavored, and you know as soon as he put extract in it that Paul will say that the almond flavor is too strong. Connie, while making the best-looking tart of the bunch, struggles in several ways, including the dreaded soggy bottom. She also can’t get her tart casing off of her bake. She shouts to Moyin, “I can’t get my bottom off!” That’s something my husband has been saying for years. Moyin rushes to help her, and Connie later rushes over to help him get his tart on its stand. Their relationship is so sweet, and we see it several times this episode. Combined with all the talk about how Moyin wants to win the whole show without winning Star Baker (which only happened once in season 10), it makes me think that this episode will end with Connie going home and Moyin winning Star Baker.

The technical is to make a millionaire’s shortbread, another British staple that is shortbread topped with a fat layer of caramel and chocolate on top. It’s basically a Twix bar, a whole slab instead of a tiny little finger (or two; don’t want to forget the left Twix). While this isn’t a terrible idea for a challenge, they didn’t give the bakers nearly enough time for the caramel to set before putting the chocolate on top, and most of the bakers turn in mushy messes with underbaked shortbread, unset chocolate, and caramel runnier than a 4-year-old’s nose. “At least it was better than Bread Week,” Nigella says. Um, both of these are a problem. I get that there needs to be a time crunch to make compelling television, at least in the minds of the producers, but setting our lovely bakers up to fail is not how it should go. The order from worst to least worst is Mo, Connie, Gabe, Moyin, and Tom, who is, of course, decent because he’s always decent.

The showstopper is based on the Hungarian dessert Grillázstorta, which sounds like a pie made out of gorillas. The bakers must make a structure out of nougatine with a praline-based cake inside of it. Ugh, nougatine. I have never ever in my life seen it outside of Baking Show. They used it even more frequently in Bake Off: The Professionals, where they have to make really elaborate structures that are entirely edible. Well, there is edible, and there is something you want to eat. Lint is, technically, edible, but do you actually want any? That’s how I feel about nougatine. You only have to learn how to make it and work with it to be on one of these shows, so why are we bothering?

During the challenge, Connie has too much to do and is starting to spiral. Paul Hollywood, of all people, gets down off his pedestal and tells Connie to go sit on the bridge and stare at the water for five minutes. I’ve never seen anything like that in the tent before. Could someone get her a five-minute YouTube meditation video to go along with it? When everyone finishes baking, Moyin goes to give her a big hug, and they talk about how special they are to each other. Oh yeah, he’s winning, and she’s going home.

Mo does a great job making a box for a baby shower complete with nougatine ribbons and adorable frosted teddy bears, and the cake is a coffee sponge with chocolate ganache that Nigella rips into with unreserved gusto that was shocking even to her. Moyin makes a crown with blue “sapphires” around it, inspired by a song that his grandmother made up about him. Inside there is an opera cake that looks absolutely immaculate. Nigella says it’s dainty but packs a whallop; Paul even manages to try the nougatine and says it’s great. Moyin, as predicted, wins.

Everyone else has a difficult time. Gabe makes a really cool-looking black sesame nougatine, so it’s black and in the shape of a boat on the waves. As cool as the outside looks, inside is a Genoise sponge with a blue mirror glaze that looks like an algae bloom that could bleach all the coral reefs. Paul says that there is no flavor to it at all. That’s not usually a problem for our Gabe. Tom makes a pub out of nougatine, and inside is a hazelnut praline cake that looks like the Wicked Witch of the West after she had water poured on her. It is just a chocolaty puddle. Paul says it’s “Not his best work.” For an English person to say that is like he just pulled down his trousers and slapped him in the face.

However, it is Connie who really struggles. She tries to make her husband Myke’s favorite kind of cake to thank him for all of his support while she’s been off in a tent in Berkshire every weekend. She takes way too long to make nougatine and barely gets her rudimentary box finished in time. Both judges love the light, creamy hazelnut cake inside, but the box literally falls apart when they open it. As predicted, Connie goes home. This is when Warrant sings “Cherry Pie” and we all sob. She and Moyin hug once again, and Moyin says that she means everything to him. She tells him that she’ll be with him every step of the way, but there are only two more episodes, so it’s not that long. But sweet, sweet wonderful Connie. She even has hugs and kisses for all of the crew on the way out. She was undone by some not-great challenges on an uneven week, but she managed to capture all of our hearts, which is like winning a whole different trophy.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: Fair Use and Foul Play
items.description: As I’ve mentioned before, the key to making a good courtroom drama — and Cupertino is on its way to being a great one — is to ensure that the lawyers facing off against our righteous heroes can make their own compelling cases. I firmly believe that strong argu
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: As I’ve mentioned before, the key to making a good courtroom drama — and Cupertino is on its way to being a great one — is to ensure that the lawyers facing off against our righteous heroes can make their own compelling cases. I firmly believe that strong arguments make for good television. But how can you do that when the opposition is defending AI slop?

In this week’s episode, an over-the-hill rapper who goes by the stage name Yungwood (Cliff “Method Man” Smith) comes to his old friend Michael Price for help with a lawsuit that is going nowhere. Yungwood relies on the income from streams of his old songs, but his numbers have dropped off precipitously ever since the major streaming services — represented here by the fictional Noisement — started hosting AI music that sounds almost identical to his. Yungwood first retained PSA’s enemy Ry Vance, who dropped the case as soon as the music-tech titans pushed back hard by hiring Bayard Diamond, Michael’s father.

There are red flags aplenty in this case for PSA. The firm still needs some quick and lucrative wins, and with the Yungwood lawsuit, they’ll be dealing with an unpredictable client who films himself nearly 24/7 for his social-media followers, making inflammatory comments that compare music-industry executives to slaveholders. They’re also up against a deep-pocketed opposition who can drain their coffers with motions and delays.

Still, a few episodes ago, Michael allowed Olivia to pursue her “crusade” against WorkSource in exchange for her promising to back some future crusade of his own. Now is the time for Michael’s crusade. Not against Noisement necessarily, but against Bayard.

The case itself provides some fantastic theater, and not just because father and son can’t stop themselves from making multiple petty objections, needling each other and infuriating the judge (Danny Burstein). No, what’s more fascinating about the way this lawsuit plays out is that it pushes the Cupertino viewers — who, I assume, are all inclined to think that AI ripoff artists are all lazy, parasitic scum — to think hard about what music is, who makes it, and who benefits from that work.

Let’s take this one by one, but out of order. First: Who makes it? On one side we have Yungwood, an artist well past his prime, whose declining streaming numbers could have just as much to do with a recent incident where he assaulted a man at a bar. But at least Yungwood can prove in court that he composes his songs himself, starting with a guitar that he actually plays. On the other side we have Purvis Beer (Amir Malaklou), who turned Yungwood’s biggest hit, “Booty Bass,” into the deceptively titled sound-alike “Bass Booty,” and who can’t even play a C chord on a piano, despite claiming to be a “born musician.”

Which raises the next question: What is music? And it’s here that this episode becomes genuinely challenging. Can Michael argue that what Yungwood does — deriving songs from a long tradition of folk music and spirituals, many of which melodically resemble “Booty Bass” — is wholly distinctive from Purvis Beer layering instrumental tracks using AI prompts? After all, both songwriters are relying on their tastes, their memory, and their relative facility with the musical tools at hand.

Of course, there has to be an end to this stalemate for the dramatic tension to resolve. And ideally it should be a break in favor of our side. So we come to the final question: Who benefits? This is where Noisement and the AI music producer Gold Artist Studio get kind of caught with their hands in the cookie jar. PSA is able to prove that Noisement is manipulating its algorithm to deprioritize Yungwood and other legacy artists in favor of the cheaper, more lucrative GAS knockoffs. When the judge pulls out his phone to listen to Jimmy Buffett and is directed toward some slop that sort of sounds like Jimmy Buffett, it’s game over for Noisement.

As has happened a couple of times in this first season, the ending is both satisfying and a bit abrupt. It feels like there’s more that could’ve been mined from this debate over musical authorship, which predates the AI boom. (But I did like that Yungwood uses the controversy to get famous again, in part by hiring a bot farm in Peru to goose his numbers.)

The biggest reason why the Yungwood story line feels curtailed is that about a third of the running time this week is dedicated to a subplot carried over from “Harper.” As Olivia suspected, her older brother, Jacob, is being scammed by a pig-butchering operation working out of Krakow. The most damning piece of evidence arrives when Jacob tries to help his “girlfriend” get through “customs” by providing personal banking information, which ends up compromising the Siffre family’s Christian publishing business.

There’s a twist here, and it’s a good one. While Olivia is working with “Josh Frank” from “One Coast Bank” to protect her parents’ accounts, she suddenly wonders if she herself is being played. If you’re the kind of person who reads every possible long-form article about frauds and swindles, you know that Olivia is right to be wary, because “saving you from a con artist” is also a common con. (Once again, there is a great New York Magazine article about this phenomenon from The Cut.)

Olivia gets Vik to help her scam the scammers, using what he calls a “beaconing payload” to track them down and infect their network with malware. Again, this is a satisfying outcome, if maybe too neat. But if I’m being honest, my biggest beef with how the One Coast subplot resolves is how dopey it looks. As the malware hits the Krakow office, all of the computers start making loud beeping noises and popping up big warning windows.
That’s the sort of thing you’d expect to see from a much cornier show, and not one as savvy about tech as Cupertino. It’s pretty sloppy … no offense to all the AI artists out there.

• We learn a bit more in this episode about Michael’s dead sister, Anna, who jumped off a balcony because she was tired of the pressure from their demanding father. She was apparently a Yungwood fan, which is another reason why Michael took this case.

• Natalia gets to put her law degree to use in this episode, filling in for Olivia in court, where she struggles to figure out how best to stand while questioning a witness. (The judge: “Try perching.”) She also laughs at Bayard when he accuses her of being a wannabe who “spread your legs for the third-richest man.” While smirking straight in his face, she whispers, “You shouldn’t drink before court.”

• Natalia makes Michael nervous by suggesting that she’s not as rich as she may need to be to keep the firm afloat. But when Michael is not around, she tells the people building her office that she needs to have her own shower and that she’ll be covering the expense from her personal account. Is Natalia making promises she can’t keep?
• A nice, realistic touch: Over the past few episodes, the cut that Olivia got on her cheek in “A.J. & Buddy” has gradually shrunk, until by the end of this episode she’s no longer wearing a bandage.

• Olivia is very flirty with Vik this week, and the episode ends with the two of them going out to dinner at a place Christy suggested — someplace very loud with a dance floor. It’s nice to see Christy enjoying herself, and yet I couldn’t help but notice that she’s still downing her booze pretty hard.

items.title: Southern Charm Season-Premiere Recap: Boys Will Be Boys
items.description: Well, we know that the season ends with Whitney asking all the guys who has a secret love child. Is it [dun, dun, DUNNNN], Austen, the lovable cad who has been dating all over Charleston; [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Craig, the unrepentant narcissist with a giant hole i
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Well, we know that the season ends with Whitney asking all the guys who has a secret love child. Is it [dun, dun, DUNNNN], Austen, the lovable cad who has been dating all over Charleston; [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Craig, the unrepentant narcissist with a giant hole in his living room ceiling; [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Shep, the newly-bearded wastrel who just got back with his ex-girlfriend; or [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Whitner, the recently buff playboy and possible performative male? Tune in this season to Southern Charm, where all the answers are revealed, including just how cute the baby is. (The baby is reportedly very cute.) If I’m putting money on it now, I would say that it’s Whitner because there is no way that the other boys would have gotten someone knocked up and we wouldn’t have known. I love you, Whitner, but are you our main suspect or a red herring?

It’s going to take us three months to answer these questions. We’re not in Maui on a cast trip; we are in Charleston where everyone is goofing off with their pets and Miss Patricia is cleaning out her cabinet of dog clothes. Talk about relatable! JK. I do not have a dog, and that imaginary dog certainly does not have clothes. We also check in with everyone. Craig went to Switzerland, where he wanted to isolate himself so that he could learn how to be alone. He did this with a luxury ski vacation. Now that he’s back in Charleston, it seems like nothing has changed, including that his assistant, Jack, is still in love with him. Madison’s baby, Teddi, is not sleeping through the night, so Madison isn’t getting much rest and still manages to look absolutely amazing. What is wrong with the rest of us?

Venita and Salley are friends once again, and they’re FaceTiming in the morning while Salley sticks her face and her extra E in a bucket of ice water that her dogs, Kevin and Boots, have already been drinking out of. Molly broke up with her dude and is just hanging out lots with Whitner (as friends), who is sending out shirtless pics with the frequency and urgency of a gay man who just downloaded Sniffies. (Straight people, do not ask Claude or Gemini or Jeeves what that is.) Venita says she’s into Whitner and Molly is like, “Are you? Are you sure? Do you want to be? How about being into someone who is not on the show? I think that is much better for you.”

All of the budding relationships come together at Venita’s Garden of Eden But Don’t Spend Too Much on the Flowers party that she holds to kick off the season. Whitner shows up with all of his shirt buttons undone to show off all the work he has been doing at the gym. Much like Venita, I have fallen for it. Salley can have my old imaginary husband, Kyle Cooke, because I have a new imaginary husband, and his name is Whitner Moylan. Yes, he is taking my last name because I can neither spell nor say his. (Also, Moylan in Gaelic means “bald,” and it’s ironic because he’s so wonderfully hairy.) Anyway, Whitner has fallen for Allie, the new girl who is a 26-year-old model that Venita knew when she was 14, when she was a modeling coach, a job that she had to go through a six-year accreditation process to practice. Yes, because she is a 26-year-old model in an amazing dress and after my husband — I already hate her. He asks her out on a date, and she accepts. Can’t wait to vomit all over that.

There’s only one problem. She was going out with Austen for a bit. Shep and his new beard (no, not a fake girlfriend to hide that he’s gay, an actual beard) pull Allie aside and ask about the relationship. He says Austen told him that they went on two or three dates and she wanted to be exclusive before being “intimate,” and so Austen said, “Maybe this isn’t for me,” and called it off. She rolls her neck and is like, “No, girl. That is not what happened.” She says that they went on a few dates; he was calling her all the time, but she is the one who stopped calling him because the whole time Salley and her extra E were blowing up his phone, and everyone was telling her that they were dating. At the very end of the episode, Allie sits down to talk to Austen, and I’m sure next week will open with her blowing him into oblivion for putting his own spin on this tale.

Yes, that means we need to talk about Salley and Austen. Do you want the short version? Let’s start with the short version. Salley is in love with Austen, and he treats her like crap. When Austen is talking to Madison at the party about his relationship with Salley, Madison tells him to stop kissing this woman who “wants to be his lady.” Austen says he didn’t know that. What? How did he not know that? That’s like going through the Wendy’s drive-thru, eating a whole square hamburger, and then being like, “How did this grease get all over my fingers?” Salley has literally told him this, but Austen is pretending like he didn’t know so that he can keep the status quo, which wildly favors him. He wants to keep going out with Salley, get all the companionship and fun of having a girlfriend, the occasional makeout when they’re drunk, but still get to date and sleep with whomever he wants. Why would he want to change it?

Meanwhile, Salley is unhappy and uncomfortable. Oh, no. Not because of Austen. Because she is wearing the dumbest dress I have ever seen in my life. It’s like she took a white pillowcase, cut out a hole for her head, trimmed off the bottom so that her underboob and midriff would show, and then put it over her head so that she can’t move her arms higher than her waist without exposing everything between her navel and neck. Who designed this dress? A blind couturier with a humiliation kink?

She’s also upset because of Austen, whom she tells everyone who will listen that she wants to be his girlfriend, even while she knows he treats her like yesterday’s doo-doo. She’s angry that, at the reunion, he called her a “bar rat” and said that not only was her hair high body count, but that her whole existence was. This is literally the problem, but no one will tell Salley. Venita tells her that he doesn’t respect her because she doesn’t respect herself. She says that she makes herself too available to Austen and acts like his girlfriend when she’s not. This is all true, but that’s not the problem at all. Austen literally tells Madison that he would have dated her, but she’s been with too many other guys that he knows. The problem is, frankly, that Salley is a slut.

I say that word with pride. I am a slut, and I am a firm advocate for sluts’ rights. That Austen thinks this way is totally stupid and antiquated, and I hate it. I especially hate that he won’t just tell Salley that, put her out of her misery, and allow her to move on to falling in love with another man who is going to treat her horribly. (I mean, PK is available.) Instead, she gets upset that Austen was wining and dining Allie but didn’t do the same to her. It makes her wonder what Allie has that she doesn’t. Sally wants to know what is wrong with her. The answer is nothing. However, what Austen sees as wrong is that she has been too promiscuous, and that makes her tainted in his eyes. Yes, it’s ridiculous, but someone please tell Salley. Let her move on. Let Austen be the villain that he always will be.

She sits him down at the party to tell him that they need to have more boundaries in their friendship. Across the party, Craig, Madison, Molly, and Rod are trying to read their lips and see what they’re saying. Honestly, the conversation about their conversation is more interesting than the conversation itself because Austen won’t be truthful with Salley, and she can’t be respectful of herself. Salley says that her hard line is that they can’t be kissing or touching anymore. Wait, that’s it. I mean, that is the baseline. She needs to tell him: no kissing, no touching, no calling her and asking her to hang out, and her dropping everything to do so. No hanging out with him and his friends and then letting him hit on other girls in front of her. No more treating her like one of the guys. No more double standard about how he can sleep with every co-ed in town, but she’s too slutty to be his wife. No more texting her about his problems late at night. No more making her think that on one hot night when they’re both oppressed by the heat of summer that he’ll eventually wake up and figure out that she has been the one all along and he will run to her house, sweat dripping in dense rivulets down his back, and shout up at her window, “Salley! It was you! It was always you!” as she throws open the shutters and jumps down from the second floor in her white nightgown to land in his arms like a dandelion seed. None of that. No more. Forever.

items.title: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: Not as Deadly as ‘Songbirds & Snakes,’ the Haymitch Origin Story Makes for a Watchable if Meandering Prequel
