Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of big-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often said that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

Set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

items.author: Cam Wolf; GQ
paragraphs: Tonight, GQ hosts its annual celebration of the biggest, most impactful, and superlatively stylish Men of the Year at the Chateau Marmont in Hollywood. In 2026, of course, no great outfit—and no great man—is complete without a wristwatch. Naturally, for the liveliest menswear party of the year, attendees are bringing out their very best timepieces.

The dress code is “modern red carpet,” and attendees have found creative ways to interpret that on their wrists. Performer of the Year Andrew Garfield, who’s been aggressively auditioning new wristwear recently, is wearing the brand-spanking-new Breguet Classique in platinum, a watch that leans all the way into simplicity with just a single hand to read both the hour and minutes. Skyler Gisondo threw down with the ultimate-classic Rolex Submariner. Michael Rider, always attuned to what’s trending in the watch world, is in a dainty Cartier Tank.
Scroll on to see all of the best watches from GQ's Men of the Year 2026 red carpet.

items.title: The Biggest Snubs and Surprises of the 2027 Grammy Nominations
items.description: mThe 2027 Grammy Awards already have a winner: women. For the first time in Grammy history, the six artists with the most nominations are all women: Raye has 11, Rosalía is close behind with nine, and Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, Ella Langley, and Olivia
items.author: Claire Valentine
paragraphs: mThe 2027 Grammy Awards already have a winner: women. For the first time in Grammy history, the six artists with the most nominations are all women: Raye has 11, Rosalía is close behind with nine, and Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, Ella Langley, and Olivia Rodrigo tie with seven (Olivia Dean received six nods, tying with Bruno Mars and Leon Thomas).

It’s not exactly surprising, given that all six artists spent the year dominating charts, playlists, and airwaves, but the nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards—announced early this morning via livestream—did have their share of upsets.

Several men who otherwise had big years—including Harry Styles, Justin Bieber, Noah Kahan, and Jack Antonoff—weren’t recognized as much as expected by the Recording Academy. Men were also completely shut out of Best Album, save for one artist: Bruno Mars. Though she did receive five nominations for Confessions of a Dancefloor: Part 2 (her first since 2010), Madonna was left out of the major categories. BTS won’t be making an appearance at all, after they decided not to submit this year following the ceremony’s addition of a controversial new Asian Pop category. And despite being a usual favorite with 19 previous nods, Doja Cat was left off the list for her most recent album, Vie.

The 2027 Grammy Awards will take place at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Sunday, February 7 at 7 p.m. ET and will air live on ABC, Disney+ and Hulu. Below, the biggest snubs and surprises of the 2027 nominations:

Styles’s fourth studio album, Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally, was a hit with fans, but didn’t resonate with the Recording Academy: Styles received zero nominations for the 2027 awards. It’s especially surprising given the fact that Styles took home Album of the Year in 2023 for Harry’s House, though he didn’t score as many big hits this year like “As It Was” or “Watermelon Sugar.”

The 29-year-old British singer-songwriter is no stranger to awards ceremonies and already had four Grammy nominations under her belt before today. Still, leading the pack with 11 nominations would be a big deal for any artist—a feat that tied her with the record for most nominations for a female artist in a year, previously held last year by Beyoncé, who also recently gave Raye her coveted co-sign.

This one can be a snub or a surprise, depending on how you look at it. Madonna’s Confessions II did get nominated four times, bringing her career record to 32 (the original Confessions on a Dance Floor won Best Electronic/Dance Album in 2007). However, her celebrated comeback record was shut out of the Big Four categories.
Snub: Gracie Abrams, Stella Lefty, Sienna Spiro

All three acts had objectively big years—Gracie Abrams with her third studio album Daughter From Hell, Stella Lefty with the viral “Boston,” and Sienna Spiro with hit “Die on This Hill”—but all three were snubbed. Abrams and Lefty were shut out completely; Spiro’s song didn’t receive as much love as expected, but she did get a nod for Best New Artist, a category she also won at this year’s VMAs, so that’s something.
Snub: Audrey Hobert and Malcolm Todd

Siblings Audrey Hobert and Malcolm Todd have both become pop phenoms over the last few years, and many speculated they might receive Best New Artist nods, but both artists were shut out of the Grammys this year.
Surprise: The women of country music

Ella Langley has been breaking records all year with her megahit “Choosin’ Texas,” so it’s no shock she’s also at the top of the list of this year’s nominations. A little more surprising is that women are dominating the country category overall this year, with all five nominations going to female artists for Best Contemporary Country Album for the first time (Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith, Megan Moroney, Kacey Musgraves, and Langley).

Despite becoming one of the most reliably popular acts in music over the past few years, especially since his 2022 breakout album Stick Season topped charts and playlists, Noah Kahan only received one nod this year for The Great Divide, in the Best Contemporary Folk Album category.
Surprise: Slayyyter, Tinashe and Underscores

It’s a big year for first-time nominees who have been quietly putting in the work: Underscores, Slayyyter and Tinashe received nods for Best Dance/Electronic Recording, with the latter two artists also receiving nods for Best Dance Pop Recording. Slayyyter, who recently sold out Madison Square Garden after a breakthrough Lollapalooza performance, is also nominated for Best Dance/Electronic Album for Wor$t Girl in America.

You might be surprised to learn that Bieber only has two Grammys for his two-decade career, and both were for collaborations. This year won’t change anything, as despite submitting his latest album Swag II and songs “Everything Hallelujah” and “Speed Demon” for several major categories, he was completely shut out.
Surprise: Angine de Poitrine

If you don’t know who Angine de Poitrine are yet, you will after watching this year’s Grammys. The experimental Canadian rock duo, who perform wearing polka-dot-covered papier-mâché masks and costumes, was nominated in several categories, including Best New Artist, Best Rock Performance, Best Alternative Music Performance, and Best Rock Album, throwing a curveball into an otherwise pretty sleepy category this year.

Björk needs no introduction, but she does need a Grammy, and this year could finally be her chance. The Icelandic singer got her first-ever nod in two of the Big Four categories, for Record and Song of the Year, for her work on Rosalía’s “Berghain.” Hopefully, the two will pair up for what would surely be an otherworldly performance.

items.title: Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond
items.description: The baton—or rather, the martini—has been passed. We officially have a new James Bond, the first in two decades. Robert Pattinson will be the next actor to don a tux and take on the role of the famed British spy.
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: The baton—or rather, the martini—has been passed. We officially have a new James Bond, the first in two decades. Robert Pattinson will be the next actor to don a tux and take on the role of the famed British spy.

After months of speculation, the news was officially announced on Monday morning via Instagram. Pattinson was actually a last-minute addition to the contender list. At one point, it seemed like every man in Hollywood was being considered for the role, with Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Jacob Elordi, and even Harry Styles in the mix. Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and Callum Turner eventually emerged as the frontrunners over the last few weeks. In late October, though, Pattinson’s name was thrown in the ring, along with Nicholas Hoult, and both actors supposedly screen-tested for the part over the weekend of October 24, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

Pattinson’s victory shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise. The actor has had an extremely successful year with critically acclaimed roles in The Drama, The Odyssey, and Primetime. He will also appear in Dune: Part Three, out next month. It’s important to note that Denis Villeneuve, director of the Dune franchise, is signed on to direct the new Bond film and probably had at least some say in the casting. He must have been impressed by Pattinson’s work on Arrakis.

It also probably helps that Pattinson has experience leading a big franchise. In 2022, the actor starred as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, and he is currently filming the sequel, which is set for release in 2028. Many thought Pattinson’s role in the DC universe would make him unavailable for the Bond films. But recent shake-ups at DC Studios, which saw co-chiefs James Gunn and Peter Safran fired last week, have left the future of that specific franchise up in the air and have seemingly freed up the actor to take on Bond.

Pattinson will take the reins from Daniel Craig, who debuted as Bond in 2006’s Casino Royale. Craig starred in five films and ended his run with No Time to Die in 2021, in which his Bond sacrificed himself to save the world. Pattinson will be the first to play Bond since Amazon MGM took creative control of the franchise last year.
According to THR, Pattinson only learned of the casting on Sunday morning, and was informed by Villeneuve himself. Those who lost out on the part were informed by producer Amy Pascal.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Pattinson is the eighth man to play Bond, following in the footsteps of Craig, Sean Connery, David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, and Pierce Brosnan.

items.title: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive
items.description: The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.
items.author: Matt Simon
paragraphs: The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”

That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”

Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”

Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”

Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.

Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”
This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

items.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
items.description: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.
items.author: Will Knight
paragraphs: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.
Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.
And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.
Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.
But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.
Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.
“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

items.title: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
items.description: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.
items.author: Paresh Dave; Zoë Schiffer
paragraphs: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.

Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.

It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.

One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.

Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”

Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

items.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
items.description: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

items.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

items.title: Anthony Mackie Says It’s ‘Hard’ to Date As an Older Man
items.description: Anthony Mackie is down in the dumps about dating. Last night, on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen, the 48-year-old actor was asked if he was planning to get married again and had the gall to claim that he’s getting rejected because he’s too old.
items.author: Grace Klara Marshall
paragraphs: Anthony Mackie is down in the dumps about dating. Last night, on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen, the 48-year-old actor was asked if he was planning to get married again and had the gall to claim that he’s getting rejected because he’s too old.
“You know, I’m an older man,” Mackie explained, “and I feel like being an older man, women don’t like older men.”

“What? That is absolutely not true!” exclaimed host Andy Cohen, a man who is surely well-versed in age-gap relationships. “Older men with Marvel money?” asked Mackie’s fellow guest and man in his 40s, Jamie Dornan, in disbelief. “Yeah, right!” Cohen said. “Excuse me … older, jacked men who look like him?” Despite all this hyping, Mackie was not reassured. “It’s hard as an older man,” he insisted. “Women don’t like older men. They like younger, fruitful men.”

This isn’t the first time Mackie has complained about his (relatively young) age interfering with his love life. In a 2025 interview with People, he said, “The idea of dating is really hard” mostly because he’s a cinematic superhero, but also because “I’m older, and I don’t do the apps.” Mackie was previously married to his childhood sweetheart, Sheletta Chapital, from 2014 to 2018, and shares four sons with her.

Look, if Mackie isn’t interested in asking a real-life woman what she thinks, he need only to look around. Just last week, Michael Bloomberg married his longtime and age-appropriate partner, Diana Taylor, at the age of 84, and Mohamed Hadid, who’s 78, got engaged to a woman 35 years his junior. All hope is not lost, especially, as Dornan implied, for the rich and the famous.

Mackie, who is both under 50 and looks about a decade younger than his actual age, may also want to check out the stats on his prospects. Beyond anecdotal data from Leonardo DiCaprio’s dating history, studies from the past few years have established that women do like older men. A 2022 Ipsos poll conducted on behalf of Cougar Life found that men are more likely to have dated someone ten or more years younger than them compared to women. Inversely, and surprisingly only to Mackie, women were found to be more likely to date someone ten or more years older than them compared to men.

I hope Mackie’s pre-midlife crisis is assuaged by this info, and he refrains from making such doofy comments going forward. If he doesn’t believe me, a 28-year-old single woman, perhaps it’s time to look inward.

items.title: Katniss and Peeta Forever
items.description: How are all my Team Peeta girls doing today? I, for one, am still buzzing. On Monday night, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson reunited on the red carpet for the premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping 14 years after the original movie hit thea
items.author: Brooke LaMantia
paragraphs: How are all my Team Peeta girls doing today? I, for one, am still buzzing. On Monday night, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson reunited on the red carpet for the premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping 14 years after the original movie hit theaters. Last night, New York felt like Panem, but in a good, non-fascist way.

Lawrence and Hutcherson, who play Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark, were joined by a number of other actors from the original movie series, making it the biggest Hunger Games reunion since the Mockingjay premiere in 2015. Woody Harrelson — who reprises his role as the older Haymitch Abernathy in the movie — and Elizabeth Banks, who played Effie in the originals — were present, as were Amandla Stenberg, Willow Shields, and Jenna Malone, who portrayed Rue, Prim, and Joanna in the original series.

Rachel Zegler and Tom Blyth, stars from the other prequel, The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, also made surprise appearances on the carpet, though they don’t appear in the new film. Sunrise on the Reaping takes place 24 years before the original series is set, following a young Haymitch (Joseph Zada) during the first Quarter Quell, which has double the number of tributes to compete to the death in the games. Ahead of the movie’s premiere, Lawrence and Hutcherson confirmed they’re reprising their roles in an epilogue.

Before the premiere, director Francis Lawrence took the stage to introduce the film, saying there were too many cast members in attendance to have them all up onstage. He announced them one by one as they stood, spread out across the audience at Alice Tully Hall. “This is the first time we’ve had three generations of Hunger Games cast together,” he said. Cue the tears.

items.title: Which Deals Are Better — Black Friday’s or Cyber Monday’s?
items.description: For more of the Cut’s favorite fashion, beauty, and home finds, sign up for the weekly Cut Shop newsletter.
items.author: Hanna Flanagan
paragraphs: For more of the Cut’s favorite fashion, beauty, and home finds, sign up for the weekly Cut Shop newsletter.

With Black Friday and Cyber Monday (a.k.a. Cyber Weekend) fast approaching, you might be wondering what the difference between the two shopping events actually is. It’s a valid question! Black Friday and Cyber Monday are pretty intertwined now, and most brands have abandoned the 24-hour timeline in favor of a weeklong sales event, so it gets confusing. Keep reading for everything you need to know about both days in order to shop strategically and take full advantage of the deals, whether you want to get discounts on giftable K-beauty products, find the perfect fashion essentials for friends and family, or spend way too much money at Nordstrom.

Traditionally, Black Friday refers to in-store deals, while Cyber Monday is dedicated to online shopping, with e-commerce sites offering doorbuster deals across all categories. But over the past few years, the so-called death of retail has caused the two shopping holidays to blur together. These days, most hard-core Black Friday shoppers would rather scour the sales section of their favorite online retailers than wake up at the crack of dawn to wait on line at Best Buy, and I don’t blame them. In response to consumer trends, every major retailer from Walmart to Reformation now offers deals both online and in-store.
Are there better deals on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

It all depends on what you’re looking for. Black Friday generally offers better deals on big-ticket items like mattresses, laptops, and TVs. Cyber Monday, on the other hand, is a better day for saving on things like small appliances, clothes, accessories, and beauty must-haves. To incentivize people to shop in-store, Black Friday deals are usually available only for a very limited time, whereas Cyber Monday deals often last for over a week. Keep in mind that most brick-and-mortars are open on Cyber Monday, so if you prefer to shop in-store (but hate the Black Friday crowds), going on Cyber Monday is your best bet.
Should you just wait for Cyber Monday?

No, you should not wait to get all your holiday shopping done on Cyber Monday. Since most retailers unveil Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals several days (and sometimes weeks!) in advance, there’s a good chance that the item in your cart will be sold out by the time Cyber Monday rolls around. (It takes place on November 30 this year with Black Friday happening on November 27.) Also, since mass retailers like Target and Nordstrom switch up their sales promos throughout the month of November, you might accidentally pass up better deals if you wait until Cyber Monday to shop.

After reading all of that, you’re probably craving some good discounts. Luckily, I’ve rounded up a few early Black Friday deals that are already live from Brooklinen, Nordstrom, Lululemon, Amazon, Gap, and more.
Update on November 17, 2026: Updated prices and checked stock for all products.

items.title: My 8-Year Battle to Get Rid of My Mom’s Stuff
items.description: My mother loved beautiful things — and a good bargain.
items.author: Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein
paragraphs: My mother loved beautiful things — and a good bargain.

When she died, my sisters and I inherited a house full of objects she had spent decades collecting: silk scarves, porcelain flowers, figurines, knitting needles, fine china. None of it came with instructions, except the jewelry.
“Don’t give away the pins,” she warned. I scribbled her last wishes into a little blue notebook. I still refer to these notes eight years later as we continue to sort through her stuff.

My mother believed she was leaving a substantial inheritance for her three daughters. All we had to do was figure out what to keep, donate, gift, sell, or toss. My sisters and I wanted to honor our mother’s wishes, but we knew — after months of agonizing — that we couldn’t keep it all.
So what exactly are we supposed to do with all our mother’s stuff?

I know I’m not alone. We are currently living through “the Great Junk Transfer.” As aging generations die or downsize, their adult children are inheriting the stuff, both meaningful and mundane, they leave behind. For many, it can become a burden. Nearly half of 2,200 people surveyed across three countries said they would “rather inherit nothing than deal with” this, according to 1-800-Got-Junk?, a removal company.
“When an object keeps its sentimental value but loses its place in your home, it gets stuck. And so do you,” wrote Brian Scudamore, founder and CEO of 1-800-Got-Junk?, about the survey.

My sisters and I have worked through our immense pile slowly but methodically. We’ve sold some, but in most cases the collector plates, porcelain figurines, stuffed animals, and plastic containers are relatively worthless. So we’ve parted with much of it in other ways — donating to local thrift stores and keeping sentimental items for ourselves and other family members.
But somehow, there’s still more to go.

We turned to Fran Ruskin, an estate-clean-out expert, to help us manage it. In several hourslong sessions, she told us which items still had resale value versus sentimental significance. The process was humbling and sometimes brutal. We learned that many of the things our mother invested in no longer held much value — at least in today’s marketplace.
“No one wants your grandmother’s china,” Ruskin told me. “And no one wants the stemware.”

Nick Fox, founder of the Millennial Inheritance, an online support group for people who have inherited weird or massive collections from their families, blames some of this on the intensity of “collector culture” and “manufactured scarcity.”

He tells stories about people who have bought in to the hype of subscription and membership-model schemes like the Bradford Exchange, Beanie Babies, Tupperware, or Precious Moments that promised “rare,” “one-of-kind,” or “limited-edition” products that would increase in value over time. (I remember when my mother became the neighborhood Cabbage Patch Kids dealer; she scored 30 or so dolls at a good price and resold them.)

“After nearly 40 years of being invited into people’s homes, here’s the biggest thing I’ve learned: People aren’t struggling with the stuff; they’re struggling with the meaning attached to it,” Scudamore told me.

We cling to objects because we feel they hold memories of the person who possessed them. Letting go can feel disrespectful to that person’s wishes, and a fear of forgetting the person we lost makes us linger a little longer.

Anthropologist Chip Colwell argues that living with things is essentially what makes us human. In his book So Much Stuff: How Humans Discovered Tools, Invented Meaning, and Made More of Everything, Colwell traces the epic history of our relationship with things, positing that humans actually can’t live, or relate to one another, without stuff.
He points to the power of specific objects, such as heirlooms, to instill continuity, cohesion, and connection across generations.
“Heirlooms are a form of memory,” Colwell writes.

Objects may even evoke a “contagious magic,” the cross-cultural perception that things still hold an essence of, and carry on a relationship with, the person who touched them. This idea illuminates why clearing out an estate can take such a heavy toll. It may feel as if we’re letting go of someone all over again when we dismantle their life and disperse their things.

Colwell told me the process of sorting through others’ belongings “can be an exercise for people to reimagine their relationship to their own things.” And these fierce emotions, said Ruskin, are what lead to families fighting over items of little monetary value but immense sentimental significance: a favorite mug, a plastic comb, a pair of dice.

For my sisters and me, selling some of our mother’s treasures has been the ultimate exercise in letting go. What I’ve realized is that while I may have to part with many of her things, I can help them find new homes with people who will cherish them.

Three years ago, my younger sister and I started a small online vintage business, trying to sell some of our shared inheritance: silver repoussé pocket mirrors, gilded frames with French countryside scenes, even a stylish mid-century ice bucket. We have picked up our mother’s penchant for collecting, scouring thrift stores and estate sales for unique treasures for the shop.

Recently, I shipped a thrifted analog Lux Robertshaw timer to a woman who explained that this exact object unlocked a childhood memory for her of sitting in the kitchen with her own mother. There was something deeply satisfying about matching an abandoned object with someone who found meaning in it again.
I like to imagine that some of our mother’s stuff is finding a new life among strangers. Sometimes, letting go is a matter of holding on in new ways.

items.title: Exclusive: Jackie Tohn Gets Candid About Esther & Sasha In 'Nobody Wants This'
items.description: Nobody Wants This’ Jackie Tohn Wants Sasha & Esther To Be Endgame
items.author: Gabrielle Bondi
paragraphs: Nobody Wants This’ Jackie Tohn Wants Sasha & Esther To Be Endgame
The star got candid about her character's journey at T-Mobile's T-Mix House last week.

Everybody wants more Nobody Wants This, especially after Season 3’s messy fallout. The latest installment, which premiered in October, delivered romantic grand gestures and juicy character drama, leaving viewers clamoring to see what happens next. Just one day before Netflix renewed the hit comedy for a fourth season, star Jackie Tohn appeared at T-Mobile’s T-Mix House in Los Angeles to celebrate the launch of the carrier’s new customizable plans — and caught up with Bustle to chat about her character Esther’s transformative and deeply relatable journey so far.

“In Season 1, Esther really had a stick up her ass. She was trying to control everything. In Season 2, she's, like, threatening to have a good time. She's like, ‘I'm fun,’ while she screams in your face,” Tohn says of Esther trying to juggle her marriage, parenthood, and having a life outside of that. “But then [in] Season 3, we see her dating. We see her out there, making the hard decisions. Choosing yourself in a relationship when so many people just stay in the thing, that's respectable.”

Nobody Wants This Season 3 sees what life is like for Esther after she initiates a separation from her husband, Sasha (played by Timothy Simons). While he struggles with dating — including a passionate but misguided hookup with Morgan (Justine Lupe) — she finds herself flourishing, even dating divorced dad Julian (Steven Weber).

While fans are divided on whether Esther and Sasha should make it work, Tohn loves that the show gives their characters room to really explore what’s right for them. “He's having this awakening. He went up to his father, he got that promotion, and he is running the company now, and he is sort of growing a pair,” she says. “And that might be hot to Esther.”

Morgan also complicates their relationship, and as Sasha sorts out his feelings for his friend after their tryst, he hooks up with Esther. Even Tohn says she’s “on the fence” about which couple is endgame. “I see so many comments on Instagram saying, ‘Oh my God, Sasha and Esther forever,’ and I see so many of those for Sasha and Morgan,” she says. “But for some reason, I want [Esther and Sasha] to be together.”

Tohn acknowledges that Esther played a bigger role in their breakup, but the series understands that relationships are far from black and white, which viewers will get to see more of in Season 4. “I know Esther is hurt, but Sasha did nothing wrong. You can't even fault him. [The show’s writers] don't want people to go home at the end of the day hating Sasha, and they don't hate Esther either,” she says. “It's like, f*ck, these are the real things. The show is so good at capturing the nuance of relationships.”

items.title: Exclusive: Aspyn Ovard Opens Up About Being In A Throuple On ‘Mormon Wives: OC’
items.description: Aspyn Ovard Doesn’t Need This
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Aspyn Ovard Doesn’t Need This
She was a social media star long before The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County came calling. With her sensitive home life in a new spotlight, can she deliver the drama and set her own terms?

When you’re famous enough to have your own dedicated snark Reddits, you get used to people asking questions — about your dating life, about the makeup you’re wearing, about how you’re raising your children. What Aspyn Ovard is less used to is having to answer back. The 30-year-old content creator has spent the past week running around Southern California for press events and interviews to promote The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, her first foray into reality TV and Hulu’s first spinoff of the Emmy-nominated phenomenon that made #MomTok a household name.

“I was very anxious,” Ovard admits over Zoom from the back of an Uber, palm trees whizzing by as she heads home to Orange County from Los Angeles, where she just recorded a podcast with her castmate and fellow influencer Avery Woods. “But I was lucky to be with the other girls for most of the stuff, so it’s nice that I didn’t have to be alone navigating it all for the first time.”

To most reality TV aficionados, Ovard is a newbie, but to the chronically online, she already has more lore than an average A-list celebrity. By 2014, before she even graduated high school, Ovard already had a million YouTube subscribers who tuned in to her lifestyle and beauty vlogs, watching her grow from a wide-eyed high schooler to a young wife and mom. She’s since expanded her platform to TikTok and Instagram, but she still doesn’t want to be called an influencer: “I usually say I’m a YouTuber if people ask, actually.”

A reality show is only as good as its cast, and Ovard resembles a producer’s dream, someone who’s already used to documenting themselves on camera and whose nontraditional romantic life — she is in a loving throuple — brings a built-in horde of curious viewers. Ovard admits she didn’t need reality TV to maintain her career, but she knew the power Mormon Wives holds as both a fan of the flagship series and a friend of some of the Utah stars. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity even though I have had so much success on my own,” she says. “It would’ve felt crazy to say no.” But taking the leap also means she’d have to divulge details about her life she adamantly kept private until now.

Ovard was born in St. George, Utah, one of the epicenters of the Mormon Church. Her family is no longer religious, but in the early 2000s, she and her four siblings were steeped in Mormon culture. “I grew up going to church when I was little, and I did end up getting baptized when I was 9. The missionaries, they got me,” she says with a smirk.

Ovard dutifully hit all the traditional hallmarks of a young small-town Mormon woman: “I got married at 19” — to her high school sweetheart (and now ex) Parker Ferris — “pregnant at 22, and wanted to have four kids by my 30s.” But the online fame she found as a content creator was already starting to break her out of her bubble. “I didn’t go on a plane until a couple of days before my 16th birthday,” she recalls. “When we started getting opportunities to travel out of the country, you realize you think in such a small way when you come from a small town.”

Ovard’s social media made her the breadwinner as she and Ferris, 31, welcomed two daughters, 7-year-old Cove and 4-year-old Lola. The couple divorced in 2024 while she was pregnant with their third child, 2-year-old Elle, and relocating to Orange County for a fresh start. Ovard said in a video that she found out a “10-year secret” Ferris had been keeping, which set the subreddits ablaze. Looking back, she didn’t realize how ominous it sounded. “I’ve said in every interview that I think the 10-year secret will be pretty underwhelming to people,” she jokes.

On Mormon Wives O.C., she finally filled in the blanks, revealing that Ferris hid his alcohol use from her while they were married — a sensitive point for Ovard, whose father died due to complications associated with alcoholism. “We’re just not each other’s people. We love differently, so we’re definitely better off as friends,” she says. “But finding that out two months after my dad had died was definitely a lot. It’s not necessarily what he did, but knowing something was hidden from you was a hard pill to swallow.”

While the divorce provided enough fodder for followers, the exes were navigating unimaginable tragedy at home. Ovard confirms on the show that one of their young daughters received a terminal cancer diagnosis three years ago, and the family doesn’t know how long she has to live. (Suspecting fans had already noted that Ovard’s collaboration with Tarte Cosmetics last year donated all net proceeds to pediatric cancer research organizations.)
“We’ve been through a lot the last couple of years, and we haven’t had a lot of things to really look forward to.”

Ovard is careful not to reveal any specifics on-screen, including which child is navigating the disease, aside from saying she received a “stable” prognosis during a scan. However, she is candid about how her daughter’s health factored into her decision to do the show: Reality TV stardom is another source of income that lets her and Ferris, who also appears on camera, maximize family time. “We’ve been through a lot the last couple of years, and we haven’t had a lot of things to really look forward to,” she tells me. “Parker being able to look at this as a career opportunity is a helpful thing for him, so we came to an agreement that we would both do the show and on the things we would share.” Regardless, Ovard won’t let the show invade her children’s privacy, blurring their faces if they appear on-screen, and her reps asked outlets to refrain from questions about how her daughter is doing.

“I was hoping my boundaries would be followed with certain things that I did not want to talk about, and it was, thankfully,” she says, then quips: “Most people just wanted to ask me about being in a throuple.”

In March of this year — before the spinoff was announced — Ovard hard-launched her relationship with a married couple, Briana “Bri” and Billy Davis. Her newfound throuple status threw everyone in her life for a loop — including herself. “There was never a moment of coming out for me,” she says. “I just kept saying, ‘Oh, you’ll never see me with a man again’ to my friends or family as I was going through the divorce process. Obviously, I was wrong. There are good ones out there.”

Ovard had been interested in dating women after her marriage ended, and she connected with Bri through Instagram in late 2024. (She prefers not to put a label on her sexuality: “Sexuality is so fluid, and I love not feeling the pressure to label mine.”) In their first conversation, Bri shared that she’s ethically nonmonogamous. “I was not in a place of looking for anything serious at all, so it didn’t really make a difference to me that she was married,” Ovard says. Despite being long-distance, things got serious quickly, with Ovard regularly flying to Bri’s home in New Jersey. “After I was with her, I was like, ‘Oh, wow. I can’t imagine ever wanting anything to do with a man,’” she recalls. “We connect on so many things. Loving a woman and being loved by a woman is so special and such a beautiful, different type of love that I’m so grateful I get to experience.”

But after a month of dating, Ovard decided she wanted to meet Billy. “I was like, ‘If he’s good enough for her, he is good enough for me,’” she says, laughing. “They were always so respectful. If I changed my mind and didn’t want to hang out with both of them, that was totally OK.”

Last fall, Bri and Billy moved across the country to Orange County to live with Ovard and her children, with whom she shares custody with Ferris. (Her ex wasn’t a huge fan of this idea at first — as seen on Mormon Wives O.C. — though she says he’s slowly starting to come around.)
“People expect it to be a lot more salacious than it is.”

Any concerns Ovard had about living as a throuple vanished upon move-in. “I didn’t have a lot of conflict resolution skills, so getting a front-row seat to two people who do have those skills has accelerated my growth in that way,” she says. “When we get asked, ‘Do you ever feel attacked by the third?’ We’re like, ‘You shouldn’t ever feel attacked by your partner.’ But we’ve all learned if it is two against one, you really have to take a look at yourself, and odds are you probably are the one in the wrong.”

She is, however, still figuring out what being a prominent face of nonmonogamy requires of her. She’s happy to dispel stereotypes by inviting cameras into her home and showcasing their love, though open discussions of their sex lives are a touchy subject. “I love to talk about that with friends because it’s a fun topic, but I’m only going to share so much,” she warns. “We get a lot of questions like, ‘Oh, would you ever add another one?’ Imagine how weird [it’d be] if I asked someone that as a hetero person in a straight relationship. People expect it to be a lot more salacious than it is, but they meet us and are like, ‘Oh, wait, they’re pretty normal.’”

Tell that to her costars. Since the first day of production, Ovard’s relationship has been a hot topic, especially among the castmates she hadn’t even met yet. Jen Affleck, a star of the flagship Mormon Wives series, moved to Orange County and leads the spinoff, which follows two polar-opposite friend groups: Ovard was already close with Woods, Bobbi Althoff, and Salomé Andrea — women with more progressive values and years of influencing experience — but wasn’t as familiar with Affleck’s friends who are still devout members of the Mormon Church: Ashleigh Pease, Madison Bontempo, Jordan McClanahan, and McCall DaPron (the older sister of OG star Mayci Neeley), who are oft referred to as “Molly Mormons.”

Within the expanded friend group, Ovard emerges as fiery and outspoken, unafraid to put herself on the front lines when culture clashes come to the forefront. During a cast trip to Palm Springs, Ovard confronted DaPron and McClanahan about their resistance to explicitly say they supported “gay rights” in spite of the Mormon Church’s practices. “We talked about politics a lot in that conversation, and that was cut out from the show. That’s Disney for you, I guess,” she says with a shrug. “I wasn’t looking for them to just say they support my relationship. I want the people I surround myself with to be aligned with supporting human rights. It’s a hill I will die on. It was hard at that moment because I don’t feel like they were understanding exactly what I was asking, but I know they were trying and have kept trying.”

Ovard isn’t that worried about all the new eyeballs she’ll get from Mormon Wives O.C. You don’t become a teen YouTube star without learning to deal with a fiery comments section. “I feel like I’ve always had thick skin doing this job,” she says. “There’s a screenshot from years ago: Someone commented on my video saying my hair was really curly, and the comment was like, ‘You don’t look good with curly hair.’ And I replied, ‘Yeah, I do.’” She’s more concerned about what her less experienced castmates are in store for: “It’s a bigger adjustment for them to go from sharing nothing to sharing everything on your socials and reality TV,” she says.

Still, when the show premieres, Ovard will be on vacation in Mexico with Bri, Billy, and her children, with plans to turn off her phone and lie on the beach. Oh, and Ferris is joining them, too. “We’re in a pretty good spot right now,” she tells me happily, as her car gets closer to home. “It’s definitely a unique relationship, but all three of us are willing to do anything we can to make him feel more comfortable and good with the situation that we’re in.”

The Mormon Wives franchise has already proved itself to be an effective star-launching vehicle: Just ask Whitney Leavitt, who leveraged her participation into starring roles on Broadway. But with everything her family’s going through, Ovard isn’t interested in a career change or world domination: “I’ve done this for 16 years now, and I’m transparently looking to keep this going for as long as I can,” she says. “I just want to spend time with my kids and be able to work the least amount possible.”

But like a great reality star, she knows how to keep you watching: “I feel like I’m slowly gathering the strength to be the person that I want to be again, and to show up for friends and myself,” she says, as we talk about what viewers might see on a potential second season. “Even getting through these press days, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, I did it.’ I can do hard things.”

items.title: Softball, Rugby, & 4 Other Underrated Sports To Watch In 2027
items.description: 6 Underrated Sports You’ll Want To Tune In To Next Year
items.author: Nali Simukulwa
paragraphs: 6 Underrated Sports You’ll Want To Tune In To Next Year
From netball to volleyball and beyond.
As the year draws to a close, nights get cozier and life finally begins to slow down. But for sports fans like me, a new restlessness sets in.

When you typically devote your days to checking score lines, the offseason can feel endless. The WNBA has already said its goodbyes for another season as the Golden State Valkyries clinched the title earlier this month. Soccer is winding down too as the NWSL championship kicks off this Saturday.

But there’s a light at the end of the tunnel: 2027 promises to be one of the biggest and most enthralling years that pro women’s sports has ever seen. Brazil will host FIFA’s Women’s World Cup in June and July, and revenue is targeted to reach $1 billion. Previously niche sports are about to get their moment in the sun too.
Out of the loop? Fear not. Whether you’re a bandwagon fan or a certified athletics buff, here’s a rundown on all of the 2027 dates you need to add to your calendar.

For the first time in history, flag football will feature at the Olympics in 2028. Ahead of its debut, the NFL and TMRW sports joined forces to unveil Premier Flag, a flag football league for both women and men, earlier this month. Backed by the likes of Tom Brady and Alex Morgan, the new league will launch in summer 2027, finally creating a destination for the sport’s elite athletes.
Exact details about the launch date and the length of the season remain under wraps, but with the Premier Flag showcase planned during Super Bowl LXI week, a first look is just around the corner.

Missing the WNBA? You’re in luck. The Netball Super League returns in February to scratch that court-sport itch. Featuring teams across England and Wales, netball brings all of basketball’s pace and high-scoring drama but is played with strictly zoned positions and without dribbling, contact, or a backboard. Since relaunching and professionalizing in 2025, the NSL has become Europe’s only elite netball league and has racked up record-breaking attendances and tripled viewership after securing broadcast deals with Sky and the BBC.

All eight teams will compete for the season’s first trophy in the Netball Super Cup on Feb. 27 before the league starts in full on March 3. As the league looks to attract new eyes, four major arena doubleheaders are scheduled throughout the year. With players vying for a roster spot at the 2027 Netball World Cup (beginning Aug. 25), this season will be one for the books.

Ilona Maher fans, prepare to be fed. Rugby returns with the HSBC SVNS on Nov. 28. Serving as a primary qualification pathway for the 2028 Olympics, the athletes will face off around the globe before the three-leg championship begins in Hong Kong (April 9-11), moves to Spain (May 21-23), and wraps up in France (May 28-30).

World Champions Australia will look to defend their title against local rivals New Zealand, but third-place challengers USA are boosted by extra funding and waiting to steal the throne. Following their success at the Paris games, entrepreneur Michele Kang, who owns three women’s soccer teams, pledged to donate $4 million to the sevens team, hoping to turn USA’s bronze to gold.
As hosts, USA’s spot at the L.A. games is secure, so all eyes turn to Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Fiji, Spain, and France, who will compete for the remaining four spots.

Hey, batter batter! As softball prepares for its first Olympic appearance since Tokyo 2020, the sport is stepping back into the spotlight. The Athletes Unlimited Softball League (AUSL) will return for its third season in 2027. With exact dates set to be announced early next year, ESPN’s new three-year broadcast deal promises to bring the league to a bigger audience than ever before. Utah Talons pitching star Montana Fouts will look to lead her side to a three-peat after securing back-to-back titles.
In the spring, eyes will turn to Australia for the Softball World Cup finals (April 5-11). The winner will seal their spot in the 2028 Olympics.
U.S. pro women’s volleyball is entering its biggest winter yet as both domestic leagues — League One Volleyball (LOVB Pro) and Major League Volleyball (MLV) — expand.

LOVB’s third season will run from Dec. 16 to April 1, growing from six to 10 teams and expanding from 60 to 110 regular-season matches. This season will welcome 66 new signings to rosters already stacked with Olympic champions like Jordan Thompson and NCAA icons like Madisen Skinner. April will see the return of the two-round, two-match postseason series, heating up the end of the season as Austin, the back-to-back champion, vies to defend their crown.

Major League Volleyball kicks off its fourth season on Jan. 7, expanding from eight to 12 teams with new franchises in Los Angeles, D.C., Minnesota, and Northern California. With reigning champions Dallas Pulse looking to defend their title, a new salary-cap exception, and weekend-heavy schedules, MLV is set for its most competitive and accessible season yet.

The PWHL drops the puck on Dec. 5, expanding from eight to 12 teams. Newly unveiled franchises in Detroit, Las Vegas, San Jose, and Hamilton will split the league into East and West, alongside a March pause for its first-ever All-Star game in Toronto. Defending champions Montréal Victoire will look to Canadian hockey GOAT, finals MVP, and captain Marie-Philip Poulin as they aim to retain their throne as two-time winners Minnesota Frost look to reclaim their top spot.
Backed by updated collective bargaining agreements boosting player wages, the third season is set to be its biggest and most equitable yet.

items.title: Selena Gomez & More It Girls Are Giving Your Go-To Summer Pants A Cozy Fall Rebrand
items.description: Just because sweater weather is in full swing doesn’t mean your closet needs a complete overhaul (unless you’re in the mood for one). You can still wear your favorite pieces from earlier this year all season long — yes, even the stuff you already shoved into t
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Just because sweater weather is in full swing doesn’t mean your closet needs a complete overhaul (unless you’re in the mood for one). You can still wear your favorite pieces from earlier this year all season long — yes, even the stuff you already shoved into the back of your closet. And one item worth digging out? Capri pants.

The once-controversial silhouette, popularized by Carrie Bradshaw, has completely won over fashion girlies like Hailey Bieber, Kendall Jenner, and Jennifer Lopez. All spring and summer, they were wearing capris with slinky tops or windbreakers.

Now that the cropped bottoms are full-blown wardrobe staples, the style set’s not letting them hibernate till May. Instead, they’re giving them a second life in their fall rotations, trading their light jackets for heavy-duty outerwear and adding cozy accessories. Apparently, bare calves aren’t just a summer thing.

In late October, Zoë Kravitz was spotted in New York filming Die Alive. Sure, the film is a dramedy, but if her recent ‘fits are any indication, it’ll turn out to be more of a fashion film. One look was especially fall mood board-worthy.

She served downtown cool in moody, monochromatic tones, pairing a collared cardigan with fitted capri pants in a matching dark navy-gray hue. For that autumnal touch, she reached for a long, dark brown suede coat that fell about the same length as her pants — keeping her calves bare, naturally.
To spruce up the dark-on-dark palette, she added a bold print. Peep her pointed-toe vintage Prada pumps covered in leopard spots.

Selena Gomez also made a case for capris in September, while out in NYC for husband Benny Blanco’s book launch. She chose a black ASTR The Label pair with a subtle ruffle hem for a touch of romance and styled them with a classic cropped Saint Laurent leather jacket — one of this year’s trending coat styles. Instead of leaning sporty, she dressed up the cropped silhouette with all-black accessories: pointed-toe slingbacks, a sleek shoulder bag, and skinny sunglasses.

Capris were also well represented in sporting venues thanks to Angel Reese, who practically branded them as her tunnel walks’ MVP. So far, she’s paired them with gold hardware-clad Schiaparelli leather in late October, and used a simple black pair as the perfect canvas for a pop of color.

Before one of her August games, Reese gave her otherwise nondescript capris a bold makeover — in Chanel, no less. She stepped into the arena in a cherry red metallic windbreaker with a cinched waist and peplum detail, a skinny belt adorned with mini bags, and peep-toe T-strap heels. For extra fall notes, she added cozy accessories, including fingerless gloves and a fuzzy red-black-and-white striped Chanel flap bag.
Get On The Short Pant Game

Consider this your sign to dig your capris out of storage before temps turn freezing. The easiest way to give them a fresher, more season-appropriate update is by styling the cropped silhouette with a thick jacket or fleece top. You can even layer a floor-length coat overtop with your calves peeking out underneath. Or you can go the Kravitz route and channel monochromatic layers in chilly palettes.

Want to tap into fall’s It girl-approved dark romance aesthetic instead? Take a cue from Gomez and swap your fave basic black pairs for whimsigoth ones — think a black pair with red flowers or a ruffled hem.
