items.title: What does motherhood look like without my best friend? | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: On page five of an eight-page letter dated 3 September 2019, my friend – whom I will call Naaz – wrote to me:
items.author: Ashwaq Masoodi
paragraphs: On page five of an eight-page letter dated 3 September 2019, my friend – whom I will call Naaz – wrote to me:

I always pray that nothing in this world may ever blur your vision of your own self. Not people, not your circumstances. One must not be delusional, but one should also never lose the grip of one’s essence. Never forget who you are, what all you have achieved, how hard you worked to be where you are today.

Naaz had never written to me before – not a note, not a postcard. We were on each other’s speed dial for as long as I could remember. But that August, the Indian state had revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status and, anticipating blowback, had throttled internet broadband, cable TV, landlines and mobile networks. Even postal services were disrupted; Naaz planned to hand-deliver her letter. Another letter tells me that on 11 August she knocked on my door for a long time. But I had already left for New Delhi, and would soon be halfway across the world.

In Kashmir, we are used to uncertainty but, in those days, it was dialled all the way up. When I left, I did not know when I would be able to speak with my parents again. We seemed to have collectively tumbled back in time to the 1990s, when separatist conflict was at its peak and, with it, the Indian state’s iron-fist policy to counter it. I was leaving for a year-long journalism fellowship at Harvard, and wracked with guilt and self-doubt: guilt over leaving when so many others could not, self-doubt over whether I would live up to the opportunity. Perhaps Naaz sensed my ambivalence, which is why she wrote those lines. She knew I might need the reminder.

Naaz first knew me as a bushy-browed teenager, travelling 110 km each day to study journalism in Baramulla, a small town in Kashmir. We met on a bus, in the spring of 2005. She was in a three-seater near the middle, in a white crewneck sweater with a Fair Isle pattern around the neckline. I took the seat beside her. I remember what she wore because my mother knit sweaters for me in that pattern, too. Within minutes, we were exchanging names, then places, then families. My mother was from the same area as her. My naanu had taught Naaz’s father. Her father had taught mine. Our meeting felt both serendipitous and predetermined.

She was seven years older than me, a science teacher, a lover of poetry. In a society steeped in existential despair, she took her vocation seriously. ‘We are the builders of Kashmir,’ she’d say. Growing up, I’d seldom encountered older people who weren’t in survival mode, always braced for the next loss or threat, who were able to support those dreaming of lives larger than the ones they’d inherited. Perhaps that’s why Naaz – thoughtful, curious, never infantilising – was so easy to like.
My friendship with Naaz quickly deepened into something closer to sisterhood

I dreamed of being a reporter. A few years after meeting Naaz, I would join a workshop led by one of Kashmir’s finest journalists. Every Sunday, at 9 am, a group of us – the youngest in their teens, the oldest in their 40s – gathered in his tiny apartment in Srinagar, thick with the smell of old books and cigarettes. We read Ryszard Kapuściński’s dispatches and watched The Battle of Algiers.
‘If we don’t tell our story, someone else will,’ he would often remind us.

My friendship with Naaz quickly deepened into something closer to sisterhood. Even when I moved away, for further studies or for work, we spoke almost daily. We would fall asleep on the phone, only to wake when the phones slipped and knocked against our faces. When I visited, we would take boat rides on Dal Lake, stroll aimlessly through the Mughal Gardens, go on long drives around Srinagar, never running out of conversation. Two young men might be construed as a security threat and attract state surveillance; a young man and woman might be seen as romantically involved and draw social scrutiny. Female friendship, on the other hand, could occupy public space more freely, without constantly defending its right to exist.

Naaz and I often joked that our ‘halal:haram’ ratio was almost identical, a way of saying we drew a similar line between the permissible and the forbidden, with many of the same compromises and contradictions. And yet we were utterly different in other ways. She would not undo what she had already done. If she left the house with her hair tied, she would keep it tied, even if it no longer made sense to do so. Whereas I agonised over everything. Naaz was surprised I could put myself in all sorts of situations as a journalist – interviewing human traffickers, reporting from conflict zones – and yet be so internally unanchored. I was driven but also anxious: I wanted professional success but, when it came, I knew only how to move past it, towards the next milestone. Naaz would shake me lightly, yanking me back to the present.
‘Can you be proud of yourself? Can you accept that you are good?’

When I returned to Kashmir after my fellowship ended, we met at her wedding. The happiest bride I have ever seen, when she saw me, she held my hands and pulled me into a tight embrace. Within months, I too was married. Despite our age difference, it felt as if something larger was aligning our lives. We became pregnant within months of each other, our conversations turning to baby names, nausea, exhaustion.
‘What do you want,’ I asked her once, ‘a girl or a boy?’
‘It doesn’t matter,’ she said. ‘I just hope the baby survives. I hope I survive.’

I remember feeling a flicker of irritation when she said that. Doom-mongering was what I did. And why would anything go wrong? Yes, she was in her late 30s, but she was healthier than most 20-somethings. Meanwhile, I fretted over how motherhood would alter the life I’d carefully built for myself, the five-year plans that I worried would now be upended. It didn’t help that my partner and I would be moving to Germany soon.
Each time I visited Kashmir, my heart clenched – that unmistakable giggle was gone

Naaz gave birth in September. Days later, she suffered an intracerebral haemorrhage – a brain bleed caused by a ruptured blood vessel, the risk of which is three times higher among women during pregnancy and in the weeks following delivery. She was the one who messaged to tell me. I should keep a tab on my vitals, she added, and not stress out over small things while pregnant. Soon after, she slipped into a coma.

A month passed before Naaz regained consciousness. Even though there were times when she seemed to be improving, the things that distinguished her began slipping away. Among the first women in her village to drive, she could no longer hold the movement of a car. A poet, she could no longer read or write. Each time I visited Kashmir, my heart clenched – that unmistakable giggle was gone, as was the way she tucked loose strands of her hair, behind her right ear specifically. Once, when I went to see her, I noticed how her dupatta, which she typically flung around her neck, was spread out over her chest. She would never wear it that way, I kept thinking to myself. As terrifying as it was to witness her suffering, so was the dissipation of things that make a person: language, memory, skill.

For more than two years, Naaz fought bravely. She passed away in March 2024 – typically, a month of birthdays in my family. That year, all through March and April, my toddler played Zum Geburtstag viel Glück in an endless loop on her music box – Happy Birthday in German, the soundtrack to my grief.

It was early morning in Berlin when I received the news. When I read the message – N is no more – I collapsed onto the prayer rug, crying into my breath so I wouldn’t wake my two-year-old. Later, when my daughter stirred, expecting me beside her as always, I moved toward her, my body performing the choreography of care as if nothing had happened. As if the mountain hadn’t fallen over me.

In Kashmir, we are used to untimely death. But how to grieve the loss of your best friend, so young, so vividly alive? And how to grieve with a two-year-old at close hand, amid meals NOW, baths NOW, nappy change NOW, tantrums NOW?
Grief, in a sense, has become intertwined with motherhood

I had known motherhood would unsettle my sense of self – what I never imagined was that it would also take away the person who held my story alongside me. In narrative psychology, identity is theorised as what Dan P McAdams calls an ‘evolving story of the self’ – an integration of one’s reconstructed past, perceived present and imagined future. This story has multiple authors. We come to know who we are through conversation, through shared recollection, through being witnessed: by our parents, our siblings, our partners, our best friends. Each holds a fragment of us, reflecting the person we are and the person we once were. Those shared memories become the story we tell ourselves about our own life. That story is never fixed. It changes as we change, and as the people who hold pieces of it enter and leave our lives. With Naaz’s death, parts of my past lost their primary witness just as motherhood began shaking the very roots of who I was.

Kashmir – my home, my muse – has changed, too. Since 2019, dissent of any sort is promptly quashed. The graffiti proclaiming azadi, freedom, has disappeared from the walls as has any public expression of separatist sentiment. Local journalists are asked to sign pledges vowing not to ‘disturb the peace’. Most of our writing group has drifted into PR or fiction; one of the youngest members was recently released after two years in prison. Like people, places also need someone to hold on to their stories. In Kashmir, bearing witness now comes at a cost.

Two years ago, I became pregnant again. As I gave birth the second time, memories from the days after Naaz’s death started playing on a loop. Grief, in a sense, has become intertwined with motherhood. It is there when I lift my son, when I chase him down the hallway. I hear his laughter and think of Naaz’s. She should have lived to experience this: the chaos, the beauty, the bone-deep exhaustion that is now my everyday.

Occasionally, in a note jotted in the margin of a book, on a walk by myself in the park, in the sheaf of letters that eventually made their way into my hands, I catch a glimpse of my earlier self: the journalist, Naaz’s best girl. I have taken to telling my daughter stories from that time, as if piecing together a self she has never known. For now, the only one she remembers is about the time a jellyfish stung me on a beach in Miami. ‘Once more… only one,’ she says, asking me again and again to act out the moment the jellyfish stung me. I oblige every time.

items.title: AnOther Loves: A Savage Mule
items.description: Animal print has endured to the point of cliché and yet it almost never gets old
items.author: Rose Dodd
paragraphs: Animal print has endured to the point of cliché and yet it almost never gets old

Animal print is iconoclastic. A semiotic marker for a maverick with a feral nature. Think of seductress Mrs Robinson in The Graduate in leopard, cheetah and zebra. Or Chris Tucker’s renegade radio-show host Ruby Rhod – in a sci-fi sculpted leopard-print catsuit – in The Fifth Element. And, of course, Elizabeth Taylor’s leopard pelt-lined opera coat in 20th-century blockbuster Cleopatra – one of the Egyptian queen’s 65 costume changes. Over the decades, Hollywood pin-ups have positioned that textile as an emblem of the raw and free, of untamable femininity. Animal print has endured to the point of cliché and yet it almost never gets old. Ferocious and timeless, these leopard-print calf-hair stilettos from Giuseppe Zanotti are named Savage Mules: with a gold-tone toe cap, rhinestones and a 105 mm heel, savage they are. A pair of shoes fit for prowling the urban jungle, they appeal to the animal within.
The Giuseppe Zanotti Intriigo Savage Mule 105 is available to shop here

items.title: Eikoh Hosoe’s Nude Photographs of Literary Rebel Yukio Mishima
items.description: On show at the Leslie-Lohman Museum: arresting photographs of the author and political dissident in his Tokyo home
items.author: Osman Can Yerebakan
paragraphs: On show at the Leslie-Lohman Museum: arresting photographs of the author and political dissident in his Tokyo home

Japanese novelist Yukio Mishima was a five-time Nobel Prize for Literature nominee whose strict dedication to traditional values often combated with his lush language and exploration of repressed sexuality. A controversial literary figure, Mishima first came across photographer Eikoh Hosoe through his images of the legendary butoh dancer Tatsumi Hijikata – the latter had interpreted the writer’s own homoerotic novel Kinjiki in 1959 in what is now considered the first genuine butoh dance. Mishima – a champion of traditionalist cultural values whose novels and stories often dealt with closeted protagonists’ struggles to fit into post-war Japanese society – saw in Hosoe a young avant-garde artist coming of age in the shadow of the Japan-US war and its aftermath, and immediately felt drawn to become the subject of his photography.

Mishima, who had established himself as a Renaissance man of literature, political activism, martial arts, modelling and acting – he published his first novel, Confessions of a Mask (1949) aged 24 – invited Hosoe to photograph him at his home in Tokyo in 1961. The author was 36 at the time, and had already starred in multiple films and gained ranks in martial arts. He posed almost entirely nude with props including mirrors, candles, a mallet, and a garden hose. His sculptural physique, which encapsulated both a militant masculinity and desire to be seen, is central to Hosoe’s darkly lit images.

The result was the photographic series, Barakei (Ordeal by Roses). The new exhibition, Props from Barakei, at the Leslie-Lohman Museum, brings together around 20 of Hosoe’s black and white photographs of Mishima from the series alongside a mixed-media installation of ropes, swords and a camera by Berlin and Singapore-based contemporary artist and poet Jason Wee.

Yasufumi Nakamori, the show’s curator, previously senior curator at Tate Modern, points at the “tension” between Mishima and Hosoe, two 20th-century Japanese figures who represent seemingly opposing social values. The novelist was a symbol of an old-world sentiment that grappled with the reality that Japan had entered US protection under a mutual post-war treaty; Hosoe was among a group of artists to emerge following the war who experimented with western styles in art. Against Mishima’s stern refusal of Japan’s capitalist growth under western influence, Hosoe represented a new wave of youth that was curious about self-expression. “[Mishima] saw an antithesis of his nationalist values in this emerging photographer,” says Nakamori.

Decorative accents in Mishima’s home – candles, large replicas of Old Master paintings, Rococo furniture – complicate his anti-western persona. His overt masculinity clashes with his vulnerable nudity and inviting postures, while the photographer’s defiant, even playful, angles disarm a man notorious for his publicly uncompromising ideals. “Hosoe masterfully construed the myth around Mishima, both visually and ideologically,” says Nakamori. His toned arms and commanding torso often blend with the bodily depictions in large replicas of Renaissance paintings which – surprisingly – populated the traditionalist author’s house.

Mishima’s body is tied and suspended by tight ropes, imbuing these photographs with a sexual undertone: “I am not sure if the series is an example of queer art per se but rather a nuanced exploration of a space where sexuality, nationalism and the body come together,” says the curator. He does, however, consider Wee’s work – which incorporates a poem he wrote about the series, woven in Morse into green and black ropes – a response to Hosoe’s development of a queer photographic vocabulary.

Today, Mishima’s legacy is complex: an ultra-nationalist who explored sexuality and vulnerability often through veiled autobiographical notes and a traditionally attractive man with a sculptural physicality, who married a literary virtuosity with maddening conservatism, intrigued by queer intimacy.

It was perhaps this alchemy that was so irresistible for the young Hosoe. The pictures owe their baroque effect to Mishima’s willingness to expose his physicality and even his home, as a figure already recognised at the time for his exploration of homosexuality. Undeniably, however, the work today is seen through the lens of Mishima’s notorious public suicide, which took place in 1970 after he trespassed a military base in Tokyo with four comrades, with the intention of taking over the government and restoring the empire. The failed coup had been planned to end with Mishima delivering his manifesto, followed by his self-disembowelment. One of his comrades then decapitated him as the final stage of his orchestrated public suicide. “Mishima believed Hosoe’s photography let him inhabit a form of lyricism in a barbaric and dissipated world,” says Nakamori. The pictures’ stylistic contortion of a body notorious for its muscular strength and political devotion resonates with his distorted public persona and gruesome public death. “He really wanted to be in that unknown place where his body could be deconstructed as a subject matter.”
Props from Barakei is on at the Leslie-Lohman Museum until 17 March, 2027

Things have been on hold – until now, that is, as the City of Helsinki has just launched an international competition for the redevelopment of the waterfront around Hanasaari, and its fortunes are about to change.
Discover the historic Hanasaari power plant

The original power plant building was erected in the post-war period between 1974 and 1976 to a design by architect Timo Penttilä. It is now an iconic complex, defining its context with its geometric, modernist volumes. The building's volumes are a mix of concrete and brick, creating a blend of utilitarian architecture and tactile composition against the backdrop of water, city and greenery.

It forms an important part of a wider 16-hectare site in this ambitious regeneration project, which aims to transform the area into a vibrant, mixed-use urban space. This will include not only the revitalised and reused power plant but also the nearby port and the wider neighbourhood.

'The launch of this idea and implementation competition marks the next step in shaping  the future of Hanasaari,' says City of Helsinki’s Mayor Daniel Sazonov. 'I am excited to see the bold, innovative ideas and inspiring proposals that will emerge for this unique waterfront area, an exceptional site in a prime location in Helsinki. I wish all participants the very best of success and creativity in this exciting competition!'
The competition is open to multidisciplinary consortia from Finland and abroad. The winning team is expected to be announced in spring 2029, with construction targeted to begin in 2031

Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).

items.title: Dan Flavin knows how to light up a room
items.description: Encountering Dan Flavin’s naked fluorescent tubes, in twos and threes, at angles, in grids and resting on the floor of Frank Gehry’s Guggenheim Bilbao, is like being invited into an improbable conversation between a maverick of minimalism via funny fuzzing lig
items.author: Harriet Quick
paragraphs: Encountering Dan Flavin’s naked fluorescent tubes, in twos and threes, at angles, in grids and resting on the floor of Frank Gehry’s Guggenheim Bilbao, is like being invited into an improbable conversation between a maverick of minimalism via funny fuzzing light and a maestro of sculptural architecture with all the swoops, ellipses, soaring oculi. Playing host to an artist of such restraint and indeed irony in Some Light, the American artist’s subtle modulations of light, form and colour alter the way we see space. Call it an encounter.

Self-trained and averse to explanation, Flavin did not call his works sculpture but propositions or situations. His tools were standard fluorescent tubes in two, four, six and eight-foot lengths and a limited range of colours. 'Electricity is my instrument,' he said. 'He worked within these deliberate limits: these colours, and the four standard lengths in which the fixtures were sold. He never altered their basic form,' says Lauren Hinkson, Curator for Collections at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York.

Yet don’t such limits often give way to art’s most interesting ruptures? Donald Judd had his bold red plinths, Carl Andre his bricks and Anne Truitt her picket fences. Flavin found his medium in 1961 while working as a guard at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and light became his life’s work. One imagines the young guard, directing visitors to exhibits, to toilets, to exits, becoming transfixed by the very apparatus of the room around him: flickering tubes that he might need to replace.

Hinkson humanises Flavin and traces how his vocabulary expanded within a basic medium that forever shows off its fixtures and fittings, like corsetry. She surfaces his own account in Artforum: 'The radiant tube and the shadow cast by its pan seemed ironic enough to hold alone. There was no need to compose. It implanted itself directly, dynamically, dramatically in my workroom wall – a buoyant and relentless gaseous image which, through brilliance, betrayed its physical presence into approximate invisibility.'

In Guggenheim Bilbao’s generous galleries, these unassuming assemblages gradually test the limits of the eye and the retina. The opening rooms show early white-light works that play warm against cool, further shifted by the daylight, which in Bilbao is moody. Stand before a two-tube work in white and warm white and as the eye adjusts, they merge like moonlight and spill onto the floor.

Next comes Corners, Barriers and Corridors, where Flavin addressed the room itself. “I knew the actual space of a room could be disrupted and played with by careful, thorough composition of the illuminating equipment,” he recalled. Colour arrives, along with grids and fence-like barriers that build volumes of colour to dissolve or heighten the space around them. Several are dedicated to artists who played the chromatic scale, Matisse and Mondrian among them. greens crossing greens (to Piet Mondrian who lacked green), 1966, is a standout: a post-and-lintel gateway that jests with the painter’s spectrum. With the cryptic titles In an artificial barrier of blue, red and blue fluorescent light Flavin dedicated this work to Judd’s son, and Judd kept a full-scale version in his Spring Street studio. Then come the white-light monuments flagging the Russian Constructivists, rising like skyscrapers or totems in a vast elliptical curved gallery.

How do you collect a work whose bulbs burn out? Flavin issued certificates on graph paper that allowed the owner to install the work and replace its tubes, and the paperwork is a graphic study in itself. Most of Some Light is drawn from the Guggenheim’s own collection, which acquired a large part of the Panza Collection. 'Beginning in 2010, with the support of the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Guggenheim undertook a decade-long study of these works called the Panza Collection Initiative,' says Hinkson. 'It focused on seven artists in the collection, Flavin among them, and looked closely at each work, its history, its certificate, its installations, trying to understand questions like: what happened with that floor piece? How could the presentations look so different? That research makes it possible to present the works on view here as Flavin intended.' Conservators now use a spectrometer to record the wavelengths each lamp gives off, she adds, so an old lamp and a new one can be compared precisely. Fittingly, the show is sponsored by Iberdrola, the global electricity and clean energy giant and a long-term patron.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The loop closes gracefully. Flavin once worked in the Guggenheim’s mailroom, shuttling documents and blueprints between the nascent museum and Frank Lloyd Wright’s office. 'He carried plans between Frank Lloyd Wright and the museum’s director, James Johnson Sweeney. So the young man who carried the architect’s plans would, years later, fill Wright’s rotunda with light,' says Hinkson. In 1971 he lit one full turn of the rotunda within a 21-artist exhibition, and in 1992 he returned to fill all of it. At 59, four years before his death, he married Tracy Harris at the museum beneath a column of rose-pink light rising through the atrium.

Throughout his career Flavin refuted religious symbolism and the spiritual messaging of light, letting his tubes speak for themselves. As he put it, bluntly, in 1967: 'My fluorescent tubes never burn out desiring a god.' Yet this was also a prolific collector of antiques and memorabilia, and a patron of the Hudson River School painters, at his homes in the Hudson Valley and on Long Island. A minimalist who filled his houses with thing called home. Some Life. Some Light.
Dan Flavin: Some Light at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao until 4 April 2027

items.title: Gustaf Westman’s brilliantly bonkers Disney homeware is now available online
items.description: Last month, Wallpaper* previewed the first three products from Gustaf Westman's 35-piece homeware collection with Disney. Over the past three weeks, alongside an immersive pop-up in Tokyo, Westman has been gradually revealing more of the glossy designs on soci
items.author: Ali Morris
paragraphs: Last month, Wallpaper* previewed the first three products from Gustaf Westman's 35-piece homeware collection with Disney. Over the past three weeks, alongside an immersive pop-up in Tokyo, Westman has been gradually revealing more of the glossy designs on social media. As of today (15 November 2026), the full collection is available to shop on his website. Ranging from large furniture to keychains, each piece is an inventive abstraction or simplification of the familiar features of the Mickey & Friends characters.
They include a mirror (€390) with a chrome tubular steel frame tracing Mickey's head and outsized ears, and a pink ceramic 'Minnie' cup (€75) to match the 'Mickey' one revealed last month.

Goofy's hat has been transformed into a side table while his legs and feet have been fashioned into a playful coffee table. There is a Mickey plate (€80) and jewellery box (€1,190), a cup based on Donald's hat (€85), a ceramic vase in the shape of Mickey's trousers (€225) and a glass one based on Goofy's hat (€440).

While many of the rounded, high-gloss ceramic pieces are available off the shelf, larger designs and those in more unusual materials and finishes are made to order. These include a freestanding 'Donald' shelf, where Donald Duck's hat, arms, belly and feet serve as display surfaces, and a 'Mickey' bar cart with a circular frame and swooping, ear-shaped handles.

The 'Pluto' lamp strikes an almost gothic note, with a yellow satin shade and long black beaded fringing, while the 'Donald' candelabra leans towards Memphis Milano with its geometric forms in enamelled cast iron. Together, the pieces make up a slightly bonkers cartoon world, with enough variety to tempt Disney devotees and Westman collectors back for more.
We sat down with Westman to find out more about the design process, his research trip to Disneyland Paris and why he thinks playfulness is important at every age.
Wallpaper*: How did the collaboration with Disney begin?
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Gustaf Westman: I was introduced to Disney by my friend and collaborator, Harry Lambert. We first connected through another project and what started as a smaller idea developed very naturally into something much bigger. I didn’t really have to think about it. Disney felt like a dream collaboration because there was already such a natural connection between their world and mine. The joy, playfulness and colour felt very intuitive, so from the first sketches there was never a sense of having to force the two together.

GW: It was very open, which gave me a lot of freedom to explore Mickey & Friends in different ways. I started by looking at the characters almost as a collection of shapes, colours and silhouettes. An ear, a bow or a particular combination of colours can be so recognisable on its own, so I kept asking how those details could become something else.

Rather than simply putting a character onto an existing product, I wanted to deconstruct them and turn those elements into the object itself. With something like the Mickey cup, the reference is immediate, whereas some pieces take a moment to realise the character references I liked having both approaches within the collection.
W*: Can you tell us about the design process?

GW: My process isn’t very methodical. I sketch a lot, I always carry a pen and paper. The first pieces I worked on were the cup and plate. It was almost as simple as looking at forms I already use in my work and asking: how do we make this recognisable as a character?

From there I could go deeper. I started looking at pictures of the characters and breaking them down into individual elements: an ear, a shape, a colour. Because Mickey & Friends have such a clear visual language, you can take those elements quite far and they remain recognisable. That gave me a lot of creative freedom, particularly with the bigger furniture pieces.
W*: You visited Disneyland Paris before designing the collection. Did anything surprise you or spark anything that found its way into the collection?

GW: I get inspired by shapes wherever I am, so of course there is an incredible amount to look at at Disneyland Paris. In some ways there is almost too much because the whole environment is so immersive. I don’t think there was one detail in the park that I saw and then directly turned into an object. It was more about experiencing the Disney world as a whole and being reminded how confidently it uses shape, colour and imagination. It reinforced the idea that I didn’t need to complicate things. The Disney aesthetic is already so strong, and there was something exciting about taking that for what it is and bringing it into my own world.
W*: What are your personal memories of Disney, and has its visual world influenced your work outside of this collaboration?

GW: Growing up in Sweden, one of my strongest Disney memories is watching Donald Duck at Christmas in some of the original Mickey movies. It’s something a lot of Swedish families do, so Disney was always part of my childhood in that way.

But working on the collection made me look much more closely at how the characters themselves were designed. I became really interested in the simplicity of those earlier 2D characters: the shapes, the colours and how little information you actually need for someone to recognise them. Mickey & Friends can be understood in a second, which I think is incredible design. That simplicity is something I relate to in my own work too. I am always interested in how you can reduce something down and still give it a very strong identity.
W*: Joy and imagination are central to your work. Why do you think that playfulness matters in the objects we live with, and does working with Disney bring a different dimension to that?

GW: I don’t think becoming an adult means everything around you suddenly has to become serious. I like objects that are functional but can also make you smile or create some kind of feeling. That playfulness has always been important in my work.

Disney adds another layer because people already have such a strong emotional connection to these characters. They remind you of being a child, watching the films or going to the Parks, and there is something very nice about being able to escape normal reality for a moment and reconnect with that feeling. With this collection, I wanted to keep that sense of joy and playfulness, but translate it into pieces that also belong in a contemporary design space.
Having already toured Tokyo with a pop-up experience this month, the full collection launches online today. The final pop-up in Paris runs next month from 4 – 6 December 2026.

Ali Morris is a UK-based editor, writer and creative consultant specialising in design, interiors and architecture. In her 16 years as a design writer, Ali has travelled the world, crafting articles about creative projects, products, places and people for titles such as Dezeen, Wallpaper* and Kinfolk.

items.title: Buffalo Zine
items.description: Buffalo Zine No. 22 continues the direction of the previous issue, staying close to what feels real to us. We chose to focus on people we genuinely relate to, those who shape our immediate world and the way we see things.
paragraphs: Buffalo Zine No. 22 continues the direction of the previous issue, staying close to what feels real to us. We chose to focus on people we genuinely relate to, those who shape our immediate world and the way we see things.

It also became a way to acknowledge the community that has supported Buffalo from the beginning. Bringing together a wide range of artists, writers, performers and creatives, the issue unfolds through first-person reflections that move between the intimate and the everyday: routines, habits, beliefs, contradictions, small rituals and defining moments.

That shift brings a different kind of presence, more personal and direct, which is exactly where we wanted to arrive. Read together, they form a collective portrait grounded in lived experience. The same approach carries through the images. The styling is their own, built from a mix of personal pieces and borrowed clothes, without imposed direction. What matters is how style exists in real life, in gestures and instinct.

At its core, this is an issue about presence, about recognising each other, exchanging perspectives and passing things on, and a community that continues to exist, grow, and sustain the magazine over time.
