Sometimes it’s seen by millions of people and sometimes it’s seen by tens of people,” said Vachon. “But our movies came to life and made it to the screen because writers and directors trusted us with their stories and actors knew we were creating an environment that enabled them to give their best performance.”

Many of the honorees spoke about the mentors and industry giants who had helped them along the way. Close said she’d promised her World According to Garp director, George Roy Hill, that she’d thank him if she ever won an Oscar. “I never got the chance to thank the man who put me in my first movie. Now I can,” she said, holding her statuette up high. Scott, the director whose prolific career output includes Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, Alien, Blade Runner, and The Martian, told a story in his video message about making his brother star in his very first project, the 1965 short film Boy and Bicycle. “I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony,” Scott said of his brother, who died in 2012. “His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

items.title: Country Music's Biggest Stars Came Together to Break Glen Powell's Balls in 'The Comeback King'
items.description: Glen Powell’s guiding principle for his career is simple: Make the kinds of movies he wants to see in the theaters. In recent years, that’s led him to do plenty of action flicks and co-lead a hit rom-com, but for his next big endeavor he’s going for the kind o
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: Glen Powell’s guiding principle for his career is simple: Make the kinds of movies he wants to see in the theaters. In recent years, that’s led him to do plenty of action flicks and co-lead a hit rom-com, but for his next big endeavor he’s going for the kind of big-event comedy that used to be plentiful in Hollywood.

The Comeback King, co-written with and directed by the king of the modern event-comedy, Judd Apatow, is about a country music star whose burgeoning career is rocked by a very public cheating scandal and breakup. The trailer for the film is set to arrive tomorrow, but a bunch of first-look images from the movie are debuting today exclusively on Rolling Stone.

“We really got to make this movie with Nashville,” Powell says, referring to not only the myriad stars who participated in the film — Miranda Lambert, Shaboozey, Brad Paisley, Jelly Roll, Megan Moroney, and Reba McEntire, to name a few — but the pro songwriters and session musicians who helped craft the film’s soundtrack. “The world feels almost Entourage-adjacent,” the actor adds with a laugh.

In the movie, Powell stars as Aubrey King, an up-and-coming country singer who seems to be enjoying his rise to superstardom (if not growing weary of gimmicky songs about beer and drinking out of a woman’s boot at every show). He’s also dating Missy, played by Madelyn Cline, the biggest pop star on the planet. But in a very Apatovian one-two twist, Aubrey catches Missy cheating on him — only for her to then seize the public narrative, claim Aubrey was unfaithful, and turn him into a pop-culture pariah.

For Powell, a big part of the fun of making The Comeback King was tackling this very familiar, very contemporary story, in the form of a big original comedy. “We’ve all watched public breakups happen, people having to navigate being on blast, and their own redemption stories,” he says. “It’s kind of untapped IP in a weird way, because it’s all kind of part of the public consciousness.”

Apatow adds, “It was really fun to talk to Glen all the time about show business and what it’s like these days to try to navigate it all. He’s someone who the world is really paying attention to, and his relationships as he’s trying to evolve as an artist.”

Aubrey’s redemption arc involves reconnecting with the kind of music he really wants to make, as well as a fresh relationship with a woman played by Cristin Milioti. What’s not really featured, but is a huge part of the movie, is that Aubrey builds his comeback from his old college, where he returns to finally complete his degree.

This is the real genesis of The Comeback King. Alongside his rise as a Hollwyood leading man, Powell has been working diligently to earn a degree from the University of Texas. (He’s still on track to graduate next spring.) Once at a party, the producer Kevin Misher told Powell this sounded like a great idea for a movie; and while Powell didn’t want to play an actor, something like a country musician sounded intriguing. Misher even suggested Apatow direct. Powell and Apatow met soon after and, over breakfast, “basically broke the bones of what this story ended up becoming,” Powell says. (Misher went on to produce The Comeback King, too.)

Powell, a Texas native, was already familiar with the world of country music, and had even spent some time in Nashville where his sister, songwriter Leslie Powell, once worked. (Leslie contributed to the Comeback King soundtrack, too.) For Apatow — who did see Willie Nelson at Radio City Music Hall when he was in the 12th grade, but ultimately was more a fan of the Who — the learning curve was slightly steeper. He credits Lukas Nelson and the songwriter Ernest with helping him understand this world and how to “represent it all in the right way.” (Funnily enough, alongside making The Comeback King, Apatow was working on a doc about Billy Strings, also set to arrive next year. “My last few years have been all about country music and bluegrass, which is what you expect from me,” he deadpans.)

As part of his process, Powell sat in on and contributed to songwriting sessions, learned guitar, and worked with a vocal coach. But that didn’t make it any easier when it came time for him to film a scene in which he sings with Lambert, Paisley, and Jelly Roll. “All of a sudden, it dawned on me that I was singing with three icons who have been doing this forever, and I’m supposed to be one of their crew,” he says. “And I was like, ‘Oh, my God, I’m such a fraud, why did I do this to myself?’ But that’s the fun part when you make a movie with country music, not about country music.”

One might think, on the flip side, these country stars would have to gird themselves for the improv-heavy environment of an Apatow film set, but the director says everyone who came through “was really hilarious, knew who they were, and was game to play.” At one point, Apatow asked Powell to contact Jelly Roll “to make sure he was comfortable with the types of jokes we were going to do. Jelly Roll responded, ‘There is literally nothing you can ask me to say that I won’t say.’ And then he was hysterical and improvised one of the best lines in the whole movie.”

Powell also hadn’t done too much improvising before working on The Comeback King, but took to it quickly. Still, he jokes, it could get grueling when Apatow and his cadre of comedians were feeding a never-ending supply of lines to further belittle an already beaten-down Aubrey. “I’m like, ‘Man, what a brutal way to go to work!’” Powell says. “The funniest comedic minds on the planet, all ganging up on me on a daily basis.”

But that “chaotic, fly-by-the-seat-of-your-pants process” was “very fruitful” for a movie like The Comeback King. “You’re showing up to set ready to make magic happen,” Powell says. “Nobody’s ever complacent and phoning it in. Everybody’s always trying to make the most of the moment. There’s an energy there that’s pretty special.”

He adds, “In an era of AI and and people outsourcing creativity, this is a movie that’s really about what it is to be human and what it is to be inspired from the right things, and not be derivative of what an algorithm wants you to be. And I’m really proud of that.”

items.title: War Recap: Man on a Mission
items.description: Well, it had to happen: Johnny’s cover is blown, and he has no one to blame but himself. This week’s episode is aptly titled: It is the juicy bit, and not just where the divorce is concerned but in terms of the narrative structure of the season. This is the mo
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Well, it had to happen: Johnny’s cover is blown, and he has no one to blame but himself. This week’s episode is aptly titled: It is the juicy bit, and not just where the divorce is concerned but in terms of the narrative structure of the season. This is the moment the story has been leading to: The firms’ respective reactions to the mole reveal will define what kind of lawyers they really are. All season long, Taylor & Byrne was positioned as “the good guys” and Cathcarts as “the bad guys,” but, perhaps as a reflection of our screwed-up world, the firms turn out to be two sides of the same self-preservationist, unscrupulous coin.

The firms cut a deal: If Taylor & Byrne agree to forget about Johnny, Cathcarts will agree to forget about Flora and the honey trap. This way, everyone leaves this infernal trial with their reputations intact. The deal is good for everyone except Johnny, who is left in the worst position imaginable. It goes without saying that he should have thought of that sooner. For most of this week’s episode — until the deal is made — he still believes he might have a shot at securing that job with Cathcarts, his only opportunity not to get the British equivalent of being disbarred. I still think he should have double-crossed, but obviously he hasn’t watched The Departed as many times as I have, so he scrambles in vain.

This week’s episode opens where we left off, with Serena realizing that Johnny is the mole. She whispers as much to Nick as soon as she gets a chance, but by that time, court is already in session. Nick and Serena are distracted as Prudence delivers her opening statement, in which she emphasizes Morgan’s visionary status and Carla’s middling acting career, and soon Smallwood becomes distracted too: Johnny texts him from his burner that he has “been rumbled.” Smallwood texts back that the job offer still stands if he can produce proof of the honey trap. I’m still caught up on how this evidence could possibly, legally be admitted in court. (I would love to hear from our helpful, informed readers on this point — sound off in the comments!)

Meanwhile, Nick and Serena try to decide what to do. Serena’s first instinct is to stop the proceedings and alert the judge that the trial has been compromised. That’s what they should do, but this is television, folks, and this episode still has 40 minutes to go. As Budgie charms the room with her opening statement — in which she encourages the judge to remember that Carla is a creative professional as they debate the creation of Zephyr — Johnny runs to the Taylor & Byrne offices hoping to get a copy of the receipt for the construction of the conservatory with which they paid off Flora, charged to Bernard’s card. He uses his make-women-stupid spell on Cleo, but it fades as the walls close in: Cleo questions the purchase of the conservatory; the ever-watchful Molly questions Johnny’s urgency; Michael questions why he wasn’t notified if there was a document needed in court; Bernard questions why he is up in his finances without asking. All this questioning happens while Johnny is literally in the elevator, and Michael snatches the receipt from his hand before the door closes.

Johnny briefly loses it in a great short montage that sees him squirm under pressure. He proceeds to Flora’s house, and on the way, calls Bella to propose a midweek getaway, since he won’t be needed in court the next day. Bella correctly identifies this as a weird suggestion to make on a Tuesday. Johnny tries to convince Flora to “do what’s right” and go to Cathcarts to confess about the conservatory, the NDA, the honey trap, everything. He tells her she has been used by Taylor & Byrne, just as he’s been used. But his desperate demeanor is sudden enough to raise Flora’s suspicion. After seven episodes of women being too easily manipulated by Johnny, they finally wake up and smell the rat.

At this point, Nick is looking for Johnny. Still in court, Nick and Serena agree that they need to speak with Bernard, and by the time they get him on the phone during recess, all the stuff with the receipt has already happened. They decide not to alert Budgie to the mole problem because there’s nothing she can do at present, and there’s nothing Johnny himself can do for Cathcarts while Budgie cross-examines Morgan. They also immediately agree that they should not tell Carla, though they might reconsider if they knew she was sleeping with the mole. I thought Johnny might try to use Carla somehow, but at least for now, he’s ignoring her calls. I fear we’re in for a soapy how could you do this to me confrontation in the finale.

The firms race to find Johnny. As Morgan worries about his performance on cross-examination (we’ll get to the trial itself after we have surveyed the depth of Johnny’s snafu), Smallwood instructs Schill to get to Johnny before “Singer,” who has disappeared from court, and offer Johnny a job lest the other side tries to “turn him” (Smallwood is familiar with The Departed). But Schill is too late; Nick has a few hours’ head start and gets to Johnny first. He waits for him in his apartment, where he threatens Johnny with criminal charges for corporate espionage and promises to ruin his career forever. When Schill calls the burner, it’s Nick who picks up (Schill hangs up right away). Nick also tells Bella everything, and she is actually mad for once. She leaves and tells Johnny to be gone when she returns. Johnny weakly apologizes to Nick, but I think the show is banking on a stronger emotional reaction for next week. Archie Renaux embodies Johnny’s desperation well; I’m eager to see him bring this character to resolution.

Nick’s brief phone call with Schill leads to the deal between the firms. Serena and Nick meet with Beatrice, Smallwood, and Schill at the Cathcarts office. At first, Cathcarts plays dumb, but when Nick assures them they have proof, they get to business. If each side can overlook their opponent’s trespasses, neither firm’s reputation will suffer and no client will have to know about anything. They come to a settlement number in about 30 seconds that will hopefully bring this God-forsaken trial to a close, so everyone can forget about honey traps and corporate spies and go have tea and shoot clay pigeons or whatever it is they do for fun. It was that easy!

This is all done without the knowledge of clients or barristers, who might be a little peeved to see their hard work so easily dismissed. Prudence and Budgie spend the day with Morgan on the stand. He oscillates between tenderness and hostility toward Carla, though he brings up her diminishing relevance as an actress as many times as possible. Prudence’s goal is to show that Carla doesn’t have any real professional involvement with Zephyr, while Budgie labors to prove that Zephyr would never have existed without Carla. Under Prudence’s examination, Morgan explains that Carla wasn’t present for most of Zephyr’s development, which took place largely in Palo Alto. By way of illustration, Prudence introduces a photo of Zephyr’s American launch party, which Carla didn’t attend because she was at the premiere of a film she wasn’t even in.

What Morgan forgets — and what evades Cathcarts’ research — is that this launch party took place on the eve of Morgan and Carla’s wedding anniversary, and that Morgan set the party date himself. Budgie argues that, knowing Carla would be at a friend’s premiere, and that their anniversary was on the next day, and that every other Zephyr executive was bringing their spouses to the function, Morgan picked a date Carla couldn’t make to purposefully exclude her and take all the credit for himself. Losing his patience, Morgan scoffs that it’s ridiculous he should have to give away “half of [his] life’s work” because he forgot an anniversary date.

But that’s not Budgie’s main point, anyway; she is only course correcting. The core of her argument is that Zephyr couldn’t have existed without Carla because the idea for Zephyr emerged in reaction to something that happened to Carla, when she was the target of a social-media pile-on and became a viral laughingstock. That was the reason Morgan and Carla went to the cottage in Normandy for a needed respite. Maintaining that Carla was a passive muse, “the Jane to his Serge,” Morgan exploited his wife’s suffering for his own gain. The truth is, he can’t recite the poem that gave Zephyr its name, which we’ve seen Carla recite by heart. He can’t even correctly remember the name of its author. If I ever need a lawyer, I’m calling Budgie.

Budgie’s perfect rhetoric puts Carla ahead, but a string of Zephyr employees — including Gillian, Eric, and an unnamed front-desk receptionist — testify in Morgan’s favor that Carla was never professionally involved with the company. Despite Serena’s encouragement that they’re still in a good position, these testimonies make Carla nervous. Morgan is thankful for his colleagues’ contributions, but he notices that Gillain seems “off.” Carla notices the same thing a bit earlier, when Gillian stops her in the hallway to offer her sympathy for how things turned out and promises to call her.

The weirdness that Morgan sensed in Gillian was nothing less than the turning gears of machination. Gillian does call Carla, as promised, and they meet covertly in Carla’s car. Gillian tells Carla about Ancker’s offer and proposes a plan: If Carla changes her strategy to go after Morgan’s Zephyr shares, rather than cash, Morgan would no longer be the majority shareholder and they could force the sale to Ancker. As a result, Carla would become a billionaire. On the stand, Gillian hinted at her intention — she testified that her contributions to the company have been reflected in her shares. With Carla, she works the overlooked-woman angle, hoping she can convince her to act out of wrath and greed. But Carla has been notoriously wishy-washy when it comes to those cardinal sins. She has gone from honey-trapping Morgan to wanting only “what’s fair”; earlier that same night, sharing an umbrella with her soon-to-be ex-husband, she almost looked wistful. Maybe this final decision will invest Carla’s character with some actual complexity and humanity, though I fear, with one episode left, it’s too late.
Representations and Acknowledgments

• With Morgan on the stand, we finally get a definition of what Zephyr actually is: “A social-media platform with strict community guidelines designed to promote positivity rather than division.” Still sounds like word salad to me, though. I can’t envision what a platform like this would actually look like, especially when a couple of episodes ago, Carla got a lot of heat on Zephyr for bombing her late-night appearance.

• At the trial, the press is present both inside and outside the courtroom. Given the prominent place the media has had in the unraveling of Carla and Morgan’s marriage, I suspect the journalists sitting in on the proceedings will play some role in the finale.

• Taylor & Byrne’s eagerness to make a deal with Cathcarts seemed anti-climactic to me. I understand they’re nervous the stuff with Flora will come out, but isn’t employing a corporate spy a much graver transgression? Is anything that happened with Flora straight-up illegal, or as illegal as planting a mole in the opponent’s firm? As Nick said last week, the espionage plot could ruin Cathcarts forever, while Taylor & Byrne established deniability about the honey trap from the get-go. I wanted to see Nick and Serena coming in for the kill. I’m hoping this isn’t the end of negotiations!

• Let’s place our bets on what will happen in the finale. I think Carla will take Gillian’s offer but backtrack at the last minute, thereby ensuring some kind of dignified ending for herself. I also think Saeed will return to the Taylor & Byrne offices and that we will finally learn what actually happened in New York, though I have very high hopes we won’t have to sit through a flashback sequence. I think we’ve seen the last of Bella, and Johnny will end up as all greedy, selfish men do: lonely and friendless. And I think Carla and Morgan will reconcile. Will we see Gabe again at all? What about Flora? Cast your predictions!

items.title: ‘Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Brad Pitt’s Sequel Is an ‘Absolute Triumph’ and a ‘Wildly Entertaining’ ‘Love Letter’ to Hollywood
items.description: David Fincher, Brad Pitt and Quentin Tarantino‘s long-awaited “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” sequel movie, officially titled “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” has been unveiled to members of the film press, who are calling the Netflix-backed tentpo
items.author: Zack Sharf
paragraphs: David Fincher, Brad Pitt and Quentin Tarantino‘s long-awaited “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” sequel movie, officially titled “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” has been unveiled to members of the film press, who are calling the Netflix-backed tentpole a “wildly entertaining” “hangout movie” that is already one of the year’s best.

“David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of #CliffBooth pops, throbs and crackles,” wrote film critic Simon Thompson. “Like Once Upon a Time… this is a love letter to LA. An eclectic, ragtag cast make this a slick and sexy romp. A salty and slower-burning side piece to Tarantino’s original with a fire final act.”

Tomatometer critic Zach Pope called the film “a PURE cinematic trifecta of Tarantino’s signature chaos, Fincher’s meticulous attention to detail, and Brad Pitt’s effortlessly charismatic Cliff Booth.”

He continued: “All wrapped into a stylish love letter to 1970s Hollywood cinema that reminds us sometimes all you need is a laid-back, wildly entertaining misadventure with a character you just LOVE spending time with. That just might turn into insanity. It’s cool, chaotic, charming, and never tries to be more than it needs to be. If you loved Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, this one’s absolutely for you. Just as it was for me.”

The Wrap’s Senior Film Reporter Drew Taylor “absolutely loved” the film. “Tarantino and Fincher are like peanut butter and chocolate (the peanut butter is profane and the chocolate dipped in blood). Stop watching anything, go see it on the biggest screen around, have the time of your life. An absolute triumph. The best,” he wrote.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is an absolute banger,” wrote Critics Choice member Ricky Válero. “An aesthetically rich film that beautifully captures the relationship between Los Angeles and the movies. Brad Pitt is as charismatic as ever. Truly one of the year’s best films.”

Variety’s Clayton Davis described the film as a “wild, hilarious hangout movie.” “Brad Pitt slides back into his beloved Oscar-winning role and gives his best performance since “Once Upon a Time in…Hollywood.” Elizabeth Debicki brings an intoxicating sensuality, and Scott Caan and Peter Weller are such a treat that they could have had triple the screen time,” he continued. “The cinematography is gorgeous. If the 2019 film was a love letter to L.A., this one is a full-on sonnet.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” features the return of Pitt as the eponymous stuntman. The movie is set in 1977, eight years after the events of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” and follows Cliff as a Hollywood studio fixer who gets in way over his head while working for a popular movie actor. The supporting cast includes Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Carla Gugino and Peter Weller, among others.

Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor for playing Cliff Booth in “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which Sony released in theaters in June 2019. The movie was acclaimed and earned a strong $410 million at the worldwide box office. “Hollywood” went on to earn 10 Oscar nominations, including best picture and best director.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” features a screenplay by Tarantino, who opted not to direct the movie because, per his retirement plan, he only plans on directing one more feature film before he leaves the director’s chair for good. The first draft of the sequel script clocked in at a whopping 230 pages, Fincher revealed to Empire magazine last month. The director cut 60 pages.
“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” opens exclusively in Imax theaters on Nov. 25 and will be available to stream on Netflix starting Dec. 23. Check out first reactions below:

items.title: Skydance Movie Studio Shakeup: Kira Goldberg Departs Netflix to Run Paramount With Don Granger, Jeff Goldstein to Retire, WB Sets Leadership
items.description: Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein have set their leadership team following Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein have set their leadership team following Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Kira Goldberg and Don Granger will serve as president of Paramount’s Motion Picture Group, and Jesse Ehrman has been elevated to president of Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group. Michael Ireland, who joined Warner Bros. earlier this year after he was let go from Paramount, will continue as president of production, reporting to Ehrmann.

Kira Goldberg was recently at Netflix as Film VP of faith, holiday, young adult and family, working on movies such as Adam McKay’s starry environmental satire “Don’t Look Up,” the sci-fi adventure “The Adam Project” and the upcoming heist thriller “The Take” with Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Granger has produced various films at Skydance, including “Jack Reacher: Never Go Back,” “Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation,” Charlize Theron’s “The Old Guard 2” and Mattel’s “Matchbox: The Movie.” Ehrman, a 20-year studio veteran, has recently worked on “A Minecraft Movie” and Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners.”

“We said it on day one: Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures are our cornerstone labels and will remain distinct. Both will continue to anchor our biggest commercial and filmmaker-driven projects, with our animation and specialty labels also remaining separate with their own creative mandates,” Goldberg and Greenstein said in a memo to staff. “Our leadership structure is designed to empower each studio and label with dedicated creative leadership, backed by an excellent corporate team that provides the expertise, resources and support to help them succeed. Together, we are building an organization with the creative ambition, resources and scale to deliver on our commitment of 30 films per year.”

Although the studios will operate separately, Paramount vets Shaun Barber and Mark Viane will oversee domestic and international distribution, respectively for both Paramount and Warner Bros. They will report to Josh Goldstine, president of worldwide marketing and distribution. With Barber and Viane’s promotions, Jeff Goldstein, a 48-year veteran of Warner Bros. Pictures who most recently served as head of global theatrical distribution, will retire. He’s expected to transition to a consulting role.

As part of the restructuring, Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation. He will stay for a period of time until he transitions to full-time producing, according to the memo. In the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, while Chris Leahy will continue to oversee the day-to-day operations of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, reporting into Dodge and Balthazor. John Lasseter remains head of Skydance Animation alongside president Holly Edwards.

Ted Lim, who was chief business officer at Warner Bros. Pictures, will be departing the company. Additionally, Josh Silverman, president of global products and publishing, will transition to lead consumer products and publishing. Meanwhile Mark Kaufman, executive VP and chief content officer of theatrical ventures, will continue to oversee shows such as the Broadway production of “The Lost Boys.”

As previously announced Jeremy Latcham is the new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, replacing James Gunn and Peter Safran. As for specialty divisions, Richard Brener will lead New Line; Lia Buman will serve as executive VP and head of global acquisitions at Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules will head Paramount Primal; Christian Parkes is overseeing Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh will be senior VP and general manager of Turner Classic Movies.

“This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry. We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership,” Goldberg and Greenstein concluded their note to staff. “We know how much work is underway across the company, and we’re grateful for the care, focus and dedication you bring to it every day. We look forward to all that we will build and accomplish together.”

items.title: ‘Madden’ Review: Nicolas Cage Plays John Madden as the Disheveled Buddha of Football in David O. Russell’s Eccentric Stunt of a Sports Biopic
items.description: You could say that every movie writes its own rules. But you can really say that about a movie in which Nicolas Cage, buried under a jowly fatsuit that makes him look like Jiminy Glick playing John Candy, portrays John Madden, the celebrated coach of the Oakla
items.author: Owen Gleiberman
paragraphs: You could say that every movie writes its own rules. But you can really say that about a movie in which Nicolas Cage, buried under a jowly fatsuit that makes him look like Jiminy Glick playing John Candy, portrays John Madden, the celebrated coach of the Oakland Raiders in their mean-machine ’70s heyday, who went on to become one of the most unhinged — and influential — TV sports commentators of his era.

In David O. Russell’s “Madden,” Cage, wearing a costume the movie never pretends you’re going to forget is a costume (it’s simply too synthetic), gives a performance that’s two parts impersonation, one part Nicolas Cage kabuki. The film’s concept is that Madden, with his outsize physique and even larger personality, was such a blustery, un-self-aware, obscenity-spewing, shoot-from-the-mouth character that wrapping Cage in this prosthetic supergeek disguise and letting him tap into the grandiose depths of his inner Cage-ness will somehow be a path toward…authenticity.

It is and it isn’t. “Madden” is a stunt biopic on cinematic amphetamines. At times, the film can feel like an extended “Saturday Night Live” sketch played straight. But it’s like an “SNL” sketch shot and edited by Scorsese. The film flashes by in a fusillade of storytelling gambits: mock documentary interviews, scenes in which Madden (in an early version of his famous telestrator) diagrams football plays right onto the screen, all spanked along by tasty period needle drops (“How Long,” “Evil Ways”) done in the jukebox-shuffle mode of “Casino.” John Madden was a gridiron genius, but his plays are easy enough to follow, because most of them are based on a chess-like fake-out — conning the players of the opposing team into thinking that this is the strategy, when the strategy is, in fact, the exact opposite of that.

“Madden” features one more stylized semi-prosthetic character: the Oakland Raiders’ owner, Al Davis, played by Christian Bale with a shark mouth and slick receding hair and a Jewish goombah accent and a princess-doll wife (an unrecognizable Sienna Miller), all of which makes you think he must be some sort of vicious criminal. But no, Davis is just Madden’s fellow monomaniac (the relentless businessman to Madden’s football artist), and these two sustain a testy friendship even once Madden leaves the team.

Spilling forward in an attention-deficit rush, “Madden” keeps you watching, but it also holds you at arm’s length. It’s a divertingly eccentric genre film that will appeal to sports fanatics, maybe mostly to sports fanatics of a certain age. In theaters (where it’s receiving a modest release), I suspect the movie will be doomed. But I could see it being a hit on streaming, and for the right reasons: In its skewed way, “Madden” is a movie crafted out of obsession. And it’s Cage’s performance that brings that to life. His Madden is OCD about football — he lives to diagram plays, to outfox the other team, to win. But his football mania is so consuming that it threatens to capsize his marriage to Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), his supportive but tough-love wife, who only wants him to be present. But he can’t be present; not really. He’s living inside his football head.

Cage captures the manic side of Madden the arrested sports fetishist, the one who lived in a state of chronic dishevelment (his clothes are ill-fitting; even his hair is ill-fitting). But the Cage feature you can’t hide are those wounded, sensitive puppy-dog eyes — the ones he’s been brandishing at audiences since “Valley Girl.” There’s an inner gentleness to Nicolas Cage, and that, ironically, is the quality John Madden had as well. He coached a team of infamous ruffians, and he would scream from the sidelines; at CBS, he barked out his game theories like a sports id let off its leash. He might have been the model for Fred Willard’s deranged color commentator in “Best in Show.” Yet he also had a strangely innocent quality. Madden was an overgrown child — a sports fanatic who never grew up. The joke of the film — its theme, really — is that it recognizes what a dysfunctional state of being that is, but it also presents Madden’s football mind as a vulgarly American state of grace.

It’s been a long time since we’ve heard the filmmaking voice of David O. Russell. His last movie, “Amsterdam” (2022), was a convoluted disaster, and his film before that, the just-okay “Joy,” came out in 2015. He had his own fall from grace (those “I Heart Huckabees” on-set tantrum videos!), and quite a fall from the ebullient glory days of “Silver Linings Playbook” and “American Hustle.” But let’s not sell him short: Those were fantastic movies that confirmed Russell’s status as a major American film artist. “Madden” isn’t close to being in their league, yet it’s crafted just well enough to let you touch the buzz of Russell’s intelligence, his attraction to the high of scruffy bad behavior, and his filmmaking joy.

The movie falls into three sections, the first set during Madden’s moment of total football triumph: the 1976 season, when he led the Raiders to victory in the AFC Championship Game, then went on to defeat the Pittsburgh Steelers in the Super Bowl. That was Madden’s only Super Bowl victory — but maybe more significantly, it was the only time his Raiders won the AFC, even though he’d led them in one winning season after another. They were a team as cursed as the Boston Red Sox, and “Madden” dives into that downbeat karma by dramatizing how it tears away at Madden’s home life. By 1979, he’s suffering from a bleeding ulcer, and Virginia won’t compete with football anymore. The only way he can save his marriage is to retire from coaching (though Al Davis will keep trying to woo him back).

The second part of the film chronicles Madden’s entrance into CBS Sports, a comedy of errors that’s also a comedy of game-changing triumph. His jabbering analysis, punctuated by “Wham!” and “Boom!,” is a rude imposition on the orderly play-calling of Pat Summerall (Joel Murray). But it’s Madden who knows the game, who has the insights, who makes sports announcing exciting.

The wild card of “Madden” — because you wouldn’t even expect this to be part of a biopic — is all the time the movie devotes to Trip Hawkins (an eagle-eyed John Mulaney), the founder of Electronic Arts, the pioneering computer-game company. He figures out early on that the Madden playbook could become the heart of a visionary digital interactive experience. Hawkins wants to turn football into a video game, but the way to make it great is to feature Madden’s plays, which Madden keeps at home in an overstuffed binder he calls The Book. It’s the ultimate treasure chest of strategic football magic tricks. Watching the stubbornly analog Madden try to adjust to the concept of squeezing football onto a computer screen becomes a hilariously touching metaphor for how our entire culture went couch-potato vicarious.

The Madden we see is a couch potato too. He’s the apotheosis of the football coach: that furious roly-poly American archetype (Lombardi, Shula, Schembechler) who’s a former so-so athlete and now operates strictly from the neck up. Madden becomes a celebrity, a pitchman for everything from Miller Lite to Tinactin, and he puts the turducken on the map — that pileup of poultry that’s a turkey, a duck, and a chicken in one. “Madden” is a turducken of a movie, a football saga stuffed inside a domestic geek romance wrapped in a Wikipedia biopic on Scorsese stimulants. What’s catchy about it is that it stays true to John Madden — to how uncool he was, and to how it was that very quality that made him the slovenly Buddha of football.

items.title: Disney Quarterly Revenue Rises 16% and Profit Doubles; Company Forecasts $3 Billion in Annual Cost Savings by 2029 Including Through Layoffs
items.description: Disney had a robust quarter, topping Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines. But CEO Josh D’Amaro, who’s been in the job for eight months, sees an opportunity for the company to become even more efficient and help fuel future growth.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Disney had a robust quarter, topping Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines. But CEO Josh D’Amaro, who’s been in the job for eight months, sees an opportunity for the company to become even more efficient and help fuel future growth.

For the three months ended Oct. 3, 2026, which is Disney’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, the Mouse House reported revenue of $25.95 billion, up 16%, and a doubling of net income to $2.61 billion. Total operating segment income rose 43%, to $4.97 billion. The company reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.77. On average, Wall Street analysts expected revenue of $25.16 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.68 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.

Overall, it was a solid quarter across Disney’s entertainment, sports and theme parks businesses. But D’Amaro and his lieutenants are looking to make Disney leaner and meaner. In their letter to shareholders accompanying the results, D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston provided an update to their “efficiency program to create incremental capacity to drive growth,” an initiative that has encompassed several rounds of job cutbacks in 2026.

“We now expect the program to realize annual run-rate operating expense savings of about $3 billion by fiscal 2029,” the execs wrote. “While these efficiencies will be used primarily to fund future growth, we do expect a portion to drop to the bottom line over time.” Disney is poised to make a significant round of layoffs in the current quarter, affecting thousands of employees, with some managers reportedly told to cut expenses by 20% on an annualized basis.

In addition, the execs said, they expect cash content spending in fiscal 2027 of approximately $26 billion, up about 9% from fiscal 2026. That includes “our increased investment in international programming and sports rights, and the timing of feature film production spend,” D’Amaro and Johnston said.

On the earnings call, D’Amaro alluded to impending job cuts. “Changes like these are not easy, and they affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company,” he said. “At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth. We make these choices because we believe so strongly in what Disney can be.”

Disney noted that its fourth quarter and fiscal 2026 results had one additional week of operations (a 53rd week) compared with the year-earlier period. The company estimates that the 53rd week contributed approximately 17 cents to full-year adjusted earnings per share.

Revenue from Disney+ and Hulu rose 22% to $5.13 billion in the September 2026 quarter, and operating income more than doubled to $824 million. Disney said it expects to complete the integration of Disney+ and Hulu before the end of 2026, with a “fully unified experience” available in December.

Starting with the December 2026 quarter, Disney will stop reporting operating income for Disney+ and Hulu. “We have made strong progress scaling our SVOD businesses and, as a result, see a long runway for growth and margin expansion at Disney Entertainment,” D’Amaro and Johnston wrote in the letter. “We no longer believe the supplemental disclosure of SVOD operating income reflects this segment focus and strategy.”

In another financial reporting change, Disney as of Q1 of fiscal 2027 will provide additional revenue disclosures for Disney Entertainment, to “provide greater visibility into how we monetize Entertainment content across distribution platforms, third-party licensing and consumer products,” the company’s execs said.

In the September quarter, Disney’s Entertainment segment overall saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income in the segment shot up 92% to $1.33 billion “due to growth in subscription and affiliate fees and higher content sales, partially offset by increased programming and production costs.”

The execs touted the company’s intellectual-property flywheel between theatrical and streaming movie releases. Disney-Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” which raked in $1.15 billion globally at the box office this summer, premiered on Disney+ on Sept. 23, and garnered 20 million views in its first five days on the platform. According to Disney, August was the highest month ever for Marvel Studios viewing, fueled by the summer theatrical success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” (released by Sony Pictures) and the debut of the “Avengers: Doomsday trailer.” During the quarter, Marvel content viewership on Disney+ more than doubled compared with its historical baseline. “Our successful rerelease of ‘Avengers: Endgame’ in late September also showed how anticipation continues to build for ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’ which arrives in theaters December 18,” D’Amaro and Johnston said in the letter.

At ESPN, revenue increased 16% to $4.61 billion. Growth in subscription and affiliate fees came from an increase of 8% from the additional week of operations in the quarter compared with the year-earlier period, 6% from higher rates and 4% from Disney’s deal with the NFL giving the league a 10% ownership stake in ESPN.

Disney Experiences revenue hit $10.11 billion in the September quarter, up 15%, with 5% of the growth in theme park admissions sales coming from higher average per capita ticket revenue. Segment operating income increased 20% to $2.25 billion. Disney Experiences saw an 11% increase in global visitors in the quarter (or a 4% increase excluding the 53rd week). “We continued to see headwinds from lower international attendance at our domestic parks in the quarter, but as expected, those headwinds moderated from the year-over-year impact observed in the third quarter,” D’Amaro and Johnston said.

For fiscal 2027, Disney is expecting double-digit growth in adjusted EPS (excluding the impact of the 53rd week in ’26). The company forecast total segment operating income growth of approximately 8%, factoring in the exclusion of equity income reporting from entertainment segment operating results. Disney expects the majority of its growth in total segment operating income and adjusted EPS for fiscal 2027 to occur in the first half of the fiscal year.

In fiscal ’27, Disney expects capital expenditures of approximately $9 billion “as we continue to execute against our strategy to turbocharge growth at Disney Experiences,” the execs said. The company invested $8.7 billion parks, resorts and other property in the 2026 fiscal year.

In August, Disney closed the sale of its 50% stake in A+E Global Media to co-owner Hearst for $1.2 billion in cash. For fiscal 2026, A+E contributed approximately $390 million in equity income to Disney’s Entertainment segment operating income.
Also Tuesday, Disney’s board declared a cash dividend of $2.00 per share payable over the course of fiscal 2027, a 33% increase over the $1.50 per share paid to shareholders during fiscal year 2026.

items.title: Skydance Film Re-Org: Kira Goldberg Joins Paramount, Jesse Ehrman Upped to Run Warner Bros.
items.description: Skydance is sorting out its film operations at both Paramount and Warner Bros. in the wake of closing its $111 billion acquisition of Warners.
items.author: Mia Galuppo; Aaron Couch; Borys Kit
paragraphs: Skydance is sorting out its film operations at both Paramount and Warner Bros. in the wake of closing its $111 billion acquisition of Warners.

Kira Goldberg is leaving Netflix, where she was one of its top film heads, overseeing faith-based, family and young adult films for the streamer. At Paramount, she will oversee film operations with longtime Skydance executive and producer Don Granger as presidents of the motion picture group.

Jesse Ehrman, a twenty-year veteran of Warners, has been elevated to president of the motion picture group at the studio. He most recently served as president of production and development. Mikey Ireland, who joined Warners in February after being laid off at Paramount, will remain as president of production at Warners.

Warner Bros. has been without a head since Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy were fired last month amid the Skydance merger. The duo had run the studio since 2022, guiding it to a best picture win with One Battle After Another earlier this year and having celebrated hits like Sinners, A Minecraft Movie and Weapons, but seeing a number of their 2026 movies bomb at the box office, most recently the Tom Cruise feature Digger.

Elsewhere in today’s announcement was the news that Jeff Goldstein, a 48-year veteran of Warner Bros. who currently serves as the head of global distribution, will be exiting the studio, taking on a consulting role.

The execs at Warners and Paramount will all report up to Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, who oversee all of film for Skydance. The new re-org was done with an eye toward accomplishing the 30-plus movie slate across the two studios and their various divisions, which include New Line and DC Studios, which recently ousted James Gunn and Peter Safran and will install Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham next month.

In the September settlement with California Attorney General Rob Bonta and other state AGs that cleared the path for the Warner Bros. merger, Skydance agreed that the combined studios must release 30 films for two years and then 32 for the next three years. There are penalties if this threshold isn’t met. For every movie that Skydance falls short of, the studio must pay $30 million to health and pension funds, split among the guilds. Additionally, a judge can force it to sell or spin out Miramax.
Read the full memo from Goldberg and Greenstein below.

The theatrical business is central to the company’s vision for the future of Skydance. We are home to more than a century of extraordinary storytelling, legendary films and an enduring impact on audiences and culture around the world. We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere.
As we shape this next chapter for Skydance, we want to share the leadership structure for the film divisions that comprise the Skydance Motion Picture Group.

We said it on day one: Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures are our cornerstone labels and will remain distinct. Both will continue to anchor our biggest commercial and filmmaker-driven projects, with our animation and specialty labels also remaining separate with their own creative mandates.

Our leadership structure is designed to empower each studio and label with dedicated creative leadership, backed by an excellent corporate team that provides the expertise, resources and support to help them succeed. Together, we are building an organization with the creative ambition, resources and scale to deliver on our commitment of 30 films per year.
Studios Business Leadership

Our corporate team brings collective expertise across key operations that ultimately support our creative output. The team comprises Courtney Armstrong, Chief Operating Officer; Mark Badagliacca, Chief Financial Officer; Brooke Robertson, EVP, Head of Global Communications & Media Relations; and Talia Robinson, EVP, Human Resources.

Josh Goldstine has been named President of Worldwide Marketing and Distribution. Shaun Barber and Mark Viane will continue to report to Josh and oversee domestic and international distribution for both Paramount and Warner Bros. Jeff Goldstein, who has worked on over 1,000 films over 48 years of an illustrious career, will retire and transition into a consulting role. Jeff is a stalwart of this industry, and as we align these two organizations, his counsel will be tremendous.

Additionally, Josh Silverman, President, Global Products & Publishing, will transition to our group to lead Consumer Products and Publishing, which will add important connectivity between our stable of IP and a key revenue stream. Mark Kaufman, EVP & Chief Content Officer, Theatre Ventures, will now report to Josh, where he will continue overseeing an acclaimed portfolio, including the Tony-winning Broadway production of The Lost Boys.
Separately, we want to let you know that Ted Lim will be departing the company. We thank him for his leadership and contributions as Chief Business Officer and wish him all the best.

Don Granger and Kira Goldberg will lead Paramount Pictures as Presidents, Motion Picture Group. Over the last year, Don has been a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output. As our slate continues to grow, so does our team, and we’re thrilled to welcome Kira. Most recently at Netflix, she oversaw a slate that included Don’t Look Up, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming Bad Day with Cameron Diaz and The Take starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Before that, she worked on films including Bohemian Rhapsody, The Post and The Greatest Showman during her tenure at Fox. Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward.

Jesse Ehrman has been elevated to President, Motion Picture Group. With over 20 years at Warner Bros., Jesse has been instrumental in many of the studio’s biggest hits including recent movies like A Minecraft Movie and Sinners, and has built lasting relationships with the studio’s most important filmmakers. Michael Ireland will continue as President of Production, reporting to Jesse. Mike’s relationships across the industry, strong eye for material and leadership experience make him an integral part of the motion picture group.

As we recently announced, Jeremy Latcham is joining us as President and Chief Creative Officer of DC Studios. James Gunn and Peter Safran will step away from their leadership roles after four years transforming and resetting the studio’s foundation and return full time to their creative work.

As part of this restructuring, Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, and has agreed to stay for a period of time until he transitions to full-time producing. We thank him for his dedication to the animation business and greatly respect his commitment to this craft.

In the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, while Chris Leahy will continue to oversee the day-to-day operations of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, reporting into Jennifer and Traci. John Lasseter remains Head of Skydance Animation alongside Holly Edwards, President, Skydance Animation.
Specialty Labels and Divisions

Our specialty labels and divisions will be led by Richard Brener, President, Chief Content Officer, New Line; Lia Buman, EVP, Head of Global Acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, Heads of Paramount Primal; Christian Parkes, Head of Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and General Manager, Turner Classic Movies.

This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry. We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership.

Our shared responsibility is to give our filmmakers, storytellers and teams the support they need to do their best work. As we continue to build out the broader organization, this leadership structure establishes a strong foundation for the work ahead.

We know how much work is underway across the company, and we’re grateful for the care, focus and dedication you bring to it every day. We look forward to all that we will build and accomplish together.

items.title: ‘3 Body Problem’ Season 2 Trailer Released: “They’re Coming to Exterminate Us”
items.description: The 3 Body Problem season two trailer is here and it features time jumps, alien threats, outer-space action and zero-gravity sex.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: The 3 Body Problem season two trailer is here and it features time jumps, alien threats, outer-space action and zero-gravity sex.
Below is the first look at the return of Netflix‘s adaptation of Liu Cixin’s acclaimed novels. The tagline for the new season is “They Are Here.”

The show from showrunners David Benioff, D.B. Weiss and Alexander Woo also has an official description: “The alien invasion nears and humanity prepares to meet them — on Earth and beyond. While a space fleet embarks on a mission that spans centuries, a secret locked inside of one man’s mind might be humanity’s only hope for survival.” As one character warns in the trailer, “They are coming to exterminate us.”
The show is set to return on Jan. 14.

The second season is reportedly shorter than the first, with Netflix confirming it will have six episodes instead of eight. Two years ago, Netflix renewed the series for second and third final seasons which will complete the adaptation.
The season has two directors familiar to Game of Thrones fans: Jeremy Podeswa helms the first half of the season and Miguel Sapochnik directs the second half.
The first season spent seven weeks in the streamer’s global Top 10 list, reaching the Top 10 in 93 countries and hitting No. 1 in 44 countries, with 46.6 million views.

The cast of 3 Body Problem season two includes returning stars Jess Hong, Benedict Wong, Jovan Adepo, Eiza González, Liam Cunningham, Marlo Kelly, Sea Shimooka, Saamer Usmani, Alex Sharp and Josh Brener. New cast members include Claudia Doumit, Ellie de Lange, Alfie Allen, David Yip and Jordan Sunshine.

items.title: Billy Evans Fires Back at Amanda Seyfried and Nathan Fielder: “It’s My Life and I Love It”
items.description: The whole point of participating in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, says Billy Evans, was to change the world’s perception of Elizabeth Holmes, the 42-year-old founder of Theranos currently serving out an 11-year sentence for defra
items.author: Seth Abramovitch
paragraphs: The whole point of participating in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, says Billy Evans, was to change the world’s perception of Elizabeth Holmes, the 42-year-old founder of Theranos currently serving out an 11-year sentence for defrauding investors.

Their young children were already beginning to feel the repercussions when filming began, Evans says, being uninvited to playdates. But in the weeks since the film’s release, he finds himself facing a host of new problems, with strangers picking apart everything from the appearance of his genitals to how the couple makes scrambled eggs.
Evans, 34, is an MIT grad whose latest business venture — a company similar in ambition to Theranos called Haemanthus — is also raising eyebrows.

He broke his silence first with a Nov. 2 “Ask Me Anything” on X, where he addressed speculation about cocaine use (he said his drugs of choice are coffee and nicotine and that his persistent screen sniffles were the result of cedar allergies). He also denied being gay (“In 2026, being gay is considerably more socially acceptable than being in love with Elizabeth Holmes,” he wrote).

He then gave a sitdown with CBS Sunday Morning over the weekend, saying he in fact loved You Can See Everything, had not consented to his nudity being shown and did not currently have plans to sue studio A24 over his depiction in the film.

But Evans has a lot more to say. In his first print interview about the film, he wants to respond to Amanda Seyfried, 40, who recently told Rolling Stone that making the film, “I became this weird Billy Evans detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage.” After filming their contentious dinner together, her opinion of him “only got worse.”

He also disputes one of the documentary’s most consequential scenes, in which Fielder and Oppenheim depict Evans holding up production over a cut of the profits. Evans says the financial terms were agreed upon two days before filming began and appearance releases were signed shortly after.

Below, Evans addresses all of that and much more, including that much-debated bag of turkey jerky, Holmes’ own thoughts on the shower scene and what, exactly, he and Holmes mean by “monuments of love.”
That’s an honest answer, but I did not prep for this at all.
Do you ever worry that the movie will be something your kids will have to carry for the rest of their lives?

At the time in which we were thinking about doing this movie, which was in February of 2023, already things were happening [to my kids], like they’d be uninvited from a play date or when we were looking at the first preschools or something. And I felt like the world had created a narrative about who their mom was that was untrue.

The goal with this film is really to let people just see her and make up their own mind, which was kind of in part why we chose Nathan. He’s a genius filmmaker. He’s insanely creative and he tells a story that only he could tell.
And your gut reaction after the first time seeing it — did you feel it helped or hindered your cause?

I’m so biased. So I think I’m really kind of the last person whose opinion matters on the subject. But to me, when Liz is on screen — and I think it’s an important distinction to make compared to recreations or reenactments — that’s just who she is. That is Elizabeth Holmes. It’s the same Liz I saw the first day I met her and it’s the same Liz now that she’s in prison. She’s insanely trusting and kind, compassionate, a bit naive, but that’s who she is. Now the problem is that people see that and they have a hard time believing it’s real. That’s been my experience for the last decade. That’s who she really is.
And what about the depiction of you?

I really didn’t like it. It’s hard to see yourself depicted in a way that frames things so intensely negative, having people scrutinize the smallest of actions, like helping your wife make eggs and it being turned into some condemnation of toxic masculinity or some controlling nature. Control is a word that I’ve never really considered in my relationship with Liz. We just infinitely trust one another.
Is she generally inept in the kitchen?

You have to remember she was running a company for 16 years. She didn’t cook at all, at all. There’s a reason why she just had green drinks. She was unable to cook. Liz could burn water. And I grew up working in kitchens. My first job was in a kitchen, so I love cooking. When Liz was pregnant, I cooked every single meal for the two years she was pregnant for us. I’d make meals for 10, 15, 20 people every night of the trial. I love cooking. She doesn’t like it at all.
There’s an expression from reality TV: “Blame it on the edit.” Do you feel that you were the victim of the edit?

I actually interpret the scene very differently than everyone else because I just don’t even think about control. So that’s not how I saw it at all. I think the criticism of it and the creepy music and then the focus on it later and Amanda’s reaction to it was different than how I interpreted it.
The one thing that everyone brings up first about you is the shower scene. I saw the New York Times did a whole story on it.

Oh, really? Yeah. I don’t read all this stuff. Look, so much of this stuff can really just be chalked up to my naivete. I always heard about you have to sign some nudity waiver. I just assumed you can’t show people naked on screen without them consenting to it. So yes, I absolutely consented to them filming me showering, but my understanding is that they wouldn’t show [my penis] in the film. It was not like I wanted to show the world myself naked.
I’ve seen people saying it was an example of you peacocking.
I’m with a bunch of dudes. There was no woman on the entire production. You grow pretty close with a group of guys.
Why do you think they chose to include it?

You should ask them. It wasn’t my decision. I wasn’t part of the process. We had lawyers reach out to them after I had heard that it had happened, pleading for them to remove it. If it was the case that I was peacocking, I wouldn’t have asked them to take it out.
And what’s Elizabeth’s opinion of that scene?

She hasn’t seen the movie, but she felt strongly about it. She’s a pretty traditional person and felt that it’s a violation of our intimacy. But for me, there’s a lot of embarrassment associated with everyone you know and their moms and the kids’ parents at drop-off having seen this.
Did I consent to them filming me? Yes. Did I consent to them showing it to the world? No. I would expect them to blur things.
But as the film goes on, there are other scenes that are harder to explain away. Are there any that really horrified you?

They were really circumstances of the situation that I’m going through. I’m not a single parent, but I am the only person that is physically with my kids five days a week and I’m raising them more or less alone. And Liz is the most incredible partner given the circumstances. She wrote two letters a day to the kids every day for the first two years she was in prison, two letters to me every day. She’s written over 3,000 letters over the course of the time she’s in prison. They are really intricate. She’ll cut up nature magazine articles that are relevant for the kids and then do these beautiful illustrations and teach them lessons through them and we read them every night.

But I’m the person who’s carrying the load here and driving them out every weekend and building a business. And I moved them away from my family in San Diego to Texas so we could all be together. So I think [people need] to understand the frustrations or the anger, which certainly exists at a system in which I feel like my wife is 100 percent innocent and wrongfully incarcerated. I certainly have frustrations.

Where I did start to get a little, I don’t know, concerned about you is a sequence where you talk about, first of all, always carrying a gun with you. Then you say that you “have vengeance in your heart.”
What was going on when you said that? Why did you say it?

Look, there’s many things that I said over the course of three and a half years that I would word so differently. There’s things that I’m embarrassed about saying or that I wish I had not said altogether. But I wasn’t thinking [at the time] about everything I said on camera. I was trying my best to open up all of me, including the bad parts in those moments of anger, sadness and frustration.

The start of filming was April 24, 2023. That was a long time ago, and I’ve grown a lot as a person over that period of time. If there’s things that I’m not embarrassed about having said three and a half years ago, then I haven’t grown enough.
Where did you see the movie, by the way? Were you with an audience?
I was, yeah. They refused to show it to me before it came out.
Did people in the audience recognize it was you?
No. No, they didn’t. I came in right before it started. I went to the opening showtime of opening day here in Austin with a friend and her mom.
I happened to be in Chicago on opening weekend, and I went to see it. It was a packed theater, and they were quite vocal.

Yeah, it was strange to see people laughing at things that I didn’t think were particularly funny. It was strange to be part of an audience where there’s an audience sentiment about something that you don’t also share, or [about which] you have more context and understanding.
In the film, when Amanda Seyfried, whose name I now know how to pronounce because of the film…
But before she even meets you, based on the footage she sees, she’s very vocal about the fact that she doesn’t like you, she doesn’t trust you, and she thinks you’re a bad influence on your wife.
Yeah, that was very strange to see.

I heard women behind me in Chicago cheering her on and clapping and saying “exactly,” as if she voiced what they had been thinking all along. Amanda becomes an avatar for everyone who doesn’t like you while they’re watching the movie. She recently doubled and tripled down on that, telling Rolling Stone that when she finally met you, she thought worse of you. How do you respond to that?

I’ve heard she was going through a lot in her life at the time in which this was being filmed, so I can understand why she’d view our relationship through a different lens than reality. I’d also say that she’s never spent any time with me and Liz together, and what she saw was not raw footage. She saw the edit that the audience saw.
And by “going through” things, you mean her own divorce?

I don’t know. I see a lot of headlines. I’d rather not comment on specifics. What I can say is Elizabeth and I have been through enormous challenges that people have read about — and some harder things that nobody knows about. Through that process, our relationship has only become stronger than it’s ever been. That’s a great testament to the love that we do have for each other, and it doesn’t matter much to me what other people think about it, because they don’t see it. They see small vignettes stitched together with music, being told by an A-list or B-list celebrity what to think about it.

But it’s my life and I love it. I’m super happy. I’ve got this incredible family. We’ve got this amazing tribe of people who have been through hell and back with us, who support us through every one of those challenges. And I’ve got two beautiful children that I get to spend every day with. If other people are unhappy about our relationship, I suggest that they invest more time in their own.
What’s your version of how it went down, what we saw on screen, where it gets quite contentious across the dinner table?

It made more sense to me after seeing the film, and hearing her say, “I want to break them up.” I didn’t understand her intentions [when she came over]. I thought we were extending an olive branch and saying, “Look, we’re not angry with you. We’re happy to engage. We don’t blame you for your portrayal of Liz [in The Dropout]. You’re an actress, you didn’t write the script, you didn’t develop the story, you didn’t do the research or lack thereof.”
What about this notion that she has something to gain personally from portraying Elizabeth? She won an Emmy for The Dropout, and they’re now saying she’s up for an Oscar for You Can See Everything.

Yeah. It seems there is an unwillingness to confront the reality of the consequences of playing a living person, especially when you readily admit 80 percent of it was made up. Then you say, “Well, but I’m really good at playing her and people can’t distinguish the difference between me and her.” Which is it? When confronted, you say it’s just a story, it’s entertainment, it’s just made up. Then when trying to convince Nathan to [cast you in a role], you say, “People can’t tell the difference between me and her.” I think that’s kind of an interesting and very fluid interpretation.
But back to the dinner. You’re saying when you saw the film, you realized she came in with the intention to break you two up. What prompted your remarks about Charlie Kirk and her career?

I’m not going to be able to recreate the exact exchange from years ago for you. I can tell you that this was not just a random burst of frustration. She clearly states her intention in the film and she lived up to that intention, but it obviously didn’t work.
She had a theory that you were controlling Elizabeth through — what’s the legal term that you had over her?

Power of attorney. Yeah, I think it’s important to talk about that for a minute. It shows her complete lack of understanding of the legal system. She’s like, “But she’s still alive!” Yeah, power of attorney is not relevant if somebody is dead. That is called a will. Power of attorney is unfortunately a requirement of being incarcerated, in our case. We’ve got two kids, we’re not married. If I need to make big decisions, that’s a way in which I can do so. I’ve got no ability to contact Elizabeth immediately when a decision or something needs to be made.

There’s decisions, like picking a legal team, in which she cannot meet with them until we set up the first conversations. And I need to be able to talk to them to understand, is this somebody that we want to work with or not? And there’s other examples — like her cell phone number. If I didn’t have access to her bank account or her cell phone bill, I wouldn’t be able to make the payment on her behalf.

That decision was made between Elizabeth and I over the course of months. Like the idea of being on X. The film criticizes me for speaking on her behalf, but I would point to the fact that Nathan is speaking on her behalf through the reenactments that he makes. Amanda is speaking on her behalf by voicing those words and has done so in the past. I am a third person doing it, but I’m the only person with her explicit authority and consent and knowledge. They don’t have that.
Well, once we’re on this topic, what about the whole tweet thing?

Well, that’s in part what I’m talking about. Liz and I talked about this. If you look at Liz’s profile on X, it’s remained unchanged since the first day we relaunched her X account in August of ’25. It says “founder of Theranos,” and then at the bottom it says, “mostly my words posted by others.”
We’ve been very clear about the fact that everything posted on our X account is not just her words from the very beginning. And that was a decision. We worded that purposely together.
That in itself wouldn’t bother me. But then they start showing these hostile tweets with swear words in them. And then it’s like, well, that’s a little weird. Did it strike you as weird?

Yeah, but it’s Twitter. This isn’t a State of the Union address. And you look at the examples that are given, it’s like in response to somebody asking for the 10th time if you can show them your feet and if you’re starting an OnlyFans account or if you’re going to start a crypto token.
Right. But you could just ignore that. Especially because she is a former CEO and is currently incarcerated.

I am not an expert at this stuff. Do I wish I would have hired some masterful team to help do this properly? Absolutely. But I was doing the best I can. I certainly made mistakes throughout the process.

There’s some element of shitposting and joking about these things. You have to remember the environment on X is where politicians and the White House press secretary or White House chief of communication or lots of powerful people who have really important positions are using similar language because of the audience and because of where it’s being said. They would not say that in a press conference. They would not say that in a shareholder letter. I think the context is important to remember.

I think it’s kind of ironic that there’s so much of a focus on me saying “F— you” to somebody. And then in the film, they’re recreating something that absolutely did not happen categorically, recreating a scene suggesting that Elizabeth and I are jumping up and down saying “we got the fucking money.”
[The interview pauses for Evans to take a call from Holmes.]
What’s the frequency of her calling?
She has 510 minutes a month on the phone, which is split between me and everyone else. If you go one second over, then it takes a whole minute from you.
Before she called, you had brought up the recreation of the pizza party negotiation with A24. So tell me, what were we misled with there? What didn’t happen?

The entire thing. Nathan says something in the film to the effect of “we had to move quickly, so we started filming before they had signed an appearance release and they refused to sign anything before we had this meeting in Los Angeles at one of his friends’ houses.”
Was there any meeting with any A24 executive?
Yes, there were. There were two senior people from A24.
Was one of them [A24 CEO] Daniel Katz?

No, not that senior. We’re not that big of a deal. It was at my friend’s house, but it was a one-story house. So this whole idea that Liz goes upstairs or something, I know it seems like a small detail, but I was at the house the other night. There’s no pretending like you’re in a completely separate room or hiding behind doors. That’s completely fictitious.
The way it’s depicted in the film is that it’s not clear when she stepped away from the table if she knew or didn’t know that you were about to ask for a percentage of the film’s profits.

On April 16, 2023, Nathan and Lance came down to San Diego. The way in which we had connected with them was through one of the producers on the project who went to high school with some of my friends. I knew him from college. His name is Jack Davis. It’s not a mystery.

It was my idea to make a movie. This was not something that she was planning to do or was really thinking about. I had spoken to a lot of different people about this — maybe 10 different documentary filmmakers and people that I thought could help tell the story. A24 was one of those groups. That introduction had come through Jack.

So Nathan and Lance then come down to San Diego on April 16, which is depicted in the film as a recreation in which Nathan is talking about David Blaine. That actually happened. On April 18, A24 made its first financial offer. On April 19, we met again in Los Angeles at my friend’s house. I wanted Nathan and Lance to know that that was on the table. On April 21, that’s the first documented transmission of an appearance release. On April 22, commercial terms, including the backend, were agreed to. Then it was handed over to the lawyers. We signed the releases a few weeks later.
So there was never a conversation where Fielder objected and said, “You can’t make a proper documentary if you’re getting paid?”

I do recall them saying, “This is atypical,” but it was not a big deal. I mean, the entire conversation maybe lasted two minutes, and they immediately said, “OK.” And then from there, it was just handed off to the team. And then we started filming on April 24.

But this idea that we were “holding up” signing an appearance release and they had already started filming is completely made up. If they didn’t think it was ethical or if they didn’t think it was fair or if they thought it was improper, they could have walked away from it.
A big thing is made in the film of her saying, “I’m not getting paid for this.”
She was not. I was. So what Liz said was true. What she said is, “I am not profiting in any way from this.” We are completely financially distinct. We are not married. We keep our assets separate.

It was the most stressful period of our life by far. [When they brought it up again three years later,] it was really hard for me to remember what Liz knew, what I knew, what the lawyers handled, what they told me after the fact. I couldn’t remember clearly, and I still don’t. I answered to the best of my ability.

They could have very easily just not made the movie. Instead they attempt to villainize me in that negotiation and recreation, and I think it takes up way too much of the movie, and I think it’s just so uninteresting.
There’s a title card at the end, a chyron, that says you relinquished your piece of the backend. Is that true?
When did you relinquish it?

They said “shortly after filming.” I can check the exact dates, but it was maybe five months ago. It suggests that I knew filming was completed. I didn’t. I thought that they were going to continue filming [past Elizabeth’s release].

They said that it would help the project. Time and time again, when there’s things that I really didn’t want to do that they said would be helpful for making a better movie and helping people see Liz more clearly, I made those sacrifices or decisions to help the project.
I have to be honest, I’m surprised you capitulated to that. You seem like a stubborn guy.
I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it.
Did you consult with her before you made that decision?

She was OK with neither of us getting paid from the very beginning. I mean, she didn’t have a strong opinion one way or another. Her problems are so much bigger than this and she really doesn’t care about money. I’m a little bit more of a realist. At the time in which these things were negotiated, I’m a single dad with two kids whose best friend’s about to be sent to prison. And at that time I didn’t have a job. I’m trying to provide for my family and I’m really scared about what’s to come.

Could we talk about the prison sequence at the end of the film? Let me ask about something kind of silly, but that I’ve seen debated, which is in the last shot of the film you’re seen sharing or eating from the bag of turkey jerky that Nathan supposedly bought for her. I’ve seen it interpreted in different ways. One is that you’re eating her turkey jerky and how selfish could you be?

That just shows how people want to see me. The machines have a lot of every item in them. I’ve got a credit card and I’ve probably spent tens of thousands of dollars on nuts and snacks over the course of the last three and a half years that we were there. I can tell you what I think happened, which is ironic because the turkey jerky’s name is Think. I actually got reached out to by the CEO of the turkey jerky company telling me, “Thank you. Our sales have increased so much and this is awesome. I really appreciate it.” And then they tried to drop off a big box of turkey jerky at a place that used to be our office.

She loves E0 on the vending machine all the way to the left, and she loves the nuts, which are E9 all the way to the right, because they have banana chips in them. I can remember a handful of times over that period that Liz requested turkey jerky, just a handful.

E0 is a different type of trail mix that has some pieces of dehydrated fruit in it. So I know the system well. Another important detail is none of the vending machines have clocks on them. I checked again last weekend. None of them have clocks on them. Nathan says he saw the time on the vending machine. That’s impossible.
