items.title: Hayley Atwell Of 'Much Ado About Nothing' On Her 4 Favorite Plays & Musicals
items.description: Callback With Hayley Atwell
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Callback With Hayley Atwell
Ahead of her Broadway debut opposite Tom Hiddleston, the actor reflects on the magic of live theater and the performances that have made her fall in love with it.

Hayley Atwell is an accomplished veteran of the London stage, but now, the actor — perhaps best known for her portrayal of Agent Peggy Carter in the Marvel Cinematic Universe — is making her Broadway debut, and she’s ready to party. Or at least throw a damn good one.

“We’re here to essentially host the audience in having an amazing party,” the actor, 44, says of the Shakespearean comedy Much Ado About Nothing, which opens Nov. 19 at the Winter Garden Theatre after a successful West End run. “We get to do it again, but in this completely different environment and a different kind of audience, which I expect will be even more raucous than in London.”

Co-starring fellow MCU star Tom Hiddleston as Benedick, the play is directed by Jamie Lloyd, who has been praised for his reimagining of works including Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Blvd. and Evita, the latter of which moves into the Winter Garden after Much Ado wraps up on Jan. 10. Much Ado received accolades in London for its high-energy campiness (picture lots of pink confetti and strobe lights) — something Atwell is here for.

She describes the production as “visceral, juicy, and gorgeous” while remaining rooted in the text. “The way [Jamie Lloyd] pitched it to me when he first offered me the role was, ‘It’s a massive party,’” she says. “Everyone’s having a great time. Some people drink a little bit too much. They stay a little bit too long. They have some feelings. Someone takes things too personally. Arguments break out. Confusions occur. We flirt with the wrong person.”

She’s also heartened by what she sees as a growing desire for the collective experience that you can only get by attending live events like a Broadway play. “When you have human beings in a room, it feels different. We can get more of a sense of each other when we’re sharing body language and just the molecules in the room changing because someone new has walked in or walked out,” she says. “That makes plays a very visceral, kind of immersive experience.
“I want to feel more alive and more connected and less numbed out from the sort of content that can kind of bore into my eyeballs that I realize I didn’t really consciously consent to.”
Ahead, Atwell shares five plays and musicals that have done just that for her.
Her first selection is August Osage County, Tracy Letts’ 2008 Pulitzer-winning dark comedy. The play follows a fractured Oklahoma family that is forced to reunite when their patriarch goes missing.

“I love plays that have a really strong ensemble, and there is a sense of real company on stage that have worked together intimately, intricately over a rehearsal period to understand the heart of the play,” she says. “But also understand their own dynamics within each other and how you always have to keep the ball in the air, and that the performance is only as strong as the people that you play with.”

Atwell learned the power of a strong ensemble during a run of Dry Powder in London. Her character, a private equity partner, often had to interrupt her casemates. “I remember coming in really hot, beginning a monologue and then realizing within about the first three lines of dialogue that I’d skipped three pages. And my fellow actors are looking at me and the terror in their eyes,” she says. “I had to keep on going and get to the end of my monologue and then try and work out what we needed to then improvise to backtrack to make sure the audience were at the same place in the script that we were.”
Sunday in the Park with George

Her second pick is Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s 1984 musical Sunday in the Park with George, which follows a fictionalized Georges Seurat. Atwell first saw the play in the West End revival starring Daniel Evans and Jenna Russell nearly 20 years ago.

“That musical encapsulates the creative process, the struggle for an artist’s identity, the struggle to have an artistic career and to maintain personal relationships. You can be selfish and also generous and fully focused on a creative career, and yet the cost of that can sometimes mean that personal relationships. In this musical, that’s where they start to falter,” she says. “And I find the tension of that really beautiful.”

Her third show is The Rocky Horror Show, the 1973 cult-classic rock musical by Richard O’Brien. “I saw it first when I was a child, probably way too young, didn’t really understand a lot of the ideas behind it, but I just loved the energy and I loved particularly Tim Curry’s performance — so magnetic,” she says. “And for me, it was about freedom. And although it’s also like a homage to the B movies and sci-fi films of back in the day, it’s very camp and it’s ridiculous and it’s silly and it’s weird and it’s bizarre.”

Her fourth selection is Shakespeare’s Hamlet, which Atwell fell in love with during a 2018 Robert Icke adaptation starring Andrew Scott. “I saw Andrew Scott playing Hamlet four times — in a play I know very well! And yet when I saw Andrew do it, I felt like I was hearing it for the first time and I felt like I was hearing it made up then and there,” she says. “He talked so openly to the audience. He felt like he was talking to every single individual in the auditorium.”

Her final pick is Medea, which Atwell saw starring Helen McCrory at the National Theatre in 2014. The play, written by Euripides in 431 BCE, tells the story of Medea, a sorceress who sacrifices her children in an act of revenge against her husband.

“Medea I think is one of the hardest roles in the canon for women to play because I think it’s one of the major taboos of our world and our society,” she says. “The idea that a woman could harm her child or her children — and how to have that as your protagonist, how a woman has to portray someone who does the absolute unspeakable, unthinkable, and that we’re having to want to engage with that feels an impossible task.”

Atwell feels McCrory handled the responsibility of Medea with grace. “Helen had, for me, as an actor such formidable courage in exposing human failings and human pain,” she says, “and how great pain and things being done to an individual can have such a devastating effect on the psyche, that then they become capable of doing the unspeakable.”

items.title: Your Horoscope This Week: November 15 To 21
items.description: R29 babes, welcome to the first week in November where it finally feels like things are moving forward again! With Mercury and Venus having officially ended their retrogrades in Scorpio and Libra, respectively, the second half of November is shaping up to have
items.author: Dossé-Via Trenou
paragraphs: R29 babes, welcome to the first week in November where it finally feels like things are moving forward again! With Mercury and Venus having officially ended their retrogrades in Scorpio and Libra, respectively, the second half of November is shaping up to have a considerably different flavor than the first. We’re entering the final week of Scorpio Season with greater clarity, passion, momentum, and sensitivity to what we truly want. After spending the past month and a half reviewing our values, relationships, and needs from every possible angle, we can finally start putting those realizations into practice. There’s a sense of relief in the air, even if we’re still figuring out exactly what comes next.

As the week begins, the moon is in Aquarius, offering us a healthy dose of emotional detachment after all the deep-diving Scorpio Season has encouraged us to do. We may find it easier to look at our circumstances objectively, laugh at situations we were taking a little too seriously, or simply enjoy being in the present moment. Then, on November 17th, the moon enters sensitive Pisces, eventually harmonizing with the Scorpio Sun on the 19th. This watery energy encourages us to be more vulnerable and honest about the realizations we’ve had throughout Mercury and Venus retrograde. Now that both planets are direct, it may feel easier to express our truth with grace and sensitivity while remaining open to hearing someone else’s perspective. Conversations that once felt intimidating could become surprisingly healing, especially when we approach them with curiosity rather than assumptions.

By the weekend, the moon enters fiery Aries just as Scorpio Season prepares to come to a close, giving us a particularly Martian burst of energy. Both Aries and Scorpio are ruled by Mars, which is currently moving through bold, expressive Leo. Translation? We may suddenly feel ready to put ourselves out there after weeks of being more introspective than usual. Maybe you finally post that photo you’ve been sitting on, experiment with a new look, tell your crush how you feel, or shoot your shot with a creative opportunity. Whatever form it takes, this weekend encourages us to embrace a little more courage, spontaneity, and visibility. We’ve spent plenty of time getting to know ourselves on a deeper level this Scorpio Season. Now it’s time to let the world see more of who we’ve become.
Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

Aries, now that Mercury and Venus are both moving forward, you may be surprised by how much easier it feels to get people on the same page. With Mercury direct in your shared-resources realm and Venus direct in your partnership zone, the first full week of both planets moving forward is ideal for strengthening the relationships that help you thrive. Perhaps you and a romantic partner are finally figuring out how to divide responsibilities more fairly, or you’re discovering that a professional collaboration works best when everyone brings something different to the table. There’s also an opportunity to become more comfortable receiving support, whether that’s financial, emotional, or practical. You don’t always have to be the one figuring everything out, Aries. Let yourself experience what happens when other people show up for you, too.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, you may feel increasingly aware of how much your priorities have evolved since late October. Rather than spending another week analyzing every emotion, take advantage of the Aquarius moon early in the week to reconnect with friends, exchange ideas, and enjoy experiences that get you out of your own head. By the weekend, the moon enters your sign, giving you an extra boost of confidence and spontaneity. With your ruling planet Mars in Leo energizing your creativity and pleasure zone, this could be the perfect time to make a bold first move,  attend an exciting event, or share something you’ve been working on. End Scorpio Season by reminding yourself how good it feels to have fun, Aries. You’ve earned it.

Taurus, your calendar may be filling up again, but this time you’re getting a lot more selective about what deserves a spot on it. With Mercury now direct in your partnership zone and your ruling planet Venus moving forward in your work and wellness realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a refreshing shift in how you manage your commitments. Maybe you’re establishing better boundaries with clients, delegating tasks to a colleague, or realizing that a professional relationship could become much more productive with a few adjustments. You may also find yourself enjoying your daily routine more, especially if you’ve been experimenting with a new fitness class, co-working space, or work schedule. The goal is to create a lifestyle that actually feels good to live, Taurus. Being booked and busy is only cute when you’re enjoying yourself.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon highlights your career and public-image zone, making the beginning of the week especially promising for professional visibility. This could be a great time to present an idea, update your portfolio, or reach out to someone whose work you admire. Then, as the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your social life gets a boost, and you may find yourself making spontaneous plans with friends or meeting people who share your interests. By the weekend, the Aries Moon encourages you to slow down and recharge behind the scenes. You’ve got plenty of exciting things brewing, Taurus, but you don’t need to attend every function or respond to every invitation. A little JOMO (joy of missing out) might be exactly what you need before Sag Season begins.

Gemini, your work-life balance is getting a much-needed software update, and this version might actually be worth keeping. With your ruling planet Mercury now direct in  Scorpio and Venus moving forward in Libra, the first full week of both planets being direct brings a refreshing combination of productivity and pleasure. You may notice that your relationships with coworkers are improving, that you’re getting more recognition for your contributions, or that a project you’ve been working on is finally becoming enjoyable again. Venus in your creativity and romance zone could also inspire you to bring more personality into your professional life, whether that’s pitching an unconventional idea, adding humor to your content, or connecting with colleagues outside the usual work setting. Who says being productive has to be boring, Gemini? You might accomplish more when you’re actually having fun.

As Scorpio Season comes to a close, the Aquarius Moon at the beginning of the week activates your travel and adventure realm, making this an excellent time to explore something outside your usual routine. You could discover a fascinating podcast, sign up for a workshop, or start planning a trip that gives you something exciting to look forward to. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your career takes center stage, and you may find yourself receiving attention from someone influential or feeling inspired to take on more responsibility. Then the Aries Moon over the weekend  energizes your friendship zone, making it a great time to organize a gathering or reconnect with people who bring out your adventurous side. Let curiosity lead the way. You never know which conversation could open your next door.

Cancer, your main-character energy is making a comeback, and this time you’ve got the confidence to back it up. With Mercury now direct in your creativity and fame zone and Venus moving forward in your home realm, you may feel increasingly comfortable  sharing more of your personality with the world. Perhaps you’re ready to film that video you’ve been overthinking, submit your work to a publication, or invite friends over for a gathering that shows off your hosting skills. You could also find inspiration in your family history, childhood memories, or cultural roots and incorporate those influences into something creative. There’s something powerful about letting people experience your perspective, Cancer, especially when you’ve spent so much time keeping your best ideas to yourself.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your intimacy and shared-resources zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for tackling practical matters involving joint finances, subscriptions, or financial commitments. Then, when the moon enters fellow Water sign Pisces on the 17th, your appetite for adventure grows. You may feel inspired to research a destination you’ve always wanted to visit, explore a new neighborhood, or connect with someone from a different cultural background. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your career sector, giving you the courage to take a professional risk. Whether you’re pitching yourself for an opportunity, reaching out to a potential mentor, or announcing an exciting project, don’t underestimate how far a little initiative could take you. The spotlight looks good on you, Cancer.

Leo, the cosmic traffic jam is finally clearing, and you’re ready to get back in the driver’s seat. With Mercury now direct in your home zone and Venus moving forward in your communication realm, the first full week of both planets being direct brings a welcome sense of ease to your everyday interactions. You may find yourself laughing more with relatives, making exciting plans with siblings, or finally enjoying a living space you’ve spent weeks trying to organize. This could also be a great time to host a dinner party, explore a new neighborhood, or invite someone over who’s been asking to see you. After all the retrograde back-and-forth, there’s something refreshing about making plans without needing a Plan B, C, and D. Let yourself enjoy the simpler pleasures of life, Leo.

As Scorpio Season enters its final stretch, the Aquarius Moon highlights your partnership zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for quality time with someone special or an exciting one-on-one collaboration. Then, when the Moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your intimacy realm gets activated, encouraging deeper conversations about your desires, finances, or future plans. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your travel and adventure zone, and with Mars in your sign, you may feel an irresistible  urge to get out of town, try something spontaneous, or say yes to an experience you’d usually overthink. A last-minute getaway or an unexpected invitation could be exactly the change of scenery you need.

Congratulations, Virgo — your ruling planet Mercury is finally behaving again! With  Mercury moving forward in Scorpio and Venus direct in Libra, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a noticeable improvement to your communication and financial affairs. Maybe an overdue payment finally arrives, a client responds to your proposal, or a conversation that previously went in circles suddenly becomes productive. You may also feel more confident promoting your work, reaching out to potential customers, or sharing your expertise with people who could benefit from it. If you’ve been considering teaching a class, offering a service, or monetizing a skill, this is an encouraging time to test the waters. Your ideas have value, Virgo, and people may be more receptive to them than you expect.

As Scorpio Season winds down, the Aquarius Moon energizes your work and wellness zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for trying a new productivity tool, switching up your workout routine, or finding a more enjoyable rhythm with your responsibilities. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your partnership realm takes center stage, and you may find yourself feeling especially appreciative of the people who make your life easier. Plan a date, celebrate a friend’s accomplishment, or spend quality time with someone whose company you genuinely enjoy. Then the Aries  Moon over the weekend activates your intimacy zone, potentially inspiring a bold conversation about a joint goal or financial commitment. You’ve spent enough time analyzing every possibility, Virgo. Give yourself permission to enjoy the progress you’re making.

Libra, your magnetism is back, your confidence is rising, and the universe may finally be ready to give you your flowers. After weeks of Venus retrograde in your sign testing your patience, the first full week of your ruling planet moving direct could feel like a breath of fresh air. You may notice people being more receptive to your ideas, compliments coming your way, or opportunities that previously seemed out of reach suddenly becoming available. With Mercury also direct in your money and self-worth zone, this could be an especially promising time to negotiate a raise, attract new clients, or treat yourself to something you’ve been saving up for. If you’ve been feeling overlooked or under-appreciated lately, the tide may be turning in your favor. Enjoy being pursued, celebrated, and recognized for everything you bring to the table.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your romance, creativity, and pleasure zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for flirting,  socializing, or getting back into a hobby that makes you feel alive. Then, when the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your wellness and daily-routine realm gets a boost, encouraging you to find a healthier balance between productivity and play. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your partnership zone, potentially bringing an exciting date, a spontaneous invitation, or a breakthrough in a close relationship. With  Mars in Leo energizing your friendship realm, someone in your social circle could even play matchmaker. Say yes to being seen, Libra. Your charm is doing some serious overtime this week.

Scorpio, is it just us, or does it feel like your birthday season is finally hitting its stride?  With Mercury now direct in your sign and Venus moving forward in Libra, this could be the most energized and confident you’ve felt all Scorpio Season. After weeks of second-guessing your decisions or feeling like you had to explain yourself a hundred different ways, you may find that trusting your instincts comes naturally again. You could feel inspired to refresh your appearance, announce a personal project, or make a decision you’ve been sitting on for far too long. Venus direct in your spirituality and solitude realm also brings a welcome sense of emotional ease, helping you feel more comfortable with where you are in life. There’s something incredibly attractive about someone who knows what they want, Scorpio, and that energy is radiating from you right now.

As your season approaches its grand finale, the Aquarius Moon begins the week in your home and family zone, making it a great time to celebrate with loved ones or enjoy the comforts of your personal sanctuary. Then, when the Moon enters fellow Water sign Pisces on the 17th, your romance, creativity, and pleasure realm comes alive. A flirtatious encounter, artistic breakthrough, or spontaneous celebration could remind you just how much fun life can be. By the weekend, the Aries Moon energizes your wellness zone, while Mars in Leo lights up your career realm. You may feel motivated to make a bold professional move, share an accomplishment, or step into the spotlight in a way that feels long overdue. End your season with a bang, Scorpio. The world is ready for more of you!

Sag, your birthday season is just one week away, and you’ve hit the cosmic jackpot by getting to experience it with both Mercury and Venus direct! After weeks of retrograde reflection, the universe is practically rolling out the red carpet for your comeback. With Mercury moving forward in your spirituality realm and Venus direct in your friendship zone, you may already notice your enthusiasm for life returning. Friends could start reaching out with invitations, exciting group plans may come together, or you might find yourself dreaming up a birthday celebration that’s a little extra this year. And why shouldn’t it be? This is your cosmic pregame, Sag! Enjoy reconnecting with your favorite people, making plans for the adventures ahead, and feeling that familiar spark of optimism returning.

As Scorpio Season wraps up, however, there’s still something delicious about enjoying a little hibernation before the festivities begin. The Aquarius Moon early in the week activates your communication zone, making it a great time to clear your inbox, organize your space, or handle errands you’ve been postponing. Then, when the moon enters  Pisces on the 17th, your home and family realm takes center stage, encouraging you to rest, enjoy homemade meals, or spend quality time with loved ones. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your romance and pleasure zone, giving you an early taste of the fiery energy that’s about to define your season. You might feel inspired to dress up, flirt, dance, or do something spontaneous just because you can. Your birthday season is almost here, Sag. Get your beauty sleep now, because things are about to get exciting!

Capricorn, the universe is finally returning your calls, and some of them could lead to opportunities worth celebrating. With Mercury now direct in your friendship zone and Venus moving forward in your career realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a refreshing wave of professional and social momentum. Perhaps a former colleague reaches out with an opportunity, someone recommends you for a project, or a connection you’ve been nurturing finally leads to something tangible. Venus direct in Libra can also make it easier to win people over professionally, especially if you’re presenting an idea, interviewing for a position, or building relationships with influential people. You’ve spent enough time waiting for the right moment. Your reputation and connections could be opening doors for you now, so enjoy the recognition!

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your money and self-worth zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for reviewing your financial progress or rewarding yourself for a recent accomplishment. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your communication realm gets a boost, and you may find yourself enjoying spontaneous conversations, neighborhood outings, or an invitation to connect with someone interesting. Then the Aries Moon over the weekend lights up your home and family zone, inspiring you to refresh your living space, host a gathering, or tackle a domestic project you’ve been putting off. With Mars in Leo energizing your shared resources realm, you might even find a creative way to split costs or make a home improvement more affordable. Let yourself enjoy the fruits of your labor, Capricorn. Life can be productive and pleasurable at the same time.

Aquarius, your comeback era is looking pretty promising, and people are starting to take notice. With Mercury now direct in your career zone and Venus moving forward in your travel and expansion realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring exciting opportunities to broaden your horizons. Perhaps you’re invited to speak at an event, collaborate with someone overseas, or share your expertise with an audience you hadn’t previously considered. If you’ve been dreaming of working remotely from another country, applying for a fellowship, or taking your career in a more adventurous direction, you may feel increasingly optimistic about your options. Venus direct in fellow Air sign Libra also makes networking across cultures and communities especially rewarding. Your world is getting bigger, Aquarius, and your talents deserve to travel far!

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the moon begins in your sign, giving you an extra boost of confidence, charisma, and emotional clarity. This is a great time to prioritize yourself, refresh your look, or initiate something you’ve been excited about. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your money and self-worth zone gets activated, encouraging you to explore ways to make your talents more profitable or celebrate a recent financial win. By the weekend, the Aries Moon energizes your communication realm, making it a fantastic time for spontaneous outings, lively conversations, or sharing something bold on social media. With Mars in Leo activating your partnership zone, someone special could even encourage you to take a leap you wouldn’t have considered on your own. Let yourself be seen, Aquarius. You have plenty worth celebrating!

Pisces, the universe is finally giving you the green light to explore, expand, and enjoy  yourself again. With Mercury now direct in your travel and adventure zone and Venus moving forward in your intimacy realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could make some of your bigger dreams feel more attainable. Maybe you’re discovering a scholarship, finding a more affordable way to travel, or receiving financial support that helps you pursue an exciting opportunity. You could also feel more comfortable discussing money with a partner or exploring ways to combine resources toward a shared goal. After weeks of reviewing your options, there’s something refreshing about realizing you have more possibilities than you initially thought. Dream big, Pisces. You may be pleasantly surprised by how much support is available when you ask for it.

As Scorpio Season comes to a close, the Aquarius Moon begins the week in your solitude and spirituality zone, encouraging you to recharge your batteries and enjoy some peaceful time away from the noise. Then, when the moon enters your sign on the 17th, the energy shifts beautifully in your favor. You may feel more magnetic, emotionally connected, and inspired to do something special for yourself, whether that’s booking a massage, going on a date, or spending time near the water. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your money and self-worth realm, potentially inspiring a spontaneous purchase, a new income idea, or the confidence to ask for  what you deserve. With Mars in Leo energizing your work and wellness zone, you could also feel motivated to invest in something that makes your everyday life more enjoyable. You’ve spent enough time weighing every possibility, Pisces. Let yourself experience some of the joy you’ve been planning for!

items.title: Shunning people who ‘look homeless’ is an aesthetic injustice | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirement
items.author: Giacomo Floris
paragraphs: Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirements of good health. They are unable to fit in and participate in the normal activities of society, such as getting a job, and they are pushed to live in dangerous and socially deprived areas. But material deprivation and social exclusion are not the only injustices suffered by unhoused individuals. They also face aesthetic injustice. This is a widely neglected source of harm associated with homelessness, which seriously impedes the ability of unhoused people to live a life of dignity and to better their circumstances.

To understand the nature of aesthetic injustice, it will be helpful to start with the more general notion of justice. Justice concerns how people should be treated, and political philosophers often say that justice requires everyone to be treated with equal respect and concern. ‘Each person,’ wrote the philosopher John Rawls in A Theory of Justice (1971), ‘possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.’ An injustice, therefore, occurs when an individual is treated in a way that is incompatible with the respect and concern that is owed to them as an equal. Harming someone is unjust because it fails to express appropriate concern for their wellbeing. Exercising arbitrary power over an individual is unjust because it violates the equal freedom that everyone is entitled to.

Aesthetic injustice is a specific kind of injustice: it consists in the wrongful treatment of individuals based on how they look. In our society, many people benefit or suffer from aesthetic injustice. As the economist Daniel Hamermesh argued in his book Beauty Pays (2011), individuals perceived as physically attractive typically command higher salaries and occupy more prestigious positions. He estimated that the best-looking people, over the course of their careers, make around $250,000 more than their less attractive colleagues. Similarly, as Sean Talamas and colleagues found, attractiveness is strongly correlated with perceived competence and intelligence – despite bearing almost no relationship to actual performance. And as the philosopher Kate Manne showed in Unshrinking (2024), fat people are often bullied, discriminated against and marginalised. These are all instances of aesthetic injustice: individuals are treated as more or less worthy of respect and concern by virtue of their outward appearance.

The outward appearance of unhoused individuals is often a reflection of their social condition. Due to the lack of sufficient resources and reliable shelter, unhoused individuals typically display signs of deterioration, such as unkempt hair and damaged skin. Their clothing is frequently dirty and ill-fitting. Additionally, many unhoused individuals exhibit visible signs of substance use disorders, such as track marks on the arms and dilated blood vessels. In the sociologist Erving Goffman’s classic study Stigma (1963), he names these aesthetic traits ‘stigma symbols’. A stigma, for Goffman, is ‘an attribute that is deeply discrediting’. By possessing these aesthetic stigmas, unhoused individuals are placed at the very bottom of the aesthetic hierarchy. They are regarded as disgusting elements of the urban landscape, whose presence in prime urban areas – areas that are desirable due to their location or historical significance – is unacceptable.

To appreciate this, consider the wide range of strategies that are adopted by many cities in order to exclude unhoused individuals from prime urban areas, such as anti-homelessness laws and ‘hostile’ architecture. Unhoused individuals are likely to be fined for loitering in commercial districts, while they are permitted to remain in socially deprived neighbourhoods. As the legal scholar Robert Ellickson put it, ‘[a] bum on a Skid Row sidewalk would never hear [“move along”] because he was exactly where the cop wanted him’ – that is, away from profitable business districts or valuable residential areas. Similarly, ‘anti-sleep’ benches and ‘ground spikes’ are widespread in parks and main commercial streets, whereas they are nowhere to be found in socially deprived areas. These measures illustrate how negative aesthetic judgments about unhoused individuals are institutionalised through public policy and urban design.

Aesthetic injustice against unhoused people is sustained and compounded by the fact that they are deprived of their capacity for self-presentation, that is, the ability to exercise reasonable control over how they present themselves to others. This is because unhoused individuals lack ‘aesthetic resources’: the materials, tools and conditions that either directly contribute to a person’s aesthetic properties or are constitutive components of them. Without access to showers, unhoused individuals are unable to maintain personal cleanliness. Without grooming products, such as soap and razors, they’re unable to keep tidy their hair, skin and facial features. As a result, unhoused people cannot shape how they present themselves to others. They cannot but look homeless.

The deprivation of the capacity for self-presentation is unjust for two reasons. First, it reinforces the social exclusion of unhoused individuals. Employers typically screen out candidates whose appearance departs from the aesthetic norms of a ‘serious’ candidate – unkempt hair, wrinkled or dirty clothing, the absence of basic grooming – whatever their actual qualifications. The injustice is therefore doubled: unhoused individuals are denied the resources needed to present themselves as employable and are then penalised for lacking a presentation they were never given the means to produce.
They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold

The philosopher Andrea Sangiovanni points to the second reason it is unjust. In his book Humanity without Dignity (2017), he contends that developing and maintaining an integral sense of self requires the fundamental ability to exercise some degree of control over how we are perceived. That is, we need to be able to manage ‘what is inner and what is outer, what is presented and what is hidden’. In intimate relationships, for example, we may choose to reveal personal vulnerabilities, while professional relationships usually demand a more formal, public-facing image.

It’s morally necessary that we have the means of choosing what to reveal, and to whom, and how to present ourselves. Wearing a suit conveys professionalism, while casual clothing indicates approachability. Wearing a kippah represents an individual’s affiliation with the Jewish community, while wearing a hijab is associated with Muslim identity. Due to the lack of adequate aesthetic resources, unhoused individuals cannot shape and control how they present themselves to others. They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold, as most people routinely do. The inability to determine one’s outward appearance is, therefore, a violation of unhoused individuals’ status as equal, self-presenting persons – in Sangiovanni’s words, ‘as beings who have a say in how [they] are to be seen by others’.

How should a just society address the aesthetic injustices suffered by unhoused individuals? To start with, the social norms of respectable appearance – that is, the aesthetic standards that determine what counts as an acceptable way of presenting oneself in public spaces – should be revised. This is not to say, of course, that all people must be regarded as equally beautiful. Rather, it is to say that no one should be excluded from prime public spaces based solely on their appearance (provided that they satisfy very minimal aesthetic standards, such as covering their genitalia). This would involve abolishing beautification projects aimed at removing unhoused individuals from public spaces. For example, in Ottawa, Canada, officers of the National Capital Commission (NCC) are authorised to remove unhoused individuals from parks and confiscate their belongings on the grounds that they are in violation of ‘beautification goals’. As one study reports, NCC conservation officers often ‘approach homeless people as garbage and do not distinguish between homeless people and their belongings as objects for removal from parks’. No one should be denied access to and enjoyment of public spaces because they are perceived as ugly.

However, revising social norms of respectable appearance is not sufficient. A just society should ensure not only that unhoused individuals have the right to live and exist in prime urban areas, but also that they have the resources necessary to exercise some control over how they appear to others. It is not enough to grant unhoused people access to public spaces independently of their appearance – it is also necessary to provide them with the opportunity to shape and control their appearance as a matter of respect for their status as self-presenting persons. In pursuit of this goal, there are many charities providing free haircuts to unhoused people and programmes offering new and gently used clothes, including business attire. These are the kinds of social initiatives that society should actively promote as a matter of justice rather than as a matter of charity, since everyone has the right to the resources necessary to determine how they appear to others, at least to some extent.

Hardly anyone denies that being homeless is an unjust social condition characterised by material deprivation and social exclusion. But this doesn’t capture the entirety of the injustice that unhoused people suffer. Part of the burden of being homeless is to be regarded as a disgusting element of the urban landscape whose presence in public areas is unacceptable. That burden is badly compounded by the denial of aesthetic resources. Without a shower, a razor, a change of clean clothes, unhoused individuals are denied what those lucky enough to be housed take for granted: a say in how to appear to the world. A just society owes the unhoused the right to be looked at without disgust, and the resources to decide, for themselves, how they wish to be seen.

items.title: The origins of the state are not agrarian but pastoralist | Aeon Essays
items.description: Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mob
items.author: Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene
paragraphs: Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.

No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.

As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.

Whoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.

Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga chariots project the military might of Mesopotamian cities, and the Abydos donkeys demonstrate their vital role in early Egyptian kingship. By the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, Central Eurasian nomads were entombing entire horse chariots – the high-tech, high-value war machines of their time – to honour their kings in Sintashta. Horse chariots later symbolised the power of the Shang and the Zhou; the latter deployed 4,000 chariots to overwhelm the former in 1046 BCE.
Building a state does not require grain, but does demand extrahuman transportation

‘The rider appears on the stage of history like a new breed of man’ – a centaur, as the German sociologist Alexander Rüstow put it in the 1950s. Eurasian nomads had long bred their mounts into the modern domestic horse, paving the way for an age of empires that would fundamentally reshape the world. Horses dominated human history for nearly four millennia. Even for maritime powers, horses remained key to conquest; from Carthage to the British, all relied on horses for inland expansion. Francisco Pizarro’s conquest of the Inkas is a prime illustration of the power of horses against an essentially pedestrian empire built on llama transportation. Horses also enabled the Comanche in North America to forge their empire and compete with European powers for nearly a century.

The Comanche Empire? Did they actually have grain to build a state? No, they had no grain – nor any agriculture, for that matter. Horse husbandry and bison hunting sustained their livelihood. In fact, all the Eurasian steppe powers – including the Mongols – relied on pastoralism. What they enjoyed most was an abundance of extrahuman transportation; what they lacked most was agricultural produce. Ultimately, building a state does not require grain, but it does demand extrahuman transportation.

Look at the political geography of the Roman and Mongol empires: the Romans could reach where ships could reach, and the Mongols could reach where horses could reach. The same is true of European colonial empires; it all comes down to the power of extrahuman transportation. Donkeys, horses and all other herd animals are the creations of pastoralists. Extrahuman transportation made the state and civilisation possible; this places pastoralism at the origin of the state and civilisation, and the Eurasian steppe at the centre of human history.

Yet the Sinocentric paradigm – the predominant vision of human history and civilisation with China at its centre – structurally erases extrahuman transportation and, with it, pastoralism, steppe empires and charisma from state formation, thereby negating the Eurasian steppe as the prime centre of human history. This framework shapes our current understanding of world history, leaving us with a view defined by entrapment, doom and despair. Becoming aware of this paradigm is essential if we are to break free from this bleak outlook, better comprehend the world we live in, and chart a brighter future.

While scholars critique world history for its Eurocentric bias, its conceptual framework and narrative are profoundly Sinocentric. This is because the origin of the state – and consequently the birth of civilisation – is the question that shapes our vision of world history. The latest authoritative iteration of this view is James C Scott’s Against the Grain: A Deep History of the Earliest States (2017), along with his The Art of Not Being Governed (2009). ‘The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability’ by Joram Mayshar and colleagues is its economic restatement. Scott, readers might counter, focuses almost exclusively on Mesopotamia and rarely mentions China. Yet his underlying framework actually rearticulates the paradigm established by the American Orientalist Owen Lattimore’s influential work, Inner Asian Frontiers of China (1940). Precisely for this reason, Scott not only frequently mentions ‘the loess soils along the Yellow River’, but also, directly quoting Lattimore, claims that ‘irrigation was spectacularly rewarding in the loess core of ancient China’.

Lattimore sought to legitimise the Republic of China’s claims over Mongolia, Manchukuo, Tibet and Eastern Turkestan. To this end, he advanced the grain thesis to locate the origins of statehood and civilisation in the Yellow River Valley, positioning China as the Cradle of the East. By mapping Frederick Jackson Turner’s American frontier thesis onto the region, Lattimore framed China as the civilised centre and reduced the aforementioned territories to ‘Inner Asia’ – a mere geohistorical frontier akin to the American West. In doing so, Lattimore abandoned the traditional conquest theory – a framework he had previously espoused – which held that both China’s early states and most of its subsequent empires were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors rather than indigenous dynamics. The rejection of the conquest theory was a repudiation of extrahuman transportation and pastoralism as forces that led to statehood, and an exaltation of sedentism and grain agriculture instead.
The paradigm owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence

The theory that entrenched Lattimore’s thesis in academia is Robert Carneiro’s circumscription hypothesis, published in the journal Science as ‘A Theory of the Origin of the State’ (1970). Not just conventional narratives, but a wide array of prominent thinkers – including Michael Mann, Jared Diamond, Francis Fukuyama and Yuval Noah Harari – popularised Carneiro’s theory in different guises. Even David Graeber and David Wengrow ultimately remain within this framework.

Drawing on Carneiro’s concept of circumscribed agricultural land, Mann’s The Sources of Social Power (1986) posits ecological and social cages with no ‘escape route’, while Diamond’s Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) similarly focuses on regions with ‘nowhere to flee’ to isolate the environmental conditions that generate the population pressure needed for the rise of the state. Fukuyama’s The Origins of Political Order (2011), however, is far more direct in delineating the primary conditions for pristine state formation: ‘that population needs to be physically constrained so that it increases in density’ and ‘that subjects cannot run away when coerced’. When Diamond wrote in Nature in 2002 that agricultural storable food surpluses ‘led to social stratification, political centralisation and standing armies’, he was merely rationalising the Lattimore-Carneiro population-pressure dogma as an ‘autocatalytic’ process. Harari’s Sapiens (2011), with its disease-ridden ‘luxury trap’, Scott’s The Art of Not Being Governed, along with his Against the Grain, and Graeber and Wengrow’s lamentation that ours is a species ‘enslaved to its crops’ all ultimately stem from the same grain thesis.

Indeed, the Lattimore-Carneiro framework relied on a population-pressure model, arguing that agriculture and sedentism triggered overpopulation, forcing the creation of hierarchies and states. However, Carneiro’s circumscription thesis required areas such as Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley and the Peruvian coast to be entirely overcrowded. Instead, empirical settlement surveys revealed that these areas lacked the demographic density to exhaust arable land, with some even experiencing depopulation during early state-formation. Because no population pressure existed to catalyse state formation, archaeological findings invalidated Carneiro’s theory.

Scott’s novelty lies neither in his rhetoric of ‘political crops’, nor in his laser-focused ‘circumscribed ecological niches’ of ‘alluvial or loess soils’, but rather in his theoretical sleight of hand: dynamic climatic circumscription. His fertile alluvial or loess soils mirror Carneiro’s circumscribed agricultural land, though on a minuscule scale, engineered by a millennium-long drought rather than geographic barriers. Ultimately, Scott repurposes Carneiro’s model of resource concentration – a resource-rich habitat that draws people from surrounding regions – yet he supercharges it with the driving force of drought. In sum, drought – simultaneously reconfiguring the physical terrain into a localised cage and driving populations inward – enables Scott to isolate the minuscule, 250-hectare footprint of Uruk as the circumscribed agricultural land. Scott’s model here is a clever manoeuvre to salvage the Sinocentric paradigm. That paradigm, as we shall see, owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence.

Whether climatic or geographical, the agricultural cage is inherently an anti-mobility framing that structurally erases pastoralism from the formation of the state. This erasure is, however, not just a conceptual flaw; it is written into the paradigm’s DNA, as the framework is fundamentally built against mobility, and actively argues for its exclusion. The erasure takes the form of epistemic theft by way of attributing the authorship of domestication of livestock and pastoralism to farmers, delaying the date of the advent of pastoralism through hyper-restrictive definitions, and relying on exclusionary framing. While the initial framework was a politically motivated, instrumental scheme, subsequent models have resulted from paradigmatic biases.

The question that led to this erasive framing was not the origin of the state in general, but its emergence in what is now China – specifically, whether it was indigenous or born of nomadic conquest. This issue was linked to a raging political dilemma: did Manchuria, and by extension the Daiching Empire (also known as the Qing dynasty), constitute a Chinese or an Inner Asian empire? This debate was a political question concerning the definition of China and the delineation of its territory. Specifically, should China be defined as ‘China proper’, restricted to the Ming provinces, or as ‘China imperial’, encompassing the domains of the Daiching Empire.

The controversy escalated into a heightened political crisis with the declaration of Manchukuo. Japanese scholarship argued that the Daiching Empire was an Inner Asian state that had conquered China, and that the Manchus were a distinct people deserving independence. The Chinese nationalist regime and its scholarship countered, arguing that the empire was inherently Chinese, and that Manchuria had been an integral part of China since antiquity. Meanwhile, contemporary critical scholarship essentially agreed with the Japanese view; the dominant framework for the origins of the state in China was the invasion theory, which argued that early Chinese states, as well as many subsequent empires, were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors. Crucially, until then, Lattimore himself had been a proponent of this theory.

The Republic of China was a legal fiction enabled by the Open Door policy (authored by US diplomats in 1899). Yet, this very regime claimed sovereignty over Mongolia, Manchuria, Eastern Turkestan and Tibet. By the 1930s, however, the Open Door order was in tatters: Outer Mongolia had declared independence in 1911, Tibet in 1912, and Manchukuo had broken away in 1932, absorbing Eastern Inner Mongolia. The rest of Inner Mongolia was ruled by a Japanese-allied government, while Eastern Turkestan declared independence in 1933.
Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours

Recognising the Daiching Empire as an Inner Asian state meant forfeiting China’s claim over all of these regions, stripping the regime of what Lattimore estimated at nearly two-thirds of its claimed territory. Worse still for the West, the Soviet Union was poised to become the ultimate beneficiary – an outcome the regime and its primary architect, the US, were determined to prevent. The regime had to ensure that its territory emerged as inherently Chinese, and scholarship was needed to substantiate this claim. This required refuting the invasion theory and reframing China as the Cradle of the East. Lattimore’s book, Inner Asian Frontiers of China, accomplished precisely this.

Executing a complete about-face from his earlier position, building on Chinese nationalist scholarship, and drawing on Turner’s American frontier thesis, Lattimore reframed Mongolia, Manchuria, Chinese Turkistan (today’s Xinjiang) and Tibet as the frontiers of China. Reducing these territories to a mere geographic area – Inner Asia – and rebranding them as mere frontiers required rendering the region stateless, tribal and barbarian. Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours; his framework thus demanded a terra nullius.

Refuting the invasion theory required disarming it of its most potent weapon of conquest – mobility – and supplanting it with an alternative framework. Lattimore accomplished this by casting mobility as an anti-state force, substituting the invasion thesis with evolutionary materialism. Inverting his earlier argument that mobility provided a ‘snowball’ effect to Mongol political organisation, Lattimore was the first to equate mobility with dispersal. He thereby transformed what was previously understood as the ultimate mobilising and concentrating mechanism into an inherently dispersive element. This reframing neutralised conquest theory, turning its defining weapon into an anti-state force.

Furthermore, by establishing mobility as the defining feature of pastoralism, and immobility as that of irrigated agriculture, Lattimore posited both a positive correlation between wealth and power and a negative one between mobility and wealth/power, thus advancing his ‘wealth versus mobility’ thesis. And by asserting that ‘grain, accumulated and stored, was beyond question the standard of real wealth in essentials’, he guaranteed ‘the ascendancy of wealth over mobility’. In this manner, Lattimore not only erased mobility as the state-making force but also established grain as that very force. In fact, Lattimore is the author of the grain thesis, and in his framework, the state emerges as a grain store.

Mobility, thus, emerged not merely as dispersal, but as a mechanism of destitution, rather than a driver of state-building. While Lattimore declared that ‘it is the poor nomad who is pure nomad,’ intellectual successors like the cultural anthropologist Marshall Sahlins observed that a nomad’s wealth ‘is a burden’ that ‘soon poses a contradiction to his mobility.’ Anatoly Khazanov pushed this thesis further, arguing that pastoralism is inherently non-self-sufficient (non-autarkic) or even anti-autarkic, thereby rendering it fundamentally incapable of producing a state.

At the same time, by mapping environmentally determined societies – specifically, forest-hunting clans, steppe-pastoral tribes, and loess-agricultural states – and adding extensive and intensive dimensions, Lattimore established population pressure as the primary catalyst for state-formation. While agriculture in general emerged as uniquely capable of generating a state, irrigated agriculture was intensive enough to trigger severe demographic strain. Identifying a continuous agricultural expanse enclosed by ‘an immense mass of inhospitable terrain’ – namely, ‘the bleak highlands’ and ‘the Inner Asian barrier lands’ on one side, and the Pacific Ocean on the other – Lattimore mapped China as a circumscribed agricultural land.

To cast China as the Cradle of the East and claim Inner Asia as a Chinese frontier, Lattimore framed Inner Asian pastoralism as a byproduct of agricultural expansion, attributing all historical agency to farmers. By claiming pastoralists were ‘akin by culture and probably by blood to the early Chinese’, he cast both populations as homologous. Dating steppe pastoralism to the 4th century BCE – as an offshoot of intensive Chinese agriculture – allowed Lattimore to monopolise the state-formation timeline and neutralise the invasion theory.

To stall the timeline of pastoralism’s emergence, he devised a hyper-restrictive definition: dismissing categories like ‘true’, ‘strict’ or ‘normal’ as overly broad, he defined ‘pastoral nomadism’ exclusively as ‘the extreme of nomadism’ or ‘the strict or extreme phases of steppe nomadism’. This framework equates pastoralism with the advent of horseback riding and, in effect, with the rise of cavalry.

To be sure, all of these claims conflicted with contemporary scholarly knowledge, including archaeology and linguistics. Back then, archaeology had shown that horse-riding nomadism and animal art emerged around 1500 BCE in the Black Sea region before spreading eastward through Mongolia to Ordos – a fact Lattimore was aware of. Similarly, linguists such as Henri Maspero had shown that the Chinese language ‘has no relation whatever, not even a distant connection with’ Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic languages. Nonetheless, Lattimore’s attribution of pastoral animal domestication to farmers and his hyper-restrictive definition of pastoralism became paradigmatic in the field. Khazanov cemented Lattimore’s thesis: he claimed that only sedentary groups with definite vegetable surpluses could domesticate animals, and characterised ‘pure pastoral nomadism’ as ‘the most extreme form’ of nomadism. In this manner, mobility and pastoralism were written out of the state-formation process.

However, modern scholarship by Melinda Zeder shows that ‘plant and animal domestication occurred at roughly the same time, with signs of initial management … reaching back to at least 11,500 cal BP [ie, 9550 BCE], if not earlier.’ Furthermore, we now know that early animal domestication ‘only took place within a subset of the geographical distribution of the wild ancestors’, unfolding ‘often in regions distant from centres of plant domestication.’ Critically, while most herd animals were domesticated via the prey pathway rather than a commensal one, pastoralists domesticated equids – donkeys and horses – via a directed pathway. Yet, by claiming that ‘specialised pastoralism, seen as an outgrowth of agriculture’ confronts the state with a ‘problem of dispersal and mobility’, Scott continues to perpetuate Lattimore’s delayed timeline and restrictive definition – even while acknowledging that agriculture and pastoralism emerged concurrently roughly 12,000 years ago.
Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated

By the 1970s, Lattimore’s framework had become the dominant orthodoxy. Elman Service, a leading neo-evolutionist, hailed it as ‘the pathfinding ecological theory’, while Morton Fried acknowledged that Lattimore ‘proposed a theory that stimulated my own’. Ultimately, neo-evolutionism displaced conquest theory as the mainstream paradigm. By positioning intensive agriculture as the sole economic foundation capable of sustaining the state, Fried’s social stratification scheme (egalitarian, rank, stratified, and state) and Service’s sociopolitical typology (band, tribe, chiefdom, and state) reinforced Lattimore’s irrigated agriculture thesis while anchoring evolutionary materialism. Consequently, the state – either as an instrument of the upper class or as a managerial institution – emerges fundamentally as an economic instrument and an evolutionary product.

By deriving the state from either social or functional differentiation, both Fried and Service rejected conquest theory. Whereas Service’s model is basically a refinement of 19th-century bourgeois materialism, Fried’s framework aligns with the Marxist model by emphasising conflict driven by internal economic differentiation. Carneiro likewise rejected conquest theory; despite his incorporating warfare and coercion, his model remains an elaboration of Fried’s framework. As one of the most influential models of neo-evolutionary thought, Carneiro’s framework was a direct product of this paradigmatic bias, and it effectively resulted in the global scaling of Lattimore’s framework. China was established as the Cradle of the East, while Inner Asia was relegated to a tribal world and ‘the barbarian “outer darkness”’. Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated until Caroline Humphrey and David Sneath deconstructed the category of ‘nomadism’ and the myth of the wandering nomad in 1999, paving the way for Sneath to later debunk the tribal model as a complete misrepresentation. Meanwhile, in a corpus of historical scholarship utilising primary sources, Christopher P Atwood compellingly demonstrates that the tribal model is untenable.

However, Scott not only resurrects Lattimore’s framework in its entirety along with its long-refuted theories but also repackages it to fit his own anarchist project. Following Lattimore, Scott maintains that Inner Asian pastoralism – along with its population – was merely a byproduct of Chinese agricultural expansion. His assertion that the Great Wall was built as much to contain Chinese taxpayers as to repel external invasions likewise mirrors Lattimore’s position. Scott’s most spectacular move is his elevation of mobility into a primary form of freedom. Lattimore’s notion of free nomads – with their ‘idea of freedom, free movement, free migration’ – nicely dovetailed with Scott’s anarchist thesis, prompting him to valorise mobility as a freedom-preserving force and recast it as the fundamental state-preventing strategy.

This conceptualisation clearly finds its echo in The Dawn of Everything (2021), where Graeber and Wengrow theorise ‘the freedom to move’ as one of the ‘fundamental, even primary, forms of freedom’. At the same time, Scott’s grain thesis, in particular, and agricultural paradigm, in general, powerfully guide our thinking, leading the two authors to declare in despair that ‘we got stuck’ and that ‘ours is a species that has become enslaved to its crops.’ Mobility thus emerged as a fundamentally anti-state, anti-domination and freedom-preserving force, albeit one that proved impotent against the all-powerful grain to which we, along with all our extrahuman transportation, are enslaved. This is how the Sinocentric paradigm was devised and how it erases pastoralism from state-formation. The objective of this paradigm is to eliminate mobility, and its theoretical frameworks inherently structure scholarly thinking and enquiry against pastoralism. Ultimately, this is how the Sinocentric paradigm traps us intellectually.

With the erasure of mobility and pastoralism and the relegation of Inner Asia into tribal barbarity, the Sinocentric paradigm monopolised state-formation in China for the Chinese while establishing China as the sole empire and civilisation within the former Daiching domain. However, there were Inner Asian empires – especially the Daiching Empire – on whose identification the integrity of the regime’s claim over Inner Asia depended. This demanded their total erasure. The method – as Lattimore himself observed in 1934 while depicting the grim reality that the Open Door policy had imposed upon the Mongols, the Manchus, the Uighurs and the Tibetans – was to ‘deny their history and surrender their national and racial identities’ and, ultimately, to conquer them conceptually. Notably, this is the exact policy that the current Chinese administration pursues today.

This meant the appropriation of all the empires that conquered China as inherently Chinese, and the construction of an everlasting Chinese empire. To achieve this, two problems had to be solved: the reality of conquests and the distinct identity of the conquering empires. Because these conquests were not isolated incidents but occurred in overwhelming numbers, a sophisticated framework had to be devised.

To appropriate Inner Asian empires, Lattimore devised the theory of Chinese dynastic cycles, a teleological device that powerfully legitimises Chinese nationalist claims through a veneer of deterministic, historical law. By reducing all empires to mere dynasties, this cycle creates the illusion of an enduring Chinese state where successive dynasties simply replace one another. Conquests are thus erased as mere changes in ruling houses while the empire itself remains intact. Consequently, the Chinese empire emerges as uniquely endless – an everlasting polity standing in stark contrast to the mortal trajectories of all other historical powers, including the Roman Empire.

To make this everlasting empire inherently Chinese and to deny the identity of the conquering empires – in contrast to British ‘accumulative’ and Russian ‘incorporative’ models – Lattimore forged ‘the third great type’: the Chinese ‘absorptive’ empire. Unlike ‘conquest’ empires, this was a ‘defensive empire’ – one that did not conquer but was conquered, yet remained Chinese by absorbing its conquerors. Consequently, the polity emerged not as a conquering political power, but as a cultural community predicated on assimilation. Furthermore, as China was established as civilisation itself, and Inner Asia was reduced to barbarity, all Inner Asian conquests represented a barbarian advancement toward civilisation. Sinicisation was a ‘standing offer of the opportunity to become civilised, to any individual or group interested in progress’ – the civilising mission.
China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles

However, Lattimore’s highly idiosyncratic conceptualisations invert reality. Empire, by definition, is an expansionist, incorporative polity; what defines an empire is expansion, and what drives it is conquest. It is also anything but culturally homogeneous; its very nature is all-encompassing, hierarchical and heterogeneous. Thus, Lattimore’s Chinese absorptive empire is a veritable anomaly. Moreover, with hundreds of mutually unintelligible varieties divided across at least eight major language groups, even the Sinitic group – let alone China as a whole – represents immense cultural diversity.

In fact, Lattimore’s ‘absorptive’ empire was the political embodiment of the Chinese nationalist narrative of assimilative power, depicting China as a solid, homogenising mass, ‘homogeneous in race, language, and culture’, where the ‘barbarians were all absorbed by the Chinese; they became Chinese like any other Chinese.’ Hence, the Manchus were all assimilated by the Chinese and became Chinese like any other; therefore, the Manchu empire was a Chinese dynasty like any other. Had all the Mongols shared the Manchu fate, the Chinese empire would have been the largest contiguous land empire the world had ever seen; then, what June Teufel Dreyer called the ‘tianxia trope’ – the idea that a Sinocentric world is the better one – would have possessed a formidable precedent.

Nevertheless, Lattimore’s framework immediately became hegemonic. China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles with a predictable Sinicisation pattern. Paired with the Chinese world order, the paradigm crystallised into unchallenged dogma. Lattimore emerged ‘as the intellectual godfather of all historians of China’ (as the sinologist Mark C Elliott put it), and the founder of Chinese frontier studies. Only in the 1990s did scholars like Pamela Crossley, Evelyn Rawski and Elliott finally break ranks to challenge the Sinicisation thesis, instigating what would become the New Qin
