One hopes instead that Pattinson is negotiating himself enough time between 007 shoots (and at least one more “The Batman” entry still on the docket) to do the odd auteur projects he clearly loves — and that adventurously chosen collaborators like Claire Denis (“High Life”) and Lynne Ramsay (“Die My Love”) can only benefit from his cachet.

In the meantime, spare a thought for the less famous guys who, for a moment there, thought they had a shot at being cinema’s longest-running action man. They’ll all be fine — I confess to some relief in particular that O’Connor, a superb and unusual hybrid of character actor and leading man, may have more time for the intrepid arthouse projects in which he thrives — and will doubtless each get some manner of boost for having been so prominently on the shortlist. Sometimes, however, the winner really does take it all in this business: For Pattinson, snagging the most in-demand role going just feels like a victory lap.

items.title: Is ‘Club Kid’ a ‘Conservative’ Movie? Only If You’re Still Living in the ’60s
items.description: One of the things I love about movies is how layered they are. When a film connects on a deep level, saying what it’s truly “about” may not be as simple as it sounds. Chasing down a movie’s inner meaning can lead you into the mystery of things. A great movie c
items.author: Owen Gleiberman
paragraphs: One of the things I love about movies is how layered they are. When a film connects on a deep level, saying what it’s truly “about” may not be as simple as it sounds. Chasing down a movie’s inner meaning can lead you into the mystery of things. A great movie can be “about” more than it seems.

Take “Club Kid.” Jordan Firstman’s ebullient and moving first feature tells a story that couldn’t be more straightforward — or, in a way, more traditional. Firstman, who gives a fantastic performance, plays Peter, a queer New York party promoter (a few decades ago we would have called him “downtown,” now he’s Brooklyn) who learns that he has a 10-year-old son, whom he fathered in a random three-way sexual encounter at one of his 4:00 a.m. club bacchanals. The kid, Arlo (Reggie Absolom), is sweet and curly-haired and British (he arrives with a chaperone from London); his mother, who raised him, recently committed suicide. The responsibility to take care of Arlo has suddenly dropped on Peter like a load of bricks. It’s something he doesn’t want and, for the time being, doesn’t have much choice about. But as he and the kid start to hang out, a tentative relationship forms, and the two begin to figure out what they might mean to each other.

What “Club Kid” is “about” is how Peter, a charming dissolute man-child, living an existence of unhinged hedonism, discovers that he wants to grow up and take care of someone besides himself. On that score, the drama is authentic and fully felt. In outline, though, it’s something we’ve seen many times before, in films from “About a Boy” to “Big Daddy.” Yet what makes “Club Kid” singular is that it’s about something larger than that.

As a filmmaker, Firstman plunges you into the world of queer club culture with a fervor and tumult and personality and lived-in detail that takes your breath away. He plunks the audience down in the middle of the shade-throwing nightbloom revels, the cocaine and ketamine binges, so that we experience the cathartic rush of drugged-out insolence, of heightened erotic excitement, of gender-flipping transgression. From the earliest days of gay liberation, the party scene was a core expression of queer freedom, and still is. What we call disco started in the underground gay clubs of the early ’70s, and part of Peter’s cachet as a promoter is that what’s he organizing is now a business, but it’s still underground. The staging of these scenes, and the acting in them, is extraordinary. Jordan Firstman makes us feel the life of the party.

And yet…he’s not merely celebrating it. Far from it. As authentic and scene-specific as they are, the party sequences in “Club Kid” signify as more than just a portrayal of the New York queer club scene. They’re also a larger snapshot of what party culture, out there in the world, has become: an arena of liberation that’s rooted in a place of physical and spiritual abandon that contains the seeds of destruction.

If you wanted to encapsulate the history of the last six decades in one sentence, you could do worse than this: Ever since the late ’60s, the party has never stopped. There are countless versions of the party, and we’ve all been to our own preferred versions. It might have been the singles bars of the disco age, or the frat-house benders that came to rule in the late ’70s — and have only grown more frenzied and predatory ever since. It might have been the industrial dance clubs of the ’80s or the raves of the ’90s. It might have been the suburban saturnalia of “Jersey Shore,” or the more contempo versions of that. It might have been the punk mosh pits, or the revels of Studio 54, or the back-to-the-underground scene of Basement. The music, the drugs, the alcohol, the hooking up, the vibe of orgiastic excess — for 60 years now, we’ve been a culture on the prowl.

In “Club Kid,” it’s not just Peter who starts to question the party culture that has fueled him. The film itself is questioning it. It’s asking, “Is this how we should be living?” And yet, because the movie dares to pose that question, there has been a backlash against it, with a chorus of voices damning the movie by branding it “conservative.” A certain number of people are looking at “Club Kid,” with its tale of a queer man who turns his back on his own personal decadence to embrace the call of family, as if it were a movie Nancy Reagan could love.

What I think the “conservative” slur misses is that Jordan Firstman, who came out of this scene, is not questioning it in a puritanical or moralistic way. He captures the honest vibrance of party culture. Yet he also captures — and this is what I think is brilliant about “Club Kid” — that whatever version of it floats your boat, the party that never stops, while rooted in a certain vibe of community, may be rooted even more deeply in the enticement we feel from getting high on ourselves. That’s the hidden seduction of party culture, the thrill and the beauty of it, and maybe the lie of it. The party doesn’t need to stop. But it might be time that we stopped seeing it as an uncut salvation without ever pausing to ask, as “Club Kid” does, what it’s doing to us.

items.title: How ‘Twilight’ Predicted Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Casting
items.description: Robert Pattinson really does have “the skin of a killer“… but in a new form.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Robert Pattinson really does have “the skin of a killer“… but in a new form.
For Twilight diehards, Monday’s announcement of Pattinson’s casting as the new James Bond might not have come as a surprise. That’s because the 2008 vampire romance film predicted it.

In the film, which launched Pattinson’s acting career, he plays the brooding Edward Cullen, a 108-year-old vampire who falls in love with human Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart). About halfway through Twilight, the first installment in the beloved film saga, Swan’s high school friend group is seen discussing the theme for the upcoming prom, which is revealed to be Monte Carlo.

“Gambling, tuxedos, and Bond, James Bond,” Eric (Justin Chon) quips in the scene. A shocked Angela (Christian Serratos) then says, “Oh my God,” as the camera cuts to a smirking Edward, opening the car door for Bella as they make their couple debut walking into school together.

In the 2008 film, Pattinson‘s Edward may have warned Stewart‘s Bella that he has “the skin of a killer“ but less than two decades later, the actor is now getting his license to kill. The Primetime actor is taking over the iconic role from Daniel Craig, who concluded his run with 2021’s No Time to Die.

The Hollywood Reporter previously reported that Pattinson was among the finalists being considered for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Nicholas Hoult. But director Denis Villeneuve and producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman ultimately thought Pattinson was perfect as the next 007.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement about his casting. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Following Monday’s news, the official X account for Twilight also posted the scene referencing James Bond and added in the caption, “It all comes back to Twilight.”

items.title: Mo Brings Plenty Hopes Real-Life Inspired ‘Marshals’ Episode Brings Justice to Late Nephew
items.description: Mo Brings Plenty, his family and community have been rocked by the untimely death of Mo’s nephew, 1923 actor Cole Brings Plenty. The 27-year-old was found dead in April 2024 after he had been reported missing. His death came between seasons one and two of the
items.author: Jackie Strause
paragraphs: Mo Brings Plenty, his family and community have been rocked by the untimely death of Mo’s nephew, 1923 actor Cole Brings Plenty. The 27-year-old was found dead in April 2024 after he had been reported missing. His death came between seasons one and two of the Yellowstone prequel, sparking his recasting (with Jeremy Gauna), a final season that honored his memory and now, an entire episode of Marshals inspired by what happened.

In Sunday’s episode of Yellowstone‘s hit CBS spinoff following Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes), titled “Roughstock,” Mo, an enrolled member of the Lakota Nations who plays the right-hand man to Broken Rock Tribe chief Thomas Rainwater (Gil Birmingham) in both Yellowstone and Marshals, searches on horseback with Kayce (Grimes) for Mo’s missing nephew (played by Will Strongheart), only to eventually find him dead, and a police department refusing to investigate the death.

The storyline is ripped from what Mo believes happened to his real nephew. In Cole’s case, the Lawrence Police Department in Kansas found no foul play involved, ruling that Cole acted alone and took his own life. Mo hasn’t stopped pushing a different narrative ever since. “For his murder to go uninvestigated, and for it to be written off as ‘no foul play,’ because they didn’t want to invest anything into it? It’s heartbreaking,” he had told The Hollywood Reporter back in March. “We’re not letting it go.”

Now that the episode has aired, Mo, who also works behind the scenes as the show’s American Indian Affairs coordinator, talks again with THR below about the bravery of the Paramount Taylor Sheridan series and Marshals showrunner Spencer Hudnut to spotlight Cole’s story on television, the emotions around reliving the tragedy of his nephew’s death, and the justice he hopes the episode can help bring to murdered and missing Indigenous people. “This is for the injustice that occurs to American Indian people and the victims who are truly victims, who are being being labeled otherwise and not being taken seriously,” he says.

This must be heavy for you, so thank you for speaking with me about the making of this episode inspired by your late nephew. Did you approach (showrunner) Spencer Hudnut about doing this, or did Spencer approach you?

It all began when my brother, Joe, Cole’s father, and I were sharing the experience of what we were going through. Spencer mentioned something about it being up to us. Saying, “I know it’s gonna be deep, and it’s hard. But it’s up to you.” We said, we have to do it. Not just for the sake of remembrance or in honoring Cole, but for all the other cases, all the other families whose cases of their loved ones not being looked at or being taken seriously and just thrown away. It was very important. And I knew it was going to be doable because the cast and crew are an amazing group of people. They all understood and had the knowledge of what we’ve experienced and gone through.
Did you have to pitch this to the studio or network to get them on board?
I think that was on Spencer. Mad respect for Spencer; even doing so, is very important.
Did you talk to Taylor Sheridan about how to handle putting this storyline into the show?

No. I knew exactly what I wanted to do. My biggest thing was that I wanted to relay the true emotions and spirit of it all, even the frustrating moments. Because it’s a roller coaster ride, and it still is today. It’s still fresh in our minds, my family’s minds, especially my brother Joel. He struggled. It was truly, truly a great loss for us.
Spencer wrote this episode. Did you collaborate?

Yes, he wrote it, and Spencer and the writing team are a great group of amazing, beautiful human beings. My brother and I went to the writers room early on, before the season even started, to spend a day with them. We talked about different things that go on within tribal councils, the political side of what goes on on a reservation, the non-political side of it and then, of course, we shared our experience of not talking about the MMIW (Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women) and MMIP (Missing and Murdered Indigenous People), but actually conveying what it’s really like to have that experience. There are hundreds and hundreds of families who have their loved ones… murdered and missing; the disappearance of loved ones just being written off as nothing.

From my previous conversations with you, this episode is very close to what you believe happened to your nephew in real life. What was it like for you to film this beat by beat, playing an uncle who loses his nephew? [Note: In the end of the episode, Kayce’s team pushes for the police to investigate the death, opening up the storyline to continue.]

It was about doing justice. But it was also good to have Luke Grimes there, and Gil Birmingham, and the crew; individuals who understood and knew. Will [Strongheart], who portrayed [Mo’s onscreen nephew] Troy, was very familiar. He came to Cole’s funeral; they all knew what we were going through, especially for me. So it was easy to fall back into that space, because I knew there were others who would be there to help me if I needed it. But at the forefront of my mind was the injustice that occurs to American Indian people and the victims who are truly victims who are being being labeled otherwise and not being taken seriously.
This is a big platform: Marshals is a mega-hit for Paramount. You will shine a light on this happening everywhere, but do you hope it moves the needle specifically with your nephew’s case?

Unfortunately, the way I see it, if a police department doesn’t want to investigate something then there’s a connection. Bottom line, hands down. Outside of that, what I hope this episode achieves is that it will drive people who are non-Native, who are unfamiliar, to go down this journey.

We mentioned MMIW, MMIP, in the past — murdered and missing Indian women and people. But to actually have a storyline that will hopefully have the audience see it through Mo’s, Kayce’s, Rainwater’s eyes? Just to be able to actually see what is going on. The positive side in this story is that law enforcement actually does get involved — the marshals, but not the police. There’s a line where the sheriff said, “Ah, this happens all the time.” I’m glad Spencer included that line because that’s really, honestly, what a lot of families hear from law enforcement when when their loved ones are found.

After we spoke the last time, the Lawrence Police Department responded to our interview with a statement. Did you see what they said? [“The entire case contains clear evidence that there was no foul play involved in Cole’s death and that Cole acted alone.”]

Oh, yeah, of course. Out of respect for my family, I encouraged my brother, Joe, to seal the records. Little did we know that it was going to give them an out. Nonetheless, I’m hoping that this episode is going to drive people to reach out to their Congress people, their senators, their governors, and say, “Hey, look, enough. Here’s the original inhabitants of this country, and here’s our treatment to them.”

But yet we speak about other nationalities in foreign countries, so we’re basically flying over mission fields to get to mission fields. We want to be the savior there, but we’re not doing it here. That’s the thing that upsets me the most, and the fact that we are tax paying people as well. First responders get their funding through tax dollars. We are forced to pay taxes, and the will of justice does not turn for us? Shame on America for that. I’m being honest. And if that’s the case, then we shouldn’t have to pay taxes. If there’s no equality and justice being served for our loved ones who are truly victimized?

What occurred in Cole’s case, there were allegations. And they let go the people they should have interviewed to get the true answers. If the police department really doesn’t want to investigate, then to me, that’s every bit of proof that there’s something to hide.

This episode included a ceremonial burial. You have worked behind the scenes to bring authenticity to this franchise for years as the American Indian Affairs coordinator. What did you especially want to show here as Mo was laying his nephew to rest?

The sacred fire… the true celebration and understanding of life. When we look at life from a spiritual perspective, it is continuous. There is no end. So that was important, because we incorporate a lot of that understanding or tradition or ceremony into our everyday lives, whether we’re assisting a family that lost a loved one or, or even ourselves, losing relatives. The spirit is forever.

One of the biggest parts of that ceremony scene was the horse. Because we’ve always had horses here in this country long before the Spanish brought theirs. The Lakota people, we have songs and ceremonies specifically for the horse that are thousands upon thousands of years old, so to have that incorporated was very important to me. To share that bit of knowledge and understanding that our people have always had, that the horse symbolizes the spiritual realm. So when Mo sees that horse, he knows his nephew made it home.
Is there anything you want to say about Cole in his memory?

If people truly believe there’s a higher power, then they have to stand up for what’s right. Regardless of what it is. My nephew, Cole, has always done that. He was a lover of life. He always gave a helping hand. He never judged anyone for who they were, what nationality, what their faith was. If someone needed help, he was there. And to turn that type of light out in a community, in this world… for us, he was the next one to carry on our traditions and knowledge. To strip us of that and do nothing about it? If people truly believe in a higher power, they better understand and know that it is the higher power who loves diversity. Because the higher power made it so from the very beginning. And if you can’t support that diversity here, this world, on this planet, then who are you to believe you’ll be welcome there?
In Marshals, the death of Mo’s nephew sounds like an ongoing story that will open up the show to explore more reservation stories, which is something Spencer Hednut said is baked into the series.

There are many stories very similar to this. Different situations and circumstances, but the outcome’s always the same. I wanted to get this message out but I had to utilize our own story, my family’s own experience. I’m hoping down the road this will give us the ability for us to be able to share more; other things that are occurring. Not always the negative things. There are positive things as well, and I want to share those too. I’m hoping people will go ahead and support stories about Indian country.
Do you feel like this was a brave thing by the show, the network, the studio to allow you to tell such a personal story?

I’m thankful to the network for giving us the opportunity. I’m thankful to the Spencer. I’m thankful that they’ve allowed us to be able to share this experience and bring it to light through the episodes. It does take great courage, because a lot of people don’t understand cultural diversity. They don’t fully understand that we as American Indian people are tax paying people, too. Like I said, we pay bills just like everyone else. We have to work for everything that we have. I’m thankful to the network and to Spencer and to the rest of the writers who supported the whole storyline.
Marshals releases new episodes Sundays at 8 p.m. on CBS and Paramount+.

items.title: Lindsay Clancy Will Face a Second Trial
items.description: On Monday, a judge said Lindsay Clancy will face a second trial this spring for the killing of her three young children, setting a retrial date for March 29.
items.author: Erica Schwiegershausen
paragraphs: On Monday, a judge said Lindsay Clancy will face a second trial this spring for the killing of her three young children, setting a retrial date for March 29.

Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her children with exercise bands before slitting her wrists and throwing herself out a second-floor window, was tried on first-degree murder charges earlier this year. While prosecutors argued that she carefully plotted the murder of her children, her defense said she was suffering from severe postpartum mental illness and should not be held criminally responsible for the deaths. The six-week trial — which sparked heated debates and conspiracy theories online — ended in a mistrial in September after jurors remained deadlocked with all but one voting that Clancy should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.

While prosecutors have not yet said what charges they’re planning to bring to trial, the fact that they agreed to a new date suggests they intend to retry her for first-degree murder, the New York Times reports. (If they had reduced the charges, Clancy could have avoided a second jury trial.) Clancy, who was paralyzed after her suicide attempt, remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital, where she’s been held since 2023. Following the mistrial in September, her defense attorney Kevin Reddington said he didn’t think she would be able to emotionally handle a second trial.

items.title: I'm Sorry, But These Faux Christmas Trees Are Too Cute
items.description: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
items.author: Alexis Bennett Parker
paragraphs: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
Beautycon is a global platform that brings together beauty enthusiasts, brands, and industry leaders to explore the latest trends, innovations, and conversations shaping the future of beauty.
All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.

I have a confession to make: I've been thinking about cheating on my Christmas tree this year. Not with another full-sized fir, but with a growing collection of miniature, colorful, and delightfully unconventional alternatives that have absolutely no business being this cute. And judging by the number of faux trees currently occupying my online shopping carts, this might be getting out of hand.

Don't get me wrong. I love traditional Christmas trees as much as the next person (and there are some ahead!). The twinkling lights, the sentimental ornaments, the excuse to rearrange your entire living room around a seven-foot centerpiece? I'm here for all of it. But somewhere between discovering a wicker tree dressed up in oversized velvet bows and a sparkly little number that looks like it belongs in a disco, I realized that holiday decorating doesn't have to be quite so serious.
In fact, the more personality, the better.

This year's faux Christmas trees are making a compelling case for abandoning the rule book altogether. We're talking sculptural silhouettes, unexpected textures, candy-colored branches, and designs that could easily double as art installations. Some are charmingly understated while others look like they were dreamed up by someone who considers more is more a personal philosophy. Naturally, I want both.

And here's the beauty of going faux: You can skip the falling needles, forget about watering anything, and keep your festive masterpiece looking fabulous year after year. Plus, who says you have to stop at one? A petite tree on your nightstand, a statement-making creation in the entryway, and something wonderfully ridiculous on your mantel sound like a perfectly reasonable decorating strategy to me.

Whether you're working with a tiny apartment, looking to give your usual holiday setup a little personality, or simply can't resist something shiny, I've rounded up the faux Christmas trees that deserve a spot on your nice list.
Fair warning: Your traditional tree might get a little jealous.

items.title: Everything We Know About Adults Season 3
items.description: Adults has officially been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu. That's not all: the studio has ordered 16 episodes for the next season. Seasons 1 and 2 only had eight episodes each, so this is a true blessing. We'll be reunited with Samir (Malik Essal), Billie
items.author: Simran Pasricha
paragraphs: Adults has officially been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu. That's not all: the studio has ordered 16 episodes for the next season. Seasons 1 and 2 only had eight episodes each, so this is a true blessing. We'll be reunited with Samir (Malik Essal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele) and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen).

Specific plot details haven’t been announced. For now, the premise remains five twenty-somethings living in Samir’s childhood home in New York, trying to navigate work, relationships, family and the delicate business of being in each other’s space constantly.

Main cast members Malik Elassal, Lucy Freyer, Jack Innanen, Amita Rao and Owen Thiele are coming back. No guest stars or recurring stars have been announced, but we will likely see Issa's new love interest, the librarian played by Mia Fowler.

n 3, according to Freyer. "[Fox]was like, 'I wanna come back next season, and the season you don’t bring me back is the season you’re gonna get cancelled,'" she told Refinery29 Australia. "And I was like, she put a curse on us, and I believe it. And now, she has to be in every season of the show for as long as it runs. And I'm like, 'OK!'"

Behind the scenes, Kronengold and Shaw remain the creators, showrunners and executive producers. Their statement about the new FX deal also acknowledged a particularly important figure in this whole operation. "We started working with FX over six years ago, back when Paul Baker was but a twinkle in all of our eyes," they joked.
Not yet, but we will update this article once there is.

The audience has grown, which is reassuring news for anyone who has been personally campaigning for their friends to watch. According to FX, Season 2 viewership increased by 60% compared with Season 1 across Hulu and Disney+ globally over its first five weeks. International viewership doubled. The network didn’t release actual audience totals, so we don't know exactly how many people joined the household.

FX Entertainment president Nick Grad also credited the show’s devoted following. "Ben and Rebecca have elevated Adults in every way, earning critical praise and a legion of devoted fans who have embraced the friend group as their own," he said in a statement.
There’s no announced release date for season three yet, but in the meantime, Australians can watch the first two seasons on Disney+.

items.title: The ex-cop on a mission to see fortune-tellers arrested | Psyche Portraits
items.description: In 2008, Bob Nygaard sat on a stool at the Neighborhood Sports Bar and Grill in Boca Raton, Florida, just before 5 pm. It was Wednesday, a night with generous happy-hour deals and the possibility of taking someone home by last call. Nygaard, a tall and brawny
items.author: Shayla Love
paragraphs: In 2008, Bob Nygaard sat on a stool at the Neighborhood Sports Bar and Grill in Boca Raton, Florida, just before 5 pm. It was Wednesday, a night with generous happy-hour deals and the possibility of taking someone home by last call. Nygaard, a tall and brawny man with a disarmingly goofy smile, had the strongest New York accent for miles. He had recently retired from a 21-year-long career as an NYPD officer. At 46, he got out when his pension kicked in, and moved down to Florida to relax.
Except he wasn’t relaxed. He was bored.

Nygaard had been a high-energy cop who didn’t get along with fellow officers because of how doggedly he pursued arrests. He probably should have known that he wouldn’t adjust to sipping Mai Tais and sitting on the beach. Shortly after arriving in Florida, he got a private investigator’s licence, using it to track down missing money or catch cheating husbands. Neither was satisfying.

He ordered a rum and Coke. He had become friendly with the bartender, who introduced him to two women sitting at the end of the bar, a nurse and a doctor. They had dinner together, swapping stories about working in medicine and the police force. Nygaard gave both women his card. Ten minutes later, his phone rang. It was the doctor. Could they meet up nearby, on a street corner outside a Chevron station? Nygaard thought she was hoping to hook up.

When she pulled up and rolled down the window, her face was half-covered in shadows. ‘I’ve never been able to tell anyone this before,’ she said from the driver’s seat. ‘I’m a medical doctor and I fell for a psychic.’ She had given more than $12,000 to a woman she met through her hairdresser. The psychic said someone had put a curse on the doctor: it explained why she was having issues with her immigration papers, and why her love life was ruined. For enough money, the curse could be lifted. Now, the doctor realised she’d been had. Nygaard had arrested conmen before. Could he help her?

From that moment on, Nygaard was never bored again. He became a PI who specialises in helping victims of psychics. And he didn’t settle cases out of court – he went after arrests to get as much money back for his clients as possible. Through word of mouth, psychic victims all over the country have sought him out. Since his first case, Nygaard has helped recover more than $5 million.

I first heard about Nygaard around a year ago, through a news article about a psychic’s arrest he had orchestrated in Philadelphia. I thought of him as part fictional detective Sherlock Holmes, part real-life Harry Houdini, who spent his later years exposing mediums. When I initially reached out over email, Nygaard didn’t respond. But after I sent a follow-up, I got a call from an unknown number a few days later. It was Nygaard: ‘I like when people don’t give up,’ he told me. He started talking fast, recounting his recent cases. What drives a retired cop, someone who busted drug dealers and burglars, to focus only on this fringe sect of society – psychics? And why was he so good at it? We made plans to meet up in the city.

On a below-freezing day in early February, I turned a narrow corner in lower Manhattan and saw a figure wearing a beige trench coat and fedora standing under the granite arch of the historic Life and Trust Bank. In my memory, steam started to rise up from the sidewalk grates, and the deserted street became the spot for a clandestine midnight meet-up. In truth, it was a clear sunny morning and Nygaard was politely waiting for me outside, but every minute spent with him can make you feel like you’re acting out a scene from a movie set in old New York. The former bank now houses a coffee shop. We walked into the cavernous lobby and ordered drinks where the bank tellers once sat.

I expected to meet a hardened law-enforcement officer with a dark past. Maybe he, or someone he loved, had been wronged by a psychic, and he had a score to settle. Or maybe he was a rationalist – someone so dedicated to an evidence-based view of the world that he wouldn’t stand for anyone proposing they could break the laws of nature.

But as we settled down with our hot drinks, I learned that Nygaard hadn’t thought about psychics at all until later in life. He had a happy, grounded childhood, he told me. He was born in Queens in 1961, and moved to New Hyde Park, Long Island, when he was four. His mother was 20 when she had him, his father only a few years older. The family, including his younger brother, ate dinner together every evening.
‘Knowing how to deal with the raccoon also helps you deal with the person’

They were a hard-working and proud unit. The family would put on their best clothes to go to the Howard Johnson’s on Jericho Turnpike for fish and chips. Nygaard was taught to always be ‘squared away’. He made his bed in the morning. His hair was always combed. ‘You pay attention to the details, to the little things,’ he said. ‘You’re clean, well dressed, polite, you’re on time.’ Even though his apartment was just around the corner from the café where we sat, he had arrived nearly 20 minutes early to make sure he wasn’t late. (Nygaard now splits his time between Florida and New York, based largely on when the New York Rangers are playing; he has season tickets.)

His sense of justice also seems to have started early. If Nygaard came home and said that all the kids were picking on someone in the schoolyard – ‘knocking them on the ground, calling him four-eyes’ – Nygaard’s father would counter: ‘You didn’t sit there and watch, did you?’

Nygaard spent summers in northeast Pennsylvania, where his grandfather had bought an old farmhouse with no running water or electricity; it relied on kerosene lamps and a well. The property reminded his grandfather of Norway. When Nygaard brought out his friends, brothers called Tommy and Richy Gambino, they had never seen a cow before. Once, they tricked another visiting city kid by telling him that chocolate milk came out of the brown cows’ udders.

In the countryside, Nygaard fostered compassion for other living things. When he was around six, he had a BB gun to shoot at cans. One day, he saw a bird, aimed his gun at it, and shot it out of a tree. Nygaard looked at it up close, examining the pellet in its belly. It wasn’t dead, but it was suffering. He killed it, to put it out of its misery, and then felt sick. ‘I never killed again,’ he told me. Yet, he also gained insights into the animalistic side of humans. When he saw a raccoon trapped inside the barn, he later recognised similar responses in perps with a warrant on them, cornered on a subway platform. ‘Knowing how to deal with the raccoon also helps you deal with the person,’ he said.

It was Nygaard’s father who wanted him to be a police officer. When Nygaard was 17, he took the police test. The job came with a pension and healthcare, Nygaard’s father would say. Plus, he could help people. But Nygaard went to college in Texas, at Southern Methodist University, majoring in business – thinking he would join the family flooring company. Then he got called to the police academy at 23.
He asked if the psychic’s last name was Marks. Stunned, the doctor asked how he had known. ‘I’m psychic,’ he joked

Police work matched his philosophy of justice: when someone broke the law, there were consequences, and it was his job to deliver them. He became obsessive about making arrests, so much so that he chafed against the other cops. When he was an officer on Long Island, there were unspoken rules about how proactive or ambitious to be, he said. Others would accuse him of creating too much paperwork. Supervisors punished him by putting him on desk duty. Yet he still managed to make arrests without leaving the station, remembering passersby with outstanding warrants, and once discovering drugs in someone’s purse. He memorised the penal code, so that he could always justify what he was doing, including a New York State law that fortune-telling was a crime.

One of Nygaard’s few police mentors was the late Jon Grow, a detective at the Baltimore Police Department. Grow co-founded the National Association of Bunco Investigators, a non-profit that helped law-enforcement officers share information about fraudsters and scams around the country. Grow passed Nygaard names and photos of scammers who had hit nearby cities. But it ‘wasn’t until that woman in that bar [in Florida] … that all of that knowledge from those years came into play,’ he said.

When the doctor asked Nygaard to help her, he asked if the psychic’s last name was Marks. Stunned, the doctor asked how he had known. ‘I’m psychic,’ he joked. Actually, the psychic in question was Gina Marie Marks, a serial offender whose last name Nygaard remembered from his conversations with Grow.

Nygaard had one stipulation for taking the doctor’s case: she would pursue an arrest no matter how much money the psychic offered her to settle. Then he found four more women who were Marks’s victims, and gathered evidence from all of them. Eventually, Marks was arrested, and the doctor got her money back.

Marks was his first psychic arrest, and that was the moment the disparate pieces of his life clicked into place. ‘All of those years, all that aggravation … fighting with the bosses … having to know the law – I never understood what it was forging me for,’ he said. ‘It was forging me for this fight.’

In early March, Nygaard and I ate dinner at a corner table at P J Clarke’s in midtown Manhattan. He was telling me about another case: in June 2010, a young woman – let’s use the name Vivian – was walking in New York City when she was approached by a woman who called herself Sarah. Sarah said she sensed an energy from Vivian and that something bad was happening in her life. Indeed, Vivian had recently been discharged from Army Officer Candidate School after an injury, and was going through a divorce.

Sarah and Vivian exchanged numbers, and Sarah later told her that she needed $90 for crystals to figure out where the negativity was coming from. By the end of the month, Sarah said she had figured it out: someone had placed a curse on Vivian, probably her stepmother. Vivian should take out $2,700 and put the money, along with rose petals and tree leaves, under her mattress and sleep on it.

Later, Sarah contacted Vivian to confirm it was her stepmother who had placed the curse. To lift it, she would have to sacrifice the $2,700. Vivian needed to bring the money, a jar, and a pair of white underwear to her apartment. Sarah filled the jar with water, wrapped an egg in the underwear, and rubbed it over Vivian’s body. In the dramatic finale of the ritual, the egg cracked open, and a dead baby corn snake fell out. The water had turned a deep, bloody red.
Psychic tricks haven’t changed much, Nygaard said. Needles emerge from a tomato. An egg cracks, and blood or dead animals spill out

Over the succeeding months, Sarah asked Vivian to send more money. In October 2013, Sarah said ‘the church’ needed $10,800, and Vivian went to the bank and took out a $12,000 loan. Vivian followed instructions to send Sarah a Cartier watch and Saks Fifth Avenue gift cards, though she was unsuccessful in leasing a Mercedes. By the time Vivian contacted Nygaard, she had lost more than $30,000.

Nygaard took Vivian’s case to the NYPD, where he was turned away. But Nygaard knew that Sarah had asked Vivian to send a watch to her address in Florida. If any part of a crime happens out of state, the whole crime can be prosecuted in that jurisdiction. Nygaard flew there to speak to a detective who agreed to help. His accumulation of evidence led to Sarah’s arrest, and Vivian’s money was returned.

Psychic tricks haven’t changed much, Nygaard told me. Needles emerge from a tomato. Something ominous comes out of a grapefruit. An egg cracks, and blood or dead animals spill out. ‘A lot of the newer ones, they stay away from that stuff, but when they want to really go for it, they go old school,’ Nygaard said.
As Nygaard ate his burger, I shared a case of my own: I had gone to see Sarah, who now goes by Emma, a couple weeks earlier, for a psychic reading. Nygaard perked up: ‘Oh, you did?’

I had nervously walked down 12th Street in the East Village until I arrived at a storefront with a green sign. I had wondered if Emma would try to scare me with a curse or some other tactic to get more money from me. I asked for a full-life reading for $150. I didn’t want to lie to be a better mark, so I brought up the most vulnerable topic I had on hand: whether my husband and I should try to have a baby. Emma looked carefully at me while I sat somewhat awkwardly in a large, velvet throne-like chair.

She asked some leading questions about my family (‘there is one family member you’re not as close to, there’s some pain there’) and my husband (‘you’re not spending as much time together these days’). Her first insight was universally obvious, and the second was untrue. I tried to keep the conversation going, but we naturally petered out around 25 minutes later. Emma asked if I would like to have my aura cleansed, because she saw I had two dark spots; it would cost an additional $250. I had budgeted only $300. I declined. Looking a little bored, Emma ended the session.

I found the interaction unimpressive, and, as I left, my sympathy for Nygaard’s clients wavered. The experience didn’t feel like a film noir; I wasn’t caught up in a seedy underbelly world of conmen who were experts at deception. The storefront space had been dumpy, and I was embarrassed to be there. I was even embarrassed for Emma, who was barefoot, possibly wearing a nightgown, and had put no effort into the reading. There were clearly children hiding behind a curtain, attempting to be quiet while their mom worked.

As a journalist who writes about science, I have covered my share of health scams. Throughout my career, I’ve spent hours carefully explaining in articles why certain wellness products don’t work and are a waste of money. There’s no scarcity of psychic scams either. Recent surveys suggest that four in 10 US adults believe in psychics, and as of 2022 the industry makes around $2 billion a year. After a few years of debunking, I accepted that scams were like a hydra’s heads: cut one off, and two more grew in its place.
Walking down the sidewalk, I hardened against the people who could fall for what I’d just experienced. If people could get tricked by that, what good was it to help them?

Across the street from P J Clarke’s, at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, I had tickets to a one-night-only performance of Houdini Speaks to the Living, a play based on letters between Harry Houdini and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Nygaard and I crossed the street into a packed auditorium, finding two empty seats near the back. The lights dimmed, and two actors walked on stage, one representing Doyle, and the other Houdini.

Doyle had dreamed up Sherlock Holmes, the ultimate logician who solved crimes by piecing together clues in ingenious ways. But Doyle was an advocate of Spiritualism, the belief that mediums could communicate with the dead, while Houdini (who once brought tricks based on the idea to his performance) came to believe that the profession was poison. In 1926, Houdini testified before the US Congress for a law that would criminalise fortune-telling. Elected officials didn’t feel it was necessarily their responsibility to help those who were duped. (Did I relate?) Ralph Gilbert, the representative for Kentucky, said that Houdini was ‘taking the matter entirely too seriously’.

The play dramatised Doyle’s attempts to convince Houdini that some mediums were credible. Houdini rebutted with counter-Spiritualism screeds, revealing how the mediums’ tricks work. He was harsh, and came across as a self-righteous know-it-all. Doyle and Houdini’s friendship ended, and they never spoke again.

At the end of the show, Nygaard was animated. I expected him to align with Houdini, especially after my encounter with Emma. Nygaard had seemed like an obvious reincarnation of the magician and his undertaking. Others think so too – Nygaard was recently invited to the Society of American Magicians’ Paranormal Investigations Committee, and regularly speaks at sceptic societies.
‘When the right con artist comes along and uses the right techniques on you … It can be more powerful than a gun’

But Nygaard felt conflicted. ‘My investigations are really not about supernatural ability,’ he said. He doesn’t care whether people can see the future. ‘I’ve never gone after a psychic and said … they should be arrested because they say they’re psychic,’ he said. He busts people for lying about what they say they’re doing with their clients’ money: buying cars and watches instead of casting spells.

We left the theatre and walked through a cold wind towards the 1 Train. ‘I’m going to take you out [to] the left field,’ he said. Nygaard told me he’s had experiences that have made him wonder about the supernatural. Sometimes, when driving a police car, he felt like the universe was taking the wheel. Once, while searching for a stolen briefcase, Nygaard heard a voice that told him to look up. He was passing by a deli, and stopped to check if the briefcase was on the roof; it was. In another instance, he was at the Chinese restaurant Wo Hop in Chinatown at 2 am when he saw, written on a dollar bill stuck to the wall, the nickname of a person who was connected to a crime he was investigating. ‘I have asked for help, and I’ve gotten answers, and I know those answers came from the universe,’ he said.

Nygaard had deep empathy for Doyle, who had lost a son in the war and wanted to speak to him again. Doyle’s grief fuelled his myopia when it came to a medium’s tricks, and when Houdini showed him it was all an illusion, it served as a reminder that his son would never return. For Nygaard, it was a perfect example of how ‘all of that learning, all of that knowledge, could go right out the window when the right con artist comes along and uses the right techniques on you … that’s how scary it is, how words can be so deceptive. It can be more powerful than a gun.’

I suddenly felt ashamed of how I felt when I left Emma. My attention had been misdirected, I realised. In being so judgmental about how someone could succumb to a bad trick, I had forgotten how much power the deceiver had.

Even Houdini remained vulnerable to wondering what if. He told his wife Bess that, if it was possible to send a message from the beyond, he would do so. For a decade, she held a seance on Halloween (the day he died) and waited. On the last one, Bess announced:

I do not believe that Houdini can come back to me, or to anyone … I do not believe that ghosts or spirits exist. The Houdini shrine has burned for 10 years … I now reverently turn out the light. It is finished. Good night, Harry.
The final moments of the show played recorded audio of Bess’s shaky voice. My stomach had tangled up into knots.
In May, Nygaard and I sat outside the Fanelli Cafe in SoHo, sharing a plate of fries in the afternoon sun.

I asked about his future. He works mostly by himself and has more cases than he can handle. He doesn’t think he could train someone to do what he does. Others might have the same investigative skills, but no one else would give psychic victims their all. He flies to other states to see clients or track psychics at the drop of a hat. He pressures police officers and prosecutors, and isn’t afraid to get in their face. His forcefulness has had consequences: in 2019, the National Association of Bunco Investigators rescinded his membership after his criticism of police handling of psychic fraud.

His dedication has required sacrifices. ‘I always did want a family, but I think what I do came at a cost,’ he said. When he was a cop, he was once on call with an officer who didn’t want to pursue an arrest because he would be late to his children’s dentist appointment. Nygaard responded: ‘Well, I guess your kids aren’t going to the dentist.’
‘You can’t have that attitude and have a relationship,’ he told me.
‘I was sitting all by myself in Florida contemplating on whether I have chosen the correct path in life’

Had I seen the movie Heat (1995), he asked, with Robert De Niro as a thief and Al Pacino as a cop? The two men are locked in a cat-and-mouse game. Near the end of the movie, they sit in a diner, comparing their lives.
‘So you never wanted a regular-type life?’ Pacino asks. He himself barely sees his family because he spends ‘all my time chasing guys like you around the block.’
De Niro replies: ‘A guy told me one time, don’t let yourself get attached to anything you are not willing to walk out on in 30 seconds flat if you feel the heat around a corner.’
That’s how Nygaard felt: ‘You want it, but you want the other thing more.’

Around a month later, on Father’s Day, I thought about Nygaard. I wondered if comparing his life with film characters who had simplistic moral drives was masking a deeper, more complex loss. The next day, I got a text from him. After spending Father’s Day alone, he had pondered the same: ‘I was sitting all by myself in Florida contemplating on whether I have chosen the correct path in life,’ he wrote. Was it all worth it?

Then, he received a message from a former client. ‘I don’t recall if you have children, but today I wanted to honour you all the same,’ she wrote. ‘You came into my life at such a strange time and the strength you provided, the direction, and how much you believed in me really made a difference and a massive impact on my life.’ Her text felt like a divine signal, he told me. ‘I felt like, through her, God was telling me: “Don’t doubt for a minute the path you have taken,”’ he wrote, ‘“because it’s the right one.”’

items.title: LUCIEN PAGÈS - FANTASTIC MAN

paragraphs: Fashion brands and media could barely exist without PRs as their dogged middlemen, and nobody in Paris does it with as much spirit as Lucien Pagès. Over the last 20 years he has built his company Lucien Pagès Communication into a publicity empire that’s behind everything cool and exciting in fashion today. The ever-present Frenchman is known for being a fixture at nearly every event and show he organises. Thanks to his knack for social media, he’s now more famous than many of his clients. However, last year Lucien suddenly disappeared from the fashion circus. Perhaps it was because he’d recently sold his business to a wealthy investor? Or maybe there were other, more personal, matters at play? The very welcoming PR mogul is now back, and ready to tell all.
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Photography by PAUL KOOIKER

One of the first things Lucien Pagès does when we meet is give me a copy of ‘Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes’ by Robert Louis Stevenson, in which the future author of ‘Treasure Island’ goes hiking with an ass named Modestine. The book was last year’s Christmas present to clients and friends. Its cover – designed and printed by Benoît Astier de Villatte, founder of highbrow ceramics, perfumes and stationery brand Astier de Villatte – depicts Lucien leading a donkey forward along the road, an arm wrapped affectionately around its neck. Lucien is from the Cévennes, which is the key context at play. He grew up in the small, remote village of Vialas, and went on to become the most influential fashion publicist of his generation.

Today Lucien, who is 51, is sat at his desk in the Paris office of Lucien Pagès Communication. It’s in the 2nd arrondissement, not far from where Boulevard Poissonière turns into Boulevard Haussmann (at which point everything suddenly seems part of the same luxury shopping wonderland thanks to department stores Galeries Lafayette and Printemps, for whose product universe some portion of supply and demand has been driven by, or at the very least ambiently massaged by, Lucien’s work). His grey hair and beard are at the longest point where the word “shaved” is allowable. He’s wearing a black T-shirt, white trousers, white Nike trainers and a Rolex watch. His thick, slightly tortoise-shell glasses point, quite exactly, to a close proximity to the worlds of fashion and design.

Lucien’s 140 or so clients include fashion brands like Calvin Klein, JW Anderson, Loewe, Sacai, Saint Laurent and Schiaparelli; beauty brands like Aesop and Humanrace; luxury hotel brands like Pellicano; silverware brands like Puiforcat; restaurant brands (okay, just restaurants) like Le Voltaire; and perfume-slash-scented-candle brands like Byredo and Diptyque. What “client” means here varies quite a lot. A PR agency’s output might involve events, press releases, dinners, shows, presentations, influencer outreach, openings and showroom invites, plus a host of intangible actions that can’t be defined or quantified. Whatever Lucien is doing, he’s always communicating. “Did you know that calling came back?” he asks. “People receive too many emails so now you have to call.” Just out of the blue? “No, I send a message. ‘Can I call you? Do you have five minutes?’”

You imagine most people would have five minutes. Leaning against a wall in the office is a framed graphic entitled ‘Lucien Pagès in one word’: a series of Yves Klein blue squares (the calling card of its creator, the Instagram account Style Not Com) containing words supplied by some of Lucien’s acquaintances. Sarah Andelman goes with “chic.” Nicolas Di Felice offers “magician.” Anthony Vaccarello contributes “malin” meaning smart, shrewd, clever.

Courtesy of the book-prompt, our first conversation is almost entirely about Lucien’s childhood, his origin story. “My grandparents had a hotel and restaurant and my parents took it over, so I grew up there,” he says. The hotel was called the Chantoiseau, or birdsong, and despite its remoteness it attracted very interesting guests. The singer Yves Duteil wrote a song about it, ‘My Cévennes Friend’ (1983), that still goes out on the radio sometimes. Lucien’s father, Patrick Pagès, had a Michelin star and was a master sommelier. President François Mitterand came for lunch once, arriving by helicopter.

Much of Lucien’s sense of fashion and popular culture came via the three TV channels then available in France: “I was obsessed with ‘Dynasty’. It was on every Saturday night. We never had an apartment inside the hotel. We had a little room. I’d see strangers in the corridor. My mum would bring me the dessert that people didn’t want and I’d eat it in front of ‘Dynasty’. It was heaven.”

One day Lucien came across a list of the best fashion schools in the country and decided he would like to go to one. The École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne (now the French Fashion Institute) was a place dominated by those you’d describe as “BCBG” or “bon chic, bon genre”: members of the French upper middle class, adherents of a certain conservative-coded chic. “I showed it to a friend of my parents because I didn’t dare talk to them about it,” Lucien remembers. “My dad was so scared I was gay. Saying I wanted to be a grand couturier would be to basically say: ‘I am indeed gay.’ So I talked to this friend and was thinking she’d help me to convince them, and she said, ‘They will never take you because you’re not BCBG.’”

They did take him. He learned about fashion history, needlework and draftsmanship, and he assumed he would be a designer. He took some internships, including a stint at Yves Saint Laurent and multiple spells at Dior in the final years of the Gianfranco Ferré era. Lucien’s first real job was with art director Marc Ascoli. “It was communication, but more the image side. We worked on Chloé’s first four campaigns with Phoebe [Philo].” He also helped organise shows for French designer Martine Sitbon, with whom Ascoli shared an office.

It was for Sitbon that he pulled off his first PR coup. “I found this fax asking for one of her dresses for Cate Blanchett, to promote a movie. I found it funny and I went to the atelier, because there were some duplicates, and I sent some dresses to the stylist without asking anyone. Cate Blanchett wore all of them, and there was a particularly bright yellow one. Everyone wrote articles about it because it was a very daring colour. It was my first PR action on my own. Because of the fax machine.”

The second time I visit, I bump into Lucien downstairs and we get into the lift together. “Can you give me ten minutes?” he says. “I have to call the New York office. There’s a bit of drama. I hope it’s not like Friday. That was just…” He imitates a fighter blocking strikes from all directions. “I just don’t want it to escalate.” I wait on one of the chairs by his door, opposite the receptionist and a vintage portrait of Kate Moss. Around 50 people work here, and Lucien is on the phone to one of the 15 in the New York branch. The London office – formed from a merger with British PR firm AIPR – has 25 staff.

When I am allowed to enter, I ask what it was about. He declines to say anything other than that today was “internal” and Friday was “external.” His office contains, by the way, around 200 oversize perfume bottles, which are part of a collection that totals nearly 400. Back in 2020, Lucien acted on a long-standing urge to own a giant classic-shaped bottle of Chanel No. 5, which led to wanting a giant heart-including-the-aorta-shaped bottle of C’est La Vie! by Christian Lacroix. He ended up finding ten of these in sizes ranging from ridiculously tiny to impractically huge (they sit Russian doll-like on the mantelpiece behind his desk), and it escalated from there. For a time he shared the bottles on TikTok, attracting as many as 600,000 views per video: there are people who know him as a fragrance collectibles influencer, nothing else. Even so, it all relates to his day job. “I’m not doing TikTok for fun,” he says. “I do TikTok to understand it.”

A publicist’s work used to be mostly about machinating behind the scenes – schmoozing editors, browbeating journalists, gatekeeping talent – but social media changed the equation. Lucien goes to almost every event the agency is involved with, then shares perfectly captured images of them via his Instagram account. With approximately 140,000 followers, including much of fashion’s core elite, that account is arguably more influential than quite a lot of the conventional media coverage he achieves. He runs through some imminent fixtures: the opening of a Paris flagship by lux-casual brand James Perse; a dinner hosted by Snapchat in honour of the wrapping-up of Pont Neuf (the bridge) by street artist JR; and a philanthropic dinner for the Pompidou Centre for which they are expecting around 1,000 guests and have commissioned an enormous flower arrangement that will resemble the tubes on the museum’s exterior. What does success look like for something like that? “That it’s open on time and it goes smoothly. Everyone’s changing their table until the last minute. You need to be sure that the new name is written by the calligrapher. You need to be sure the tables match the most recent changes.”

In a phone call, Business of Fashion editor-at-large Tim Blanks places Lucien in a small tradition of fashion PRs who become almost as well known as the clients they represent. “There is a PR person at any given moment whom everybody wants to be their PR person,” he says. “Before Lucien was Karla Otto. Before that there was Ed Filipowski at KCD. And in the ’90s, Michèle Montagne had all the cool people.”

Blanks – a friend and contact of Lucien’s from the early days – admires his “nose for the new and interesting,” which was evident from the beginning. Lucien founded the agency in 2006. His first client was American designer Adam Kimmel, with whom he shared an office in the Marais (Kimmel later became chief creative officer of WeWork, so office sharing is a theme for him). Other early clients included Jonathan Anderson and Simon Porte Jacquemus.

“He had a very small but amazingly interesting client list and it was already sort of global,” says Blanks. “Adam was from New York. Chitose Abe [the Sacai founder was Lucien’s second client] was from Tokyo – people that you actually wanted to cover. He has this very winning way of actually making you take interest in his clients because you want to. This is an asset for a PR person because you love him and you want to do something for him. So you will go to the thing that he wants you at without dragging your heels and going, ‘Oh, do I have to?’ If you really, really trust their taste and they’re telling you about somebody you haven’t heard about, somebody new that they’re representing, there’s obviously a much stronger chance that you listen.”

It’s the first day of Paris Fashion Week Men’s and, as ever, a driver will ferry Lucien between events and appointments. We find the car, a Mercedes, out on the boulevard and climb into the back. A bag has been stashed there containing a change of clothes in case needed. We’re on the way to the SS27 show of the label Rescha, by emerging designer Charlotte Chowdhury (formerly with Jacquemus).

As we drive across town Lucien mentions a piece ‘Architectural Digest’ published last year about his relationship with the Chantoiseau hotel. His father died 15 years ago, and although his mother, Christiane, tried to run it as a guest house for a time, that project proved short-lived. “It was costing more than it was bringing in, with some very strange people passing by,” he says. “I was, like, ‘Enjoy your house if you want to stay there, but I don’t want you to be in danger. I don’t want you to work for nothing.’” So now the 20-room hotel is simply his mother’s house but filled with the paraphernalia of Lucien’s universe: ceramics by Astier de Villatte, cushions and vases by India Mahdavi, a library of magazines in the former wine cellar.

But the point about the ‘Architectural Digest’ piece is that Lucien partly credits the memories it dredged up – his father died from cancer – for his noticing, the day after he did the interview, an irregularity in his testicle that turned out to be a tumour. “Maybe thinking about my dad saved me, because I paid attention to it.” Lucien had surgery but the cancer spread and he went through four rounds of chemo before getting the all-clear.

“It’s a trauma, in my life. My dad died from cancer at 62 and me, I got it at 50. He was treated and, without going into detail, it was very, very tough for him… So I was, like, ‘Okay, now it’s happening to me,’” he says. Did it make him want to change anything? “No. I wanted my life to be back as it was. Not because it was perfect but because I didn’t want what happened to exist, so the way for me to erase that moment was to go back to how things were.” Even so, after the first round, Lucien married his boyfriend of nine years. “It was just, ‘Okay: maybe it’s time to arrange your life.’”

We arrive at the Musée Guimet, France’s national museum of Asian art, an ideal backdrop for Rescha’s Franco-Indian aesthetic. Lucien receives a briefing. “We have ‘Le Monde’ coming through… Angelo Flaccavento…” He and Charlotte take a selfie together and confer for a while, then she’s summoned away by the guy who does TikTok for ‘Le Figaro’, France’s leading centre-right broadsheet. Lucien tells me Vogue Runway have pledged to attend, which is great as they’ve never covered Rescha before, though they haven’t decided whether or not to write a review. He heads backstage, asking if anyone knows where the whiteboard is: he wants to check the final looks. It’s the first time the agency has worked with Rescha. “It’s a special moment: the first one,” he says. “It’s the one I always remember.”

The moment approaches to allow guests in, and the room thins out. It’s important that people aren’t left waiting outside (it is the hottest day in history, heading towards a high of 39ºC), but a shoot has just finished and there are still a couple of models around who should not be seen off duty. I am shown to my allocated chair, where I sit next to Iris de la Villardière, co-founder of jewellery brand Viltier. She lights up warmly at the mention of Lucien’s name. The show starts. A few chiselled men – in sparkly sarees and cotton poplin shirts – appear among the largely female cast.

By the time I re-enter the entrance area, Lucien has left for the Saint Laurent show, shortly to start in the rotunda of the Bourse de Commerce. Near a giant Cambodian statue I run into Louise Chen, the famous DJ. “Lucien’s a sweetheart,” she says. “He’s everywhere, involved in everything, yet still manages to be charming to someone like me.”

Later, the Rescha Instagram account is filled with story reposts from fashion media and notable guests including South Asian community platform Diet Paratha (“She Worked at Jacquemus + Wales Bonner so OFC her PFW Show Was Beautiful”), ‘Women’s Wear Daily’ (“Ones to Watch for Men’s Spring 2027”), ‘Purple’ (“Backstage Rescha S/S 2027, PFW”), ‘Numéro’, ‘Grazia’, ‘L’Officiel’ and ‘L’Etiquette’. Tableware entrepreneur Alice Moireau self-identifies as “a @rescha.paris girl” to her 125,000 or so followers. Vogue Runway, alas, do not show.

The launch party for the new issue of ‘Acne Paper’ at the Jardin du Palais Royal is packed. Everyone is waving identical black fans to cool themselves down, making it feel like the summer party of an influential secret society. There’s an exhibition in the shop – images of a woman lying in multicoloured paint – but most guests are spilled out into a cordoned-off area in the gardened square. The theme is “Autoportrait,” described in a blurb as “where the magazine turns the gaze towards its publisher for the first time exploring the ideas that have shaped the house over three decades.”

Lucien’s agency has been helping to compile the American names on the guest list. I find him standing in front of the gate, talking to four people who are facing him and not each other. He is friendly and warm but there’s an inscrutability to him as well, a perennial sense there’s more he could theoretically say but won’t. About what, you’re not sure. He greets a revolving cast of interlocutors: a shinily black-clad Lauren Sherman from Puck, then Edouard Benadava, chief content officer at communications and production group The Independents. “I’m building our content vertical,” Edouard says.

The Independents acquired Lucien Pagès Communication back in 2024, adding it to a communications “vertical” (i.e. companies sharing an industry or theme) that also includes Karla Otto and AIPR. But although Lucien no longer owns the agency, the operational side remains the same. “There is more financial reporting, of course, so you feel the numbers more, but that’s why they leave me very free,” says Lucien. “People have fantasies about the group. It looks powerful, but in the end we do the same job. They just want me to perform in the best way possible.”

It’s a 40ºC evening. Desperate for hydration, I walk over to a bar surrounded by people with five-or six-figure Instagram followings: Syrian-Swedish painter Jwan Yosef, avant-garde surfer Michael February. I spot Lucien heading away along the ornate arcade. Is he leaving? “Yes!”

Lucien’s agenda this week also includes the launch of a “queer library” by Aesop, a cocktail reception for Meta, and shepherding guests through showrooms from relevant brands such as Our Legacy, God’s True Cashmere and JW Anderson. The latter is on the Rue du Louvre. It’s laid out and organised as if a retail outlet, and indeed it will be a pop-up store a little later this year. There’s a pair of floral Chelsea boots, a sweatshirt displaying the phrase “Anonymous Nude,” and a soft, brown replica of a squirrel. Lucien arrives, checks in with his door staff, then introduces me to Adam Iezzi, founder of AIPR, who merged with Lucien’s UK operation just over a year ago. “When you’re a PR you meet a lot of other PRs, but there’s no one else that I wanted to get into bed with,” Adam says.

The presentation for the new collection of Californian brand ERL is in a completely pink room with flowers painted onto the walls. Models lounge on cuboid blocks. On one plinth is a small pile of paperbacks. There is an Old English Sheepdog in the room, which seems to be part of the show. ‘Candy Girl’ (1963) by Frankie Valli & The Four Seasons, a proper diner-after-high-school number, is playing.

Is it meant to feel a bit David Lynch? “Maybe a bit Barbie,” says Lucien. It’s our last encounter. On Sunday, he’ll fly to Corsica for Jacquemus. Earlier this week, he tells me, ten influencers got trapped in the lift to his office. This doesn’t surprise me: it felt relatively full with two of us in it, and so certainly wasn’t designed to take that many people, or influencers. “Now nobody can use the lift in our whole building. I’m quite ashamed.” A guest kisses him on both cheeks. Another squeezes his arm: “C’est magnifique! C’est beau, eh?”

Does Lucien have an armoury of solutions for dealing with sticky situations? “When there’s a problem, we have to find a way for everyone to save face so we can move on. For a long time you could say, ‘It was a misunderstanding.’ But we’ve used it too much. People are starting to say, ‘No, it’s not a misunderstanding.’ And you’re, like, ‘Fuck, I tried the “misunderstanding.” It didn’t work.’”

Collaborative guest lists are a hornet’s nest. Lucien remembers an event “for someone very rich” where they were asked to get rid of a guest who’d slipped onto a supplementary list compiled by someone else. “They’d received the invitation and !SVP’d so what could I do? I couldn’t disinvite her. So I created what looked like a mass mail-out, saying that due to unfortunate circumstances, and because of security, we weren’t actually allowed to invite any more people and please accept our apologies. But in fact only one person received it. The person wasn’t offended because she imagined she was one of many.”

Lucien left hospital on 20 December 2025 and was back in the office on 8 January. “It was difficult for me because I work in fashion and I came back with no more hair and a fat face. I decided I didn’t care. I went to events.” It had been a lot thanks to his non-attendance that people caught wind of his illness. If his job had only involved emails, they wouldn’t have noticed: he never stopped replying to them. The idea to make a new edition of ‘Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes’ came during treatment. “I was finishing a journey, and it made me think of Stevenson, you know?” But despite the Cévennes coming up a lot, Lucien wants to disavow the appearance of hanging on to the past. “I’m not nostalgic for my childhood. I wouldn’t go back there for anything.”

As for actually reading the Stevenson book, the instinctive reaction is to think, “Well the contrast couldn’t be bigger could it?” Travelling around small villages in the 1870s versus achieving visibility for luxury brands in the 2020s. Another way of looking at it though is that it’s a powerful testimony to the power of PR, simply given how many people go to the region because of it. I’m not saying a press officer called Stevenson in 1878 to invite him on a “trip,” just that cultural gestures can have a long-lasting impact. There is a business in Vialas, near the Chantoiseau, where you can rent a donkey and follow Stevenson’s route. Vaguely related, the grandson of Yves Duteil, who wrote the song about the hotel, is now doing an internship with Lucien.

items.title: Сведения и описание программного обеспечения в сфере информационных технологий.
items.description: В «Снобе» мы используем и развиваем собственные информационные технологии. Это не просто часть нашей работы, а основа всего проекта. В нашем IT-отделе мы решаем следующие задачи:
paragraphs: В «Снобе» мы используем и развиваем собственные информационные технологии. Это не просто часть нашей работы, а основа всего проекта. В нашем IT-отделе мы решаем следующие задачи:
- Создаем, улучшаем и поддерживаем все наши веб-ресурсы, включая сайт Snob.ru.
- Консультируем по вопросам, связанным с веб-разработкой и работой сайтов.
- Предоставляем онлайн-доступ к нашему контенту и различным цифровым сервисам.
- Разрабатываем собственные инструменты для работы с интернет-рекламой — от размещения до аналитики.
Ядро нашей IT-системы — это, конечно, федеральное сетевое издание Snob.ru.

Для того, чтобы вы могли удобно читать нас, а редакция — быстро и эффективно публиковать материалы, мы создали мощную собственную платформу. Это не стандартное коробочное решение, а наша уникальная разработка:
- Удобная система управления контентом (CMS), которая позволяет нашим редакторам создавать материалы в самых разных форматах, легко менять дизайн и структуру главной страницы и разделов.
- Автоматическая публикация контента не только на сайте, но и в наших социальных сетях и новостных агрегаторах.

Эта платформа полностью разработана нашей командой с использованием современных технологий: на фронтенде (то, что вы видите) используются HTML, CSS, TypeScript и JavaScript (с фреймворками Vue 2 и Vue 3); бэкенд (основная логика) написан на Python (с Django), а данные хранятся в базе PostgreSQL. Такая «кухня» позволяет нам быть гибкими и постоянно развивать функционал.

Сайт Snob.ru полностью кроссплатформенный. Это значит, что вы можете комфортно читать нас с любого устройства — компьютера, планшета или смартфона, на любой операционной системе (Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android, iOS). Мы позаботились о том, чтобы контент выглядел отлично везде.
Наша собственная разработка и круглосуточная поддержка в режиме 24/7 обеспечивают стабильную работу всего проекта, позволяя обрабатывать более 2 500 000 уникальных визитов в месяц.
Описание функциональных характеристик программного обеспечения
Программное обеспечение представляет собой современную систему управления контентом (CMS) сайта snob.ru, которая предназначена для следующих целей:
1. Работа редакции и контент-команд
- Позволяет оперативно создавать и публиковать материалы в различных форматах (новость, статья, интервью, тест и др.).
- Даёт возможность легко настраивать дизайн, менять структуру главной страницы и разделов без необходимости программирования.
- Поддерживает совместную работу над контентом, включая редактуру, модерацию и планирование публикаций.
2. Онлайн-платформа для авторов и читателей
- Предоставляет инструменты для ведения личных блогов, публикации авторских материалов и взаимодействия с аудиторией.
- Включает функции рейтингов и обсуждений, что помогает пользователям находить единомышленников и формировать сообщества.
- Подходит как для индивидуальных авторов, так и для организаций, желающих создать удобную площадку для обмена мнениями и контентом.
3. Онлайн-платформа для программы лояльности — Клуб «Сноб»
