items.title: Matt Damon Reveals Ben Affleck’s Review of ‘The Odyssey’ — and the One Performance He Couldn’t Stop Talking About
items.description: The Odyssey‘s awards season campaign is in full swing, with Matt Damon, Tom Holland, John Leguizamo, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Himesh Patel and Elliot Page taking part in a screening event in Los Angeles on Saturday night.
items.author: Kirsten Chuba
paragraphs: The Odyssey‘s awards season campaign is in full swing, with Matt Damon, Tom Holland, John Leguizamo, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Himesh Patel and Elliot Page taking part in a screening event in Los Angeles on Saturday night.

The group united for a 40-minute Q&A to discuss their experience on Christopher Nolan’s hit film, while also paying plenty of compliments to each others’ performances. And though he wasn’t in attendance, Robert Pattinson stole the show, as Damon revealed that “Ben Affleck probably talked to me for 20 minutes about just Rob after he saw the movie.”

“When they talk about a brave performance — Ben goes, ‘You had the benefit of all of the might and power of Christopher Nolan storytelling at your back’ and I went, ‘Yeah’ and he goes, ‘Rob had all of the weight and heft and power of Christopher Nolan’s storytelling coming down on him. And the way he did it, it was like watching a guy run into an avalanche,'” Damon told the crowd at the Academy Museum. “Any moment that he could be more cowardly, more hateable, you could see his wheels turning. ‘How could I make this even worse for myself?’ And it was so fun to watch because he’s such a dynamic actor and so interesting.”
There was also plenty of praise for Damon himself, as the cast noted how much the star had to go through physically and emotionally to play the role of Odysseus.

Patel recalled how one day when they were shooting some brutal scenes on the seas, “A bunch of the guys on the boat, they were they were starting to like flag, and Matt turned around to us and he said, ‘I know this is hard, but how many actors are in SAG? Every single one of them would die to be where you are right now.’ And we were like, ‘Well, we can’t argue with that.’ I mean, that’s completely true. Shut up, get on with it,” adding that even during the taxing moments, Damon would be “smiling, happy, just loving it.”

Holland shouted out the scene between Damon and Anne Hathaway when Odysseus has returned to Ithaca but is still in hiding, saying he wasn’t supposed to be on set that day but wanted to come see the actors in action.

“Watching you guys go the distance in that scene just really set the tone for us of the level that we should all aspire to be at for a movie like this,” Holland said. “I couldn’t do that yet. I need a few more years.”

Damon also spoke about Nolan’s specific take on Odysseus, saying, “His adaptation made it really clear what he wanted: that weariness, that regret, that shame. It’s this foundational story in Western literature, and it’s about homecoming and this idea, this kind of twist, that he wasn’t actually ready to go home was kind of shocking from an academic standpoint… when I got to that line the first time I read the script, where Annie says, ‘You were the people from the sea,’ I literally just put the script down for a second. I was very shocked.”

Elsewhere in the chat, Holland added to his previous comments that this role was his last chance to play a boy (“I can grow facial hair now!”), emphasizing “it was a really sort of cathartic experience for me because it really felt like a farewell to sort of the first chapter of my career.” Theron teased that in her part as Calypso, “like Tom, I felt like this was the last time that I would get to play a young girl.”

Many of the stars also spoke about their fear of being the one to derail Nolan’s epic, with Zendaya admitting in her role as Athena she was “incredibly nervous” because “I did not want to be the one that was going to mess up this take, especially when you’re shooting on IMAX film and you can hear the sound of it going. You’re like, ‘I want to make sure that whatever I contribute to this, I’m giving just as much as everyone here is clearly giving.’ So it gave me a lot of anxiety.” But, she continued, “It helped that Tom came to set that day [of shooting her Battle of Troy scene] and he was like in the corner, like, ‘You got this, you’re doing good!'”

items.title: Shooting Matt Damon in the Desert and Leaning Into Discomfort
items.description: It was a beautiful day to be indoors. In barren Lancaster, California, the temperature had hit the mid-90s, and the feels-like figure in my weather app topped triple digits. We were professional. We were stoic. But at a certain point, you just give in to the h
items.author: Adam Baidawi
paragraphs: It was a beautiful day to be indoors. In barren Lancaster, California, the temperature had hit the mid-90s, and the feels-like figure in my weather app topped triple digits. We were professional. We were stoic. But at a certain point, you just give in to the heat of the desert. At a certain point, you wilt a little.

Matt Damon, mercifully, never did. Damon may be the least-debated pick in GQ Men of the Year history—he’s still riding the billion-dollar wave of The Odyssey, one of the great cinematic accomplishments this century. Damon was also, by some distance, the most unbothered man on that desert set, and all while being the only one wearing heavenly black tailoring (a peak-lapel Norton & Sons jacket, and glorious mohair Celine pants). It was Bourne-esque. Odyssean, even! Three decades into being a film star, Damon has familiarity with endurance, both creative and literal. In his cover story, he walks our Frazier Tharpe through the physical cost of making Christopher Nolan’s epic, up to and including a night in Scotland on which he didn’t sleep at all. The piece is a portrait of a movie star who still treats the job as a job, most of all when it is inconvenient, unfair, or uncomfortable.

Discomfort has been something of a theme for me this year. I will confess that I knew 2026 would be an administrative ordeal from the moment I accepted this new role at GQ. There was a move from London to New York (including a cat, whose opinion was not consulted). There was a home to find. And there was the discovery that the land of the free has impressive disdain for a grown man with no credit score. None of it was enjoyable. All of it, I think, is good for me.

I have the good fortune to work with many brilliant editors and writers. A recurring note I like to give is: Where is the tension? Without tension, there’s no story. I am not a confrontational person, but I find confrontation on the page irresistible. I want you to stumble, in every issue of GQ, onto something uncomfortable, or uncomfortably new. A magazine that agrees with you from cover to cover is a magazine that you have already read. And I would hate to do that to you.

This issue does not let you off lightly. After some life advice from an honest-to-God astronaut who went deeper into space than anyone that’s ever lived, you’ll read about Chris Rock’s unvarnished thoughts on divorce, discomfort, and reclamation, and Andrew Garfield’s very real anxieties in playing Sam Altman, the complicated man who’s been described as the Oppenheimer of our time. From there, we hang out with the men risking the unknown to get hot on peptides, which is, for better or worse, the defining male-vanity story of 2026.

A few months ago I started putting my email address in these letters (adam@gq.com). You’ve been generous. You’ve been thoughtful. A handful of you have been unhinged. But one note showed up way more than I thought it would: NO POLITICS, PLEASE.

I understand the impulse. I know These Modern Times are stressful, and wouldn’t it be nice if GQ were a place of apolitical tranquility? Alas. GQ has always taken men seriously as full human beings, and full human beings can handle tough conversations, opposing viewpoints, and a little gray area. There’s nothing noble about steering clear of the uncomfortable.

Which brings me to our special package on Cornell, anchored by a dispatch from campus by Savannah Sobrevilla. It is about an alleged sexual assault. It is also about the men on the sidelines of sexual assault. Some of the young men we meet through the story are students who are earnestly and inelegantly trying to grapple with how serious the alleged crimes are, with the crude and cruel culture that surrounds them, and with what role, exactly, they play in exacerbating that culture—or could play in diminishing it. It’s not easy reading, but not everything should be. ✦
Photography by Richard Burbridge
Hair by Johnnie Sapong using Leonor Greyl
Tailoring by Susanna Badalyan
Sets by Heath Mattioli for Frank Reps
Production by Kendal Steensen and Felix Cadieu for NEIGHBORS
A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “A Paean to Discomfort.”

items.title: Get to Know the Watchmaker Behind John Mayer’s Latest Pick-Up
items.description: When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help establish new indies. This week, Mayer is co-signing a hyper-limited-edition piece from FVF Genève, a watchmaker you should get to know.

FVF Genève is the brainchild of Spanish-born, Geneva-based watchmaker Franc Vila. Mayer is wearing his latest release: FVF2 Time & Day “Happy Monday,” made in partnership with American watch and jewelry retailer Material Good. On his Instagram, Mayer referred to the collaborators as a “Trifecta of Greatness.” There’s more to this piece than its mesmerizing mother-of-pearl, though. The watch’s design celebrates the idea that, if you love what you do, Monday mornings are actually something to look forward to.

The “Happy Monday” is a limited edition of seven pieces, each of which is engraved with a different day of the week on its rotor. The design is a reminder, as the brand says, that “each day is an opportunity to embrace our calling.” It helps, of course, that this message is delivered by a truly beautiful movement with black-polished surfaces, plenty of beveling and polishing, and great typography. Then there’s the rad day-of-the-week indicator on the dial. Situated between 6 and 9 o’clock, it takes the shape of a subtle gold track with a letter for each day of the week in French. To go with the “Happy Monday” theme, “Lundi” (Monday in French) is the only day represented by a standout green letter.

The dial is the showstopping element on this piece. It’s executed in a sparkly deep-blue mother-of-pearl and accented with thick gold-tone printing in the form of an outer minute track, a sub-seconds display between 4 and 5 o’clock, and bisecting lines that create a classically inspired “sector” design. The interplay of the sector when combined with mother-of-pearl is unusual enough, but add in the retrograde day-of-the-week indicator, and you’ve got a truly compelling combo.

The watch’s 39.5mm case is made out of Grade 5 titanium and features a Titalyt treatment—an electrochemical surface treatment that creates a ceramic-like layer and increases durability and hardness. F.P. Journe is a big fan of this treatment, and FVF uses it to great effect here. The finishing gives the Happy Monday a dark, industrial aesthetic that plays off the mother-of-pearl and gold tones on the dial for a distinctive feel. The watch comes on a matching beads-of-rice bracelet with straight endlinks, further adding to the interplay between vintage and modern inspiration. Finally, the crown and date corrector are located on the left side of the case rather than the right, where they typically sit.

Limited to just seven pieces—not including a unique piece that went to Material Good’s Yoni Ben-Yehuda—the $125,000 Happy Monday is the latest independent watch to receive a co-sign from super-collector John Mayer. Despite his role as Audemars Piguet's “Creative Conduit," Mayer has been known to support high-end independent makers such as F.P. Journe, and famously helped propel Vanguart onto the horological stage over the past year.

Vila, who established his eponymous luxury watch brand in the early 2000s, is a prime candidate to receive his flowers from the modern collecting community: marrying avant-garde case and dial designs with high complications. Vila sold his initial brand in the late 2000s, but he’s now having another go at creating modern classics with FVF. He’s come at the right time. It’s boom times for independent watchmakers as collectors try to identify the next big thing, and a co-sign from Mayer makes FVF a strong candidate to catch fire.

items.title: Inside the First Competition Between Historic Vintage Timepieces
items.description: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

In the automotive world, high-end cars have gone head-to-head since the early 1920s. Judges didn’t evaluate them based on their speed, though—in a Concours d’Élégance, the prize goes to the best-looking vehicles. The tradition continues today in picturesque sites around the world where collectors submit their often very high-end vintage, classic cars. Surprisingly, there has never been an event for vintage timepieces.

Aurel Bacs, the famous auctioneer whose longstanding association with Phillips has shaped the watch collecting world, endeavored to change that. “It began with a meeting where I said, ‘I have a dream,’” he said in a press release. For the very first iteration of this competition, Bacs and Phillips partnered with Swiss heavyweight Vacheron Constantin. They expected to receive maybe 100 to 200 submissions, but the jury was forced to whittle down 550 of them to 34 finalist watches, whose owners were flown out from across the world for the Concours held at the Hôtel Président in Geneva.

“It was the most beautiful evening in the field ever,” Bacs said. At the Hôtel Président, around 200 attendees gathered, along with a jury of 14 watch-industry experts including Bacs himself, Ben Clymer of Hodinkee, writer and historian Nick Foulkes, longtime watch journalist Roberta Naas, and others. Watches could only be submitted for consideration in one category (Chronographs, Métiers d’Art, Chronomètre Royal, Astronomical Complications, Multiple Complications, Design, and Chiming Mechanisms) and were judged based on nine criteria: authenticity, elegance, rarity, impact on the history of Vacheron Constantin and/or on watchmaking in general, provenance, technicality, métiers d’art (artistic crafts), state of preservation, and emotional dimension.

The jurors deliberated over several hours until the winners of the seven categories and a Best of Show were finally selected. Following a cocktail reception, everyone gathered on the lower floor of the Hôtel Président to see the results from the watch world’s first Concours d'Élégance.

The first category featured a smattering of some of the maison’s most important wristwatches, including a highly rare ref. 4072 in stainless steel from 1940. However, it was a yellow gold pocket-watch chronograph from 1929 that won the day. The result was such a surprise that the audience, intimately familiar with the historical importance of pocket watches, audibly gasped inside the room. It made me wonder if these old-fashioned timepieces could regain their lost position as the pinnacle of watch collecting. This piece certainly warranted the love it received: in excellent condition and featuring a white enamel dial with dual registers in an “up-down” configuration, it’s a beautiful timepiece.

This category celebrates handcrafts such as enameling and gem-setting, and it featured a smattering of truly spectacular pieces—mostly sub-40mm wristwatches in precious metals with wild cloisonné or Grand Feu champlevé enamel dials depicting landmasses or animals.
However, a stunning pocket watch set with blue sapphires throughout the bezel and Roman indices won out.

When an older American gentleman stepped on stage to collect his prize, he explained to a stunned crowd that not only had his great-grandfather, Dr. Otto von Frangeš, been given the watch by His Majesty Alexander I of Yugoslavia, its original owner, but that he wore it while sitting in the motorcade during the king’s assassination in France in 1934. Otto’s middle son, Nikola, eventually smuggled the watch out of Yugoslavia by sewing it into the lining of his wife’s jacket as they fled the Iron Curtain in the late 1940s.

In 1907, Vacheron launched the Chronomètre Royal sub-brand, specifically built to endure a life sailing the seas. The model’s parts were anti-magnetic and resisted rusting. The dials were made out of enamel, which could also stand up to the moist atmosphere without rusting. Because they were critical to maritime navigation, timing precision was of the utmost importance, and models from this line frequently won observatory trials (which tested for a watch’s accuracy) that ran from the 1800s to the mid-1900s. Given all that information, the winner is a bit of a shocker: a ref. 2215 from 1976 that exemplifies the qualities of the line but modernizes them in many ways. It doesn’t even feature a full set of numerals, trading them out for a few diamond-set indices. In his acceptance speech, the owner said he wears it on the weekends with jeans.
Astronomical Complications

The Astronomical Complications category is dear to the heart of anyone who appreciates a good moonphase display and also includes timepieces equipped with a triple-calendar, a complete calendar, or a perpetual calendar. Though more modern pieces, such as a skeletonized QP wristwatch from 1987, made it to the final round, it was a wildly neat (and unique) platinum-cased “Cioccolatone” from 1957 that won out. Housed in a 34mm x 43mm rectangular case and equipped with a complete calendar, it’s owned by a dapper Italian collector, who beamed as he collected the prize with his grown son. This would not be this pair’s first time at the podium…

This is a loaded category for Vacheron, which famously makes the most complicated pocket watch and wristwatch in the world, with 57 and 41 complications, respectively. To be eligible in this category, watches were required to have at least two complications—child’s play for VC.

Spanning everything from an enamel-dialed, minute-repeating, split-seconds chronograph pocket watch from 1901 to several Patrimony watches from the 1990s, the winner was the “Don Pancho.” Delivered in 1940, this diminutive yellow-gold timepiece with minute repeater, day, and retrograde date indications was once the world’s most complicated wristwatch. Double-signed by Brooking in Madrid, it sold for roughly $740,000 at auction back in 2019.

A more subjective category, perhaps, than the others, Design included watches “featuring Vacheron Constantin’s signature design, either in the case or through the time display.” One entrant, for example—a wild time-only ref. 4695 dress watch—featured incredibly intricate lugs and a Maltese Cross-type dial. But the winner was nothing short of revelatory. Once again owned by the aforementioned tall Italian gentleman, the possibly unique ref. 6213 is an automatic world timer from 1957 in yellow gold. Based upon Louis Cottier’s famous system, it is so rare that even Clymer admitted he had never heard of it before the competition. The owner’s son described his father returning home with it one day when he was a boy, excited beyond belief that he had finally tracked it down after years of searching.

This category included pocket watches or wristwatches fitted with a minute repeater, quarter repeater, half-quarter repeater, or grand sonnerie—a mechanism that automatically strikes the hours and quarter-hours every 15 minutes. Incredibly, among the entrants was a red gold quarter-repeater pocket watch from the early 1820s with a stunning guilloché dial. However, the winner was another pocket watch dating to 1926 and cased in platinum. Its ultra-thin design, black Breguet numerals, Breguet blued steel handset, and simple silver dial belied the complex mechanism within. The visibly emotional American gentleman who owns it recalled how, as a boy, he would open a chest of drawers, remove his grandfather’s pocket watch, and listen to its minute repeater.

A bonus category, Best of Show went to a truly spectacular wristwatch: a ref. 6448 in platinum with diamond-set indices. Seemingly a simple time-only dress watch, this tremendous piece—which was produced in just three examples in the early 1960s—boasts a hand-wound, 13-ligne minute-repeater movement. Housed in a brushed-finish case with incredible teardrop lugs, it’s the only known example in this metal, and it was notably the last minute-repeating reference produced by the brand for nearly 30 years.

Nominally, the crowd at the awards ceremony was there to judge the merits of a watch, but I left emotionally moved by the stories each watch owner shared about their timepieces. As the very first concours for watches, the format will no doubt be repeated in the future—either by Vacheron, adopted by other brands, or done as a more traditional multi-brand event like the Concours d’Élégance at Pebble Beach.

items.title: Why This 251-Year-Old Watchmaker Is Suddenly Hotter Than Ever in 2026
items.description: Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.

Founded in the late 18th century by perhaps the world’s most famous watchmaker, Abraham Louis-Breguet, the eponymous brand was once the horologer to royalty. (He famously made a watch for Marie Antoinette that she unfortunately, ahem, never got the chance to wear.) Breguet is responsible for the tourbillon, an early self-winding mechanism, his famous namesake numerals that nearly every brand in Switzerland uses now, and much more. But despite its massive contributions to horology, the brand's pieces haven't caused frenzies among collectors like those from Rolex, Patek Philippe, or even Cartier. However, like Dune’s Bene Gesserit, the watchmaker’s plans are apparently measured in centuries. Recent signals point to the idea that Breguet may be entering a new golden era as collectors come around to its exquisitely made timepieces.

Follow the money, and you’ll quickly find evidence of Breguet’s glow-up. Late last month, at Monaco Legends Group’s fall watch auction, a 1970s-era piece previously owned by a 50-year veteran Breguet watchmaker sold for €221,000. That was nearly of the beginning of the brand's impressive run of auction that makes us wonder, What’s going on with Breguet these days?
From one master watchmaker to the next

Abraham Louis-Breguet isn’t the only hallowed watchmaker to steer the brand. Legendary names like George Daniels, F.P. Journe, and Michel Parmigiani have contributed to the brand’s legacy. At auction, many collectors are keying in on a period of Breguet led by Daniel Roth from the mid-’70s to 1987. After he left Breguet, Roth went on to found his own successful brand that now sells for six figures at auction. The combination of these two powers is proving irresistible to today’s collectors.

The Ref. 3050A was a signature piece of Roth’s reign at Breguet and epitomizes the designer’s contributions to the brand. Roth introduced the first modern piece from the manufacturer with a perpetual calendar. The piece’s guilloché dial is also a signature of the Roth era. The watch sold for €85,800 at the end of October.
Classique Perpetual Calendar ref. 3057

The 3057 was the successor to Roth’s first watch at Breguet, the 3050. The big change is the transparent caseback. This lovely semi-skeletonized perpetual calendar hammered for some 200% above its estimate—not a huge surprise considering Breguet made only a couple of these a year when they were in production. Notably, thanks to the addition of that exhibition caseback, we can see the pretty, highly decorated automatic movement.
Classique Complications ref. 3355PT00PA0

It’s platinum. It’s skeletonized. It’s got a tourbillon. It’s got a matching bracelet. It’s accompanied by all its factory goodies. What else could one ask for in a pre-owned Breguet? Still, a $387,000 hammer price is a remarkable outcome.
Classique Grandes Complications ref. 5447

This oversized perpetual-calendar minute repeater, likewise executed in platinum, commanded almost $271,000 at Phillips this weekend—proof positive of the appeal of classical Breguet looks mixed with modern movement technology and finishing.
Classique Tourbillon ref. 3357

An evolution of the Daniel Roth-era ref. 3350, this gorgeous tourbillon wristwatch features one of the hallmarks of Breguet’s signature style: a beautifully guilloché dial combined with blued steel hands and a Roman-numeral minute track.
The defining watches of modern Breguet

Breguet took a significant left turn in the 1950s when it began producing the Type XX flyback chronograph for French military aviators. It still serves as an important pillar in the brand’s lineup today.
Classique Tourbillon ref. 3350

Introduced in the late 1980s, the ref. 3350 is Breguet’s first wrist-worn tourbillon—a significant milestone for the brand that invented the complication. Emblematic of the Daniel Roth era of Breguet production, it has since become a neo-vintage classic.

Released in 2025 in celebration of the firm’s 250th birthday, the Classique Souscription uses a single hand to tell the time against a Grand Feu enamel dial mirroring vintage Breguet pocket watches. Just this week, the maison followed it up with the platinum version seen above.

The Expérimentale 1 is the first step in a new collection of envelope-pushing, ultra-complicated watches. Fitted with advanced materials, the “1” features watchmaking’s very first high-frequency tourbillon, which beats at an astounding 10 Hz. This is a great way forward for modern Breguet—a model that embraces the brand’s tradition as the industry's most inventive watchmaker.

Now a quarter-millennium old, Breguet has one of the most extensive histories of any watchmaker still in operation, with records reaching back generations. Its finishing is exceptional; its complications are rooted in some of the earliest experiments by one of the world’s most famous horologists; and its designs are superb. As prices continue to skyrocket for watches at auction, especially for hotshot newcomers, it’s exciting to see one of the most storied brands in history catch fire, too.

items.title: The Many Faces of John Malkovich
items.description: There’s a problem with the size of John Malkovich’s head—or, more precisely, with the headshots depicting his likeness, which the London-based artist Goshka Macuga plans to use as masks in W’s annual Art Issue cover shoot. The black and white portraits of Malk
items.author: Jen Wang
paragraphs: There’s a problem with the size of John Malkovich’s head—or, more precisely, with the headshots depicting his likeness, which the London-based artist Goshka Macuga plans to use as masks in W’s annual Art Issue cover shoot. The black and white portraits of Malkovich are laid out neatly in a grid at Milk Studios, in Los Angeles, like some sort of evidence table proving just how wildly varied and storied the actor’s five-decade-long career in film, television, and theater has been. We have Malkovich clean-shaven, or with a swath of scruff; here is Malkovich in a white powdered wig, and there, with no hair at all. There are Malkoviches in rakish hats, Malkoviches looking professorial in glasses, and one Malkovich sporting a Dior blouse with an Elizabethan neck ruff at the premiere of his latest film, Wild Horse Nine, at the Venice Film Festival, where his deft turn as a terminally ill CIA agent earned him the festival’s best actor prize and an immediate front-runner position in this year’s Oscars race.

“On guys, when they stand up in a suit, these heads will be too small,” says Macuga, wearing Miu Miu pants and a pale pink vintage top, as she gestures toward the photographs. She pulls a stainless steel ruler out of its casing to figure out with the photographer, Jeff Henrikson, the correct ratio for the portraits. (Eventually, the too-small Malkovich visages are easily corrected with larger paper and a guillotine trimmer delivered via Amazon.) Macuga, a Turner Prize nominee whose work can be found in the permanent collections of the Tate, MoMA, and Fondazione Prada, among others, was born and raised in Soviet-era Warsaw. She only encountered the kind of art that she wanted to make at 17 years old, when she got ahold of her first copy of Art in America, a scarce commodity in Communist Poland. She exudes warmth and an improv actor’s enthusiasm for spontaneity.

“Lots of artists like to have a very stable practice: Go to the studio, make the same stuff,” she says. “I like the opposite. I like something completely new. John and I will be literally thrown into this thing for a few hours to produce images that will become representative of him and me,” she said, then laughed. “It could go very well, or it could go very badly.”

The concept behind the shoot is a matryoshka doll of references. It pays homage to Macuga’s Exhibition M, a large-scale jacquard tapestry commissioned by MoMA, about the role of the museum as an institution. That tapestry, in turn, was inspired by a 1954 photo of André Malraux, which depicted the French novelist and art theorist leaning against a double grand piano, surrounded by images included in the second book of his trilogy, Le Musée Imaginaire de la Sculpture Mondiale. In June of this year, Macuga expanded upon her MoMA commission at Art Basel with Exhibition M: A Re-enactment, a mixed-media installation and performance featuring three actors masked with portraits of Malraux, Macuga, and former MoMA director Alfred H. Barr Jr., who moved around soft sculptures Macuga had created from the same fabric as the MoMA tapestry.

It is an interesting coincidence that heads are something of a theme in this collaboration between Macuga and Malkovich, considering that the majority of Wild Horse Nine is set on Rapa Nui, aka Easter Island, home to the mythical moai statues. “They’re so enormous, some of them, you really can’t imagine,” Malkovich says of the Polynesian monoliths during our preshoot interview from his home in Lexington, Massachusetts, where he lives to be close to his two granddaughters. “The heads were just dragged”—from the island’s main quarry to a variety of locations—“and set up by ropes, which seems crazy beyond belief. I think they all got knocked over in a big tidal wave in the ’60s, and so they had to be set up again. That makes me tired just thinking of it.”

Wild Horse Nine is set in 1970s Chile, on the eve of Augusto Pinochet’s military coup. It follows CIA operatives Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell) as they take a sightseeing detour to Rapa Nui while U.S.-assisted political upheaval is being plotted in Santiago. Somewhat reminiscent of the critically acclaimed In Bruges, Wild Horse Nine is director Martin McDonagh’s second film about strangers in a strange land—or two hit men in a foreign country, as it were—and crackles with hilariously profane, existential banter. The friendship between Chris and Lee is the beating heart of McDonagh’s black comedy—a product of Malkovich and Rockwell’s natural rapport, along with their mutual commitment to rehearsing scenes “hundreds of times,” by Malkovich’s count. Malkovich offers high praise for his costar, whom he’s known for 25-odd years. “Sam’s very funny, and he’s also a real student of acting. He watches films 10 or 20 times as much as I do,” he says, likening Rockwell’s kinetic acting chops to an expert dolphin trainer at SeaWorld. “He knows what to do to make them jump really high out of the water to get their fish.”

At the start of Wild Horse Nine, Malkovich’s character, Chris, is dying of cancer, suffering memory loss, and ruing his life choices, many of which involved getting a lot of innocent people killed. “Chris is looking back at his life and realizing, You know what? I don’t think the end does justify the means,” Malkovich says. In Chris’s hazy swirl of remembering and forgetting, aided by a steady supply of morphine injections, he finds spiritual communion not so much with the moai, as expected, but with the remote island’s wild horses.

While he’s worked with horses throughout his career—notably, playing real-life horse trainer Lucien Laurin in Disney’s feel-good Thoroughbred-racing film Secretariat—Malkovich finds the equine species somewhat inscrutable. “You can spend all day shooting a gun an inch from a horse’s ear, and it doesn’t seem to notice. It just goes on with its life. But if it sees a small plastic bag blowing in the wind across a field four miles away, it freaks out and takes off at a full gallop, like a lunatic. They’re in their own world,” he says, with admiration. “They do their own thing.”

The same can be said for Malkovich himself. “Doing his own thing” is one way to characterize the 72-year-old actor’s artistic legacy, which began with the Steppenwolf Theatre Company, in Chicago, and has ranged well beyond acting to classical music and opera collaborations, winemaking, and fashion design. He’s seemingly at home in any kind of environment, even a complicated photo shoot like the one Macuga has prepared. Once he settles in, he starts riffing and is in little need of direction. Take the first setup, with the group of his 10 doppelgängers, all dressed identically in black suits and ties to match Malkovich’s Ralph Lauren outfit. “It looks like Pulp Fiction,” Macuga says, excitedly. (And a little like the scene from Being John Malkovich where “John Malkovich” enters the portal to his own brain and encounters an entire restaurant full of Malkoviches uttering only one word: “Malkovich.”) After the initial shots have been taken of the seated group, Malkovich breaks away from the pack and begins to improvise his own movements. While the other Malkoviches remain in their chairs, the original turns away from the camera, spreads his legs, and bends all the way over to touch his feet, thrusting his backside in the air until his face peeks out from between his legs. Moments later, he straightens up like a man half his age.

In another group photo, in which all the suited men are standing, Malkovich—now outfitted head to toe in Bottega Veneta, with the leather lapel of his jacket finished in the Italian house’s signature intrecciato—poaches the measuring tape from the tailor adjusting everyone’s cuffs and hems in between shots and assumes her role, taking the measurements of the would-be Malkoviches surrounding him. In preparation for a solo shot, Malkovich emerges from his makeshift dressing room in an oversize Loewe coat, and Macuga unearths an old Prada ad featuring the actor in a black trench as a reference. Henrikson asks the room if anyone knows the year the ad debuted. “Nineteen-eighty-eight,” Malkovich says with certainty. (The photograph is actually from Prada’s first menswear ad campaign, shot by Peter Lindbergh for fall/winter 1995, but who cares?)

“Super amazing!” Macuga shouts, pleased with her collaborator’s self-direction as he tries out a variety of poses. Although adapting the ideas behind Exhibition M, which involved countless hours of research, for a fast-paced fashion shoot with a legendary actor whom she’s met only this afternoon has had the meticulous artist “very stressed” throughout the day, Malkovich’s willingness—and ability—to bring his own ideas to the space allows Macuga to finally relax in a folding chair and be a delighted spectator.

In his 1999 review of Being John Malkovich for The Independent, titled “Bald, Blank, Brainy. It Can Only Be John Malkovich,” esteemed British film critic and historian David Thomson declared, “Malkovich is not a Hollywood leading man—audiences find him, variously, chilly, unattractive, repulsive, or anathema.” Which may explain why, despite how often he is the most compelling player to watch in his 90-plus films, Malkovich has spent his career in a kind of liminal space between great character actor and bona fide movie star. His performance in Wild Horse Nine may finally convince audiences that Malkovich is, in fact, both—not that he’s particularly concerned with accolades. “It’s very nice that people care or think about it at all. I’m lucky to have a job and incredibly fortunate to do pretty much exactly what I wanted to do my whole life. That’s already an award,” he says. “I’ve worked with great directors: Bertolucci, Antonioni, Spielberg, Jane Campion, and on and on and on. But the gift is the work, of course. Most people spend their entire lives doing things they’re not terribly interested in, to put food on the table and send their kids to school and do what humans do: get by.”

So what would Malkovich like his work to stand for, if trophies are of little interest? Much like his character Chris, he desires contemplation. “I think the point of a movie is to cause people to reflect on their lives, on their choices, on what they’ve done or haven’t done or should have done or might’ve done or couldn’t do, and how that affects them. Good films or plays or novels, great artwork, great music, ask a question: What’s important to us and why? How do we live?”

items.title: What Richard Avedon Taught Ron Howard About Fashion
items.description: Ron Howard has been to “exactly one” fashion show in his life, and he couldn’t tell you the designer. “I’m not great at this!” says the Oscar-winning director with an affable laugh. “Fashion is not my area.”
items.author: Faran Krentcil
paragraphs: Ron Howard has been to “exactly one” fashion show in his life, and he couldn’t tell you the designer. “I’m not great at this!” says the Oscar-winning director with an affable laugh. “Fashion is not my area.”

Calling into W from his California office, Howard sounds like everybody’s dad, which—at least culturally—he is. A child sitcom actor turned acclaimed director, Howard is responsible for indelible American movies like Apollo 13 and How the Grinch Stole Christmas, box office hits like Splash, cult-favorites like Arrested Development, and a series of documentaries about The Beatles and Jim Henson that consider how genius happens—and how it always hits a limit without a human spirit to keep it in check.

But when Howard decided to explore this same theme through the lens of photographer Richard Avedon, he hit a small, stiletto-inflicted snag: “I don’t know very much about the fashion world,” or, he admits, how photographers and models can build entire universes in a single unmoving frame. “My daughter Bryce has tried to tell me,” he says, referring to the actress Bryce Dallas Howard, who has modeled for image-makers like Ellen von Unwerth and Norman Jean Roy. “I’m not sure dads listen to their daughters that much, but I get it now.”

Viewers of Avedon, the 104-minute documentary out today on Netflix, will come away with the same education. Howard seamlessly shuffles Avedon’s still photographs into interviews with luminaries like Calvin Klein, Twiggy, Penelope Tree, and Tina Brown. (“Wasn’t she so great in it?!” Howard asks with football-coach enthusiasm of the storied editor. “I love her line, ‘You’ve got to bite the hand that needs you.’”) He also reckons with the way Avedon, who worked as a photographer from 1944 until his death in 2004, moved between high-profile magazine work with Marilyn Monroe, Bob Dylan, and Gisele and documentary images that showed Americans the segregated South, a generation of abandoned war veterans, and the lives of child farmworkers.
“I often use these [documentary] projects as a way to better understand the world,” Howard says of his approach.

“My lack of knowledge—I often find it to be really useful when I delve into a subject, whether it's scripted or a doc. What I really do is share what it is I've learned with audiences.” He was especially intrigued that he knew Avedon’s imagery—teenage Brooke Shields in her Calvin Klein jeans; Janis Joplin with a leaden expression and an airy bell-sleeved blouse; Sharon Stone nearly whacking Clint Eastwood with a bejeweled clutch as she waved on the Oscars red carpet—but wasn’t aware that the same person was behind the camera the whole time.
An early visit to Avedon’s archives at MoMA helped hatch the plan for the film, which traces the photographer’s journey from Merchant Marine to fashion royalty.

“I don't really believe in ghosts haunting me,” Howard says of his visit to Avedon’s most personal creative work. “My daughters, Paige, Jocelyn, and Bryce, are pretty witchy, as is my wife. So they’d have a different experience in the archives, I think. But for me, what I did begin to feel in the archives is a connection between Avedon and some people, alive and dead, who've been very meaningful in my life and whose company I really, really enjoy. His energy was so different from mine. He was highly extroverted, you know? These are qualities that I don't quite have, but I admire them.”

He also began to connect Avedon’s fashion work with the painstaking magic of movie-making. “I never thought of the great still photographers as directors, as choreographers of story and narrative,” Howard admits. That changed for him during the making of this film. Meeting models like Penelope Tree, he says, “made me realize they’re performers…I began to understand that they're creating characters and playing scenes and moments.” He pauses a moment. “Is that a little bit obvious to you?” he asks. “I know. I know. But even in a world that is as adjacent to mine, I could go through my lifetime without understanding what it takes to make a great fashion moment.”

Now, Howard says, he gets it. Mostly. “I will say, I still dress the same. Every once in a while, fashion rotates to a point where I'm right in step, and then the clock keeps ticking,” he says. “But every 10 or 12 years, I look like I'm dialed right in.”

items.title: These ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Have Lost Their Dark Matter
items.description: The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
items.author: Robin George Andrews
paragraphs: The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.

Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.

But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses—using the motions of their stars as a proxy—the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?

A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter—their gas and dust—swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three new galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.
It’s a convincing explanation for many experts—one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.

Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.

These bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark-matter-lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars—and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.
That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji said.

What, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s—and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin—cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a stealthy type of neutrino? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs? Some have even opined that it could be primordial black holes as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.

“We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” said Daniel Whiteson, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter is matter.”

Dark matter, which makes up 27 percent of the universe—and 85 percent of all matter—interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.

“You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” said Chamkaur Ghag, a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding says no.”

So when DF2 was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawaii to track the motions of those stars to estimate the galaxy's total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark-matter-deficient galaxy ever spotted.

In 2019, they observed DF4, another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists announced that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.
That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce around an origin story.

Dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.

“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said Aaron Romanowsky, an astronomer at San Jose State University.
Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.

It’s reminiscent of the Bullet Cluster, two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter got torn asunder during the collision.
Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.

Kinwah Wu, a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.

Stacy McGaugh, an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he said. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.

“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.

Most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.

That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist Mordehai Milgrom. “MOND says: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.

MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull—for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances—the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.

Dark matter has long been the favored theory for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a significant blow in 2015 when the US-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves—ripples in the fabric of the universe—for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.

DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji said.
“I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson said. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”
The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.

Original story reprinted with permission from Quanta Magazine, an editorially independent publication of the Simons Foundation whose mission is to enhance public understanding of science by covering research developments and trends in mathematics and the physical and life sciences.

items.title: Google DeepMind Staff Tap the UK Government to Escalate Their Unionization Fight
items.description: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab.
items.author: Joel Khalili
paragraphs: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab.

On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application with the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions.

The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm that the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership.

The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression that their demands weren’t being taken seriously.

“They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.”

“We respect the right of employees to make an informed decision about whether or not to join a union,” Google DeepMind spokesperson Tom Hewett tells WIRED in a statement. “We have consistently listened to both those seeking to unionize and those opposed, and have acted in good faith from the outset. We remain committed to constructively participating in this process, and have maintained open and transparent communication with our employees and the unions throughout.”
The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Alphabet, Google’s parent company, removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development.

“When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.”

The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts.
“We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee.
The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations.

“We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.”

In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote.
The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK.

“It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.”
Update 11/12/26 3:50pm ET: This story has been updated to add a statement from Google DeepMind.

items.title: Get SteamOS Easily Running on Your Mac
items.description: Most of my Steam collection won't run on my Mac. It's not (entirely) my fault.
items.author: Justin Pot
paragraphs: Most of my Steam collection won't run on my Mac. It's not (entirely) my fault.

I will be the first to admit that my collection is mostly old indie games, all of which work fine on Windows. Less so on the Mac. Apple stopped supporting 32-bit games back in 2019 when it released macOS Catalina. A good chunk of my Steam library has a "No" symbol next to it because of that restriction. And next year it will get even worse: macOS will drop support for running Intel Mac applications, which could leave even more games unplayable (though Apple claims that certain older games will keep working).

But there's another way. A free, open source app called FX Steam Launcher boots the ARM version of SteamOS—the operating system that powers Valve's Steam Deck gaming handheld—right on your Mac, using a combination of a virtual machine and compatibility layers. You will need a Mac with an Apple Silicon processor, as Intel Macs aren't supported, running macOS 15 or later. I set this up recently, connected a controller, and I've been playing all kinds of games that are otherwise unplayable on my MacBook Air.

It wasn't even hard to set up. To get started, download the application, mount the DMG file, and drag the app to your Applications folder. The first time you launch the application, a pop-up will offer to download and install SteamOS for you in a virtual machine.

Click Create New Disk, and you'll be asked a few questions. The most important step is the hard drive size—the default is 64 GB, which is plenty, but consider allocating more space if you plan on installing multiple large games. You can also choose the drive location, if you like, and set a password for opening SteamOS.

Click Create, and the application will download SteamOS and install it in a virtual machine. I recommend using this time to pair a game controller with your Mac in System Settings under Bluetooth. FX Steam Launcher works with most current gamepads, including Xbox, DualSense, DualShock, and Made for iPhone. I used a Nintendo Pro Controller.

Eventually, you will see the login screen, where you can enter your Steam credentials. Once you're in, you'll see your Steam library. The virtual machine operates like an actual Steam Deck, which takes some getting used to if you've never used one. It divides your library into games known to work in SteamOS and those that might work, which is helpful. A lot of my games started running immediately, with full gamepad support.

This isn't a drop-in solution for every game. SteamOS itself is quite fiddly, and you're now running it in a virtual machine. In some cases, I needed to tweak the graphics settings for games to run correctly. For Psychonauts, specifically, I had to download a user-made patch to get the controller working properly—but I'd have needed that fix for an actual Steam Deck too. When a game ran poorly, I frequently found the solution by Googling and finding actual Steam Deck owners who ran into similar problems.

There is a limit to the processing power you get out of a Mac, especially if you (like me) are using a MacBook Air. And a virtual machine, by definition, doesn't have access to all of your machine's capabilities. But the list of compatible games, compiled from other users, shows which devices have successfully played various titles. Check that page for your favorite games before you dive in.

If nothing else, this is a lot easier than my previous method for running Windows games on a Mac, which involved setting up a version of Wine that's no longer supported. I even got a few non-Steam games installed. Sideloading on SteamOS means booting into Desktop Mode, which you can find in the SteamOS sidebar under Power. You'll end up in a Linux-based desktop, complete with a web browser. You can download games, put them in the folder of your choice, and point Steam to them. I couldn't add custom art, but I got multiple games up and running this way.
Honestly, Valve should update the official Steam Mac client with similar compatibility tech so it can run Windows games natively. It would be a huge hit with Mac users.

If you're a power user, I recommend checking out the settings for FX Steam Launcher, which you can open from the menu bar or with the keyboard shortcut Command-comma. You can change the resolution for your virtual Steam Deck, configure the sound to your liking, and submit game statistics.

It's remarkable software. And, with an HDMI cable and a gamepad, you can plug your MacBook into your TV and game from your couch. That's what I plan on doing when I'm done writing this article (which I guess is right now).

items.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
items.description: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while a
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

items.title: The Best Under-$25 Gifts for Everyone on Your List
items.description: If luxury gifts aren’t in the cards for you this year, that makes two of us. In this economy? I’m giving my friends and family members cute and thoughtful gifts that also happen to be affordable. If you like the sound of that, you’re in the right place. Read o
items.author: Hanna Flanagan; Chinea Rodriguez
paragraphs: If luxury gifts aren’t in the cards for you this year, that makes two of us. In this economy? I’m giving my friends and family members cute and thoughtful gifts that also happen to be affordable. If you like the sound of that, you’re in the right place. Read on for the best under-$25 gift ideas this holiday season, from charms and trinkets to beauty gift sets and a candle that isn’t boring.
A fancy pen doesn’t have to cost a ton. Gift this supersmooth copper pen to anyone who loves to journal. It comes with refill ink so they can use it forever, and it doesn’t smear or bleed.

En Route’s tarnish-proof jewelry is my go-to for everyday hoops and the occasional dressier hoop. These waterdrop earrings are versatile enough to dress up for a holiday party or wear with your day-to-day outfits.

Slippers are the perfect holiday gift, no matter their age or style, because they’re useful and cozy. This faux-fur pair is cool enough for the Gen-Zer on your list, but your bestie will love them too.
Grip socks are essential for any Pilates class, and they don’t have to be boring. This stripy pair from Cacti Wellness looks good on and off the reformer.

When you’re shopping for under-$25 items that are nice enough to gift, packaging makes all the difference. This Glossier hand cream comes in a squeezable red rubber pod that feels festive and special.

items.title: Mercury and Venus Retrogrades Are Over But the Chaos Isn’t
items.description: Temp check: How are we feeling, hmm? The past several weeks have been nothing short of nutty, and the combo-platter retrograde has certainly been to blame. Both Mercury (the planet of communication) and Venus (symbolizing our values) have been going backwards,
items.author: Aliza Kelly
paragraphs: Temp check: How are we feeling, hmm? The past several weeks have been nothing short of nutty, and the combo-platter retrograde has certainly been to blame. Both Mercury (the planet of communication) and Venus (symbolizing our values) have been going backwards, wrecking havoc in virtually every aspect of our lives.

But on November 13 — yes, Friday the 13th (naturally) — both Mercury and Venus go direct, concluding their retrograde motions and entering the final phase: retroshade. So what does that mean? Is this hellscape finally going to freeze over? Are you going to be okay? Behold! Everything you need to know about the dramatic end to this very tumultuous season — and exactly what it means for you.
Wait, so Mercury retrograde is over?!

Yes, friend — finally. On October 24, Mercury went backward, beginning its three-week chaos-fest around communication, travel, transportation, technology, and basically everything we rely on for our day-to-day lives. Phew. From missed connections to technological malfunctions to conversations that escalated to flipping tables, Mercury retrograde has been keeping us on our toes.

Mercury goes retrograde approximately three or four times per year, so while it’s hardly a rare astrological occurrence, each backbend has its own unique characteristics. In this case, Mercury went retrograde in Scorpio, the zodiac sign associated with secrets, intimacy, power, and transformation, meaning that in addition to the usual logistical calamities, this retrograde had a particularly psychological dimension.

Scorpio is the detective of the zodiac, determined to uncover whatever is lurking beneath the surface. So over the past three weeks, even the most ordinary conversations may have revealed deeper layers: clandestine motives, power imbalances, and even ancient insecurities. It’s been a lot!
And Venus retrograde is over, too? That’s a thing!?

Oh, honey, is it ever! Exactly three weeks before Mercury went backward, on October 3, Venus — the planet of values, romance, and worthiness — began its own retrograde cycle, initiating a powerful period of reflection around love, desire, and, perhaps most importantly, confidence.Venus retrograde is considerably less common than Mercury retrograde, occurring approximately once every 18 months and lasting about 40 days. During this time, everything Venus governs becomes subject to reevaluation, from our romantic relationships, to our financial habits, to our personal aesthetics, and to our understanding of self-worth. You may have found yourself reconsidering relationships, questioning your professional arrangements, or even realizing that the version of self you’ve been presenting no longer matches the person you’ve become. And perhaps these revelations have been uncomfortable — especially as they’ve shifted our status quo. But that’s the entire point.

You see — from even an astronomical perspective — Venus undergoes a remarkable transformation during its retrograde, transitioning from an evening star (rising during sunset) to a morning star (rising before sunrise). And astrologically, this celestial metamorphosis mirrors our own emotional evolution: We enter the retrograde with one understanding of ourselves, venture into unfamiliar territory, and emerge with an entirely new perspective.

This particular Venus retrograde began in Scorpio before moving backward into Libra, two zodiac signs that explore relationships from very different angles. Scorpio is concerned with intimacy, vulnerability, and the complicated dynamics of trust, while Libra focuses on partnership, reciprocity, and finding balance. Together, these energies encouraged us to explore the intersection of our individual needs and our expectations of others. And as we prepare to wrap up this retrograde, it’s abundantly clear just how much has changed.
So… what does it mean that they were both retrograde together — and ending their retrogrades the same day?

The day Mercury retrograde began (October 24) was the same exact day Venus formed its “inferior conjunction” with the Sun — the exact halfway point of Venus retrograde — when Venus shifted her place in the sky and transformed from an evening star into a morning star. In other words, just as Venus was delivering some of the most significant revelations of her entire retrograde cycle, Mercury added an extra layer of intensity, asking us to investigate how we express these breakthroughs.

Of course, there have also been plenty of challenges along the way, both logistically (through delays, travel snafus, and technological meltdowns) and emotionally (via misunderstandings, strange disagreements, and even heightened suspicions). But this Mercury retrograde has also offered us the opportunity to examine situations from perspectives we may not have previously considered. When Mercury goes backward, we also find ourselves altering our point of view — and sometimes looking at something at a different vantage yields the exact breakthrough we’ve been searching for.

All in all, this Mercury-Venus retrograde combo-platter has shifted virtually every aspect of reality. Anecdotally, I’ve witnessed more breakups, career changes, and friendship shake-ups over the past six weeks than I’ve encountered during the rest of the year. People are standing up for themselves, reevaluating their commitments, and demanding more from their lives, which naturally means that certain outdated dynamics are beginning to fall away. And while these changes can be challenging, the past six weeks have also been tremendously inspiring, particularly because these pivots are rooted in a deeper understanding of personal worth.
And now, on Friday, November 13, both Mercury and Venus are ending their retrogrades on the very same day.
So now what? What’s “retroshade?”

Before you pop the bubbly, there’s one more important piece of the puzzle we need to discuss. Every planetary retrograde consists of three distinct phases: the pre-retrograde shadow, the retrograde itself, and the post-retrograde shadow. Before a planet stations retrograde, it travels across the section of the zodiac where it will soon go backward (the shadow period), introducing themes and circumstances that will become increasingly significant when the planet formally reverses. Then, as the planet flips (retrograde), and it retraces those same degrees, encouraging us to reconsider whatever unfolded during the initial passage. Finally, when the planet stations direct, it travels across that territory for a third and final time (retroshade), giving us an opportunity to integrate the insights we’ve gained along the way.

Although Mercury and Venus are both officially moving forward on November 13, they will continue traveling through their post-retrograde shadow periods, which means we’ll be revisiting some of the same themes that have been developing since early October. Fortunately, this final phase offers us an opportunity to approach familiar circumstances with a completely different understanding of ourselves.

Mercury’s post-retrograde shadow will last through November 30, during which time the planet of communication will retrace its steps through Scorpio, helping us revisit unresolved conversations, clarify misunderstandings, and make sense of the information we’ve uncovered. If you’ve been struggling to articulate something important, you may find that the words begin coming together more easily over the next few weeks.

Venus’s post-retrograde shadow, meanwhile, will go through December 15, giving us an additional time to integrate this bounty of revelations surrounding our relationships, finances, and self-worth. Venus will retrace the territory she covered through Libra and Scorpio, encouraging us to revisit the circumstances that initially prompted us to reconsider our priorities. Think of this retroshade as the integration phase: A gentle onboarding that teaches us how to adjust to our new reality and prepares us to step into this brand-new tomorrow.

First and foremost: movement! With Mercury and Venus finally going direct, conversations that have been postponed, decisions that have felt overwhelming, and situations that have been stuck in limbo will begin gaining momentum. We’ve spent the past six weeks discovering what we want, what we deserve, and what needs to change, and now it’s time to figure out what to actually do with that information. Whatever revelations have emerged, consider how you can begin making choices that put them into action. You’ll soon discover that the best part of the retrograde season is what happens next.
